name: Biochemistry
description: Complete study manual · 30 practical class topics

topics.title: Introduction to metabolism. Nutritional biochemistry. The coenzyme function of vitamins. The concept of metabolism

goals.text: To teach the student the concept of metabolism, its stages, catabolism and anabolism, metabolic pathways and the methods of studying them, the biochemical basis of nutrition, the nonessential and essential components of food, the coenzyme function of vitamins and the biochemistry of milk.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of metabolism, catabolism and anabolism;
the stages of metabolism (digestion, absorption, intermediary metabolism, excretion of end products);
the three stages of catabolism and the common pathway;
the functions and daily requirements of the main nutrients;
the essential amino acids, fatty acids and other factors;
the water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins and their coenzyme forms;
the causes of hypovitaminosis, avitaminosis and hypervitaminosis;
the methods of studying metabolism.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: match vitamins with their coenzymes;
perform qualitative reactions for vitamins and evaluate the result;
calculate the energy value of a diet.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Hypervitaminosis** occurs mainly with the fat-soluble vitamins (A and D), because they accumulate in tissues: vitamin A hypervitaminosis — headache, liver damage, a teratogenic effect in pregnancy; vitamin D hypervitaminosis — hypercalcemia, calcinosis of the kidneys and vessels. An excess of water-soluble vitamins is excreted in the urine (except B~12~, which accumulates in the liver for years).

blocks.text: **Metabolism** is the sum of the chemical reactions that take place in a living organism and provide its exchange of matter and energy with the external environment. Metabolism consists of two interrelated directions:

items: **Catabolism (dissimilation)** — the breakdown of complex substances into simpler ones; mainly oxidation reactions, energy is released (exergonic), part of it is stored in the form of ATP; NADH and NADPH are formed.

**Anabolism (assimilation)** — the synthesis of complex substances (proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids) from simple ones; energy is consumed (endergonic), and NADPH is used mainly as the reductant. Catabolic and anabolic pathways are often not the same: they proceed through different enzymes, are located in different compartments of the cell (for example, fatty acid oxidation — in the mitochondria, synthesis — in the cytosol) and are regulated separately. **Amphibolic pathways** (for example, the Krebs cycle) serve both catabolism and anabolism.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: Stages of metabolism (drawn after Sobirova R.A., 2006)

blocks.text: Stages of metabolism

items: **Digestion** — the breakdown of food polymers into monomers in the gastrointestinal tract by enzymes (proteins → amino acids, polysaccharides → monosaccharides, fats → fatty acids, glycerol, monoacylglycerols).
**Absorption** — the passage of monomers through the intestinal wall into the blood and lymph.
**Intermediary (intracellular) metabolism** — the conversion of monomers in cells: their breakdown (to obtain energy) and the synthesis of the body’s own substances.
**Excretion of end products** — CO~2~ (lungs), H~2~O, urea, uric acid, creatinine, ammonium salts (kidneys), bilirubin derivatives (intestine).

blocks.text: A **metabolic pathway** is a chain of transformations of a substance through successive enzymatic reactions; its starting substance is the **substrate**, the intermediates are **metabolites**, and the end product is the **product**. Metabolic pathways may be linear (glycolysis), cyclic (the Krebs cycle, the ornithine cycle) or branched. Each pathway usually has one **key (rate-limiting) enzyme**: it catalyzes the slowest reaction, controls an irreversible reaction and determines the overall rate of the pathway.

parts.text: All catabolic pathways converge on **acetyl-CoA** and are completed through the **Krebs cycle + respiratory chain**. Therefore the main part of the body’s energy (≈ 90% of ATP) is formed in the mitochondria by oxidative phosphorylation.

blocks.text: Methods of studying metabolism

items: **At the level of the whole organism**: balance experiments (nitrogen balance), calorimetry, respiratory quotient; determination of metabolites in blood and urine.
**At the organ level**: perfusion of an isolated organ, angiostomy (arteriovenous difference).
**At the tissue and cell level**: tissue slices, homogenates, cell cultures, isolation of organelles by differential centrifugation.

**Molecular methods**: the **labeled atoms** method (isotopes ^14^C, ^3^H, ^15^N, ^32^P) — tracing the fate of metabolites; enzyme inhibitors; genetic methods (knockout organisms, mutants); chromatography, mass spectrometry (metabolomics).
**Clinical methods**: inborn errors of metabolism (the metabolite before the blocked enzyme accumulates) — “experiments of nature.”

blocks.text: **Nutrition** is a component of metabolism that meets the body’s need for energy and plastic material. The main components of food: proteins, fats, carbohydrates (macronutrients), vitamins and minerals (micronutrients), water and dietary fiber.

blocks.text: The daily energy expenditure of adults is 2200–3500 kcal depending on physical activity (in women 1800–2800 kcal).
Essential components of food
**Essential (indispensable)** substances are not synthesized in the body, or not in sufficient amounts, and must come with food:

items: **8 essential amino acids**: valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan; partly essential in children — **arginine and histidine**.
**Essential (polyunsaturated) fatty acids**: linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3); arachidonic acid is formed from linoleic acid.
**Vitamins** (vitamin D and niacin are partly synthesized).
**Minerals**: macroelements (Na, K, Ca, Mg, P, Cl) and trace elements (Fe, Zn, Cu, I, Se, F, Co, Mn, Mo).

parts.text: Essential amino acids: **“Very Lazy Ivan Takes Me Late For Tea”** — Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Threonine, Methionine, Lysine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan.

blocks.text: **The biological value of proteins** is the degree to which a dietary protein is converted into the body’s proteins; it depends on the content of essential amino acids and on digestibility. Egg and milk proteins have the highest biological value; plant proteins are often deficient in lysine (wheat), methionine (legumes) or tryptophan (maize).
Age-related nutrition. Biochemistry of milk
Because of growth, children’s requirement for protein (2–4 g/kg) and energy per 1 kg of body weight is 2–3 times higher than in adults. Breast milk is the most appropriate food for the infant.

blocks.text: **Colostrum** is secreted in the first days after delivery: it is rich in protein (especially secretory IgA) and provides immune protection.

**Vitamins** are low-molecular-weight organic substances that are not synthesized in the body, or not in sufficient amounts, and are needed in small quantities (mg, µg); they are neither an energy source nor plastic material, but most of them are part of **coenzymes**. They are divided into **water-soluble** (B group, C) and **fat-soluble** (A, D, E, K) vitamins.

parts.text: **Hypervitaminosis** occurs mainly with the fat-soluble vitamins (A and D), because they accumulate in tissues: vitamin A hypervitaminosis — headache, liver damage, a teratogenic effect in pregnancy; vitamin D hypervitaminosis — hypercalcemia, calcinosis of the kidneys and vessels. An excess of water-soluble vitamins is excreted in the urine (except B~12~, which accumulates in the liver for years).

blocks.text: **Causes of hypovitaminosis and avitaminosis:** insufficient intake with food (exogenous); impaired absorption (gastrointestinal diseases, absence of Castle’s intrinsic factor — B~12~), increased requirement (pregnancy, growth, illness), suppression of the intestinal microflora by antibiotics (K, B group), the action of **antivitamins** (endogenous).

**Antivitamins** are substances similar in structure to a vitamin that block its coenzyme function: methotrexate (a folate antagonist — antitumor), dicoumarol and warfarin (vitamin K antagonists — anticoagulants), isoniazid (a B~6~ antagonist), avidin (binds biotin).

parts.text: Thiamine deficiency is common in chronic alcoholism: pyruvate dehydrogenase activity falls, pyruvate and lactate accumulate in the blood, and an energy deficit develops in the brain (Wernicke encephalopathy). Such patients must be given thiamine before glucose — otherwise glucose oxidation uses up the thiamine reserve completely and worsens the condition.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: qualitative reaction for vitamin B~1~ (thiochrome reaction)

items: Add to a test tube 1 drop of 5% thiamine solution, 5 drops of 10% NaOH and 1–2 drops of 5% potassium ferricyanide (K~3~[Fe(CN)~6~]) solution.
Add 5–10 drops of isobutyl (or butyl) alcohol, shake and wait for the layers to separate.

Observe the alcohol layer under ultraviolet light. **Result and analysis:** in an alkaline medium thiamine is oxidized to form **thiochrome** — the alcohol layer **fluoresces** blue under ultraviolet light. This reaction is the basis of the quantitative determination of thiamine.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: reduction reaction for vitamin B~2~

items: Add to a test tube 10 drops of riboflavin solution (yellow) and 5 drops of concentrated HCl.

Drop in a small piece of metallic zinc (Zn). **Result and analysis:** with the release of hydrogen riboflavin is reduced: the yellow color turns first pink and then colorless (leucoflavin). Under the action of atmospheric oxygen the color returns. This shows the property of FMN and FAD to accept and donate hydrogen (oxidation-reduction).

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determination of vitamin C with 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol (Tillmans reaction)

items: Pour into a test tube 2 ml of ascorbic acid solution (or fruit juice) and 1 ml of 2% HCl.

From a burette titrate dropwise with blue 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol solution until a pink color persists for 30 s. **Result and analysis:** ascorbic acid is a strong reductant — it reduces the blue dye to the colorless leuco form. Once all the ascorbic acid has been oxidized, the excess dye gives a pink color in the acidic medium. The amount of vitamin C is calculated from the volume of dye used.

blocks.text: Experiment 4: calculating the energy value of a diet

items: Determine from the table the amount (g) of protein, fat and carbohydrate in the student’s daily food.
Calculate the energy: E = protein × 4 + fat × 9 + carbohydrate × 4 (kcal).
Find the share (%) of each nutrient in the energy and compare it with the norm (protein 12–15%, fat 25–30%, carbohydrate 55–60%).

skills.title: Skill: evaluating a diet

items: Determine the amount of protein, fat and carbohydrate in the diet.
Calculate the total energy value and compare it with expenditure.
Check the share of animal protein (≥ 50%) and the sources of essential amino acids.
Evaluate the sources of vitamins (especially C, D, B group, folate) and minerals (Fe, Ca, I).
Conclusion: the diet is adequate, excessive or deficient; give a recommendation for correction.

skills.title: Skill: biochemical justification of a vitamin deficiency

items: Identify the clinical signs (for example, anemia, dermatitis, neurological signs).
Recall which vitamin is part of which coenzyme.
Identify the reaction and enzyme in which this coenzyme takes part and which is impaired.
Name the metabolite that accumulates (for example, pyruvate in B~1~ deficiency, methylmalonic acid in B~12~ deficiency).
Explain the laboratory confirmation and the principle of treatment.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 48-year-old man has abused alcohol for 15 years and is poorly nourished. In the emergency department he was found to have confusion, impaired eye movements and an unsteady gait. Blood pyruvate and lactate levels are increased.
cases.ask: Which vitamin deficiency is suspected? Why do pyruvate and lactate accumulate? What should be taken into account in treatment?
cases.answer: Vitamin B~1~ (thiamine) deficiency — Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamine diphosphate is the coenzyme of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. In its deficiency pyruvate is not converted to acetyl-CoA, accumulates and is reduced to lactate (lactic acidosis); the Krebs cycle slows down and an ATP deficit develops in the brain. In treatment thiamine is given parenterally before glucose.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: People living in areas where they eat only maize were observed to have dermatitis on sun-exposed areas of skin, diarrhea and memory loss.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is its biochemical cause?
cases.answer: Pellagra — niacin (vitamin PP) deficiency (“3 Ds”: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). In maize niacin is in a bound (non-absorbable) form and tryptophan is low — so the synthesis of niacin from tryptophan is also insufficient. Niacin is part of NAD^+^ and NADP^+^; when they are deficient many dehydrogenase reactions are impaired, and rapidly renewing tissues (skin, intestinal epithelium) and the nervous system are damaged.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 9-month-old child is fed only cow’s milk and semolina porridge and is rarely taken outdoors. Examination shows a flattened occiput, a “rosary” on the ribs and “bracelets” on the wrists. Blood alkaline phosphatase is increased and phosphate is decreased.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the biochemical mechanism.
cases.answer: Rickets — vitamin D deficiency. Lack of sunlight reduces the synthesis of cholecalciferol in the skin, and the diet is also poor in vitamin D. The active form calcitriol (hydroxylated in the liver and kidney) provides the absorption of Ca^2+^ and phosphate in the intestine; in its deficiency bone mineralization is impaired and osteoid tissue increases (osteoblast activity — alkaline phosphatase rises). Treatment: vitamin D, sunbathing, proper feeding.

topics.title: Structure and mechanism of action of enzymes. Kinetics of enzyme reactions. Regulation of enzyme activity

goals.text: To teach the student the chemical nature and structure of enzymes, their active and allosteric sites, cofactors and coenzymes, classification and nomenclature, mechanism of action, properties, the dependence of reaction rate on temperature, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate, inhibitors and types of inhibition, methods of regulating enzyme activity and the basics of medical enzymology; to master the determination of salivary amylase activity.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the protein nature of enzymes, simple and complex enzymes, the concepts of apoenzyme, cofactor and coenzyme;
the structure of the active site and the allosteric site;
the 7 classes of enzymes and the principles of naming;
the mechanism of enzyme action (lowering of the activation energy, the enzyme–substrate complex);
the properties of enzymes: specificity, thermolability, pH dependence;
the Michaelis–Menten equation and the meaning of Km and Vmax;
the types of inhibition and drugs that are enzyme inhibitors;
the methods of regulating enzyme activity;
the diagnostic significance of isoenzymes and organ-specific enzymes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine salivary amylase activity by the Wohlgemuth method;
determine the type of inhibition from a Lineweaver–Burk plot;
clinically evaluate changes in serum enzyme activity.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Order of the classes: **“Over The Hill Lies Ivan’s Little Town”** — Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, Ligases, Translocases.

blocks.text: **Enzymes** are biological catalysts formed in living cells that accelerate chemical reactions. Almost all enzymes are **proteins** (except RNA molecules with catalytic activity — **ribozymes**). The science that studies enzymes is **enzymology**.

items: **Simple enzymes** consist only of amino acids (pepsin, trypsin, ribonuclease).

**Complex enzymes (holoenzyme)** = a protein part (**apoenzyme**) + a nonprotein part (**cofactor**). The cofactor may be a metal ion (Zn^2+^, Mg^2+^, Fe^2+^, Cu^2+^, Mn^2+^) or an organic substance — a **coenzyme**. A coenzyme firmly (covalently) bound to the apoenzyme is called a **prosthetic group** (for example, FAD in succinate dehydrogenase). The **active site** is the part of the enzyme molecule that binds the substrate and provides its chemical transformation. It is formed from amino acid residues located in different parts of the polypeptide chain when the tertiary structure forms, and consists of two parts:
**the binding (contact) part** — recognizes and binds the substrate (determines specificity);
**the catalytic part** — carries out the chemical transformation (often serine, histidine, cysteine, aspartate and glutamate residues).

blocks.text: The **allosteric site** is a part located outside the active site that binds regulatory molecules (**effectors**). When an effector binds, the conformation of the enzyme and of its active site changes: an **activator** increases activity, an **inhibitor** decreases it. Allosteric enzymes usually consist of several subunits (quaternary structure).

**Isoenzymes** are forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction but differ in structure, physicochemical properties and tissue distribution. For example, **lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** is a tetramer built of H and M subunits, with 5 isoenzymes: LDH1 (H4) — heart muscle, LDH5 (M4) — liver and skeletal muscle. **Creatine kinase**: MM — skeletal muscle, MB — heart, BB — brain.

According to the classification of the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, enzymes are divided into **7 classes** by the type of reaction they catalyze. Each enzyme has a 4-number code (EC 1.1.1.27 — LDH). The working name: substrate name + type of reaction + “-ase” (lactate dehydrogenase).

blocks.text: For any chemical reaction to start, molecules must overcome the **activation energy** barrier. Enzymes carry the reaction along another route with a lower activation energy and increase its rate 10^8^–10^12^ times. The equilibrium of the reaction and the overall energy change (ΔG) do not change.
Stages of an enzyme reaction:
E + S ⇄ ES → EP → E + P

items: Binding of the substrate to the active site — formation of the **enzyme–substrate complex (ES)**.
Strain (deformation) of bonds in the substrate, formation of the transition state.

Release of the product; the enzyme remains unchanged. Two models of how the substrate fits the active site: E. Fischer’s **“lock and key”** model (rigid fit) and D. Koshland’s **“induced fit”** model — when the substrate binds, the conformation of the active site changes and “adapts” to the substrate (the modern view).

blocks.text: Chemical mechanisms of catalysis: acid-base catalysis, covalent catalysis (the substrate temporarily forms a covalent bond with serine or cysteine in the active site), metal ion catalysis, approximation and correct orientation of substrates.
**Specificity** is the selective action of an enzyme on a particular substrate or type of reaction:

items: **absolute** — on only one substrate (urease — urea, arginase — arginine);
**relative (group)** — on a group of substrates with the same bond (pepsin, lipase, phosphatases);

**stereospecificity** — on only one stereoisomer (L-amino acid oxidase, D-glucose enzymes). **Thermolability.** For every 10 °C rise in temperature the reaction rate doubles, but above 40–50 °C the enzyme protein denatures and its activity falls. The **temperature optimum** of human enzymes is 37–40 °C. At low temperature enzyme activity decreases, but the enzymes do not denature (reversible inactivation) — the cold storage of organs is based on this.

blocks.text: **pH dependence.** Each enzyme has a **pH optimum**; it depends on the ionization of groups in the active site and of the substrate.

blocks.text: **Dependence on enzyme concentration.** When the substrate is in excess, the reaction rate is directly proportional to the amount of enzyme. The determination of enzyme activity is based on this.

**Dependence on substrate concentration.** When the substrate is low, the rate increases in direct proportion to it; as the substrate increases, all enzyme molecules become occupied and the rate approaches its maximum (Vmax) — a **hyperbolic curve**. This dependence is expressed by the **Michaelis–Menten equation**:

The **Michaelis constant (K~m~)** is the substrate concentration (mol/l) at which the reaction rate equals half the maximum rate. K~m~ shows the **affinity** of the enzyme for the substrate: the smaller the K~m~, the higher the affinity. For example, the K~m~ of hexokinase for glucose is ≈ 0.1 mmol/l (high affinity, it works even when glucose is low), while that of glucokinase is ≈ 10 mmol/l (it works only when glucose is high — in the liver after a meal).
To find K~m~ and V~max~ precisely, the double-reciprocal plot — the **Lineweaver–Burk plot** (1/v against 1/[S]) — is used: the straight line crosses the y-axis at 1/V~max~ and the x-axis at −1/K~m~.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: The Michaelis–Menten curve and the Lineweaver–Burk plot; the effect of inhibitors (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Units of enzyme activity:** the international unit (IU, U) — the amount of enzyme that converts 1 µmol of substrate per minute; the **katal** (SI) — the amount of enzyme that converts 1 mol of substrate per second (1 U = 16.67 nkat). **Specific activity** is the activity per 1 mg of protein.
**Inhibitors** are substances that reduce enzyme activity.

items: **Irreversible inhibition** — the inhibitor binds covalently to a functional group of the active site: organophosphorus compounds (sarin, chlorophos) with the serine of acetylcholinesterase, aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase, heavy metals (Hg^2+^, Pb^2+^) with SH groups, cyanides with the iron of cytochrome oxidase.
**Reversible inhibition:**

**Competitive** — the inhibitor is similar in structure to the substrate and competes with the substrate for the active site. Its effect can be abolished by increasing the substrate concentration. **K~m~ increases, V~max~ does not change.** Examples: malonate — succinate dehydrogenase; sulfonamides — folate synthesis from para-aminobenzoic acid in bacteria; methotrexate — dihydrofolate reductase; statins — HMG-CoA reductase.

**Noncompetitive** — the inhibitor binds outside the active site and changes the enzyme’s conformation; the effect does not disappear even when the substrate is increased. **V~max~ decreases, K~m~ does not change.**
**Allosteric inhibition** — binding of an effector to the allosteric site (see below).

parts.text: Many drugs are enzyme inhibitors: ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril — angiotensin-converting enzyme), statins (HMG-CoA reductase), allopurinol (xanthine oxidase — in gout), proton pump inhibitors (H^+^,K^+^-ATPase), NSAIDs (cyclooxygenase), neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase — in myasthenia). In methanol poisoning ethanol is given: ethanol **competes** with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase and slows its conversion into toxic formaldehyde.

items: **Change in the amount of enzyme** — induction or repression of synthesis (under the action of hormones and substrates; for example, cortisol induces the enzymes of gluconeogenesis, insulin induces glucokinase) and the rate of degradation.
**Activation of proenzymes (zymogens)** — partial proteolysis: trypsinogen → trypsin (enteropeptidase), pepsinogen → pepsin (HCl), blood clotting factors, the complement system.

**Covalent modification** — **phosphorylation–dephosphorylation**: protein kinases phosphorylate serine, threonine or tyrosine residues at the expense of ATP, and phosphoprotein phosphatases remove the phosphate. For example, glycogen phosphorylase is activated when phosphorylated, whereas glycogen synthase becomes inactive.
**Allosteric regulation** — binding of an effector. Often the end product of a metabolic pathway inhibits the first (key) enzyme — **negative feedback** (feedback inhibition).
**Protein–protein interaction** — binding or dissociation of regulatory subunits (activation of protein kinase A by cAMP: the regulatory subunits dissociate).
**Compartmentalization** — the location of enzymes in different compartments of the cell.

blocks.text: Medical enzymology includes three directions:

items: **Enzyme diagnostics** — determination of enzyme activity in blood serum. When cells are damaged (cytolysis), intracellular enzymes are released into the blood. **Organ-specific enzymes** indicate the damaged organ.
**Enzymopathology** — diseases associated with congenital or acquired enzyme deficiency (phenylketonuria — phenylalanine hydroxylase, galactosemia, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency).
**Enzyme therapy** — the use of enzymes as drugs: pancreatin (digestive insufficiency), streptokinase and alteplase (dissolving thrombi), asparaginase (in leukemia), hyaluronidase.

blocks.text: **Immobilized enzymes** are enzymes attached to an insoluble carrier; they can be used again and again and are more stable. Glucometer test strips and biosensors (glucose oxidase) work on the basis of such enzymes.
Experiment 1: determination of salivary amylase activity by the Wohlgemuth method

**Principle of the method:** amylase breaks down starch to dextrins and maltose. Starch gives a blue color with iodine, dextrins — violet-red, maltose — no color. Saliva is serially diluted and the smallest amount that completely breaks down the starch is found.

items: Rinse the mouth with water, collect 1 ml of saliva and dilute it with 9 ml of distilled water (1 : 10).

Pour 1 ml of saline into each of 10 test tubes. Add 1 ml of diluted saliva to tube 1, mix and transfer 1 ml of it to tube 2; serially dilute in this way up to tube 10 (1 ml is discarded from the last one). Degree of dilution: 1 : 20, 1 : 40 ... 1 : 10 240.
Add 2 ml of 0.1% starch solution to each tube, mix and place in a 38 °C thermostat for 30 minutes.
Cool the tubes (to stop the reaction) and add 1 drop of 0.1% iodine solution to each.

Identify the most diluted tube in which the starch has been completely broken down (yellow color, no blue). **Calculation:** amylase activity (A) is the number of ml of 0.1% starch solution broken down by 1 ml of undiluted saliva at 38 °C in 30 minutes. For example, if the yellow color is in the tube diluted 1 : 160: A = 2 ml × 160 = 320.

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** normal salivary amylase activity is **160–320 units** (Wohlgemuth). Urinary amylase (diastase) is normally 16–64 units; it rises sharply in acute pancreatitis.
Experiment 2: demonstrating the specificity of enzymes

items: Pour 1 ml of diluted saliva into each of two test tubes.
Add 1 ml of 1% starch to tube 1 and 1 ml of 1% sucrose solution to tube 2; keep at 38 °C for 15 minutes.

Perform the Trommer (or Fehling) reaction in both tubes: add 1 ml of 10% NaOH and 3–5 drops of 1% CuSO~4~ and heat. **Result and analysis:** in tube 1 a red precipitate (Cu~2~O) — starch has been broken down to maltose, a reducing sugar. In tube 2 the reaction is negative — amylase does not break down sucrose (sucrose is acted on by sucrase). This shows the relative (group) specificity of the enzyme.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: effect of temperature, activators and inhibitors on amylase activity

items: Keep a saliva + starch mixture in three tubes at 0 °C (ice), 38 °C and 100 °C (previously boiled saliva) for 10 minutes; test with iodine.

To three other tubes add, respectively, 1% NaCl (activator), 1% CuSO~4~ (inhibitor) and water, and keep with saliva + starch at 38 °C; test with iodine from time to time. **Result and analysis:** at 38 °C starch is broken down quickly; on ice — very slowly (reversible inactivation); with boiled saliva — not at all (denaturation). Cl^-^ ions activate amylase (breakdown speeds up), Cu^2+^ ions inhibit it.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of inhibition from a Lineweaver–Burk plot

items: Draw the straight lines of 1/v against 1/[S] without inhibitor and with inhibitor.
If the lines cross on the y-axis (1/V~max~) — V~max~ is unchanged and K~m~ has increased: **competitive inhibition**.
If the lines cross on the x-axis (−1/K~m~) — K~m~ is unchanged and V~max~ has decreased: **noncompetitive inhibition**.
Conclude whether increasing the substrate concentration can abolish the inhibition.

Take into account the dynamics of the enzyme rise (CK-MB rises in 3–6 hours, peaks in 1–2 days).
Compare the conclusion with the clinical data.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After working in a newly renovated warehouse, a patient was brought to hospital with profuse salivation, sweating, constricted pupils, bronchospasm and muscle twitching. Serum cholinesterase activity is sharply reduced. An organophosphorus pesticide had been used in the warehouse.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical mechanism of the condition. On what principle is treatment based?
cases.answer: Organophosphorus compounds phosphorylate the serine residue in the active site of acetylcholinesterase and inhibit the enzyme irreversibly. Acetylcholine is not broken down and accumulates in the synapses — muscarinic (salivation, sweating, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia) and nicotinic (fasciculations, paralysis) signs develop. Treatment: atropine (blocks muscarinic receptors) and enzyme reactivators — oximes (pralidoxime): they remove the phosphate group from the serine and reactivate the enzyme (effective in the first hours, before the phosphorylated enzyme “ages”).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient drank methyl alcohol by mistake. He was prescribed intravenous ethyl alcohol solution and fomepizole.
cases.ask: On what biochemical principle is this treatment based?
cases.answer: Methanol is converted by alcohol dehydrogenase into formaldehyde and then into formic acid — they damage the optic nerve and cause metabolic acidosis. Ethanol is a substrate of the same enzyme and competes with methanol (it has a higher affinity for the enzyme); fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase. As a result the conversion of methanol into toxic products slows down, and it is excreted unchanged through the kidneys and lungs (hemodialysis is also used).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 35-year-old patient suddenly developed severe girdle-like pain in the upper abdomen. Urinary diastase is 1024 units, and serum lipase and α-amylase are sharply increased.
cases.ask: Which organ is damaged? Why has enzyme activity increased?
cases.answer: Acute pancreatitis. When pancreatic cells are damaged (premature activation of proteolytic enzymes inside the gland — conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin, autolysis), amylase and lipase are released into the blood. Because amylase is a small molecule, it passes through the kidneys into the urine — urinary diastase rises (normal 16–64 units). Lipase is more specific for pancreatitis and persists longer in the blood.

topics.title: Biological membranes. Membrane receptors. Signal transduction pathways into the cell

goals.text: To teach the student the chemical composition, structure, functions and general properties of biological membranes, the routes of transport of substances across the membrane, the types of membrane receptors, signal transduction into the cell and the systems of second messengers, and the significance of membrane damage in pathology.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the lipid and protein composition of membranes and the fluid mosaic model;
the functions of membranes;
the general properties of membranes: transverse asymmetry, fluidity, selective permeability;
the types of passive and active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis;
the types of membrane receptors;
the systems of G proteins, adenylate cyclase and phospholipase C, and the second messengers;
tyrosine kinase receptors and receptors linked to ion channels;
the causes and consequences of membrane damage.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the type of transport according to the substance;
explain the mechanism of hormone action by the signal transduction system;
determine the osmotic resistance of erythrocytes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase** uses 30–40% of the cell’s ATP (up to 70% in the brain). It maintains the membrane potential, cell volume and the Na^+^ gradient for secondary active transport. **Cardiac glycosides** (digoxin) inhibit this enzyme: Na^+^ increases inside the cell, Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchange weakens, Ca^2+^ accumulates and myocardial contraction becomes stronger.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The consequence of cell damage is the release of intracellular enzymes into the blood (cytolysis). Therefore an increase in blood ALT, AST, CK and LDH activity is a biochemical sign of membrane damage.

sections.title: 1. Structure and chemical composition of biological membranes

blocks.text: **Biological membranes** are lipid-protein structures 6–10 nm thick that surround the cell and its organelles. The cell has a plasma membrane and internal membranes (the membranes of the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria and lysosomes).

Membranes contain **lipids** (≈ 40%), **proteins** (≈ 50–60%) and **carbohydrates** (2–10%, as part of glycolipids and glycoproteins). In the myelin sheath lipids make up 75–80%, in the inner mitochondrial membrane proteins ≈ 75%.
Membrane lipids:

items: **Phospholipids** — glycerophospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol) and sphingomyelin. They are **amphiphilic**: a hydrophilic “head” and two hydrophobic “tails” (fatty acid residues). In water they form a **lipid bilayer**.
**Glycolipids** — cerebrosides, gangliosides (mainly in the outer layer; receptor and antigen function).
**Cholesterol** — regulates the rigidity and fluidity of the membrane (a “buffer”): at high temperature it reduces fluidity, at low temperature it prevents solidification. **Membrane proteins:**
**Integral (transmembrane)** proteins — span the bilayer (channels, carriers, pumps, receptors).
**Peripheral** proteins — bound to the membrane surface by ionic and hydrogen bonds.

**Anchored** proteins — attached through a lipid “anchor” (a fatty acid, prenyl, glycosylphosphatidylinositol). **Fluid mosaic model** (S. Singer and G. Nicolson, 1972): the membrane is a fluid lipid bilayer in which proteins “float” and can move laterally.

sections.title: 2. Functions and general properties of membranes

blocks.text: Functions:

items: **Barrier** — separates the internal environment of the cell and organelles, compartmentalization.
**Transport** — selective passage of substances.
**Receptor (signaling)** — reception of hormones, mediators and other signals.
**Enzymatic** — membrane-bound enzymes (respiratory chain, ATP synthase, adenylate cyclase).
**Energy conversion** — formation of an electrochemical gradient in the mitochondria and ATP synthesis.
**Intercellular contact** — gap junctions, adhesion molecules, antigenicity (blood groups, histocompatibility antigens).
**Electrogenic** — generation of the membrane potential and conduction of excitation. **General properties:**

**Transverse asymmetry** — the composition of the outer and inner leaflets differs: the outer leaflet is rich in phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin and glycolipids, the inner in phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine. The movement of lipids from one leaflet to the other (“flip-flop”) is very slow and is carried out by special enzymes (flippases). Carbohydrate parts are only on the outer surface (glycocalyx).
**Fluidity** — lateral movement of lipids and proteins; fluidity increases when unsaturated fatty acids increase and when the temperature rises, while cholesterol and saturated fatty acids reduce it.
**Selective permeability** — small hydrophobic molecules (O~2~, CO~2~, steroids) pass freely; ions and polar molecules pass only through special proteins.

parts.text: In apoptosis phosphatidylserine moves to the outer leaflet of the membrane — this is an “eat me” signal for macrophages. When platelets are activated, phosphatidylserine also moves outward and forms a surface for the clotting factor complexes.

blocks.text: **Carriers** (uniport, symport, antiport) have enzyme-like properties: specificity, saturation (V~max~), competitive inhibition. For example, GLUT4 is insulin-sensitive (muscle, adipose tissue): insulin moves it from intracellular vesicles to the membrane.

parts.text: **Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase** uses 30–40% of the cell’s ATP (up to 70% in the brain). It maintains the membrane potential, cell volume and the Na^+^ gradient for secondary active transport. **Cardiac glycosides** (digoxin) inhibit this enzyme: Na^+^ increases inside the cell, Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchange weakens, Ca^2+^ accumulates and myocardial contraction becomes stronger.

blocks.text: Signaling molecules (**ligands**, first messengers) are hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and growth factors. Hydrophilic ligands (peptide hormones, catecholamines) do not cross the membrane and act through **membrane receptors**; hydrophobic ligands (steroid and thyroid hormones, calcitriol) cross the membrane, bind to **intracellular (nuclear) receptors** and change gene transcription.

blocks.text: The G protein system

**G proteins** are GTP-binding heterotrimeric proteins (α, β, γ subunits). At rest the α subunit is bound to GDP. When the receptor is activated, GDP is exchanged for GTP, α-GTP dissociates and acts on the effector enzyme; the α subunit’s own GTPase activity hydrolyzes GTP to GDP and terminates the signal.

items: **Gs** — activates adenylate cyclase (cAMP ↑);
**Gi** — inhibits adenylate cyclase (cAMP ↓);

**Gq** — activates phospholipase C. **The adenylate cyclase system:** adenylate cyclase forms **cAMP** from ATP. cAMP binds to the regulatory subunits of **protein kinase A** and releases the catalytic subunits; these phosphorylate target proteins (phosphorylase kinase, hormone-sensitive lipase and others). cAMP is broken down to AMP by **phosphodiesterase** (caffeine and theophylline inhibit phosphodiesterase and prolong the action of cAMP).

blocks.text: **The inositol phosphate system:** phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP~2~) into two second messengers: **inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP~3~)** — releases Ca^2+^ from the endoplasmic
reticulum; **diacylglycerol (DAG)** — together with Ca^2+^ activates **protein kinase C**. Many effects of Ca^2+^ are carried out through the protein **calmodulin**.

parts.text: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the α subunit of the G~s~ protein and abolishes its GTPase activity — the G protein stays permanently active, cAMP rises sharply in the intestinal epithelium, and Cl^-^ and water move into the intestinal lumen — severe diarrhea. Pertussis toxin, in contrast, blocks the G~i~ protein. Nitroglycerin releases NO and dilates vessels through cGMP; sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, which breaks down cGMP.

blocks.text: Membrane damage is a key link in the pathogenesis of many diseases:

items: **Lipid peroxidation (LPO)** — free radicals (O~2~

−, ^•^OH) oxidize polyunsaturated fatty acids; membrane permeability increases, enzymes and receptors fail. Antioxidant defense: vitamins E and C, glutathione, superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase.
**Activation of phospholipases** (ischemia, excess Ca^2+^) — phospholipids are broken down.
**Detergent action** — excess bile acids and fatty acids.
**Mechanical and osmotic damage**, the membrane attack complex of the complement system, bacterial toxins.
**Congenital defects** — a defect of membrane skeleton proteins (spectrin) — hereditary spherocytosis; ion channel diseases (channelopathies) — cystic fibrosis (the CFTR Cl- channel).

parts.text: The consequence of cell damage is the release of intracellular enzymes into the blood (cytolysis). Therefore an increase in blood ALT, AST, CK and LDH activity is a biochemical sign of membrane damage.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of the osmotic resistance of erythrocytes

items: Pour 1 ml each of NaCl solutions from 0.7% to 0.2% (in steps of 0.02–0.05%) into test tubes.
Add 1 drop of blood to each tube, mix and leave for 1 hour (or centrifuge).
The tube with the highest concentration in which the solution has turned pink and there is a sediment — **minimal resistance** (onset of hemolysis).

The tube in which there is no sediment at all and the solution is clear red (“lacquered blood”) — **maximal resistance** (complete hemolysis). **Evaluation:** normally minimal resistance is 0.46–0.48% and maximal 0.32–0.34% NaCl. In hereditary spherocytosis resistance decreases (hemolysis begins at a higher concentration), in thalassemia and iron deficiency anemia it increases (thin, flat erythrocytes).

blocks.text: **Analysis:** in a hypotonic medium water enters the erythrocyte by osmosis, the cell swells, its membrane ruptures and hemoglobin is released. Resistance depends on the membrane composition, the state of the cytoskeleton and the cell shape (surface/volume ratio).
Experiment 2: effect of a detergent and temperature on membrane permeability (demonstration)

items: Pour 2 ml of an erythrocyte suspension in 0.9% NaCl into three test tubes.
Add 3 drops of 1% bile salt (or saponin) to tube 1 and 3 drops of ethanol to tube 2; heat tube 3 at 60 °C for 10 minutes.

Compare with the control tube. **Result and analysis:** under the action of a detergent and heating, membrane lipids and proteins are disrupted — hemolysis (the solution is clear red). This shows the consequence of loss of membrane integrity.

items: Determine the nature of the substance: a small hydrophobic molecule, an ion, a polar molecule or a macromolecule.

Check whether there is saturation and specificity — the participation of a carrier.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient who came from an endemic area has watery “rice-water” diarrhea of up to 15–20 liters a day, severe dehydration and a fall in blood pressure. Vibrio cholerae was detected in the stool.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical mechanism of the diarrhea. Why is glucose added to the rehydration solution?
cases.answer: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the α subunit of the G~s~ protein in enterocytes; its GTPase activity is lost and adenylate cyclase is permanently activated. cAMP rises and, through protein kinase A, phosphorylates the CFTR Cl^-^ channel — Cl^-^, followed by Na^+^ and water, moves into the intestinal lumen. The glucose in the oral rehydration solution provides, through SGLT1 (Na^+^-glucose symport), the absorption of Na^+^ and, with it, of water by osmosis; this carrier is not impaired by cAMP.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with chronic heart failure takes digoxin. After losing potassium because of diarrhea, he developed nausea, yellowish spots in his vision and heart rhythm disturbances.
cases.ask: What is the mechanism of action of digoxin? Why does hypokalemia increase the toxicity?
cases.answer: Digoxin inhibits Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase in cardiomyocytes — Na^+^ increases inside the cell, the Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchanger removes less Ca^2+^, Ca^2+^ accumulates in the cell and contraction becomes stronger (a positive inotropic effect). Digoxin competes with K^+^ for the same site on the ATPase: when K^+^ falls, digoxin binds to the enzyme more and its effect (toxicity) increases — arrhythmias develop.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An 8-year-old child has recurrent jaundice, anemia and an enlarged spleen. The blood smear shows small spherical erythrocytes, and osmotic resistance is reduced: hemolysis begins at 0.60% NaCl. His father has the same disease.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? What is its biochemical basis?
cases.answer: Hereditary spherocytosis (Minkowski–Chauffard disease). Because of a defect of membrane skeleton proteins (spectrin, ankyrin), the lipid bilayer is poorly bound to the cytoskeleton, pieces of membrane are lost, the erythrocyte becomes spherical and its surface/volume ratio decreases. Such cells tolerate swelling poorly (reduced osmotic resistance) and are trapped and destroyed in the spleen — hemolytic anemia, raised bilirubin (jaundice), splenomegaly.

topics.title: Biological oxidation

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the concepts of energy metabolism and biological oxidation, high-energy compounds and the significance of ATP, the structure and components of the respiratory (electron transport) chain, the mechanism of oxidative phosphorylation (the chemiosmotic theory), substrate-level phosphorylation, respiratory control and the P/O ratio, respiratory chain inhibitors and uncouplers, and mitochondrial diseases.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: exergonic and endergonic reactions and their coupling;
high-energy compounds and the ATP–ADP cycle;
the types of biological oxidation (dehydrogenation, electron donation, oxygen addition);
the complexes and carriers of the respiratory chain and their arrangement according to redox potentials;
the chemiosmotic theory of oxidative phosphorylation and how ATP synthase works;
the reactions of substrate-level phosphorylation;
the P/O ratio and respiratory control;
respiratory chain inhibitors and uncouplers;
extramitochondrial oxidation and reactive oxygen species.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine succinate dehydrogenase activity by the Thunberg method;
determine catalase and peroxidase activity;
give a biochemical explanation of respiratory chain disorders in poisonings.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Uncouplers used as a weight-loss agent (2,4-dinitrophenol) have caused fatal hyperthermia — because energy is converted not into ATP but into heat, and body temperature rises uncontrollably. In hyperthyroidism oxidation and phosphorylation are also partly uncoupled: patients are heat-intolerant, sweat, and their basal metabolic rate is increased.

blocks.text: Reactions in the living cell are of two types: **exergonic** (free energy is released, ΔG < 0, proceeds spontaneously) and **endergonic** (energy is consumed, ΔG > 0). Endergonic reactions proceed **coupled** with exergonic reactions; the universal mediator of this coupling is **ATP**.

**High-energy compounds** are substances that release a large amount of free energy on hydrolysis (ΔG°’ < −30 kJ/mol): ATP and other nucleoside triphosphates (GTP, UTP, CTP), creatine phosphate, phosphoenolpyruvate, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA.

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Standard free energy of hydrolysis of some phosphate compounds
head: Compound
ΔG°’, kJ/mol

blocks.text: The intermediate value of ATP allows it to accept energy from compounds with a higher potential and pass it on to those with a lower potential. In the human body an amount of ATP close to body weight (≈ 40–60 kg) is formed and broken down per day, yet at any moment the body contains only ≈ 50–100 g of ATP — the **ATP–ADP cycle** turns over very rapidly.
Routes of ATP formation:

items: **Oxidative phosphorylation** — in the mitochondria at the expense of the respiratory chain energy (≈ 90%).

**Substrate-level phosphorylation** — direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate to ADP: in glycolysis (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → 3-phosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate) and in the Krebs cycle (succinyl-CoA → succinate, GTP is formed).

blocks.text: **Biological oxidation** is the sum of the oxidation-reduction reactions that take place in living cells. Oxidation is the removal of electrons (and often of hydrogen atoms), reduction is their addition. Hydrogen atoms removed from substrates (2H^+^ + 2e−) pass to **NAD^+^** or **FAD**, are then delivered to oxygen through the **respiratory (electron transport) chain**, and water is formed. This process is called **tissue respiration**.

The respiratory chain is located in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. Electrons move along the carriers from the side with a low (negative) **redox potential** to the side with a high (positive) one: NAD^+^/NADH (−0.32 V) → ... → ½O~2~/H~2~O (+0.82 V). The total potential difference is ≈ 1.14 V and the free energy released is ≈ 220 kJ/mol (from NADH).

blocks.text: **Cytochromes** are heme-containing proteins; their iron passes between the Fe^3+^ ⇄ Fe^2+^ states and carries one electron at a time.

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: The respiratory chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane, the proton gradient and ATP synthase; sites of action of inhibitors (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Oxidative phosphorylation** is ATP synthesis coupled to electron transport in the respiratory chain. Its mechanism is explained by **P. Mitchell’s chemiosmotic theory** (1961, Nobel Prize 1978):

items: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from the matrix into the **intermembrane space** at the expense of the energy of electron transport.
The inner membrane is impermeable to protons — an **electrochemical proton gradient** (ΔμH+) is formed: a chemical part (ΔpH ≈ 0.5–1) and an electrical part (Δψ ≈ 150–180 mV).

Protons return to the matrix only through the **F~o~ channel of ATP synthase**; this flow drives the rotation of F~1~ (rotational catalysis, P. Boyer) and the synthesis of ATP from ADP + P~i~. The **P/O ratio** is the number of ATP molecules formed per 1 atom of oxygen (2 electrons). According to current data, oxidation of NADH yields **≈ 2.5 ATP** and oxidation of FADH~2~ (succinate) **≈ 1.5 ATP** (older textbooks give whole numbers — 3 and 2).

blocks.text: **Respiratory control** is the dependence of the rate of respiration (O~2~ consumption) on the ADP concentration. When ATP is used and ADP increases, ATP synthase speeds up, the proton gradient decreases and the respiratory chain speeds up. When ADP is low, the gradient is high and the electron flow slows down. Thanks to this, ATP formation is matched to the cell’s needs.
ATP is exported to the cytosol by the **ADP/ATP translocase** (antiport); phosphate enters by symport with H^+^.
Transfer of cytosolic NADH into the mitochondria
The inner membrane is impermeable to NADH; the hydrogen of NADH formed in the cytosol in glycolysis enters through **shuttle mechanisms**:

items: **The malate-aspartate shuttle** (liver, heart, kidney) — hydrogen passes to NAD^+^ in the mitochondria (≈ 2.5 ATP).
**The glycerol phosphate shuttle** (skeletal muscle, brain) — hydrogen passes to FAD (≈ 1.5 ATP).

blocks.text: **Uncouplers** are substances that uncouple oxidation from phosphorylation. In **brown adipose tissue** the protein thermogenin (UCP-1) is a physiological uncoupler: it returns protons to the matrix and the energy is released as heat — **non-shivering thermogenesis** in newborns and hibernating animals.

parts.text: **Cyanide poisoning**: cytochrome oxidase is blocked, the tissues cannot use oxygen (venous blood is as red as arterial blood, O~2~ is not used), anaerobic glycolysis increases and lactic acidosis develops. Treatment: sodium nitrite (converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which binds cyanide — cyanmethemoglobin), sodium thiosulfate (converts cyanide into the less toxic thiocyanate with the participation of rhodanese), hydroxocobalamin. **In CO poisoning** hemoglobin is converted to carboxyhemoglobin and cytochrome oxidase is also inhibited; treatment — oxygen (hyperbaric oxygenation).

Uncouplers used as a weight-loss agent (2,4-dinitrophenol) have caused fatal hyperthermia — because energy is converted not into ATP but into heat, and body temperature rises uncontrollably. In hyperthyroidism oxidation and phosphorylation are also partly uncoupled: patients are heat-intolerant, sweat, and their basal metabolic rate is increased.

blocks.text: ≈ 90% of oxygen is reduced to water in the respiratory chain; the rest is used by other routes:

items: **Oxidases** — pass hydrogen directly to O~2~, forming H~2~O~2~ (amino acid oxidases, xanthine oxidase).

**Oxygenases** — attach oxygen atoms to the substrate: **monooxygenases** (hydroxylases, cytochrome P450 — in the endoplasmic reticulum, metabolism of xenobiotics and steroids) and **dioxygenases**. **Reactive oxygen species (ROS)** are incompletely reduced active forms of oxygen: the superoxide anion radical (O~2~^−^), hydrogen peroxide (H~2~O~2~), the hydroxyl radical (^•^OH). They are formed by the “leakage” of electrons from the respiratory chain, in phagocytes (NADPH oxidase — the “respiratory burst”) and under ionizing radiation. Normally ROS take part in killing bacteria and in signaling, but in excess they damage lipids, proteins and DNA (oxidative stress).

blocks.text: Antioxidant defense:

items: enzymes: **superoxide dismutase** (2O~2~^−^ + 2H^+^ → H~2~O~2~ + O~2~), **catalase** (2H~2~O~2~ → 2H~2~O + O~2~), **glutathione peroxidase** (contains selenium; converts H~2~O~2~ to water at the expense of reduced glutathione), glutathione reductase (uses NADPH);
nonenzymatic antioxidants: vitamins E and C, β-carotene, glutathione, uric acid, bilirubin.

blocks.text: The mitochondria have their own DNA (mtDNA); it encodes 13 proteins of the respiratory chain and is inherited only **through the mother**. Mutations of mtDNA or of nuclear genes encoding respiratory chain proteins cause **mitochondrial diseases**. They mainly affect tissues with high energy needs — the brain, skeletal and heart muscle, the optic nerve: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS syndrome (myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes), Kearns–Sayre syndrome. Their common biochemical sign is increased blood lactate and pyruvate.
Experiment 1: determination of succinate dehydrogenase activity by the Thunberg method

**Principle of the method:** succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) removes hydrogen from succinate and passes it to an artificial acceptor — methylene blue; methylene blue is reduced and becomes colorless (the leuco form).

items: Mince muscle tissue and wash it with water (to remove endogenous substrates).
Put equal amounts of tissue into two test tubes. Add 2 ml of 2% sodium succinate to tube 1 and 2 ml of water to tube 2 (control).
Add 2 drops of 0.01% methylene blue to each and cover with a layer of petroleum jelly oil to keep air out.

Place the tubes in a 37 °C water bath and observe the time of decolorization. **Result and analysis:** in the tube with succinate methylene blue decolorizes faster — SDH oxidizes succinate to fumarate. In the control decolorization is very slow. If **malonate** is added to a 3rd tube together with succinate, decolorization slows down — competitive inhibition.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of catalase activity

items: Pour 1 ml of 3% hydrogen peroxide solution into a test tube.
Add 1 drop of blood (or liver homogenate).

Repeat in another tube with boiled blood. **Result and analysis:** when fresh blood is added, vigorous foaming (O~2~ bubbles) occurs — catalase breaks down H~2~O~2~ into water and oxygen. With boiled blood there is no reaction — the enzyme is denatured. Catalase activity is determined quantitatively by the Bach–Zubkova method: the undecomposed H~2~O~2~ is titrated with potassium permanganate.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determination of peroxidase activity (benzidine or guaiac test)

items: Pour 1 ml of diluted blood (or potato juice) and 5 drops of benzidine (or guaiac resin) solution into a test tube.
Add 3–5 drops of 3% H~2~O~2~.

blocks.text: **Result and analysis:** a blue (or blue-green) color appears — peroxidase (in blood, the pseudoperoxidase activity of hemoglobin) oxidizes the substrate at the expense of the oxygen of H~2~O~2~. This reaction underlies the detection of occult blood in stool and urine.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A person rescued from a fire was brought in unconscious. The skin is pink-red, blood lactate is sharply increased, and the oxygen content of venous blood is close to that of arterial blood. Cyanide and CO were released from the burning synthetic materials.
cases.ask: Why is there a lot of oxygen in the venous blood? What is the cause of the lactic acidosis? Which antidotes are used?
cases.answer: Cyanide and CO block cytochrome oxidase (complex IV) — electrons do not pass to oxygen and the tissues cannot use it (tissue, or histotoxic, hypoxia), so the venous blood remains rich in oxygen. Once oxidative phosphorylation stops, ATP is formed only by anaerobic glycolysis — pyruvate is reduced to lactate and lactic acidosis develops. CO also forms carboxyhemoglobin with hemoglobin (red skin). Treatment is given by the set emergency protocol: oxygen (including hyperbaric oxygenation) and the antidotes used against cyanide (hydroxocobalamin, nitrite and thiosulfate preparations).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A gym member bought a “fat burner” online — 2,4-dinitrophenol — and took it. A few days later his body temperature rose to 41 °C, with profuse sweating, tachycardia and shortness of breath.
cases.ask: How does this substance act? Why did hyperthermia develop?
cases.answer: 2,4-dinitrophenol is an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation: it carries protons into the matrix bypassing ATP synthase, and the proton gradient is lost. The respiratory chain works continuously (O~2~ consumption rises sharply), but little ATP is formed and the energy is released as heat. The body cannot dissipate this heat — uncontrollable hyperthermia, a life-threatening condition. The substance is not a medicine and its use is dangerous.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 14-year-old adolescent has exercise intolerance, muscle weakness and recurrent stroke-like attacks. Blood lactate is increased at rest. His mother also has a mild myopathy; his father is healthy.
cases.ask: Which group of diseases is suspected? Why is lactate increased? What does the pattern of inheritance indicate?
cases.answer: A mitochondrial disease (MELAS syndrome is suspected). Because of a defect of respiratory chain proteins, NADH oxidation and ATP formation are impaired; the NADH/NAD^+^ ratio rises and pyruvate is reduced to lactate — lactic acidosis. The tissues with the greatest energy needs (brain, muscles) are affected. Transmission of the disease through the mother points to a mutation of mitochondrial DNA, because mitochondria pass to the zygote only from the egg cell.

topics.title: The common pathways of catabolism

goals.text: To teach the student the common pathways of catabolism — the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate and the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, their enzymes, coenzymes, energy yield, regulation, anabolic (amphibolic) functions and link with the respiratory chain, and the biochemical basis of hypoenergetic states.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the significance of the common pathways of catabolism;
the structure, coenzymes and reaction of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex;
the reactions, enzymes and products of the Krebs cycle;
the regulation of the Krebs cycle and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex;
the energy yield of the cycle and its link with the respiratory chain;
the anabolic functions of the cycle and the anaplerotic reactions;
the causes and consequences of hypoenergetic states.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the amount of ATP formed in the oxidation of glucose and pyruvate;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Oxygen does not take part in the Krebs cycle itself, but the cycle works only under **aerobic conditions**: NAD^+^ and FAD are reoxidized only in the respiratory chain. When oxygen is lacking, NADH accumulates and the cycle stops.

sections.title: 1. The concept of the common pathways of catabolism

blocks.text: The specific catabolic pathways of carbohydrates, fats and amino acids (glycolysis, β-oxidation, amino acid breakdown) lead to the common metabolites — **pyruvate** and **acetyl-CoA**. Their further oxidation proceeds through reactions common to all substances:

items: **Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate** — pyruvate → acetyl-CoA;
**The citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle, tricarboxylic acid cycle)** — oxidation of the acetyl residue to CO~2~;

**The respiratory chain and oxidative phosphorylation** — transfer of hydrogen atoms to oxygen and ATP synthesis. These processes take place in the **mitochondrial matrix** (the Krebs cycle enzymes, except succinate dehydrogenase, which is in the inner membrane) and provide the main part of the body’s energy.

blocks.text: Pyruvate formed in the cytosol in glycolysis enters the mitochondria through a special carrier and is converted to acetyl-CoA by the **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC)**:
Pyruvate + NAD^+^ + CoA-SH → Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H^+^ + CO~2~
The reaction is **irreversible**; therefore glucose cannot be synthesized from acetyl-CoA (the reason why glucose is not formed from fatty acids).

blocks.text: **Regulation.** PDC activity is:

items: **inhibited** by the products — acetyl-CoA and NADH (high ATP/ADP and NADH/NAD^+^), and also by **phosphorylation** (PDH kinase phosphorylates E~1~ and makes it inactive; acetyl-CoA, NADH and ATP activate the kinase);
**activated** by pyruvate, ADP, NAD^+^, CoA, Ca^2+^ (during muscle contraction) and **dephosphorylation** (PDH phosphatase; insulin activates it).

parts.text: **In thiamine deficiency** (alcoholism, beriberi) the PDC and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase do not work — pyruvate and lactate increase in the blood, and an energy deficit develops in the brain and heart (Wernicke encephalopathy, “wet” beriberi — heart failure). **Arsenite** binds the SH groups of lipoic acid and inhibits the PDC. Congenital PDC deficiency — severe lactic acidosis and neurological disorders in children; a ketogenic diet is used.

blocks.text: The cycle was discovered in 1937 by **H. Krebs** (Nobel Prize 1953). In the cycle the two-carbon acetyl residue of acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate and is oxidized in 8 successive reactions to two molecules of CO~2~, while oxaloacetate is regenerated.

blocks.text: Starting from pyruvate (adding the NADH of the PDC): 10 + 2.5 = **12.5 ATP** (15 by the old calculation). The aerobic oxidation of glucose yields a total of **30–32 ATP** (36–38 by the old calculation) (topic 6).

parts.text: Oxygen does not take part in the Krebs cycle itself, but the cycle works only under **aerobic conditions**: NAD^+^ and FAD are reoxidized only in the respiratory chain. When oxygen is lacking, NADH accumulates and the cycle stops.

blocks.text: The rate of the cycle is matched to the cell’s energy needs. The main regulated enzymes are those that catalyze the irreversible reactions:

blocks.text: General principle: **high ATP and NADH** (enough energy) — the cycle slows down; **high ADP, NAD^+^ and Ca^2+^** (energy expenditure, muscle contraction) — the cycle speeds up. In addition, the rate of the cycle depends on the availability of oxaloacetate.

sections.title: 6. Functions of the Krebs cycle. Anaplerotic reactions

blocks.text: **Catabolic (energy) function** — oxidizing the acetyl residue to CO~2~ and supplying NADH and FADH~2~ to the respiratory chain.
**Anabolic functions** — the cycle metabolites are raw material for synthesis:

items: oxaloacetate → phosphoenolpyruvate → **glucose** (gluconeogenesis);
oxaloacetate → **aspartate**, α-ketoglutarate → **glutamate** (transamination);
citrate moves to the cytosol and gives acetyl-CoA → **synthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol**;
succinyl-CoA + glycine → **heme synthesis**. For this reason the cycle is considered an **amphibolic** pathway.

blocks.text: **Anaplerotic (“filling-up”) reactions** replenish the metabolites withdrawn for synthesis:

items: **Pyruvate carboxylase** (biotin, ATP): pyruvate + CO~2~ → oxaloacetate — the most important; acetyl-CoA activates it allosterically (when acetyl-CoA increases, its “partner” oxaloacetate increases too);
formation of α-ketoglutarate from glutamate (glutamate dehydrogenase, transamination);
formation of succinyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine (propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; requires B~12~).

parts.text: In starvation and diabetes mellitus oxaloacetate is used up in gluconeogenesis; the acetyl-CoA formed in the liver from the β-oxidation of fatty acids cannot fully enter the Krebs cycle and is directed to the synthesis of **ketone bodies** (topic 9).

blocks.text: A **hypoenergetic state** is a fall in ATP formation in the cell below its needs. Causes:

items: **Alimentary** — starvation, lack of nutrients and vitamins (B~1~, B~2~, PP, B~5~);
**Hypoxic** — lack of oxygen (respiratory and circulatory failure, anemia, CO poisoning);
**Histotoxic** — inhibition of respiratory chain enzymes (cyanides), the action of uncouplers;

**Mitochondrial diseases** — congenital defects of respiratory chain and Krebs cycle enzymes. Consequences: ion pumps fail (cell swelling), synthetic processes weaken, anaerobic glycolysis increases and lactic acidosis develops; the most sensitive organs are the brain and the heart.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of citric acid in urine (Deniges reaction)

items: Pour 2 ml of urine, 0.5 ml of 10% H~2~SO~4~ and 0.5 ml of 5% KMnO~4~ solution into a test tube and heat to boiling.

After decolorization add 1 ml of mercuric sulfate reagent (Deniges reagent). **Result and analysis:** citric acid is oxidized to acetone dicarboxylic acid, which gives a white precipitate with mercuric sulfate. Normally 0.2–1.2 g of citrate is excreted in the urine per day; it binds calcium and prevents the formation of kidney stones (hypocitraturia is a risk factor for stone formation).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of pyruvate in urine (sodium nitroprusside test)

items: Add to a test tube 2 ml of urine, 0.5 ml of 10% NaOH and 3–5 drops of freshly prepared 5% sodium nitroprusside solution.

Observe the color that appears, then add 1 ml of concentrated acetic acid. **Result and analysis:** if pyruvate is present, a deep orange-red color forms in the alkaline medium and turns violet when acetic acid is added. An increase of pyruvate in the urine (normal 10–25 mg per day) is characteristic of B~1~ hypovitaminosis, diabetes mellitus, hypoxia and PDC deficiency.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase in muscle tissue by malonate

items: Put equal amounts of washed minced muscle into three test tubes.

Add 2 ml of succinate to tube 1, 2 ml of succinate + 1 ml of malonate to tube 2, and 2 ml of water to tube 3 (control); add 2 drops of methylene blue and a layer of petroleum jelly oil to all of them.
Compare the time of decolorization at 37 °C.

blocks.text: **Result and analysis:** in the tube with malonate decolorization slows down — malonate is similar in structure to succinate and competes with it for the active site. Increasing the amount of substrate (succinate) reduces the inhibition.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 6-month-old child has had low muscle tone, developmental delay and seizures since birth. Blood lactate and pyruvate are sharply increased, the lactate/pyruvate ratio is normal, and alanine is also increased. The condition worsens after carbohydrate food.
cases.ask: Which enzyme deficiency is suspected? Why do carbohydrates worsen the condition? What diet is recommended?
cases.answer: Congenital deficiency of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Pyruvate is not converted to acetyl-CoA and accumulates; it is converted to lactate (LDH) and to alanine (transamination). Carbohydrates form pyruvate through glycolysis and increase the acidosis. Because the brain obtains energy mainly from glucose oxidation, the neurological disorders are severe. Treatment: a ketogenic diet (low in carbohydrates, high in fats) — fatty acids and ketone bodies give acetyl-CoA bypassing the PDC; in some patients high-dose thiamine is effective.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After rats were given an inhibitor of one of the Krebs cycle enzymes, succinate accumulated in the tissues while the amounts of fumarate and malate decreased.
cases.ask: Which enzyme is inhibited? Name a possible inhibitor. How does this affect energy metabolism?
cases.answer: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) is inhibited; malonate is its classic competitive inhibitor. Succinate is not converted to fumarate and the cycle stops: the following metabolites and oxaloacetate decrease, acetyl-CoA cannot enter the cycle; less FADH~2~ and NADH are formed and ATP synthesis falls. Increasing the succinate concentration partly overcomes the inhibition.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient after prolonged starvation, blood glucose is 3.0 mmol/l, ketone bodies are sharply increased and acetone is detected in the urine.
cases.ask: How does the activity of the Krebs cycle in the liver change in starvation? Why do ketone bodies increase?
cases.answer: In starvation, under the action of glucagon and cortisol, gluconeogenesis in the liver increases and oxaloacetate is used for it (it leaves for the cytosol as malate). At the same time the β-oxidation of fatty acids coming from adipose tissue increases and a lot of acetyl-CoA is formed. Because oxaloacetate is lacking, acetyl-CoA cannot form citrate and is not fully oxidized in the Krebs cycle — in the liver mitochondria it is converted into acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate (ketone bodies); these serve as an energy source for other tissues (brain, muscle).

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of dietary carbohydrates and their significance, the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates (including age-related features), the fate of the absorbed monosaccharides in the tissues, the synthesis and breakdown of glycogen in the liver and muscles and their regulation, aerobic glycolysis, the transfer of the hydrogen of cytosolic NADH into the mitochondria, and the glycogenoses and aglycogenoses.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The two glycogen “stores” serve different purposes**: liver glycogen maintains the level of **blood glucose** (between meals, ≈ 12–24 hours); muscle glycogen is an energy source only for the muscle’s **own contraction**.

blocks.text: Carbohydrates provide 55–60% of the energy of food; the daily requirement of adults is 350–450 g. The main dietary carbohydrates are: **polysaccharides** — starch (amylose and amylopectin), glycogen (little in meat), cellulose and other dietary fiber; **disaccharides** — sucrose (glucose + fructose, α1→β2), lactose (galactose + glucose, β1→4), maltose (2 glucose, α1→4); **monosaccharides** — glucose, fructose.

**Functions of carbohydrates in the body:** energy (1 g → 4 kcal), storage (glycogen), plastic and structural (glycoproteins, proteoglycans, glycolipids, the ribose and deoxyribose of nucleotides), protective (mucous substances), receptor and recognition (glycocalyx, blood group antigens), and a carbon skeleton for the synthesis of other substances (amino acids, fats).

**Dietary fiber** (cellulose, pectin, hemicellulose) is not digested in humans, but it increases intestinal peristalsis, binds and removes cholesterol and bile acids, and serves as food for the beneficial microflora.

items: **Glucose and galactose** — symport with Na^+^ through **SGLT1** (secondary active transport, against the gradient);
**Fructose** — facilitated diffusion through **GLUT5**;
from the enterocyte into the blood — through **GLUT2** in the basolateral membrane. The absorbed monosaccharides reach the liver first through the **portal vein**.

parts.text: **Lactase deficiency** (milk intolerance) — in a large part of the world’s population lactase activity falls after childhood for genetic reasons (primary); in intestinal diseases (enteritis, celiac disease) it is secondary. Undigested lactose passes into the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it and form gases (H~2~, CO~2~, CH~4~) and organic acids — bloating, pain, osmotic diarrhea. Diagnosis: the hydrogen breath test, a lactose load. Treatment: a lactose-free diet, fermented milk products (in which lactose is partly broken down by bacteria), lactase preparations. **In newborns** congenital lactase deficiency is rare but runs severely.

sections.title: 3. Entry of glucose into the cell and its phosphorylation

blocks.text: Glucose enters the cell through **GLUT** transporters: GLUT1 (erythrocytes, the blood-brain barrier), GLUT2 (liver, pancreatic β-cells, enterocytes, kidney — high K~m~), GLUT3 (neurons — low K~m~), **GLUT4** (skeletal muscle, heart, adipose tissue — **insulin-dependent**).
In the cell glucose is phosphorylated at once and can no longer leave the cell:
Glucose + ATP → Glucose-6-phosphate + ADP

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Hexokinase and glucokinase
head: Feature
Hexokinase (I–III)
Glucokinase (hexokinase IV)
rows: Supplies the tissue even when glucose is low
Retains excess glucose in the liver after a meal

blocks.text: **Glucose-6-phosphate** is the “crossroads” of carbohydrate metabolism: it can enter glycolysis, glycogen synthesis or the pentose phosphate pathway, or (in the liver) be converted into free glucose by glucose-6-phosphatase.

**Glycogen** is a branched polymer of glucose (α1→4 bonds, with an α1→6 branch every 8–12 residues). It is stored mainly in the **liver** (≈ 100–120 g, 5–6% of its mass; to maintain the blood glucose level) and in **skeletal muscle** (≈ 300–400 g, 1–2% of its mass; only for the muscle’s own energy).

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Synthesis and breakdown of glycogen (drawn after Sobirova R.A., 2006; Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: Glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis)

items: Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase/glucokinase, ATP).
Glucose-6-phosphate ⇄ glucose-1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase).
Glucose-1-phosphate + UTP → **UDP-glucose** + PP~i~ (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase); the pyrophosphate is hydrolyzed — the reaction is irreversible.
The glucose residue of UDP-glucose is attached to the end of the glycogen chain by an α1→4 bond — **glycogen synthase** (the key enzyme). The “primer” protein for a new chain is **glycogenin**.
The **branching enzyme** (amylo-1,4→1,6-transglycosylase) transfers a piece of the chain and forms an α1→6 branch. Adding one glucose to glycogen costs 2 high-energy bonds (ATP and UTP).

blocks.text: Breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis)

items: **Glycogen phosphorylase** (the key enzyme; coenzyme — pyridoxal phosphate) cleaves α1→4 bonds from the end of the chain with phosphate (phosphorolysis): glycogen(n) + P~i~ → glycogen(n−1) + glucose-1-phosphate.
The **debranching enzyme** (transferase + amylo-1,6-glucosidase) removes the branch point, and free glucose is released.
Glucose-1-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase).

**In the liver**: glucose-6-phosphatase → free glucose → into the blood. **In muscle** there is no glucose-6-phosphatase — glucose-6-phosphate enters glycolysis (muscle glycogen does not serve to maintain blood glucose).

blocks.text: Regulation of glycogen metabolism
Glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase are regulated in **opposite** directions — through **phosphorylation–dephosphorylation**:

items: **When phosphorylated**: phosphorylase is **active**, glycogen synthase is **inactive** → glycogen is broken down.
**When dephosphorylated**: phosphorylase is inactive, glycogen synthase is **active** → glycogen is synthesized.

head: Hormone
Tissue

Result
rows: Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase is phosphorylated; glycogen synthase is phosphorylated
β-receptors → cAMP (in the liver also α1 → IP~3~, Ca^2+^)
Activates phosphodiesterase and phosphoprotein phosphatase; induces glucokinase

blocks.text: **Allosteric regulation:** in muscle AMP and Ca^2+^ (during contraction) activate phosphorylase; in the liver glucose inhibits phosphorylase; glucose-6-phosphate activates glycogen synthase.

parts.text: **The two glycogen “stores” serve different purposes**: liver glycogen maintains the level of **blood glucose** (between meals, ≈ 12–24 hours); muscle glycogen is an energy source only for the muscle’s **own contraction**.

blocks.text: **Glycolysis** is the breakdown of glucose in the cytosol to **pyruvate** (10 reactions). Under aerobic conditions pyruvate is converted in the mitochondria into acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle to CO~2~ and H~2~O — **aerobic oxidation**. Under anaerobic conditions pyruvate is reduced to lactate (topic 7).

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Reactions of glycolysis; the key enzymes and the reactions in which ATP is formed (drawn after Sobirova R.A., 2006; Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: The two stages of glycolysis:

items: **The preparatory stage** (energy is consumed): glucose is phosphorylated at the expense of 2 ATP and split into two triose phosphates.

**The stage of oxidation and energy production**: glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is oxidized (NADH is formed) and 4 ATP are formed in two substrate-level phosphorylation reactions (phosphoglycerate kinase, pyruvate kinase). **The overall equation of glycolysis (aerobic):**

blocks.text: Glucose + 2NAD^+^ + 2ADP + 2Pi → 2 Pyruvate + 2NADH + 2H^+^ + 2ATP + 2H~2~O
**Key (irreversible) enzymes:** hexokinase (glucokinase), **phosphofructokinase-1** (the main one), pyruvate kinase.

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Regulation of phosphofructokinase-1
head: Activators
Inhibitors
rows: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (increases under the action of insulin; the strongest activator)
Citrate (enough products of the Krebs cycle)

blocks.text: **Pyruvate kinase** is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (a “feed-forward signal” from the preceding step) and inhibited by ATP and alanine; in the liver it is phosphorylated and inactivated under the action of glucagon.
Transfer of the hydrogen of cytosolic NADH into the mitochondria

Under aerobic conditions the NADH formed in glycolysis must be oxidized in the respiratory chain, but the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to NADH. The hydrogen passes through **shuttle mechanisms**:

items: **The malate-aspartate shuttle** (liver, kidney, heart): in the cytosol oxaloacetate is reduced to malate at the expense of NADH, malate enters the mitochondria, is oxidized back to oxaloacetate and NADH is formed in the matrix (≈ 2.5 ATP). Oxaloacetate returns in the form of aspartate.

**The glycerol phosphate shuttle** (skeletal muscle, brain): dihydroxyacetone phosphate is reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate at the expense of NADH; the FAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase of the mitochondrial membrane reoxidizes it and the electrons pass to CoQ (≈ 1.5 ATP).

blocks.text: **The Pasteur effect** is the fall in glucose consumption under aerobic conditions: when oxygen is present, more ATP and citrate are formed and they inhibit phosphofructokinase.
**Glycogenoses** are congenital deficiencies of the enzymes of glycogen breakdown; glycogen (sometimes of abnormal structure) accumulates in excess in the tissues.

head: Type

Main features
