Muscle pain and cramps on exercise, myoglobinuria; lactate does not rise

blocks.text: **Aglycogenosis** (glycogenosis 0) is a deficiency of liver **glycogen synthase**: almost no glycogen accumulates, there is severe hypoglycemia between meals (morning seizures), and hyperglycemia with a rise in lactate after a meal. Frequent feeding and starch at night are recommended.

parts.text: **In von Gierke disease** glucose-6-phosphate is not converted into glucose — the liver cannot release glucose into the blood by glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis. The accumulated glucose-6-phosphate goes into glycolysis and lactate and pyruvate increase (lactic acidosis); through the pentose phosphate pathway more purines are formed and uric acid rises (gout); the synthesis of fats from acetyl-CoA increases (hyperlipidemia, fatty degeneration of the liver). Treatment — frequent feeding, raw corn starch at night (it is broken down slowly).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: iodine reaction for starch and glycogen

items: Pour 1 ml of 1% starch and 1 ml of 1% glycogen solution into two test tubes.

Add 1 drop of Lugol’s solution to each; then heat and cool. **Result and analysis:** starch gives a blue color and glycogen a red-brown one (iodine enters the spiral of the polysaccharide and forms a complex; because the branches of glycogen are short, the color is different). On heating the spiral is destroyed and the color disappears; on cooling it returns.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: the Trommer reaction for reducing carbohydrates

items: Pour 1 ml each of 1% glucose, sucrose and lactose solutions into test tubes.
Add to each 1 ml of 10% NaOH and 3–5 drops of 1% CuSO~4~ (the blue Cu(OH)2 precipitate dissolves).

Heat the upper part to boiling. **Result and analysis:** with glucose and lactose a yellow (CuOH) and then a red-brick (Cu~2~O) precipitate forms — they are reducing sugars (they have a free hemiacetal hydroxyl). Sucrose gives no reaction (both hemiacetal hydroxyls are used in the glycosidic bond), but after hydrolysis with acid it gives a positive reaction.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: the Seliwanoff reaction for fructose

items: Add to a test tube 1 ml of 1% fructose solution and 1 ml of Seliwanoff reagent (a solution of resorcinol in concentrated HCl); heat to boiling.

Compare with glucose. **Result and analysis:** fructose (a ketose) quickly gives a red color — in acid it is converted into hydroxymethylfurfural, which forms a colored compound with resorcinol. With glucose (an aldose) the color develops very slowly and is weak. Sucrose is also positive (it contains fructose). This reaction is used to detect fructose in urine (fructosuria).

skills.title: Skill: calculating the ATP formed in the oxidation of glucose

items: Write down that glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Determine through which shuttle the cytosolic NADH passes (malate-aspartate — 2.5, glycerol phosphate — 1.5 ATP).
Add 2 NADH (5 ATP) for the conversion of 2 pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.
Add 20 ATP for the oxidation of 2 acetyl-CoA in the Krebs cycle.
Show that the total is 30–32 ATP; compare it with anaerobic conditions (2 ATP).

skills.title: Skill: identifying the type of glycogenosis

items: Determine which organ is affected: the liver (hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia) or the muscle (exercise intolerance, myoglobinuria).
Evaluate the degree of hypoglycemia and the rise in lactate, uric acid and lipids.
Analyze the result of the glucagon test: if glucose does not rise — glycogen is not being broken down.
Determine the deficient enzyme and the type of glycogenosis.
Explain the principle of the diet.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 1-year-old child has an enlarged abdomen (the liver extends 5 cm below the costal margin), a “doll’s face” and growth retardation. In the morning, fasting glucose is 1.8 mmol/l, and lactate, triglycerides and uric acid are increased. After glucagon was given, glucose did not rise and lactate rose further.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain all the biochemical changes.
cases.answer: Von Gierke disease (glycogenosis type I) — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Glycogen accumulates in the liver (hepatomegaly); because the last reaction of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is blocked, glucose is not released into the blood — severe fasting hypoglycemia; glucagon increases glycogenolysis, but glucose-6-phosphate goes into glycolysis and lactate rises. The excess of glucose-6-phosphate increases purine synthesis through the pentose phosphate pathway (uric acid ↑), and through glycolysis more acetyl-CoA and glycerol are formed and fat synthesis increases (hyperlipidemia). Low insulin and high glucagon also raise lipids.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 22-year-old man feels severe pain and cramps in his muscles during the first minutes of a gym session; after a rest he can continue exercising (the “second wind” phenomenon). After heavy exercise his urine was brown. In the ischemic exercise test blood lactate did not rise.
cases.ask: Which enzyme is deficient? Why does lactate not rise? Explain the “second wind” phenomenon.
cases.answer: McArdle disease (glycogenosis type V) — deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase. Muscle glycogen is not broken down, and at the start of exercise no glucose-6-phosphate is formed for glycolysis — an ATP deficit, muscle cramps, damage to muscle cells and release of myoglobin into the urine (brown urine). Because there is no glycolysis, lactate does not rise. The “second wind” — after a few minutes blood flow increases and more glucose and fatty acids reach the muscle from the blood, so the energy supply improves.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 25-year-old woman complains of bloating, rumbling and loose stools 1–2 hours after drinking milk. She tolerates kefir and cheese well. In the hydrogen breath test, hydrogen in the exhaled air rose sharply after a lactose load.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the mechanism of the signs and why she tolerates fermented milk products.
cases.answer: Lactase deficiency (in adults, primary: a genetically determined fall in lactase activity). Lactose is not broken down or absorbed in the small intestine; in the large intestine it is osmotically active and retains water (osmotic diarrhea), and bacteria ferment it to H~2~, CO~2~ and short-chain acids (flatulence, pain; a rise in H~2~ in the breath). In fermented milk products most of the lactose has been broken down by lactic acid bacteria, and cheese contains very little lactose.

topics.title: Gluconeogenesis. The pentose phosphate pathway. Fructose and galactose metabolism. Glucose homeostasis

goals.text: To teach the student anaerobic glycolysis and its significance, gluconeogenesis, the Cori and glucose-alanine cycles, the reciprocal regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate pathway of glucose oxidation, the metabolism of fructose and galactose and their hereditary disorders, and the regulation and age-related features of blood glucose homeostasis; to master the determination of blood glucose with a glucometer and by the enzymatic method.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the reactions of anaerobic glycolysis and alcoholic fermentation and their energy yield;
the substrates of gluconeogenesis, the “bypass” reactions and the energy cost;
the Cori and glucose-alanine cycles;
the reciprocal (opposite) regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis;
the stages and significance of the pentose phosphate pathway;
the metabolism of fructose and galactose, hereditary fructose intolerance and galactosemia;
the normal blood glucose level and its hormonal regulation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine blood glucose with a glucometer and by the glucose oxidase method;
evaluate a glucose tolerance test;
give a biochemical explanation of the causes of hyper- and hypoglycemia.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate** is the “key” to glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver: insulin increases its formation and thereby glycolysis, while glucagon (through cAMP) decreases it and increases gluconeogenesis.

blocks.text: When oxygen is lacking (intense muscle work, hypoxia) or in cells without mitochondria (**erythrocytes**), pyruvate is reduced to lactate by **lactate dehydrogenase**:
Pyruvate + NADH + H^+^ → Lactate + NAD^+^
This reaction regenerates NAD^+^ for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and allows glycolysis to continue without oxygen.
**The overall equation of anaerobic glycolysis:** Glucose + 2ADP + 2Pi → 2 Lactate + 2ATP + 2H~2~O

The energy yield is **2 ATP** (≈ 15 times less than in aerobic oxidation), but it is fast and needs no oxygen. Anaerobic glycolysis is characteristic mainly of erythrocytes, the retina and lens of the eye, the renal medulla, white muscle fibers and tumor cells.

**Alcoholic fermentation** (in yeast): pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO~2~ (pyruvate decarboxylase, TDP) → ethanol (alcohol dehydrogenase, NADH). Fermentation is used in baking bread and in making wine and beer.

parts.text: **Lactic acidosis** — blood lactate > 5 mmol/l and pH < 7.35 (normal lactate 0.5–2.2 mmol/l). Causes: tissue hypoxia (shock, heart failure, sepsis, severe anemia — type A), liver failure (lactate is not used in gluconeogenesis), metformin, thiamine deficiency, mitochondrial diseases (type B). Tumor cells break glucose down to lactate even in the presence of oxygen
— the **Warburg effect**; this underlies the detection of tumors in PET scanning (^18^F-fluorodeoxyglucose).

blocks.text: **Gluconeogenesis** is the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate substances. It takes place mainly in the **liver** (≈ 90%) and in the **renal cortex** (up to ≈ 40% in prolonged starvation). Its significance: maintaining blood glucose during starvation, when the glycogen store is exhausted (after 12–24 hours) — the brain (≈ 120 g per day), the erythrocytes and the renal medulla need glucose.

**Its substrates:** lactate (working muscle, erythrocytes), **glucogenic amino acids** (alanine, glutamine and others — from the breakdown of muscle proteins), **glycerol** (from lipolysis in adipose tissue), propionate (from odd-chain fatty acids). **Fatty acids and acetyl-CoA do not give glucose** (the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible).
Gluconeogenesis uses the reversible reactions of glycolysis, but the three irreversible reactions of glycolysis are bypassed by **four special “bypass” reactions**:

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Gluconeogenesis: substrates and the reactions that bypass the irreversible steps of glycolysis (drawn after Severin E.S.)

head: Glycolytic enzyme

rows: 1) Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO~2~ + ATP → oxaloacetate (biotin)
2) Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK): oxaloacetate + GTP → phosphoenolpyruvate + CO~2~
Cytosol (and mitochondria); induced by cortisol and glucagon
Cytosol; inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
Endoplasmic reticulum; only in the liver and kidney

blocks.text: Oxaloacetate does not cross the mitochondrial membrane — it leaves for the cytosol in the form of malate (or aspartate).
**Energy cost:** the synthesis of 1 glucose from 2 pyruvate consumes **6 high-energy bonds** (4 ATP + 2 GTP) and 2 NADH.
Regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are regulated **reciprocally**: when one is activated the other is inhibited (otherwise a “futile cycle” would waste ATP).

Glycolysis

↓ fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls; pyruvate kinase is phosphorylated and inactive
↑ induction of PEPCK, glucose-6-phosphatase and aminotransferases; breakdown of proteins (substrate)

parts.text: **Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate** is the “key” to glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver: insulin increases its formation and thereby glycolysis, while glucagon (through cAMP) decreases it and increases gluconeogenesis.

blocks.text: The Cori cycle and the glucose-alanine cycle

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: The Cori cycle and the glucose-alanine cycle (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **The Cori cycle** — lactate formed in working muscle and erythrocytes reaches the liver through the blood, is converted into glucose and returns to the muscle. The muscle’s “oxygen debt” is repaid at the expense of the liver’s energy.

**The glucose-alanine cycle** — in muscle, pyruvate takes the amino group from amino acids and is converted into alanine; in the liver alanine is converted back into pyruvate (gluconeogenesis), while the ammonia goes into urea synthesis. This cycle carries nitrogen from the muscle in a harmless form.

blocks.text: **The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)** is an alternative route of glucose-6-phosphate oxidation; it takes place in the cytosol. It does not form ATP; its main products are **NADPH** and **ribose-5-phosphate**.

blocks.label: Figure 7.3
blocks.caption: The oxidative and non-oxidative stages of the pentose phosphate pathway (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **The oxidative stage** (irreversible): glucose-6-phosphate → 6-phosphogluconolactone → 6-phosphogluconate → ribulose-5-phosphate + CO~2~. **2 NADPH** are formed in the two dehydrogenase reactions. The key enzyme is **glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)**; it is activated by NADP^+^ and inhibited by NADPH; insulin induces it.

**The non-oxidative stage** (reversible): with the participation of **transketolase** (coenzyme — TDP, B~1~) and **transaldolase**, pentoses are converted into fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (returning to glycolysis) or, conversely, ribose-5-phosphate is formed from glycolytic intermediates. **The significance of NADPH:** synthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol and steroid hormones (the liver, adipose tissue, mammary gland and adrenal cortex are the organs with the most active PPP); keeping glutathione in the reduced state (protection of erythrocytes from oxidative stress); microsomal oxidation (cytochrome P450); NADPH oxidase in phagocytes (the bactericidal “respiratory burst”).

parts.text: **Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency** is the most common enzymopathy (X-linked; frequent in areas where malaria is widespread). Little NADPH is formed in the erythrocytes and glutathione is not reduced; when oxidizing drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurans), infections or **fava beans** are involved, hemoglobin is oxidized and precipitates (Heinz bodies), and an **acute hemolytic crisis** develops.

blocks.text: **Fructose** (in fruit, honey and sucrose) is metabolized mainly in the liver:
Fructose → (**fructokinase**, ATP) → fructose-1-phosphate → (**aldolase B**) → dihydroxyacetone phosphate + glyceraldehyde → glycolysis or gluconeogenesis

Fructose “bypasses” phosphofructokinase-1, so it is broken down rapidly in the liver and its excess is directed to fatty acid synthesis (high fructose intake is a risk factor for fatty degeneration of the liver and hyperlipidemia).
**Galactose** (part of lactose):

Galactose → (**galactokinase**) → galactose-1-phosphate → (+ UDP-glucose, **galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, GALT**) → UDP-galactose + glucose-1-phosphate; UDP-galactose → (**epimerase**) → UDP-glucose

Vomiting after fructose (juice, fruit, sucrose), severe hypoglycemia, liver and kidney damage; fructose-1-phosphate accumulates and P~i~ and ATP fall

Mainly cataract (galactose → galactitol accumulates in the lens)

parts.text: **Galactosemia** is part of the newborn screening program. As soon as the diagnosis is made, the child is switched to **lactose-free and galactose-free** feeding (soy formulas) — this prevents fatal complications. The cause of the cataract: galactose is reduced by aldose reductase to **galactitol**, which does not leave the lens and, by its osmotic effect, draws in water and damages the fibers.

blocks.text: The blood glucose level is strictly regulated, because the brain and erythrocytes obtain their energy mainly from glucose.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Normal blood glucose values (adults, fasting)
head: Material
Normal value

blocks.text: **Sources of blood glucose:** dietary carbohydrates (absorption — 2–3 hours), liver glycogenolysis (between meals, ≈ 12–24 hours), gluconeogenesis (in prolonged starvation). **Its consumption:** oxidation in the tissues, synthesis of glycogen and fats; above 10 mmol/l glucose passes into the urine (the **renal threshold** is 8.9–10 mmol/l).

Glycogenolysis in the liver and muscle; reduces insulin secretion
Induction of gluconeogenesis enzymes; breakdown of proteins in muscle; reduced uptake of glucose in the periphery
Counter-insular action, absorption in the intestine (T~3~, T~4~)

blocks.text: **Age-related features:** in the first days of life newborns have physiological hypoglycemia (small glycogen store, immature gluconeogenic enzymes); the risk is higher in preterm infants and in infants of mothers with diabetes. In old age glucose tolerance decreases.

**Glycoproteins and proteoglycans** are complex proteins that contain carbohydrate: glycoproteins (immunoglobulins, hormones, membrane proteins) have short branched oligosaccharides; proteoglycans have many long glycosaminoglycan chains (connective tissue — topic 22). Their carbohydrate part is formed from glucose through UDP-sugar nucleotides.
Experiment 1: determination of blood glucose by the glucose oxidase method

**Principle of the method:** glucose oxidase oxidizes glucose to gluconolactone and H~2~O~2~; peroxidase, at the expense of H~2~O~2~, oxidizes a chromogen (4-aminoantipyrine + phenol) and forms a pink compound (the Trinder reaction). The intensity of the color is proportional to the glucose concentration.

items: Pour 2 ml of working reagent (glucose oxidase, peroxidase, chromogen) into each of three test tubes.
Add 20 µl of serum (plasma) to tube 1, 20 µl of standard glucose solution (5.55 mmol/l) to tube 2 and 20 µl of water to tube 3 (control).
Mix and keep at 37 °C for 15 minutes.
Measure the optical density against the control at 500–510 nm on a photometer (or a biochemical analyzer). **Calculation:** C (mmol/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × 5.55

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** in venous plasma the fasting norm is 3.9–6.1 mmol/l; 6.1–6.9 — impaired fasting glycemia; ≥ 7.0 (on two occasions) — diabetes mellitus; < 3.3 — hypoglycemia.
Experiment 2: determination of glucose in capillary blood with a glucometer

items: Wash and dry the hand, wipe the pad of the finger with alcohol and wait until the alcohol evaporates.
Insert the test strip into the glucometer (check that the code matches).
Puncture the side of the finger with a lancet and wipe away the first drop.
Touch the second drop to the application area of the test strip.

After 5–10 s read and record the result. **Analysis:** the glucose oxidase (or glucose dehydrogenase) immobilized on the test strip oxidizes glucose; the electrons pass to the electrode and an electric current is generated (an electrochemical biosensor). The glucometer is intended for self-monitoring; the diagnosis is made in the laboratory in venous plasma. Causes of error: alcohol left on the finger, the first drop, squeezing out the blood (tissue fluid), an expired test strip, a sharp change in hematocrit.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: evaluating a glucose tolerance test (from a case)

The subject gives blood on an empty stomach (after 8–14 hours of fasting), then within 5 minutes drinks **75 g of glucose** dissolved in 250–300 ml of water (in children 1.75 g/kg, up to 75 g); blood is taken again after 2 hours.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Two days after taking a sulfonamide drug, a 30-year-old man developed weakness, jaundice and dark urine. Blood hemoglobin is 85 g/l, indirect bilirubin is increased, and Heinz bodies were found in the erythrocytes. He has had the same condition before after eating a bean dish.
cases.ask: Which enzyme deficiency is suspected? Explain the mechanism of the hemolysis.
cases.answer: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. In erythrocytes NADPH is formed only in the pentose phosphate pathway; through glutathione reductase it keeps glutathione in the reduced state. An oxidizing drug (sulfonamide) or the substances of beans generate H~2~O~2~ and free radicals; because glutathione is not regenerated, hemoglobin and membrane proteins are oxidized, hemoglobin precipitates and forms Heinz bodies, and the erythrocytes are destroyed — acute hemolytic anemia, a rise in indirect bilirubin (jaundice) and hemoglobinuria.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: When a 6-month-old child was started on fruit juice and sweetened porridge as complementary food, pallor, sweating, vomiting, seizures and liver enlargement were observed after meals. While breastfed, the child had no complaints.
cases.ask: Which disease is suspected? Explain the mechanism of the hypoglycemia.
cases.answer: Hereditary fructose intolerance — aldolase B deficiency. Fructose (juice, sucrose) is converted in the liver by fructokinase into fructose-1-phosphate, but it is not broken down and accumulates. Phosphate and ATP are consumed in this process (hypophosphatemia, ATP deficit — liver damage). Fructose-1-phosphate inhibits glycogen phosphorylase and aldolase — glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis stop and severe hypoglycemia develops. Breast milk contains no fructose. Treatment — complete exclusion of fructose, sucrose and sorbitol from the diet.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old man drank a lot of alcohol for 2 days without eating. He was brought in unconscious: blood glucose 2.1 mmol/l, lactate increased.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of alcoholic hypoglycemia.
cases.answer: In starvation the liver glycogen is exhausted within 24 hours and blood glucose is maintained by gluconeogenesis. In the liver ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase and generates a lot of NADH; the NADH/NAD^+^ ratio rises sharply. As a result pyruvate is reduced to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate — the main substrates for gluconeogenesis (pyruvate, oxaloacetate) are lacking and gluconeogenesis stops. Hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis develop. Help: intravenous glucose (thiamine first).

topics.title: Structure, functions, digestion and transport of lipids

goals.text: To teach the student the classification, structure and significance of the lipids of food and of the human body, the digestion and absorption of fats (including the features of the child’s body), the significance of bile acids, the resynthesis of fats in the intestinal wall, the formation and transport of chylomicrons and blood lipoproteins, the significance of lipoprotein lipase, and the disorders of fat digestion.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of lipids and the structure of their main representatives;
the functions of lipids in the body;
the essential fatty acids;
the stages and enzymes of fat digestion and the role of bile acids;
the absorption of the products of fat digestion and their resynthesis in the intestinal wall;
the types, composition and functions of lipoproteins;
the significance of lipoprotein lipase;
the causes of steatorrhea.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: demonstrate the emulsifying action of bile acids;
determine lipase activity;
evaluate the indices of the blood lipid profile.

blocks.text: **Lipids** are a group of substances insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (ether, chloroform, benzene) that contain fatty acids or their derivatives.

blocks.title: Table 8.1. Classification of lipids
head: Group
Representatives
Structure
rows: Palmitic (C16:0), stearic (C18:0), oleic (C18:1), linoleic (C18:2, ω-6), α-linolenic (C18:3, ω-3), arachidonic (C20:4, ω-6)
Long-chain carboxylic acids; saturated and unsaturated
Glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + a nitrogenous base or inositol
Sphingosine + fatty acid (ceramide) + phosphocholine or carbohydrates
Cholesterol, bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D

blocks.text: Functions in the body:

items: **energy** — the oxidation of 1 g of fat gives 9 kcal; TAG is the main energy store (10–15 kg in adipose tissue — enough for 40 days of starvation);
**structural** — phospholipids, glycolipids and cholesterol form the basis of membranes;
**regulatory** — steroid hormones, eicosanoids, second messengers (DAG, IP~3~);
**protective and heat-insulating** — the subcutaneous fat layer, the fat around internal organs;
a source of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and necessary for their absorption;

**bile acids** — digestion and absorption of fats; **surfactant** (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) — keeps the alveoli from collapsing. **Essential fatty acids** are linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3): humans have no enzymes that introduce a double bond further than carbon 9 from the carboxyl group. Sources: vegetable oils (sunflower, corn, linseed), fish oil (eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids — ω-3). Their deficiency causes dermatitis, growth retardation and impaired wound healing.

blocks.text: The daily fat requirement of adults is 80–100 g; ≈ 90% of it is TAG.

**In the oral cavity and the stomach** fats are hardly digested in adults: gastric lipase has low activity (its pH optimum is 4–5, while gastric juice is strongly acidic) and the fat is not emulsified. **In newborns**, however, the lingual and gastric lipases play an important role: the gastric medium is less acidic, the fat of milk is already emulsified, and breast milk also contains its own lipase.
**In the small intestine** the main digestion of fats takes place:

items: **Emulsification** — the breaking up of large fat droplets into small ones; this is helped by the salts of **bile acids** (surface-active substances), peristalsis and the CO~2~ bubbles formed by bicarbonate. Emulsification increases many times over the surface on which lipase acts.
**Hydrolysis** — by the enzymes of the pancreas: – **pancreatic lipase** (its activating protein is **colipase**) cleaves the ester bonds of TAG at

blocks.text: positions 1 and 3: TAG → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 fatty acids; – **phospholipase A~2~** (activated by trypsin) removes the fatty acid at position 2 from a
phospholipid → lysophospholipid; – **cholesterol esterase** breaks down cholesterol esters into cholesterol and a fatty acid.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Digestion and absorption of fats and their resynthesis in the intestinal wall (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: Bile acids

**Bile acids** are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol (the key enzyme is 7α-hydroxylase). The **primary** bile acids are cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid; they are **conjugated** with glycine or taurine (glycocholic and taurocholic acids) and enter the intestine with the bile as sodium and potassium salts. In the intestine, under the action of bacteria, the **secondary** bile acids — deoxycholic and lithocholic acid — are formed.

The functions of bile acids: they emulsify fats; activate lipase; form **mixed micelles** with the products of digestion and provide for their absorption; are necessary for the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; keep cholesterol dissolved in the bile.

**The enterohepatic circulation:** ≈ 95% of the bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, return to the liver through the portal vein and are secreted into the bile again (6–10 times a day). Only ≈ 0.5 g/day is lost in the feces — this is the main route by which cholesterol is removed from the body.

sections.title: 3. Absorption of the products of digestion and their resynthesis

blocks.text: Monoacylglycerols, long-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and lysophospholipids form **mixed micelles** with bile acids and are delivered to the surface of the enterocytes; the lipid components cross the membrane by diffusion (and through special carriers), while the bile acids remain in the intestinal lumen. **Short- and medium-chain** fatty acids (C4–C12) are absorbed without micelles and pass directly into the blood of the portal vein (they are abundant in milk fat; in malabsorption, food with medium-chain TAG is prescribed).
**Resynthesis in the enterocytes** (in the endoplasmic reticulum):

items: the fatty acids are activated: fatty acid + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA (acyl-CoA synthetase);
**the monoacylglycerol pathway**: 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG;

phospholipids are formed from lysophospholipids, and cholesterol esters from cholesterol (the ACAT enzyme). **The significance of resynthesis:** dietary fats are converted into fats characteristic of the human body (the fatty acid composition changes); the products of digestion are “carried away” from the intestinal cell, which allows absorption to continue; the TAG becomes part of the transport form — the chylomicrons.

blocks.text: The resynthesized lipids are assembled together with the protein **apo B-48** into **chylomicrons**, which leave by exocytosis into the **lymph** (the intestinal lymph capillaries — the “lacteals”) and enter the blood through the thoracic duct (this is why the serum is cloudy after a fatty meal — **alimentary lipemia**).

parts.text: **Steatorrhea** is an increase of fat in the feces (> 7 g per day). Causes: **lack of bile** (obstructive jaundice, obstruction of the bile ducts, liver diseases) — emulsification and micelle formation are impaired; **lipase deficiency** (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, a pancreatic tumor); **impaired absorption** (celiac disease, Crohn disease, resection of the ileum). The feces are shiny, sticky, large in amount and have a sharp odor. Consequences: deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (night blindness, osteomalacia, bleeding), a shortage of essential fatty acids, weight loss.

blocks.text: Lipids are insoluble in water, so they are transported in the blood in **lipoproteins** — lipid-protein complexes. The core of a lipoprotein particle contains hydrophobic lipids (TAG, cholesterol esters), and its surface amphiphilic substances — phospholipids, free cholesterol and **apoproteins**.

**Functions of the apoproteins:** forming the structure of the particle (apo B-48, B-100), activating enzymes (apo C-II — lipoprotein lipase, apo A-I — LCAT), binding to receptors (apo B-100 and apo E — LDL receptors).

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Metabolism of lipoproteins: the exogenous and endogenous pathways and reverse cholesterol transport (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: Lipoprotein lipase

**Lipoprotein lipase (LPL)** is an enzyme located on the surface of the capillary endothelium (bound to heparan sulfate); it hydrolyzes the TAG of chylomicrons and VLDL. The fatty acids formed enter the tissues: in **muscle** they are oxidized (energy), in **adipose tissue** they are converted back into TAG and stored. LPL is activated by **apo C-II**; its synthesis in adipose tissue is increased by **insulin** (after a meal fat goes into store), and in muscle by starvation and physical activity. Heparin releases LPL from the endothelium into the blood (the **“clearing factor”** — lipemic serum becomes clear).

The **remnant chylomicrons**, emptied of TAG, are taken up by the liver (through apo E); VLDL are converted into IDL and LDL. LDL enter the tissues by endocytosis through **LDL receptors** (topic 10).

parts.text: **Congenital deficiency of LPL or apo C-II** (type I hyperlipoproteinemia) — chylomicrons rise sharply in the blood: the serum is “milky”, triglycerides > 10–20 mmol/l, with attacks of acute pancreatitis, xanthomas on the skin and enlargement of the liver and spleen. Treatment — a diet with sharply restricted fat (medium-chain TAG are allowed, because they do not form chylomicrons).

Experiment 1: the emulsifying action of bile acids

items: Pour 2 ml of water into each of three test tubes.
Add 2 drops of vegetable oil to tube 1, 2 drops of oil + 5 drops of bile (or 1% sodium cholate) to tube 2, and 2 drops of oil + 5 drops of 1% sodium carbonate to tube 3.

Shake all of them vigorously and leave for 5–10 minutes. **Result and analysis:** in tube 1 the oil quickly rises to the top (the emulsion is unstable). In the tube with bile a stable, milky emulsion forms — bile acids lower the surface tension of the droplets. In the tube with sodium carbonate the emulsion is also more stable — soap is formed with the free fatty acids of the oil.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of pancreatic lipase activity and the effect of bile

items: Pour 10 ml of milk (or a fat emulsion) and 2 drops of phenolphthalein into each of two flasks; neutralize with 0.1 N NaOH to a pale pink color.
Add 1 ml of pancreatin solution to flask 1 and 1 ml of pancreatin + 1 ml of bile to flask 2; keep at 37 °C.

Every 10 minutes take 1 ml from the flasks and titrate with 0.05 N NaOH to a pink color (for 30–40 minutes). **Result and analysis:** with time the amount of NaOH used for titration increases — lipase breaks down TAG and forms fatty acids. In the flask with bile this happens faster: the bile acids emulsify the fat, increase the surface on which lipase acts and activate the lipase.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: assessing the lipemia of serum and interpreting the results of the lipid profile (from a case)

items: Compare serum taken on an empty stomach and 3–4 hours after a fatty meal (demonstration or figure).
Leave the lipemic serum in the refrigerator (+4 °C) overnight: if a “cream” layer forms on top — chylomicrons; if the serum itself remains cloudy — there is a lot of VLDL.
Compare the lipid profile results given by the teacher with the normal values and calculate the atherogenic index.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the cause of steatorrhea

items: Confirm the increase of fat in the feces (coprogram: neutral fat or fatty acids).
If there is a lot of neutral fat (TAG) — lipase deficiency (pancreatitis): fecal elastase-1 is reduced.
If there are many fatty acids and soaps — lack of bile or impaired absorption.
If there is jaundice, acholic feces and raised conjugated bilirubin in the blood — obstruction of the bile ducts.
Check for signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and recommend a diet.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating the lipid profile

items: Compare the values of total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL and HDL cholesterol with the normal values.
Calculate the atherogenic index.
Determine which lipoproteins are increased (CM, VLDL or LDL).
Suggest the cause: diet, obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hereditary factors.
Assess the risk of atherosclerosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 50-year-old patient has yellow skin and sclerae, itching, colorless (acholic), shiny and bulky stools and dark urine. Ultrasound revealed a stone in the common bile duct. The clotting time is prolonged.
cases.ask: Why has the fat in the feces increased? Explain the clotting disorder.
cases.answer: Because the stone has blocked the bile duct, bile acids do not reach the intestine: fats are not emulsified, the surface on which lipase acts is small, and mixed micelles are not formed — the products of digestion are not absorbed and leave with the feces (steatorrhea). There are no bilirubin derivatives (stercobilin) in the feces — they are acholic. Fat-soluble vitamins are also not absorbed; because of vitamin K deficiency the γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X in the liver is impaired — the clotting time is prolonged. Vitamin K is given parenterally.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-year-old child has recurrent attacks of severe abdominal pain (acute pancreatitis), yellow nodules on the skin and buttocks (eruptive xanthomas) and enlargement of the liver and spleen. The fasting serum is milky and, after being left in the refrigerator, formed a creamy layer on top; triglycerides are 25 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its biochemical mechanism and the principle of treatment.
cases.answer: Type I hyperlipoproteinemia — deficiency of lipoprotein lipase (or of its activator apo C-II). The TAG of the chylomicrons is not hydrolyzed and the chylomicrons stay in the blood for a long time (even in the fasting state) — the serum is milky and in the refrigerator a “cream” layer floats to the top. Excess triglycerides are broken down by pancreatic lipase in the capillaries of the pancreas and form toxic fatty acids — pancreatitis. Treatment: sharp restriction of long-chain fats in the diet; medium-chain TAG are allowed, because they are absorbed into the portal vein without chylomicrons.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 5-year-old child with cystic fibrosis is underweight and thin even though the appetite is good. The stools are bulky, fatty and strong-smelling; there is a lot of neutral fat in the feces and elastase-1 is sharply reduced. He sees poorly in the evening.
cases.ask: What is the cause of the steatorrhea? Explain the “night blindness.” What treatment is needed?
cases.answer: In cystic fibrosis a defect of the CFTR Cl- channel makes the pancreatic secretion thick and it blocks the ducts; the gland tissue undergoes fibrosis — lipase and the other enzymes do not reach the intestine (exocrine insufficiency). TAG is not broken down — there is a lot of neutral fat in the feces. Fat-soluble vitamins are not absorbed: vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin synthesis and vision in the dark deteriorates. Treatment: pancreatic enzyme preparations (pancreatin) with meals, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), a high-calorie diet.

topics.title: Intermediary metabolism of fats

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the storage and mobilization of fats in adipose tissue (lipolysis and lipogenesis) and their regulation, the formation of fats from carbohydrates, the transport and β-oxidation of fatty acids, the oxidation of glycerol, the biosynthesis of fatty acids and its regulation, the synthesis and breakdown of ketone bodies, and the metabolism of the main phospho- and glycolipids.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the synthesis of TAG and lipolysis in adipose tissue and their hormonal regulation;
the transport of fatty acids in the blood and their entry into the cell;
the carnitine shuttle system and the four reactions of β-oxidation;
the energy yield of the oxidation of palmitic acid;
the oxidation pathway of glycerol;
the stages, enzymes and regulation of fatty acid synthesis;
the synthesis and use of ketone bodies and the causes of ketosis;
the main pathways of synthesis and breakdown of phospholipids and glycolipids.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine ketone bodies in urine and evaluate the result;
calculate the ATP formed in the oxidation of a fatty acid;
explain the changes in fat metabolism in starvation and diabetes mellitus.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The brain and erythrocytes do not use fatty acids as an energy source**: fatty acids bound to albumin hardly cross the blood-brain barrier, and erythrocytes have no mitochondria. In prolonged starvation the brain obtains 2/3 of its energy from **ketone bodies**.

blocks.text: **Adipose tissue** is the body’s main energy store (15–25% of body weight in healthy adults). In adipocytes TAG is formed from two sources: from the fatty acids released from chylomicrons and VLDL by lipoprotein lipase, and from glucose (glucose → glycerol-3-phosphate, excess glucose → acetyl-CoA → fatty acids).
**TAG synthesis (lipogenesis)** — in the liver and adipose tissue:
glycerol-3-phosphate + 2 acyl-CoA → phosphatidic acid → (phosphatase) → diacylglycerol + acyl-CoA → **TAG**

In adipose tissue glycerol-3-phosphate is formed only from **glucose** (reduction of dihydroxyacetone phosphate), because adipocytes have almost no glycerol kinase. For this reason the accumulation of TAG in adipose tissue depends on the availability of glucose and insulin. The liver does have glycerol kinase.
**Lipolysis (mobilization of fats)** — the hydrolysis of TAG to glycerol and fatty acids in starvation, physical work and stress:

items: **Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL)**: TAG → diacylglycerol + FA;
**Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)**: DAG → monoacylglycerol + FA (the key, regulated enzyme);
**Monoacylglycerol lipase**: MAG → glycerol + FA.

Effect

Phosphodiesterase is activated (cAMP ↓), HSL is dephosphorylated; LPL, glucose entry and lipogenic enzymes ↑

blocks.text: The **fatty acids** released by lipolysis are bound in the blood to **albumin** (free, “non-esterified” fatty acids) and transported to muscle, heart, liver and kidney. **Glycerol** goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase converts it into glycerol-3-phosphate and then into dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which enters glycolysis (energy) or gluconeogenesis (glucose).

parts.text: **The brain and erythrocytes do not use fatty acids as an energy source**: fatty acids bound to albumin hardly cross the blood-brain barrier, and erythrocytes have no mitochondria. In prolonged starvation the brain obtains 2/3 of its energy from **ketone bodies**.

blocks.text: **β-oxidation** is the oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondrial matrix with the successive removal of two-carbon fragments (acetyl-CoA) (F. Knoop, 1904). It takes place mainly in the heart, skeletal muscle, liver and kidney.
**1. Activation of the fatty acid** (in the cytosol, on the outer mitochondrial membrane):
Fatty acid + CoA-SH + ATP → Acyl-CoA + AMP + PP~i~ (acyl-CoA synthetase; 2 high-energy bonds are used)
**2. Transport of the acyl residue into the mitochondria — the carnitine shuttle system.** The inner membrane is impermeable to acyl-CoA:

items: **carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I)** (outer membrane) transfers the acyl group to carnitine → acylcarnitine; this is the **key (regulated) step of β-oxidation**;
**carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase** carries the acylcarnitine into the matrix;

**CPT-II** in the matrix transfers the acyl group back to CoA. CPT-I is inhibited by **malonyl-CoA**, the first product of fatty acid synthesis — so synthesis and breakdown do not occur at the same time.

blocks.text: **3. The β-oxidation cycle** — four reactions:

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Activation of fatty acids, the carnitine shuttle system and the reactions of β-oxidation (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **Dehydrogenation** — acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD): acyl-CoA → trans-Δ2-enoyl-CoA + **FADH~2~**;
**Hydration** — enoyl-CoA hydratase: → L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA;
**Dehydrogenation** — 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD^+^): → 3-ketoacyl-CoA + **NADH**;

**Thiolytic cleavage** — thiolase (+ CoA-SH): → **acetyl-CoA** + an acyl-CoA shortened by two carbons. The shortened acyl-CoA starts the cycle again. For a Cn fatty acid with an even number of carbons there are (n/2 − 1) cycles and n/2 acetyl-CoA are formed.

blocks.text: The high energy value of fats is due to the fact that fatty acids are more reduced than carbohydrates.

The oxidation of **unsaturated fatty acids** needs additional enzymes (isomerase, reductase); each double bond means one FADH~2~ less. From **odd-chain fatty acids** propionyl-CoA is formed at the end → methylmalonyl-CoA → (B~12~) succinyl-CoA → it can enter gluconeogenesis. **Very long chain** fatty acids (C22 and longer) are first shortened in the **peroxisomes** (here H~2~O~2~ is formed instead of FADH~2~).

parts.text: **Carnitine or CPT deficiency** and **medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency**: during starvation or illness fatty acids are not oxidized — **hypoketotic hypoglycemia** (ketone bodies are not formed and there is not enough ATP for gluconeogenesis), muscle weakness, cardiomyopathy and liver damage; one of the causes of sudden infant death syndrome. Treatment: avoiding long fasts, frequent carbohydrate feeding, carnitine preparations.

blocks.text: Fatty acids are synthesized in the **cytosol**, mainly in the **liver**, **adipose tissue** and the **lactating mammary gland**; the source is **acetyl-CoA** formed from excess carbohydrates. Synthesis increases under the action of **insulin**, after a carbohydrate-rich meal.

**1. Export of acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytosol (the citrate shuttle).** Acetyl-CoA does not cross the mitochondrial membrane: it forms citrate with oxaloacetate, citrate leaves for the cytosol and is split again into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate by **citrate lyase** (ATP). Oxaloacetate is converted into malate and then, by **malic enzyme**, into pyruvate, and **NADPH** is formed.
**2. Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA** (the key reaction):
Acetyl-CoA + CO~2~ + ATP → **Malonyl-CoA** + ADP + P~i~ — **acetyl-CoA carboxylase** (coenzyme — **biotin**)

**3. Fatty acid synthase** — a multienzyme complex (a dimer with 7 active sites in each subunit and an acyl-carrier part — the **pantetheine group** (B~5~)). In each cycle 2 carbons are added from malonyl-CoA (CO~2~ is released); **2 NADPH** are used for the reduction. In 7 cycles **palmitic acid** (C16:0) is formed.
The overall equation of palmitate synthesis:
8 Acetyl-CoA + 7 ATP + 14 NADPH + 14 H^+^ → Palmitate + 8 CoA-SH + 7 ADP + 7 P~i~ + 14 NADP^+^ + 6 H~2~O
**Sources of NADPH:** the pentose phosphate pathway (the main one) and malic enzyme.

**Elongation and desaturation:** palmitate is elongated in the endoplasmic reticulum to stearate and longer; desaturases introduce a double bond at position Δ9 (stearate → oleate). Linoleic and linolenic acids are not synthesized.

Inhibited by
rows: Glucagon, adrenaline (cAMP → phosphorylation); AMP kinase (low energy)

blocks.text: **Ketone bodies** are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. They are synthesized from acetyl-CoA only in the **liver mitochondria** (ketogenesis), are carried by the blood to other tissues and are oxidized there as an energy source.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: Synthesis of ketone bodies in the liver and their use in peripheral tissues (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Synthesis:** 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase) → **HMG-CoA** (HMG-CoA synthase — the key enzyme) → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA (HMG-CoA lyase). Acetoacetate is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate at the expense of NADH or spontaneously decarboxylated to acetone.

**Use:** the heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and, in prolonged starvation, the **brain**. β-Hydroxybutyrate is oxidized to acetoacetate; acetoacetate is converted by **succinyl-CoA-acetoacetate-CoA transferase** into acetoacetyl-CoA and then into 2 acetyl-CoA. **The liver has no such transferase** — it does not use ketone bodies, it only “exports” them.

**Ketogenesis increases** when a lot of acetyl-CoA is formed and oxaloacetate is lacking: starvation, a carbohydrate-free (ketogenic) diet, prolonged physical work, **diabetes mellitus** (insulin deficiency — lipolysis and β-oxidation increase sharply and oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis).

Normally blood ketone bodies are 0.1–0.5 mmol/l and they are not detected in urine by routine methods. **Ketonemia** and **ketonuria** are seen in starvation and diabetes; because ketone bodies are strong acids, when a lot of them accumulate **ketoacidosis** develops (the pH falls); acetone leaves with the breath and gives a “rotten apple” odor from the mouth.

parts.text: **Diabetic ketoacidosis** is a life-threatening complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus: hyperglycemia (> 13–15 mmol/l), ketone bodies > 3 mmol/l, pH < 7.3, reduced bicarbonate; Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, coma. Treatment — insulin (it stops lipolysis and ketogenesis), fluids and potassium.

blocks.text: **Synthesis of glycerophospholipids** (in the endoplasmic reticulum) — on the basis of phosphatidic acid or diacylglycerol:

items: **phosphatidylcholine** and **phosphatidylethanolamine** — through the CDP-choline (CDP-ethanolamine) pathway; phosphatidylcholine is also formed from phosphatidylethanolamine by three methylations at the expense of S-adenosylmethionine;
**phosphatidylinositol** — CDP-diacylglycerol + inositol;

**lipotropic factors** (choline, methionine, vitamin B~12~, folate, serine) are needed for the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine and for the export of TAG from the liver in VLDL; when they are lacking, **fatty degeneration of the liver** develops. **Sphingolipids** are synthesized on the basis of **sphingosine**, formed from serine and palmitoyl-CoA: sphingosine + fatty acid → ceramide; ceramide + phosphocholine → **sphingomyelin**; ceramide + carbohydrates → **cerebrosides, gangliosides**.

blocks.text: **Breakdown:** phospholipids by phospholipases (A~1~, A~2~, C, D); sphingolipids are broken down in the lysosomes by specific hydrolases. Congenital deficiencies of these enzymes are the **sphingolipidoses** (lysosomal storage diseases, topic 10).
Experiment 1: determination of ketone bodies in urine (Legal test)

items: Pour into a test tube 1 ml of urine, 0.5 ml of 10% NaOH and 0.5 ml of freshly prepared 10% sodium nitroprusside solution.
Observe the red color that appears.

Add 1 ml of concentrated acetic acid. **Result and analysis:** if acetone and acetoacetate are present, a red color forms in the alkaline medium; when acetic acid is added it turns **cherry-red (violet)** — a positive result. Creatinine also gives a red color in alkali, but after acetic acid it turns yellow (which excludes a false positive). β-Hydroxybutyrate is not detected by this test.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of acetoacetate in urine (Gerhardt test)

items: Pour 2 ml of urine into a test tube and add 10% iron (III) chloride solution dropwise (the phosphates precipitate; filter off the precipitate).

Add a few more drops of FeCl~3~ to the filtrate. **Result and analysis:** if acetoacetate is present, a **red-brown (wine) color** appears. On heating, acetoacetate is converted into acetone and the color disappears (whereas the color given by salicylates persists on heating).

blocks.text: Experiment 3: detection of ketonuria with test strips (from a case)

items: Dip the test strip into the urine for 1–2 s and shake off the excess on the edge of the container.

After 60 s compare the color with the scale (−, +, ++, +++). **Evaluation:** positive in starvation, vomiting (especially in children — the acetonemic state), a carbohydrate-free diet and decompensated diabetes mellitus. In diabetes ketonuria is seen together with glucosuria.

items: Assess the glycemia: hyperglycemia + ketosis — diabetes mellitus; normo- or hypoglycemia + ketosis — starvation, vomiting, a ketogenic diet.

Take the history into account (alcohol, not eating, pregnancy, acetonemic vomiting in children).
Explain the biochemical mechanism (the insulin/glucagon ratio, lack of oxaloacetate).
State the principle of treatment (insulin, glucose, fluids).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 17-year-old adolescent has complained for 3 days of thirst, passing a lot of urine, vomiting and abdominal pain. The breathing is deep and noisy and there is an odor of acetone from the mouth. Blood glucose is 22 mmol/l, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 8 mmol/l; glucose and ketone bodies (+++) were found in the urine.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the mechanism of the rise in ketone bodies.
cases.answer: Ketoacidotic decompensation of type 1 diabetes mellitus. When insulin is lacking, glucagon and the counter-insular hormones predominate: hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue is activated and lipolysis increases sharply, so a lot of fatty acids reach the liver; because malonyl-CoA is low, CPT-I is not inhibited, β-oxidation increases and a lot of acetyl-CoA is formed. Since oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis, acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle and is converted into ketone bodies. They are acids — metabolic acidosis (compensated by Kussmaul breathing), and acetone leaves with the breath. Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration. Treatment: insulin, fluids, potassium.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 2-year-old child with influenza, after not eating for 18 hours, developed lethargy, vomiting and seizures. Blood glucose is 1.9 mmol/l, ketone bodies were not detected, and ammonia and liver enzymes are increased. Medium-chain acylcarnitines are increased in the blood.
cases.ask: Which enzyme deficiency is suspected? Why does the hypoglycemia occur without ketosis?
cases.answer: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. In starvation energy is obtained mainly from the oxidation of fatty acids; because the enzyme is lacking, β-oxidation stops — acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies are not formed (hypoketosis), and there is not enough ATP or acetyl-CoA (an activator of pyruvate carboxylase) for gluconeogenesis — hypoglycemia. Medium-chain acyl-CoAs bind to carnitine and accumulate in the blood (they are detected by tandem mass spectrometry). Treatment: avoiding long fasts, giving glucose during illness.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old woman on a diet with almost all carbohydrates excluded (a “keto diet”) has an odor of acetone from the mouth and ketone bodies (++) in the urine. Blood glucose is 4.2 mmol/l and the pH is normal.
cases.ask: Is this condition dangerous? Explain its mechanism and how it differs from diabetic ketoacidosis.
cases.answer: Physiological (dietary) ketosis. When carbohydrates are low, insulin is low and glucagon relatively high: lipolysis and β-oxidation increase, the liver forms a lot of ketone bodies and they serve as an energy source for muscle and brain. But insulin is not absent altogether — it keeps lipolysis in check, so ketone bodies stay at a moderate level (0.5–3 mmol/l), the buffer systems neutralize them, the pH is normal and glucose is normal. In diabetic ketoacidosis, by contrast, there is almost no insulin: ketones exceed 3 mmol/l and acidosis and hyperglycemia develop.

topics.title: Metabolism of complex lipids. Cholesterol metabolism. Regulation of lipid metabolism

goals.text: To teach the student sterols and steroids, the significance and biological functions of cholesterol in the body, the biosynthesis of cholesterol and its regulation, its transport in the blood, the significance of LDL receptors and lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase, the routes of removal of cholesterol from the body, the biochemical basis of hypercholesterolemia, atherosclerosis and gallstone disease, and the dyslipoproteinemias and sphingolipidoses; to master the determination of serum cholesterol by the enzymatic method.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure, sources and functions of cholesterol;
the stages of cholesterol biosynthesis and the regulation of HMG-CoA reductase;
the transport of cholesterol in the blood, LDL receptors and reverse transport;
the routes of removal of cholesterol from the body;
the biochemical basis and risk factors of atherosclerosis;
the biochemical basis of gallstone disease;
the types of dyslipoproteinemia and the sphingolipidoses;
the age-related normal values of the lipid indices.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine total cholesterol in serum by the enzymatic method;
calculate the atherogenic index and evaluate the lipid profile.

sections.title: 1. Sterols and steroids. The significance of cholesterol

blocks.text: **Steroids** are substances based on the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene ring. **Sterols** are steroid alcohols with a hydroxyl group at position 3; the main sterol of animals is **cholesterol** (C~27~H~45~OH). The body contains ≈ 140 g of cholesterol; ≈ 90% of it is in the cells (in membranes) and the rest in the blood.
The biological functions of cholesterol:

items: **structural** — a component of membranes, regulating their fluidity and permeability; abundant in the myelin sheath;
a basis for the synthesis of **bile acids** (liver);
synthesis of the **steroid hormones**: cortisol, aldosterone (adrenal cortex), testosterone, estrogens, progesterone (gonads, placenta);

synthesis of **vitamin D~3~** — in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol under ultraviolet light. **Sources:** food (0.3–0.5 g per day: egg yolk, meat, liver, butter) and endogenous synthesis (≈ 0.8–1 g per day; ≈ 50% in the liver, the rest in the intestine, skin and adrenal cortex). Plant foods contain no cholesterol (phytosterols reduce the absorption of cholesterol in the intestine).

blocks.text: **Age-related features:** in childhood a lot of cholesterol is needed for myelination and growth; breast milk is rich in cholesterol. Blood total cholesterol rises with age: in children 2.5–4.5 mmol/l, in adults the desirable value is < 5.2 mmol/l; in women, after the menopause, LDL rises as estrogens fall.

sections.title: 2. Biosynthesis of cholesterol and its regulation

blocks.text: Cholesterol is synthesized in all nucleated cells, mainly in the **liver**, in the cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum, from **acetyl-CoA**. One molecule of cholesterol costs 18 acetyl-CoA, 36 ATP and 16 NADPH.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: The main stages of cholesterol biosynthesis and its regulation (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: 3 acetyl-CoA → **HMG-CoA** (β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl-CoA) — in the cytosol (unlike ketone body synthesis, which takes place in the mitochondria).
HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH → **mevalonate** — **HMG-CoA reductase** (the key enzyme, in the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum).
Mevalonate → activated isoprenoid units (C5, at the expense of ATP) → geranyl and farnesyl pyrophosphate → **squalene** (C30).
Squalene is cyclized to **lanosterol** and then, in ≈ 20 reactions, converted into **cholesterol**.

blocks.title: Table 10.1. Regulation of HMG-CoA reductase
head: Mechanism
Effect
rows: Intracellular cholesterol (through the transcription factor SREBP)
When it is high — the synthesis of the enzyme and of LDL receptors falls and the enzyme is degraded faster
Activates it by dephosphorylation; increases its synthesis
Increase the synthesis of the enzyme (but the removal of cholesterol and the number of LDL receptors increase more — hence hypercholesterolemia in hypothyroidism)
Competitive inhibitors; cholesterol in the cell falls and LDL receptors increase — LDL in the blood decreases

blocks.text: Cholesterol is transported in the blood in lipoproteins (topic 8); ≈ 2/3 of total cholesterol is in the form of **cholesterol esters**.

**Transport to the tissues.** The VLDL synthesized in the liver are converted in the blood by LPL into IDL and then into **LDL** — ≈ 70% of blood cholesterol is in LDL. LDL enter cells by endocytosis through **LDL receptors** (which recognize apo B-100 and apo E) (M. Brown and J. Goldstein, Nobel Prize 1985).

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Entry of cholesterol into the cell through the LDL receptor and regulation of the intracellular cholesterol level (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: When free cholesterol increases inside the cell: the synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase and of LDL receptors falls, and **ACAT** (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase) is activated, so the excess cholesterol is stored as esters.

**Reverse transport. HDL** (apo A-I) are formed in the liver and intestine as “flat discs”; they take free cholesterol from peripheral cells through the ABCA1 transporter. **Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT)** (activated by apo A-I) transfers a fatty acid from phosphatidylcholine to cholesterol and forms cholesterol esters; these move into the core of the HDL and the particle becomes spherical. HDL deliver cholesterol to the **liver** (SR-B1 receptors) or pass the cholesterol esters to other lipoproteins. For this reason HDL are **antiatherogenic** lipoproteins.
**Removal.** Cholesterol is not broken down to CO~2~ and H~2~O in the body. It:

items: is converted in the liver into **bile acids** (≈ 0.5 g per day; the key enzyme is 7α-hydroxylase) and leaves with the bile;
passes unchanged with the bile into the intestine; part of it is reabsorbed, and the rest is converted by bacteria into **coprostanol** and excreted with the feces;
a small amount leaves with sebum, and the metabolites of steroid hormones with the urine.

blocks.text: **Atherosclerosis** is a chronic disease in which lipids (mainly cholesterol and its esters) accumulate in the intima of large and medium arteries and fibrous plaques form. Its complications — ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, stroke — are among the main causes of death in the world.
The biochemical stages of atherogenesis:

items: Damage to the endothelium (hypercholesterolemia, arterial hypertension, smoking, hyperglycemia, homocysteine).
LDL enter the intima and are **oxidized** or glycated there (modified LDL).

Monocytes move into the intima and become macrophages; they take up modified LDL without limit through **scavenger receptors** (these receptors are not regulated by cholesterol) — **foam cells** are formed.

Under the action of inflammatory cytokines smooth muscle cells proliferate and collagen accumulates — a plaque with a fibrous cap forms; rupture of the plaque causes thrombosis. **Risk factors:** raised LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, high lipoprotein(a), arterial hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity, physical inactivity, heredity, age and male sex.

blocks.text: **The atherogenic index (A.N. Klimov):** AI = (total CH − HDL-CH) / HDL-CH; normal < 3.0; > 4 — high risk.

parts.text: **Familial hypercholesterolemia** (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) — a mutation of the LDL receptor gene (autosomal dominant). In heterozygotes (≈ 1:250) total cholesterol is 8–12 mmol/l and ischemic heart disease appears at 30–50 years; in homozygotes (≈ 1:1 000 000) cholesterol is 15–25 mmol/l, with tendon xanthomas and myocardial infarction in childhood. LDL do not enter the cells, and the cell, sensing cholesterol as “low”, does not reduce its synthesis. Treatment: statins, ezetimibe (reduces absorption in the intestine), PCSK9 inhibitors and, in severe cases, LDL apheresis.

blocks.title: Table 10.2. The Fredrickson classification of the dyslipoproteinemias (main types)
head: Type
Increased lipoproteins
In the blood
Cause (primary)
Atherogenicity
rows: Deficiency of LPL or apo C-II
Defect of the LDL receptor (familial hypercholesterolemia)
Familial hypertriglyceridemia; often secondary (diabetes, obesity, alcohol)

blocks.text: **Secondary** dyslipoproteinemias: diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, obesity, alcoholism, certain drugs.

In bile, cholesterol is kept dissolved by forming micelles with bile acids and phosphatidylcholine. When their ratio is disturbed (too much cholesterol or too few bile acids and phospholipids), the bile becomes **supersaturated with cholesterol (“lithogenic”)**; cholesterol crystals precipitate in the gallbladder and **cholesterol stones** form (≈ 80% of all stones). Risk factors: female sex, pregnancy, estrogens, obesity, rapid weight loss, a high-calorie diet, reduced motility of the gallbladder, diseases of the ileum (bile acids are not reabsorbed).

**The biochemical basis of treatment: ursodeoxycholic** (and chenodeoxycholic) acid preparations — they increase the bile acid pool, improve the solubility of cholesterol in the bile and reduce cholesterol synthesis in the liver (they dissolve small cholesterol stones); surgery (cholecystectomy). **Pigment stones** (calcium bilirubinate) form in hemolytic anemias and infection of the bile ducts.

sections.title: 6. Regulation and disorders of fat metabolism

blocks.text: **In the fed state** (insulin ↑): the synthesis of fatty acids and TAG from glucose increases (in the liver) and VLDL are formed; in adipose tissue LPL is activated and fat is stored; lipolysis is inhibited.
**In starvation** (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol ↑): lipolysis in adipose tissue increases, fatty acids are oxidized in muscle and liver, and ketone bodies are formed in the liver.

**Obesity** is an increase of adipose tissue resulting from a prolonged excess of energy intake over expenditure (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m^2^). Adipose tissue is an endocrine organ: it produces **leptin** (a satiety signal acting on the hypothalamus), adiponectin and cytokines. In obesity, leptin resistance, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and arterial hypertension develop — the **metabolic syndrome** (topic 15). **Obesity in children** is usually related to overeating and physical inactivity; rarely it is caused by a defect of the leptin gene or of its receptor.
**Sphingolipidoses** are congenital deficiencies of the enzymes that break down sphingolipids in the lysosomes; the lipids accumulate mainly in nervous tissue, the liver and the spleen.

Deficient enzyme

rows: Developmental regression, blindness, a “cherry-red spot” on the retina
Painful neuropathy, kidney and heart damage (X-linked)

blocks.text: In some sphingolipidoses (Gaucher, Fabry) **enzyme replacement therapy** is used.
Experiment 1: determination of total cholesterol in serum by the enzymatic method (on a biochemical analyzer)
Principle of the method (CHOD-PAP):

items: **Cholesterol esterase**: cholesterol esters + H~2~O → cholesterol + fatty acids;
**Cholesterol oxidase**: cholesterol + O~2~ → cholest-4-en-3-one + H~2~O~2~;
**Peroxidase**: 2H~2~O~2~ + 4-aminoantipyrine + phenol → pink quinoneimine + 4H~2~O. The intensity of the color is proportional to the amount of total cholesterol (500 nm).
Pour 1 ml of working reagent into each of three test tubes.
Add 10 µl of serum to tube 1, 10 µl of standard (5.17 mmol/l) to tube 2 and 10 µl of water to tube 3.
Mix and keep at 37 °C for 10 minutes.
Measure the optical density against the control at 500 nm (automatically on the analyzer). **Calculation:** C (mmol/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × 5.17

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** < 5.2 mmol/l — desirable; 5.2–6.2 — borderline high; ≥ 6.2 — high. The sample is taken after 12–14 hours of fasting.
Experiment 2: qualitative reaction for cholesterol (Liebermann–Burchard reaction)

items: Pour 1 ml of a solution of cholesterol in chloroform into a dry test tube.
Add 10 drops of acetic anhydride and 1–2 drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (take care!).

Observe the change of color. **Result and analysis:** first a pink, then a blue and finally a **green** color appears — cholesterol is dehydrated by sulfuric acid and forms colored compounds. This reaction used to be the basis of the quantitative determination of cholesterol (the Ilk method).

blocks.text: Experiment 3: interpreting the results of the lipid profile (from a case)

Using the results given by the teacher: compare total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL and HDL cholesterol with the normal values; calculate the atherogenic index; determine the type of dyslipoproteinemia by the Fredrickson classification. If LDL-CH was not measured directly, calculate it with the Friedewald formula (when TG < 4.5 mmol/l): LDL-CH = total CH − HDL-CH − TG / 2.2.

items: Make sure the blood is taken after 12–14 hours of fasting.
Compare total CH, TG, HDL-CH and LDL-CH with the normal values.
Calculate the atherogenic index.
Assess them together with the other risk factors (age, sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, heredity).
Determine the type of dyslipidemia and recommend excluding secondary causes (hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 12-year-old child was found to have hard nodules over the Achilles tendons (tendon xanthomas) and yellow patches on the eyelids (xanthelasmas). Total cholesterol is 16 mmol/l and triglycerides are normal. His father died of myocardial infarction at 38, and his mother’s cholesterol is 9 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain its biochemical mechanism. Why may the effect of statins be limited?
cases.answer: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) — a mutation in both alleles of the LDL receptor gene (both parents are heterozygotes). LDL do not enter cells and accumulate in the blood; the cells sense a “shortage” of cholesterol and do not reduce HMG-CoA reductase and synthesis. The excess LDL is taken up by macrophages through scavenger receptors — xanthomas and early atherosclerosis. Statins act mainly by increasing the number of LDL receptors; if the receptors do not work at all, the effect is small — LDL apheresis, PCSK9 inhibitors and other methods are needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old obese woman (BMI 34 kg/m^2^) complains of attacks of severe pain under the right costal margin after fatty food. Ultrasound revealed small radiolucent stones in the gallbladder.
cases.ask: What is the likely chemical composition of the stones? Explain the mechanism of their formation.
cases.answer: Cholesterol stones (radiolucent). Obesity, female sex and estrogens increase cholesterol synthesis in the liver and its secretion into the bile, while the synthesis of bile acids falls relatively; the bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol (lithogenic). Reduced motility of the gallbladder helps crystals to form. Small cholesterol stones can be dissolved with ursodeoxycholic acid; with frequent attacks — cholecystectomy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 55-year-old man smokes and his blood pressure is 160/95 mm Hg. Tests: total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/l, HDL-CH 0.9 mmol/l, triglycerides 2.2 mmol/l.
cases.ask: Calculate the atherogenic index and LDL-CH. Assess the risk.
cases.answer: AI = (6.8 − 0.9) / 0.9 ≈ 6.6 (normal < 3.0). Friedewald formula: LDL-CH = 6.8 − 0.9 − 2.2 / 2.2 = 6.8 − 0.9 − 1.0 = 4.9 mmol/l (desirable < 3.0). HDL is low, LDL and TG are high — atherogenic dyslipidemia. Together with smoking and arterial hypertension the risk of cardiovascular disease is very high. Recommendations: stopping smoking, diet, physical activity, statins, control of blood pressure.

topics.title: Digestion of proteins, absorption of amino acids and their distribution among tissues

goals.text: To teach the student the significance of proteins in the body, nitrogen balance and the biological value of proteins, the dynamic state of body proteins, the digestion of proteins in the gastrointestinal tract and its regulation, normal and pathological gastric juice, the absorption of amino acids and their distribution to the tissues, the features of protein digestion in children, and the putrefaction of proteins in the intestine and the detoxification of its products; to master the determination of the acidity of gastric juice.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the functions of proteins and the daily requirement;
the types of nitrogen balance and their causes;
the biological value of proteins and protein deficiency;
the composition of gastric juice, the formation and functions of HCl;
the proteolytic enzymes, their activation and specificity;
the mechanisms of amino acid absorption;
the features of protein digestion in children and food allergy;
the products of putrefaction and their detoxification in the liver.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the total acidity and free and bound HCl of gastric juice by titration;
determine indican in urine and evaluate the result;
calculate the nitrogen balance.

sections.title: 1. The significance of proteins. Nitrogen balance

blocks.text: Proteins carry out many functions in the body: **plastic** (the structure of cells and tissues), **catalytic** (enzymes), **transport** (hemoglobin, albumin, transferrin), **protective** (immunoglobulins, clotting factors), **regulatory** (peptide hormones), **contractile** (actin, myosin), **energy** (1 g → 4 kcal; in starvation). Proteins are the source of **nitrogen** and of the **essential amino acids** for the body.
**Nitrogen balance** is the difference between the nitrogen taken in with food and the nitrogen excreted from the body (mainly as urea). 1 g of nitrogen corresponds to ≈ 6.25 g of protein.

blocks.title: Table 11.1. Types of nitrogen balance
head: Type
Essence
When it is seen
rows: In healthy adults on an adequate diet
Growth in children, pregnancy, recovery after illness, the action of anabolic hormones
Starvation, protein deficiency, severe illness, burns, injuries, sepsis, tumors, diabetes mellitus, excess cortisol, old age

blocks.text: **The daily requirement for protein** in adults is 0.8–1.0 g/kg (≈ 70–100 g), at least half of it animal protein; in children 1.5–4 g/kg (most in newborns), and more in pregnant and breastfeeding women, in athletes and during recovery. The **protein minimum** (the smallest amount needed to maintain nitrogen equilibrium) is ≈ 30–50 g.

**The biological value of proteins** depends on their content of essential amino acids and on their digestibility: egg and milk proteins are high; plant proteins are lower (the limiting amino acids: wheat — lysine, legumes — methionine, maize — tryptophan and lysine). Eating different plant proteins together (for example, grain + legumes) increases the biological value.

parts.text: **Protein-energy malnutrition** is one of the main causes of child mortality in developing countries. **Kwashiorkor** — energy in the diet is relatively adequate but protein is sharply reduced: edema because of hypoalbuminemia, fatty degeneration of the liver, changes of the skin and hair, reduced immunity. **Marasmus** — both protein and energy are lacking: severe wasting, loss of muscle and adipose tissue, no edema.

blocks.text: **The dynamic state of body proteins.** The body’s proteins are constantly broken down and resynthesized: ≈ 300–400 g of protein is renewed per day (more than the amount that comes with food) — ≈ 75% of the amino acids released by breakdown are reused. The half-life of proteins differs: pancreatic enzymes and insulin — minutes to hours; liver enzymes — hours to days; hemoglobin — 120 days (the life of the erythrocyte); collagen — months to years. Intracellular proteins are broken down in the **lysosomes** (cathepsins) and in the **proteasomes** (the ubiquitin-dependent pathway).

**The species and tissue specificity of proteins**: the protein composition of every species and tissue is genetically determined; therefore, if foreign proteins enter the body undigested (for example, parenterally), they cause an immune response. Dietary proteins are broken down to amino acids and lose their “species specificity”.

sections.title: 2. Digestion of proteins in the stomach

blocks.text: Proteins are not digested in the oral cavity. Gastric juice (1.5–2.5 l per day) contains **hydrochloric acid**, **pepsinogens**, mucus (mucin) and Castle’s intrinsic factor.
**The formation of HCl** — in the **parietal cells** of the fundic glands: by carbonic anhydrase CO~2~ + H~2~O → H~2~CO~3~ → H^+^ + HCO~3~
−; H^+^ is pumped into the gastric lumen in exchange for K^+^ by **H^+^,K^+^-ATPase** (the “proton pump”), and Cl^-^ leaves through channels; HCO~3~
− passes into the blood in exchange for Cl^-^ (the “alkaline tide” after a meal).

**The functions of HCl:** it denatures and swells proteins (opening the peptide bonds to enzymes); converts pepsinogen into pepsin and creates the optimal pH for pepsin (1.5–2); has a bactericidal action; regulates gastric emptying and the release of secretin in the duodenum; improves the absorption of iron (Fe^3+^

**Pepsin** is synthesized in the chief cells as inactive **pepsinogen**; under the action of HCl and by **autocatalysis** a fragment of 42 amino acid residues is removed from the N-terminus and active pepsin is formed. Pepsin is an **endopeptidase**: it cleaves the peptide bonds formed by aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan) and leucine; proteins are broken down into large polypeptides. **Gastricsin** (pH 3–3.5) is important in the newborn’s stomach. Newborns also have **chymosin (rennin)**, the enzyme that curdles milk casein.

**Regulation of gastric juice secretion:** nervous (the vagus — acetylcholine), humoral (**gastrin** — released by the G cells of the antrum under the action of protein products and distension of the stomach; **histamine** — through H~2~ receptors), and inhibitors — somatostatin, secretin, a low pH.

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Normal acidity of gastric juice (fasting, in titration units)
head: Index
Normal (t.u.)

blocks.text: **Pathological gastric juice: a hyperacid state** (gastritis, peptic ulcer, Zollinger–Ellison syndrome — gastrinoma); **hyposecretion and achylia** (atrophic gastritis, gastric cancer, pernicious anemia — no HCl and no intrinsic factor). Pathological components: **lactic acid** (fermentation by bacteria in the absence of HCl — suspicion of gastric cancer), **blood**, bile.

parts.text: **The biochemical basis of treating acid-related diseases: antacids** (aluminium and magnesium hydroxides) neutralize HCl; **H~2~ blockers** (famotidine) block the action of histamine; **proton pump inhibitors** (omeprazole) irreversibly inhibit H^+^,K^+^-ATPase — the most powerful antisecretory agent. The main etiological factor in peptic ulcer is Helicobacter pylori (with the help of urease it breaks urea down to ammonia and survives in the acidic medium; the urea breath test is based on this).

sections.title: 3. Digestion of proteins in the intestine

blocks.text: The pancreatic proteases are synthesized as inactive **proenzymes** (this protects the gland tissue from self-digestion; the gland also contains a **trypsin inhibitor** protein). In the duodenum **enteropeptidase** (enterokinase) removes a hexapeptide from trypsinogen and forms **trypsin**; trypsin then activates the remaining trypsinogen by autocatalysis, as well as the other proenzymes.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: Activation of the proteolytic enzymes (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.title: Table 11.3. Specificity of the proteolytic enzymes
head: Enzyme
Type
Peptide bonds cleaved
rows: On the amino side of aromatic amino acids and leucine
On the carboxyl side of lysine and arginine (basic amino acids)
On the carboxyl side of aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp)
Bonds of small neutral amino acids (glycine, alanine, serine)
Removes amino acids from the C-terminus (B — lysine and arginine)
Removes amino acids from the N-terminus
