blocks.text: Endopeptidases break the chain into fragments from inside, while exopeptidases release free amino acids from its ends. The last stage of digestion takes place on the surface of the enterocytes (membrane digestion) and inside them.

parts.text: **Acute pancreatitis** — premature activation of the pancreatic enzymes inside the gland (diseases of the bile ducts, alcohol, trauma): trypsin activates the other proenzymes, phospholipase A~2~ and elastase, and the gland tissue digests itself (autolysis, necrosis) and the blood vessels are damaged. Amylase and lipase rise in the blood. Principles of treatment: fasting (to reduce secretion), protease inhibitors (aprotinin — historically), pain relief, infusion therapy.

sections.title: 4. Absorption and distribution of amino acids

blocks.text: Free amino acids and di- and tripeptides are absorbed in the small intestine:

items: free L-amino acids — by **symport with Na^+^** (secondary active transport) — with separate carriers for neutral, basic and acidic amino acids and imino acids;
di- and tripeptides — by **symport with H^+^** (PepT1), and they are broken down inside the enterocyte;

**the γ-glutamyl cycle (Meister cycle)** — entry of amino acids into the cell with the participation of glutathione (renal tubules, intestine, brain). The absorbed amino acids reach the liver through the **portal vein**; the liver retains part of them (synthesis of plasma proteins, gluconeogenesis, urea) and passes the rest into the general circulation. **The amino acid pool** is the free amino acids in the blood and cells (≈ 35 g). Its sources: dietary proteins, breakdown of body proteins, synthesis of nonessential amino acids. Its uses: protein synthesis, synthesis of nitrogenous compounds (heme, creatine, nucleotides, biogenic amines), production of energy and glucose.

blocks.text: **Distribution among tissues**: in starvation muscle proteins are a source of amino acids (they are released mainly as alanine and glutamine); the liver is the center of amino acid metabolism; the kidney uses glutamine and excretes ammonium ions.

**Congenital absorption disorders: Hartnup disease** (a defect of the carrier of neutral amino acids, especially tryptophan — pellagra-like signs), **cystinuria** (a defect of the carrier of cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine — cystine stones in the kidney).

sections.title: 5. Features of protein digestion in children

items: The acidity of gastric juice is low (pH 3–5) and pepsin activity is low; **gastricsin** and **chymosin** play an important role.
In the first months of life the permeability of the intestinal mucosa is high — some proteins (**IgA** and IgG of the colostrum) are absorbed undigested by **pinocytosis** (passive immunity).

For this reason foreign dietary proteins (cow’s milk proteins, egg, wheat gluten) may also be absorbed partly undigested and cause **food allergy**. This is why complementary food should be introduced at the right time and gradually.
**Celiac disease** — an immune reaction to the gluten (gliadin) of wheat, barley and rye: atrophy of the villi of the small intestine, malabsorption; treatment — a gluten-free diet.

sections.title: 6. Putrefaction of proteins in the intestine and detoxification of its products

blocks.text: Amino acids that have not been absorbed undergo **putrefaction** in the large intestine under the action of bacteria (decarboxylation, deamination, breakdown of side chains) and toxic substances are formed.

blocks.label: Figure 11.2
blocks.caption: The products of putrefaction and their detoxification in the liver (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.title: Table 11.4. The main products of putrefaction
head: Amino acid
Product of putrefaction

blocks.text: The products of putrefaction reach the **liver** through the portal vein and are detoxified there (topic 26): first by **microsomal oxidation** (for example, indole → indoxyl, skatole → skatoxyl), then by **conjugation** — with active sulfate (PAPS) or with **UDP-glucuronic acid**. The soluble conjugates formed are excreted in the urine. For example, the potassium salt of indoxyl sulfate is **indican**.

The amount of indican in the urine (normally 10–20 mg per day) shows the intensity of putrefaction: it rises in intestinal obstruction, constipation, lack of HCl in the stomach (achylia), bacterial overgrowth in the large intestine and a diet rich in protein. In liver failure the products of putrefaction and ammonia are not detoxified — **hepatic encephalopathy** (topic 25).
Experiment 1: determination of the acidity of gastric juice by titration (Töpfer method)

**Principle of the method:** the acids of gastric juice are titrated with 0.1 N NaOH in the presence of two indicators. **Dimethylaminoazobenzene** (which changes from red to yellow at pH 2.9–4.0) shows free HCl; **phenolphthalein** (pink at pH 8.2–10) shows the total acidity.

items: Measure 5 ml of filtered gastric juice into a flask and add 1–2 drops of dimethylaminoazobenzene and 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein (a red color means free HCl is present).
Titrate from a burette with 0.1 N NaOH until the red color turns **orange** — mark 1 (free HCl).
Continue the titration until a **yellow** color appears — mark 2.

Titrate until a **pink** color appears — mark 3 (total acidity). **Calculation:** the result is expressed in titration units (t.u.) — the number of ml of 0.1 N NaOH needed to neutralize 100 ml of gastric juice: X = NaOH used (ml) × 20 (for 5 ml of juice).
Free HCl = NaOH used up to mark 1 × 20;
Total acidity = NaOH used up to mark 3 × 20;

Total HCl (free + bound) = the mean of marks 2 and 3 × 20; bound HCl = total HCl − free HCl. **Evaluation:** total acidity 40–60, free HCl 20–40, bound HCl 10–20 t.u. If there is no free HCl — **achlorhydria**; if there is neither HCl nor pepsin — **achylia**.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of lactic acid in gastric juice (Uffelmann reaction)

items: Add to a test tube 1 ml of 1% phenol solution and 1 drop of FeCl~3~ (a violet color — iron phenolate).

Add gastric juice dropwise. **Result and analysis:** if lactic acid is present, the violet color turns **yellow-green** (iron lactate). In a healthy person there is no lactic acid in the gastric juice; it appears as a result of bacterial fermentation in the absence of HCl (achylia, gastric cancer).

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determination of indican in urine (Obermayer reaction)

items: Pour 2 ml of urine and 2 ml of Obermayer reagent (a solution of FeCl~3~ in concentrated HCl) into a test tube and mix.

Add 1 ml of chloroform, invert several times and wait for the layers to separate. **Result and analysis:** indican is hydrolyzed to indoxyl, which is oxidized to **indigo blue** and colors the chloroform layer blue. The intensity of the color corresponds to the amount of indican; a deep blue color shows that putrefaction in the intestine has increased.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the nitrogen balance

items: Determine the amount of protein taken in with food (g) and convert it into nitrogen: N = protein / 6.25.
Determine the urea nitrogen in the daily urine and add 2–4 g (losses with feces, skin and other nitrogenous substances).
Compare the nitrogen taken in and excreted.
Determine the type of balance (equilibrium, positive, negative).
In a negative balance analyze the cause (starvation, a catabolic state) and reassess the protein requirement.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating a gastric juice analysis

items: Compare the total acidity and the free and bound HCl with the normal values.
Assess the pathological components (lactic acid, blood, bile).
Determine the state: hyperacid, hyposecretion, achlorhydria, achylia.
Name the possible diseases (peptic ulcer, atrophic gastritis, gastric cancer, pernicious anemia).
Give the biochemical basis of the principle of treatment (antisecretory agents or replacement therapy).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 60-year-old patient has a reduced appetite, aversion to meat, weight loss and a feeling of heaviness in the epigastrium. Gastric juice analysis: total acidity 10 t.u., no free HCl, the Uffelmann reaction positive. Blood hemoglobin is 95 g/l.
cases.ask: Evaluate the gastric juice analysis. Why has lactic acid appeared? Which disease is suspected?
cases.answer: Achlorhydria (no free HCl, sharply reduced total acidity) and lactic acid in the gastric juice. Without HCl the stomach loses its bactericidal property; when food is retained in the stomach, bacteria ferment carbohydrates and form lactic acid. Aversion to meat, weight loss, anemia and lactic acid raise the suspicion of gastric cancer — endoscopy and biopsy are needed. The anemia is related to chronic blood loss and impaired iron absorption (no HCl).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 40-year-old man complains of pain in the upper abdomen on an empty stomach and at night; the pain decreases after food or after taking soda. Gastric juice: total acidity 90 t.u., free HCl 70 t.u. The urea breath test is positive.
cases.ask: Evaluate the condition. Explain the biochemical basis of treatment.
cases.answer: A hyperacid state — duodenal ulcer (associated with Helicobacter pylori). With the help of urease H. pylori breaks urea down into NH~3~ and CO~2~ (the labeled CO~2~ is detected in the breath test), surrounds itself with an alkaline “cloud”, damages the mucosa and increases gastrin secretion. Treatment: a proton pump inhibitor (it blocks H^+^,K^+^-ATPase and sharply reduces HCl secretion) + antibiotics (eradication); antacids are symptomatic. Soda (NaHCO~3~) neutralizes HCl and relieves the pain, but it forms CO~2~ and causes acid rebound — it is not recommended.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient with chronic constipation the Obermayer reaction in the urine is strongly positive (a deep blue color). He eats a lot of protein food.
cases.ask: What does this result show? Write the pathway of indican formation.
cases.answer: Indican in the urine is increased — putrefaction of proteins in the large intestine has increased (because of constipation the intestinal contents stay for a long time, and there is a lot of protein). The pathway of formation: tryptophan → (bacteria) → indole → portal vein → microsomal oxidation in the liver → indoxyl → conjugation with active sulfate (PAPS) → indoxyl sulfate → its potassium salt (indican) → urine. Recommendation: more dietary fiber and fluid, treatment of the constipation.

topics.title: The common pathways of amino acid metabolism. Aminotransferases. Decarboxylation of amino acids

goals.text: To teach the student the fate of the absorbed amino acids, the common pathways of amino acid catabolism — transamination (the aminotransferases and the coenzyme function of vitamin B~6~), direct and indirect oxidative deamination, the decarboxylation of amino acids, the formation, functions and detoxification of the biogenic amines, and the significance of histamine in allergy and inflammation; to master the determination of aminotransferase activity in serum.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the pathways of transformation of amino acids in the cell;
the transamination reaction, the aminotransferases and the role of pyridoxal phosphate;
the clinical and diagnostic significance of ALT and AST and the De Ritis ratio;
direct and indirect (transdeamination) deamination;
the significance and regulation of glutamate dehydrogenase;
the fate of the carbon skeleton of amino acids (glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids);
the decarboxylation reaction and the biogenic amines;
the detoxification of the biogenic amines (MAO, COMT) and the significance of inhibitors of these enzymes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine ALT and AST activity in serum on a biochemical analyzer;
evaluate aminotransferase activity clinically;
explain the mechanism of drugs that affect the metabolism of the biogenic amines.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Transdeamination** is the **main route** of deamination of amino acids. α-Ketoglutarate and glutamate act as “carriers” in this process and deliver the amino groups to GDH. In skeletal muscle there is little GDH, and deamination there proceeds through the **purine nucleotide cycle** (AMP deaminase).

blocks.text: The amino acid pool of the cell is used in the following ways:

items: **Protein synthesis** — the main route.
**Synthesis of nitrogenous compounds**: purine and pyrimidine bases, heme, creatine, carnitine, biogenic amines, hormones (thyroxine, adrenaline), neurotransmitters, glutathione, nicotinamide.

**Catabolism** — removal of the amino group (transamination, deamination) and oxidation of the carbon skeleton or its conversion into glucose and ketone bodies. The catabolism of amino acids increases especially when the diet is rich in protein, in starvation and in diabetes mellitus. The **ammonia** formed is detoxified (topic 13).

blocks.text: **Transamination** is the transfer of the α-amino group of an amino acid to an α-keto acid; a new amino acid and a new α-keto acid are formed. The reaction is **reversible** and no ammonia is released. It was discovered by A.E. Braunstein and M.G. Kritzman (1937).
L-amino acid + α-ketoglutarate ⇄ α-keto acid + L-glutamate

**Aminotransferases (transaminases)** belong to the class of transferases; they are found in almost all tissues, in the cytosol and the mitochondria. Their coenzyme is **pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)**, a derivative of vitamin B~6~. PLP accepts the amino group from the amino acid and is converted into **pyridoxamine phosphate**, then passes it to the keto acid (a “ping-pong” mechanism).
Most aminotransferases use **α-ketoglutarate** as the acceptor of the amino group — as a result the amino groups are collected in **glutamate**.

head: Enzyme
Reaction
Main location
rows: Liver (cytosol) — a lot; less in the kidney, muscle and heart
Heart, liver (cytosol and mitochondria), skeletal muscle, kidney

blocks.text: **The significance of transamination:** synthesis of nonessential amino acids (from keto acids); collection of the amino groups of amino acids in glutamate (for subsequent deamination); the link between amino acid catabolism and gluconeogenesis (alanine → pyruvate, aspartate → oxaloacetate); the malate-aspartate shuttle; transport of nitrogen between tissues.
The clinical significance of the aminotransferases
Normally the activity of ALT and AST in the blood is low. When cells are damaged (cytolysis) they are released into the blood:

blocks.title: Table 12.2. Aminotransferases in serum (37 °C, kinetic method, adults)
head: Enzyme
Men
Women

items: **In hepatitis** (viral, toxic) **ALT rises sharply** (10–100 times), ALT > AST; the rise of ALT begins 1–2 weeks before the jaundice.
**In myocardial infarction AST** rises after 6–12 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and returns to normal in 4–7 days; ALT changes little.

**In alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis** AST > ALT (mitochondrial AST is released; in alcoholism a lack of PLP lowers ALT more). **The De Ritis ratio** = AST / ALT; normally 1.33 ± 0.42. **< 1** — liver damage (viral hepatitis); **> 2** — myocardial infarction, alcoholic liver damage.

blocks.text: **Deamination** is the removal of the amino group from an amino acid in the form of **ammonia**. Its types: oxidative, reductive, hydrolytic and intramolecular. In humans the main type is **oxidative deamination**.
Direct oxidative deamination
Only **glutamate** is actively deaminated — by **glutamate dehydrogenase** (GDH; in the mitochondria, especially active in the liver):
L-Glutamate + NAD^+^ (NADP^+^) + H~2~O ⇄ α-Ketoglutarate + NH~3~ + NADH + H^+^

The reaction is reversible: in the reverse direction it binds ammonia and synthesizes glutamate. GDH is an **allosteric** enzyme: **ADP and GDP** (low energy) activate it — the catabolism of amino acids increases; **ATP, GTP and NADH** inhibit it.

The direct deamination of other amino acids is of little importance: **L-amino acid oxidase** (FMN; very low activity), D-amino acid oxidase (FAD; for D-amino acids coming from bacteria), serine and threonine — through dehydratases (PLP), histidine — through histidase.
Indirect deamination (transdeamination)
Most amino acids are deaminated in **two steps**:

items: **Transamination**: the amino acid passes its amino group to α-ketoglutarate → glutamate;
**Oxidative deamination of glutamate** (GDH): glutamate → α-ketoglutarate + NH~3~.

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: Indirect deamination (transdeamination): transamination and the oxidative deamination of glutamate (drawn after Severin E.S.)

parts.text: **Transdeamination** is the **main route** of deamination of amino acids. α-Ketoglutarate and glutamate act as “carriers” in this process and deliver the amino groups to GDH. In skeletal muscle there is little GDH, and deamination there proceeds through the **purine nucleotide cycle** (AMP deaminase).

blocks.text: **Reductive amination** (the reverse of transdeamination) — the synthesis of nonessential amino acids: α-ketoglutarate + NH~3~ (GDH) → glutamate → other amino acids through transamination.

sections.title: 4. The fate of the carbon skeleton of amino acids

blocks.text: After the amino group has been removed, the carbon skeletons of the 20 amino acids are converted into 7 common products: pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate and oxaloacetate. They are oxidized in the Krebs cycle (energy) or:

items: **glucogenic amino acids** (those converted into pyruvate or Krebs cycle metabolites) — give glucose through gluconeogenesis: alanine, serine, glycine, cysteine, aspartate, asparagine, glutamate, glutamine, arginine, histidine, proline, methionine, valine, threonine;
**ketogenic amino acids** (those that give acetyl-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA) — only **leucine** and **lysine**;
**mixed** (gluco-ketogenic): isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan.

sections.title: 5. Decarboxylation of amino acids. The biogenic amines

blocks.text: **Decarboxylation** is the removal of the carboxyl group from an amino acid as CO~2~; the product is a **biogenic amine**. The reaction is catalyzed by **decarboxylases** (lyases); their coenzyme is **pyridoxal phosphate** (B~6~). The reaction is irreversible.

blocks.caption: Formation of the main biogenic amines (drawn after Severin E.S.)

Function
rows: A mediator of allergy and inflammation (vasodilation, increased permeability, bronchospasm, itching — H~1~); secretion of gastric juice (H~2~); a neurotransmitter in the CNS
A neurotransmitter (mood, sleep, appetite); intestinal motility; constricts vessels; platelet aggregation; melatonin is formed from it in the pineal gland
The main inhibitory mediator of the CNS

parts.text: **Histamine** is released from mast cells and basophils in allergic reactions: urticaria, Quincke edema, bronchospasm, and a sharp fall of blood pressure in anaphylactic shock. **Antihistamines**: H~1~ blockers (diphenhydramine, loratadine, cetirizine) — in allergy; H~2~ blockers (famotidine) — reduce the secretion of gastric juice. In vitamin B~6~ deficiency the activity of glutamate decarboxylase
falls and GABA decreases — **seizures** in newborns (B~6~ is given together with isoniazid treatment).

blocks.text: Detoxification of the biogenic amines
So that the action of the biogenic amines is short, they are broken down quickly:

items: **Monoamine oxidases (MAO)** — on the outer mitochondrial membrane, containing FAD; oxidative deamination: R-CH~2~-NH~2~ + O~2~ + H~2~O → R-CHO + NH~3~ + H~2~O~2~. MAO-A breaks down serotonin and noradrenaline, MAO-B dopamine. The aldehydes formed are oxidized to acids (serotonin → 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid; catecholamines → vanillylmandelic acid) and excreted in the urine.
**Diamine oxidase (histaminase)** — oxidizes histamine, putrescine and cadaverine.
**Methylation** — **catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)** methylates catecholamines at the expense of S-adenosylmethionine; histamine is also methylated.

parts.text: **MAO inhibitors** (moclobemide — MAO-A, selegiline — MAO-B) and **selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors** (fluoxetine) are antidepressants: serotonin and noradrenaline increase in the synapse. In Parkinson disease (a lack of dopamine in the substantia nigra) **L-DOPA** (levodopa) is used — it crosses the blood-brain barrier, which dopamine cannot, and is converted into dopamine in the brain; it is given together with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa). If a patient taking MAO inhibitors eats food rich in tyramine (hard cheese, wine), a hypertensive crisis (the “cheese reaction”) may develop. **Pheochromocytoma** (a catecholamine-producing tumor) is diagnosed by a rise in vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrines in the urine; a **carcinoid tumor** by a rise in 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in the urine.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of ALT and AST activity in serum on a biochemical analyzer (kinetic method)
Principle of the method (IFCC):

items: **ALT**: L-alanine + α-ketoglutarate → pyruvate + L-glutamate; pyruvate + NADH + H^+^ → lactate + NAD^+^ (the indicator enzyme is **lactate dehydrogenase**);
**AST**: L-aspartate + α-ketoglutarate → oxaloacetate + L-glutamate; oxaloacetate + NADH + H^+^

blocks.text: → malate + NAD^+^ (the indicator enzyme is **malate dehydrogenase**). NADH absorbs light at 340 nm while NAD^+^ does not; the **rate of fall** of the optical density is proportional to the enzyme activity. Pyridoxal phosphate is added to the reagent (to avoid a falsely low result in B~6~ deficiency).

items: Pour 1 ml of working reagent (substrates, NADH, LDH or MDH, PLP) into a cuvette and warm it at 37 °C for 5 minutes.
Add 100 µl of serum and mix.
After 1 minute measure the optical density at 340 nm and record it every minute for 3 minutes (automatically on the analyzer).
Calculate the mean ΔE/min. **Calculation:** activity (IU/l) = ΔE/min × F (F is the factor for the reagent and cuvette, derived from the molar absorption coefficient of NADH; for example, 1746).

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** compare with the normal values in the table and calculate the De Ritis ratio. Hemolyzed serum falsely raises AST (erythrocytes contain a lot of AST).
Experiment 2: determination of the aminotransferases by the Reitman–Frankel method (colorimetric) (a historical method)

**Principle of the method:** the pyruvate formed in transamination (or the pyruvate formed spontaneously from oxaloacetate) forms a hydrazone with **2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine**; in an alkaline medium it gives a red-brown color. The intensity of the color is proportional to the amount of pyruvate and therefore to the enzyme activity. The result is expressed in µmol pyruvate / (hour · ml); normal values: ALT 0.1–0.68, AST 0.1–0.45 mmol/(hour · l).
Experiment 3: the ninhydrin reaction for amino acids

items: Add to a test tube 1 ml of 1% glycine solution (or a protein hydrolysate) and 5 drops of 0.1% ninhydrin solution.

Boil for 1–2 minutes. **Result and analysis:** α-amino acids give a **blue-violet** color with ninhydrin (Ruhemann’s purple): the amino acid undergoes oxidative deamination and decarboxylation, and the ammonia released forms a colored compound with ninhydrin. Proline and hydroxyproline give a yellow color. This reaction underlies the detection of amino acids in chromatography.

skills.title: Skill: clinical evaluation of an aminotransferase result

items: Compare ALT and AST with the normal values for the sex; determine how many times they are increased.
Calculate the De Ritis ratio.
If it is < 1 — think of cytolysis of hepatocytes (hepatitis); if > 2 — damage to the myocardium or muscle, alcoholic hepatitis.
Compare with the other indices: bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, GGT (liver); CK-MB, troponins (heart).
Check that there is no hemolysis in the sample.

skills.title: Skill: explaining the mechanism of a drug that affects the metabolism of a biogenic amine

items: Determine which step the drug acts on: synthesis (decarboxylase), the receptor, reuptake or breakdown (MAO, COMT).
State how the amount of the biogenic amine changes in the synapse or in the tissue.
Explain the clinical effect (antidepressant, antihistamine, antiparkinsonian).
Indicate the adverse effects and the interaction with food (tyramine).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 25-year-old patient has weakness, loss of appetite, nausea and heaviness under the right costal margin; jaundice appeared 3 days later. Tests: ALT 1200 IU/l, AST 680 IU/l, bilirubin 85 µmol/l (mainly conjugated and free), HBsAg positive.
cases.ask: Calculate the De Ritis ratio and interpret the result. Why has ALT risen more?
cases.answer: De Ritis = 680 / 1200 ≈ 0.57 (< 1) — cytolysis of hepatocytes (acute viral hepatitis B). ALT is located mainly in the cytosol of hepatocytes and is most abundant in the liver; when the membrane is damaged it is the first to be released into the blood. A large part of AST is in the mitochondria — it is released in quantity only in deep (necrotic) damage. The rise of ALT begins before the jaundice and is a sensitive sign of the activity of hepatitis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 58-year-old man says he had severe pain behind the sternum 8 hours ago. Tests: AST 180 IU/l, ALT 45 IU/l, CK-MB and troponin I sharply increased.
cases.ask: Calculate the De Ritis ratio. Which organ is damaged?
cases.answer: De Ritis = 180 / 45 = 4 (> 2) — damage to the myocardium. The heart muscle contains a lot of AST and little ALT; in myocardial infarction the cardiomyocytes undergo necrosis and AST, CK-MB, LDH1 and troponins are released into the blood. AST rises after 6–12 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and normalizes in 4–7 days; today the troponins are considered the most specific marker.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient taking a MAO inhibitor for depression ate hard cheese and drank red wine at a party, after which he developed a severe headache, sweating and palpitations; his blood pressure is 210/120 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical mechanism of this condition.
cases.answer: The “cheese reaction” — a hypertensive crisis. Cheese and wine contain a lot of tyramine (the decarboxylation product of tyrosine). Normally it is broken down by MAO in the intestinal wall and the liver. When MAO is inhibited, tyramine passes into the blood and displaces noradrenaline from the sympathetic nerve endings (an indirect sympathomimetic); because noradrenaline is also not broken down by MAO, its effect is stronger — the vessels constrict and blood pressure rises sharply. People taking MAO inhibitors are forbidden foods rich in tyramine.

topics.title: Detoxification of ammonia. Metabolism of individual amino acids and its hereditary disorders

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the sources and toxic action of ammonia, the routes of its temporary and final detoxification, the synthesis of urea and its link with transamination and the Krebs cycle, the types and consequences of hyperammonemia, the metabolism of serine, glycine, methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, one-carbon groups and transmethylation, and the congenital diseases of amino acid metabolism; to master the determination of urea in serum.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the sources of ammonia and the mechanisms of its toxic action;
the temporary binding of ammonia (glutamine, alanine) and the formation of ammonium salts in the kidney;
the reactions, enzymes, energy cost and regulation of the ornithine cycle;
the normal values and the changes of urea in blood and urine;
congenital and acquired hyperammonemias;
the significance of tetrahydrofolate and one-carbon groups;
the metabolism of methionine, S-adenosylmethionine and transmethylation, and homocysteine;
the metabolism of phenylalanine and tyrosine and its congenital diseases.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine urea in serum and evaluate the result;
determine phenylpyruvate in urine (the Fölling test);
give a biochemical explanation of the cause of hyperammonemia.

blocks.text: Sources of ammonia:

items: deamination of amino acids (mainly the oxidative deamination of glutamate);
hydrolysis of amides (glutamine, asparagine);
oxidation of biogenic amines by MAO;
deamination of purine and pyrimidine bases (adenine, cytosine);

putrefaction of proteins and breakdown of urea by bacteria in the intestine (it reaches the liver through the portal vein). About 15–20 g of ammonia is formed per day in the human body, but its level in the blood is very low: **11–35 µmol/l** (normally < 50 µmol/l).

blocks.text: **Its toxic action** (especially on the brain):

items: in the brain ammonia forms glutamate with α-ketoglutarate (reductive amination) — **α-ketoglutarate falls**, the Krebs cycle slows down and ATP formation decreases;
glutamate and glutamine increase — **osmotic swelling** of the astrocytes (glutamine) and a disturbed balance of neurotransmitters (glutamate ↓ or ↑, GABA ↑);
NH~4~

blocks.text: + disrupts K^+^ channels and Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase, and the membrane potential changes;

items: the blood pH shifts to the alkaline side. Clinical signs: nausea, vomiting, lethargy, tremor, seizures, coma.

sections.title: 2. Temporary detoxification and transport of ammonia

blocks.text: The ammonia formed in the tissues is bound at once and transported to the liver and kidney in nontoxic forms:

items: **Synthesis of glutamine** (the main route; brain, muscle and other tissues): glutamate + NH~3~ + ATP → **glutamine** + ADP + P~i~ — **glutamine synthetase**. Glutamine is the main transport form of ammonia (the most abundant amino acid in the blood).
**Formation of alanine** (muscles): pyruvate is transaminated into alanine and goes to the liver — the **glucose-alanine cycle** (topic 7).

**Synthesis of asparagine** (less important). **In the kidney** glutamine is broken down by **glutaminase** into glutamate and NH~3~; NH~3~ passes into the tubular lumen, binds H^+^ and is excreted in the urine as **ammonium salts** (NH~4~

blocks.text: +) (≈ 0.5–1 g per day). This process **increases sharply in acidosis** — an important mechanism by which the kidney maintains the acid-base balance (topic 29).

The **final detoxification** of ammonia is the synthesis of urea in the **liver**. The cycle was discovered by H. Krebs and K. Henseleit (1932). Urea is a slightly toxic, highly water-soluble, neutral substance; ≈ 80–90% of the body’s nitrogen is excreted in this form.

Enzyme

Citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate + AMP + PP~i~

blocks.text: **The sources of the two nitrogens of the urea molecule:** the first is **ammonia** (from the deamination of glutamate and the glutaminase reaction), the second is **aspartate** (from the transamination of oxaloacetate). In this way the nitrogen of all amino acids is delivered to the cycle through transamination.
**Energy cost:** 3 ATP for one urea (**4 high-energy bonds**, because one ATP is split into AMP + PP~i~).

**The link with the Krebs cycle (the “Krebs bicycle”):** the **fumarate** formed in the ornithine cycle is converted in the Krebs cycle into malate and oxaloacetate; oxaloacetate is transaminated back into **aspartate** and returns to the ornithine cycle. The NADH formed in the malate dehydrogenase reaction recovers part of the energy spent on urea synthesis.
Regulation:

items: **N-acetylglutamate** (acetyl-CoA + glutamate; its synthesis is activated by arginine) is the obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I;

with a protein-rich diet and in starvation (when amino acid catabolism increases) the synthesis of the cycle enzymes is induced (glucagon, cortisol). **Normal values of urea:** in serum **2.5–8.3 mmol/l**; in the urine **20–35 g** (333–583 mmol) per day.

A protein-rich diet, strong catabolism (burns, fever, tumors), gastrointestinal bleeding

blocks.text: **Hyperammonemia** is an increase of the ammonia level in the blood.
**Congenital (primary) hyperammonemias** are congenital deficiencies of the ornithine cycle enzymes (≈ 1:25 000–35 000 newborns):

head: Disease
Deficient enzyme
Changes in blood/urine
rows: Hyperammonemia type II (the most common, X-linked)
NH~3~ ↑↑, glutamine ↑; orotic acid ↑ in the urine (carbamoyl phosphate goes into pyrimidine synthesis)
Arginine ↑↑; spastic paraparesis, NH~3~ rises less

blocks.text: In newborns, in the first days of life (when protein intake begins), refusal to feed, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and coma are seen. Treatment: restriction of protein, **sodium benzoate** and **phenylbutyrate** (they conjugate with glycine and glutamine and remove nitrogen bypassing urea), supplements of arginine or citrulline, hemodialysis, liver transplantation.

**Acquired (secondary) hyperammonemia** — mainly in **liver cirrhosis and failure**: urea synthesis falls and the ammonia of the portal vein bypasses the liver through portocaval anastomoses and enters the general circulation — **hepatic encephalopathy** (topic 25). In children, taking aspirin during viral infections may cause **Reye syndrome** (damage to the mitochondria, hyperammonemia, fatty degeneration of the liver, encephalopathy); for this reason aspirin is not recommended for children with fever.

sections.title: 5. Metabolism of one-carbon groups. Serine and glycine

blocks.text: **Tetrahydrofolate (THF)** is the active form of folic acid (B~9~); it is formed by dihydrofolate reductase (NADPH). THF carries **one-carbon groups** (methyl −CH~3~, methylene =CH~2~, methenyl =CH−, formyl −CHO, formimino). The main sources of one-carbon groups are **serine** (serine + THF → glycine + N5,N10-methylene-THF; serine hydroxymethyltransferase, PLP) and **glycine** (the glycine cleavage system).

**One-carbon groups are used for:** the synthesis of purine nucleotides (atoms C2 and C8), the synthesis of **thymidylate** (dUMP → dTMP), the regeneration of methionine (homocysteine → methionine), and the interconversion of serine and glycine.

Syntheses in which **glycine** takes part: proteins (every third amino acid of collagen), heme (succinyl-CoA + glycine), creatine, purines, glutathione, conjugation of bile acids (glycocholic acid), detoxification of benzoic acid (hippuric acid).

parts.text: **Sulfonamides** competitively inhibit the synthesis of folate from para-aminobenzoic acid in bacteria (humans obtain folate from food) — a bacteriostatic effect. **Methotrexate** inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — a lack of THF stops the synthesis of thymidylate and purines; rapidly dividing tumor cells die. **Folate deficiency** — megaloblastic anemia; in pregnancy — neural tube defects in the fetus (which is why folic acid is prescribed when a pregnancy is planned).

blocks.text: **Methionine** is an essential amino acid and the main **donor of methyl groups** in the body. With ATP it forms **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)**. SAM gives its methyl group to various acceptors — **transmethylation** (by methyltransferases):

items: noradrenaline → **adrenaline**;
guanidinoacetate → **creatine**;
phosphatidylethanolamine → **phosphatidylcholine** (choline);
**methylation** of nucleotides and DNA (epigenetic regulation of gene expression);

synthesis of carnitine and melatonin; detoxification of foreign substances and hormones (catecholamines — COMT). After giving up its methyl group, SAM is converted into **S-adenosylhomocysteine** and then into **homocysteine**. The fate of homocysteine:
**remethylation** — it returns to methionine: the methyl donor is N5-methyl-THF and the coenzyme is **methylcobalamin (B~12~)** (methionine synthase);
**transsulfuration** — with serine it forms cystathionine (cystathionine β-synthase, **B~6~**) and then **cysteine**; cysteine → taurine, glutathione, sulfates (PAPS).

parts.text: **Hyperhomocysteinemia** (normal blood level 5–15 µmol/l) is seen in deficiency of B~12~, folate or B~6~, in renal failure or in congenital enzyme defects (cystathionine β-synthase — **homocystinuria**: dislocation of the lens, skeletal changes, mental retardation, early thrombosis). Homocysteine damages the endothelium and is an independent risk factor for **atherosclerosis and thrombosis**. In B~12~ deficiency N5-methyl-THF is not used and accumulates (the “folate trap”) — the other forms of THF fall and megaloblastic anemia develops.

blocks.text: **Phenylalanine** (essential) is converted into **tyrosine** mainly in the liver by **phenylalanine hydroxylase** (coenzyme — **tetrahydrobiopterin, BH~4~**). From tyrosine are formed: the **catecholamines** (dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline), **melanin** (tyrosinase in melanocytes) and the **thyroid hormones** (T~3~, T~4~); the final catabolism of tyrosine leads through homogentisic acid to **fumarate** and **acetoacetate**.

parts.text: **Screening for phenylketonuria** is carried out in all newborns on days 3–5 of life (the Guthrie test or tandem mass spectrometry). Once the diagnosis is made, the child is put on a **diet low in phenylalanine** (special formulas; tyrosine becomes essential for such patients). If the diet is started early, mental development is almost normal. Mothers with PKU must follow the diet during pregnancy as well — otherwise a high phenylalanine level causes microcephaly and heart defects in the fetus. One source of phenylalanine is **aspartame** (an artificial sweetener).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of urea in serum by the urease method

**Principle of the method: urease** breaks urea down into ammonia and CO~2~; the ammonia forms **blue indophenol** with phenol and hypochlorite (catalyzed by sodium nitroprusside) (the Berthelot reaction). The intensity of the color is proportional to the amount of urea (546–600 nm). Analyzers use a kinetic method: the ammonia is measured by the consumption of NADH in the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction (340 nm).

items: Pour 1 ml of urease-containing buffer solution into each of three test tubes.
Add 10 µl of serum to tube 1, 10 µl of standard (for example, 8.33 mmol/l) to tube 2 and 10 µl of water to tube 3; keep at 37 °C for 10 minutes.
Add the phenol-nitroprusside and alkaline hypochlorite reagents and keep at 37 °C for another 10 minutes.
Measure the optical density against the control on a photometer. **Calculation:** C (mmol/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × Cstandard

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** the normal value is 2.5–8.3 mmol/l. It is evaluated together with creatinine (kidney function).
Experiment 2: determination of phenylpyruvate in urine (Fölling test)

items: Pour 1 ml of fresh urine into a test tube and add 2–3 drops of 10% iron (III) chloride solution.

Observe the change of color within 30–60 s. **Result and analysis:** if phenylpyruvate is present, a **blue-green** color appears (it fades within a few minutes) — suspicion of phenylketonuria. False positives: some drugs (salicylates — violet), bilirubin, homogentisic acid (a transient blue color). The result is confirmed by measuring phenylalanine in the blood.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determination of homogentisic acid in urine (demonstration)

items: Pour 2 ml of urine from a patient with alkaptonuria (or a solution of homogentisic acid) into each of two test tubes.

Add 1 ml of 10% NaOH to one of them and shake it in air. **Result and analysis:** in an alkaline medium homogentisic acid is oxidized quickly and gives a **black-brown** color; in the tube without alkali the urine darkens slowly over several hours in air.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the cause of a change in blood urea

items: Compare the urea level with the normal value.
If it is increased — assess creatinine: if both are increased — renal failure; if the urea/creatinine ratio is very high — a prerenal cause (dehydration, gastrointestinal bleeding, catabolism).
If it is decreased — check liver function (albumin, prothrombin time, ammonia).
Take the diet into account (the amount of protein).
Draw a conclusion and recommend further tests.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the cause of hyperammonemia

items: Consider the patient’s age: in newborns — congenital enzyme defects; in adults — liver diseases.
Analyze the results of testing the blood amino acids (citrulline, arginine, glutamine) and the urinary orotic acid.
Determine the enzyme that is blocked (orotic acid ↑ — ornithine carbamoyltransferase; citrulline ↑ — argininosuccinate synthetase).
Explain the principles of treatment (protein restriction, benzoate, phenylbutyrate, arginine, dialysis).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 3-day-old boy refused to breastfeed and developed vomiting, lethargy and seizures. Blood ammonia is 450 µmol/l (normal < 50), glutamine is increased, citrulline is low, and orotic acid is sharply increased in the urine.
cases.ask: Which enzyme is deficient? Why is orotic acid increased? State the principles of treatment.
cases.answer: Ornithine carbamoyltransferase deficiency (hyperammonemia type II; X-linked, which is why it is severe in a boy). Carbamoyl phosphate is not converted into citrulline (citrulline is low), accumulates in the mitochondria, leaves for the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis, increasing orotic acid. Ammonia is not detoxified — in the brain α-ketoglutarate falls, glutamine accumulates (swelling) and encephalopathy develops. Treatment: temporarily stopping protein, glucose (to reduce catabolism), sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate (which remove nitrogen as hippuric acid and phenylacetylglutamine), arginine and, in severe cases, hemodialysis; later a protein-restricted diet and liver transplantation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Newborn screening found a blood phenylalanine level of 1200 µmol/l (normal < 120). Tyrosine is reduced.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? What are the consequences if it is not treated? What is the essence of the diet?
cases.answer: Classic phenylketonuria — phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Phenylalanine is not converted into tyrosine, accumulates and is transaminated into phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate and phenylacetate (a “mousy” odor in the urine). A high phenylalanine level blocks the transport of other large neutral amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan) into the brain, myelination is impaired and the synthesis of neurotransmitters (dopamine, serotonin) falls — if untreated, severe mental retardation and seizures; melanin is low — the skin and hair are pale. Treatment: from the first weeks of life a diet low in phenylalanine (special formulas) with tyrosine supplements; blood phenylalanine is monitored regularly.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 60-year-old vegetarian woman has weakness, numbness in the legs and memory loss. The blood shows megaloblastic anemia, homocysteine 45 µmol/l (normal 5–15) and increased methylmalonic acid.
cases.ask: Which vitamin is deficient? Why are homocysteine and methylmalonic acid increased?
cases.answer: Vitamin B~12~ (cobalamin) deficiency (low in the diet of vegetarians — it is found only in animal products). Methylcobalamin is the coenzyme of methionine synthase: when it is lacking, homocysteine is not converted into methionine (hyperhomocysteinemia — a risk of thrombosis and atherosclerosis), N5-methyl-THF accumulates (the “folate trap”) and the other forms of folate fall — the synthesis of thymidylate and DNA is impaired (megaloblastic anemia). 5′-deoxyadenosylcobalamin is the coenzyme of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: when it is lacking, methylmalonic acid accumulates; abnormal fatty acids are incorporated into myelin and damage the nervous system (subacute combined degeneration). Treatment — parenteral B~12~.

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the digestion of nucleoproteins, the functions of nucleotides, the synthesis of purine nucleotides (the de novo and salvage pathways), its regulation and their breakdown, the formation of uric acid, hyperuricemia and gout, the synthesis and breakdown of pyrimidine nucleotides, the biosynthesis of deoxyribonucleotides and thymidylate nucleotides, the disorders of nucleotide metabolism and the drugs that act on these pathways; to master the determination of uric acid in blood and urine.

items: determine uric acid in serum and evaluate the result;
perform the murexide test for uric acid;
explain the biochemical basis of the treatment of hyperuricemia.

sections.title: 1. Functions of nucleotides. Digestion of nucleoproteins

blocks.text: **Nucleotides** are compounds consisting of a nitrogenous base (purine: adenine, guanine; pyrimidine: cytosine, uracil, thymine), a pentose (ribose or deoxyribose) and 1–3 phosphate residues.
Functions:

items: monomers of the nucleic acids (DNA, RNA);
**energy** — ATP is the universal energy carrier; GTP (protein synthesis, gluconeogenesis), UTP (glycogen synthesis), CTP (phospholipid synthesis);
components of **coenzymes** — NAD^+^, NADP^+^, FAD, CoA;
**second messengers** — cAMP, cGMP;
**activated intermediates** — UDP-glucose, CDP-choline, S-adenosylmethionine, PAPS;

**allosteric effectors** — they regulate the activity of many enzymes. **Digestion of nucleoproteins:** in the stomach nucleoproteins are split into the protein part (histones) and the nucleic acids; in the intestine the pancreatic **nucleases** (DNase, RNase) break the nucleic acids down into oligonucleotides, **phosphodiesterases** into mononucleotides, **nucleotidases** into nucleosides, and **nucleosidases (phosphorylases)** into the nitrogenous base and the pentose. The purine and pyrimidine bases that come with food are almost not used for the synthesis of nucleic acids in the body — they are broken down. Therefore nucleotides are **not an essential factor**: they are synthesized from amino acids and other simple substances.

blocks.text: De novo synthesis

Purine nucleotides are synthesized mainly in the **liver**, in the cytosol, on the basis of **phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP)** — the purine ring is “assembled” step by step on ribose-5-phosphate.
**Sources of the atoms of the purine ring:** glycine (C4, C5, N7), the amide nitrogen of glutamine (N3, N9), aspartate (N1), CO~2~ (C6), N10-formyl-THF (C2, C8).

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: De novo synthesis of purine nucleotides and the salvage pathway (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: Ribose-5-phosphate + ATP → **PRPP** (PRPP synthetase).
PRPP + glutamine → 5-phosphoribosylamine — **amidophosphoribosyltransferase** (the **key enzyme**).
In 9 reactions **inosine monophosphate (IMP)** is formed (6 ATP are used).

From IMP: **AMP** (the amino group of aspartate, the energy of GTP) and **GMP** (the amide group of glutamine, the energy of ATP). **Regulation:** PRPP synthetase and amidophosphoribosyltransferase are inhibited by the end products — **AMP, GMP and IMP** (negative feedback), while PRPP activates them. In addition there is **reciprocal regulation**: GTP is needed for the synthesis of AMP and ATP for the synthesis of GMP — this keeps the balance of adenine and guanine nucleotides.

blocks.text: The salvage (reutilization) pathway
The free purine bases formed by the breakdown of nucleotides combine with PRPP and are converted back into nucleotides — energy is saved:

items: **hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)**: hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP; guanine + PRPP → GMP;
**adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT)**: adenine + PRPP → AMP. The salvage pathway is especially important in the **brain** and erythrocytes (where de novo synthesis is low).

parts.text: **Lesch–Nyhan syndrome** — complete congenital deficiency of **HGPRT** (X-linked recessive, in boys). The salvage pathway does not work: PRPP accumulates and sharply increases de novo synthesis, so purines

are formed in excess and broken down — **severe hyperuricemia**, uric acid stones, gouty arthritis; neurological disorders (choreoathetosis, mental retardation) and **self-injury** (biting the lips and fingers). Allopurinol reduces the hyperuricemia but does not correct the neurological signs.

sections.title: 3. Breakdown of purine nucleotides. Uric acid

blocks.text: Purine nucleotides are converted by nucleotidases, adenosine deaminase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and guanase into **hypoxanthine** and **xanthine**, and then by **xanthine oxidase** (which contains molybdenum, FAD and Fe; active in the liver and intestine) into **uric acid**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Breakdown of the purine bases to uric acid and the xanthine oxidase inhibitors (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: In humans and other primates uric acid is the **end product** of purine metabolism (in most mammals it is converted by **uricase** into the readily soluble allantoin; humans do not have this enzyme). Uric acid is a weak acid and at physiological pH is in the form of **urate** (sodium urate); it is poorly soluble in water. About 2/3 of it is excreted by the kidneys and 1/3 through the intestine. Uric acid is also a strong **antioxidant**.

head: Material
Normal value

blocks.text: **Adenosine deaminase deficiency** — dATP accumulates in lymphocytes and inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, DNA synthesis stops — **severe combined immunodeficiency** (no T and B lymphocytes); the first gene therapy was used in exactly this disease (topic 18).
**Hyperuricemia** is a rise of uric acid in the blood (> 420 µmol/l in men, > 360 in women).
**Primary hyperuricemia** (in ≈ 90% of cases — a hereditary reduction of urate excretion by the kidney; less often — increased synthesis: raised PRPP synthetase activity, partial HGPRT deficiency).
Secondary hyperuricemia:

items: increased formation — extensive breakdown of cells: leukemias, lymphomas, chemotherapy of tumors (**tumor lysis syndrome**), hemolytic anemia, psoriasis; food rich in purines (meat, liver, kidney, fish, beer), excess fructose, type I glycogenosis;

reduced excretion — renal failure, thiazide diuretics, low-dose aspirin, lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis (lactate and ketone bodies compete with urate for secretion), alcohol, lead poisoning. **Gout** is a disease in which urate crystals (monosodium urate) are deposited in joints and tissues. **Acute gouty arthritis** — most often the 1st metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe; the crystals are taken up by neutrophils and inflammatory mediators are released (severe pain, swelling, redness). In chronic gout **tophi** (deposits of urate under the skin), **urate stones** in the kidney and urate nephropathy develop.

blocks.title: Table 14.2. The biochemical basis of the treatment of hyperuricemia and gout
head: Group
Drug
Mechanism
rows: Allopurinol (an analogue of hypoxanthine; alloxanthine — its active metabolite), febuxostat
Reduce the formation of uric acid; hypoxanthine and xanthine (which are more soluble) are excreted; the salvage pathway uses up PRPP and so also reduces de novo synthesis
Reduce the reabsorption of urate in the renal tubules
Break uric acid down into allantoin (in tumor lysis syndrome)

blocks.text: **Diet:** restriction of purine-rich food, alcohol (especially beer) and fructose-containing drinks, drinking plenty of fluid, alkalinization of the urine (urate becomes more soluble).

sections.title: 5. Synthesis and breakdown of pyrimidine nucleotides

blocks.text: The pyrimidine ring is first assembled free and then attached to PRPP:

items: Glutamine + CO~2~ + 2ATP → carbamoyl phosphate — **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II** (in the cytosol; the **key enzyme**; inhibited by UTP, activated by PRPP and ATP). (Unlike carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I of the ornithine cycle: that one is in the mitochondria and uses NH~3~.)
Carbamoyl phosphate + aspartate → carbamoyl aspartate (aspartate carbamoyltransferase) → dihydroorotate → **orotic acid** (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase — in the mitochondria).
Orotate + PRPP → orotidine monophosphate → **UMP** (a bifunctional enzyme — **UMP synthase**: orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase).
UMP → UDP → **UTP** → **CTP** (CTP synthetase, the amide group of glutamine). In humans the first three enzymes are combined in one multifunctional protein (CAD).

blocks.text: **Breakdown:** cytosine and uracil → β-alanine, NH~3~, CO~2~; thymine → β-aminoisobutyric acid. The products are readily soluble in water and do not cause diseases like hyperuricemia.

parts.text: **Hereditary orotic aciduria** — UMP synthase deficiency: a lot of **orotic acid** in the urine (crystals), megaloblastic anemia (not enough pyrimidine nucleotides and DNA synthesis; it is not cured by folate or B~12~),

growth retardation. Treatment — **uridine**: it is converted into UMP and makes up the shortage of nucleotides, and through UTP it inhibits carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II and reduces the formation of orotic acid. Orotic aciduria is also seen in ornithine carbamoyltransferase deficiency (topic 13), but there is hyperammonemia there and no anemia.

sections.title: 6. Synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides and thymidylate nucleotides

blocks.text: **Ribonucleotide reductase** reduces ribonucleoside **diphosphates** (ADP, GDP, CDP, UDP) to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates. The reductant is **thioredoxin** (which is regenerated at the expense of thioredoxin reductase and NADPH). The enzyme is regulated allosterically in a complex way: **dATP** is an inhibitor for all substrates and ATP an activator; the various dNTPs change the substrate specificity and keep the balance of deoxyribonucleotides. The activity of the enzyme is highest in the S phase of the cell cycle.

**Thymidylate nucleotides:** dUMP + N5,N10-methylene-THF → **dTMP** + dihydrofolate — **thymidylate synthase**. Dihydrofolate is converted back into THF by **dihydrofolate reductase** (NADPH). These reactions are vital for rapidly dividing cells (tumors, bone marrow, intestinal epithelium).

blocks.text: In the first days of life the blood uric acid of newborns is high (a lot of cells, especially erythrocytes, are broken down) and urate crystals may be deposited in the renal tubules — a **uric acid infarct** (a physiological state; the urine is brick-red and it passes within 1–2 weeks). During growth the synthesis of nucleotides is intense. Hyperuricemia is more common in old age and, in women, after the menopause (estrogens increase the excretion of urate).
Experiment 1: determination of uric acid in serum by the uricase method

**Principle of the method: uricase** oxidizes uric acid to allantoin, CO~2~ and **H~2~O~2~**; peroxidase, at the expense of H~2~O~2~, oxidizes a chromogen and forms a colored compound (the Trinder reaction, 520 nm). The intensity of the color is proportional to the amount of uric acid.

items: Pour 1 ml of working reagent (uricase, peroxidase, chromogen) into each of three test tubes.
Add 25 µl of serum to tube 1, 25 µl of standard (for example, 357 µmol/l) to tube 2 and 25 µl of water to tube 3.
Keep at 37 °C for 10 minutes and measure against the control at 520 nm. **Calculation:** C (µmol/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × Cstandard

blocks.text: **Evaluation:** 200–420 µmol/l in men, 140–360 in women. Ascorbic acid (a strong reductant) can use up the H~2~O~2~ and falsely lower the result.
Experiment 2: the murexide test for uric acid

items: Put a small amount of uric acid (or scrapings from a urate stone) into a porcelain dish and add 2–3 drops of concentrated nitric acid.
Evaporate carefully on a water bath (a red-yellow residue).

After cooling, add 1 drop of 10% ammonia solution. **Result and analysis: violet-red** color appears (murexide — the ammonium salt of purpuric acid); with NaOH it is blue-violet. This reaction is characteristic of purines and uric acid; it is used to determine the chemical composition of kidney stones.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: microscopic examination of uric acid crystals in urine (demonstration)

items: Place a drop of the urine sediment (after centrifugation) on a slide.

Examine under the microscope. **Result and analysis:** in acidic urine, uric acid crystals are yellow-brown and rhomboid, barrel-shaped or in rosettes; amorphous urates form a brick-red sediment. Large amounts indicate a urate diathesis or a tendency to urate stones.

Assess creatinine and kidney function.
Take drugs (diuretics, aspirin), alcohol, diet and chemotherapy into account.
Choose the principle of treatment: a xanthine oxidase inhibitor or a uricosuric agent.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 50-year-old man ate a lot of meat and drank beer at a party, and at night woke up with severe pain at the base of his big toe: the joint is swollen and red, and cannot be touched. Uric acid in blood is 610 µmol/l. Needle-shaped crystals were found in the joint fluid.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the causes of the hyperuricemia and of the attack. State the principles of treatment.
cases.answer: Acute gouty arthritis. Purine-rich food (meat) and beer (purines + alcohol) increased uric acid formation; in the metabolism of alcohol lactate accumulates and reduces urate secretion in the kidney. When uric acid exceeds the saturation limit, monosodium urate crystals precipitate in cooler peripheral joints; neutrophils engulf them and release inflammatory mediators. During an attack — colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids; afterwards, long-term — allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor), diet, restriction of alcohol, plenty of fluid.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a patient with lymphoma, 2 days after chemotherapy was started the volume of urine fell sharply. Uric acid in blood is 950 µmol/l, potassium and phosphate are increased, calcium is decreased, creatinine is increased.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Explain its mechanism and the measures for preventing it.
cases.answer: Tumor lysis syndrome. Under the action of chemotherapy many tumor cells break down and the purines of their nucleic acids are converted into uric acid; intracellular K^+^ and phosphate enter the blood, and phosphate binds calcium and causes hypocalcemia. Uric acid crystallizes in the renal tubules and causes acute renal failure. Prevention: allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy (it breaks uric acid down to the much more soluble allantoin), plenty of fluid (hydration), monitoring of electrolytes.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 1-year-old child was found to have megaloblastic anemia and growth retardation. Treatment with folate and B~12~ gave no effect. Orotic acid in the urine is sharply increased, ammonia in blood is normal.
cases.ask: What disease is this? Why does the anemia not respond to folate and B~12~? What is the treatment?
cases.answer: Hereditary orotic aciduria — deficiency of UMP synthase. Orotic acid is not converted into UMP and is excreted in large amounts in the urine; pyrimidine nucleotides (UTP, CTP, dTTP) are lacking, and DNA synthesis is disturbed in rapidly dividing cells (megaloblastic anemia). The disease is caused not by a deficiency of folate or B~12~ but by an enzyme defect, and for that reason vitamins have no effect. The normal ammonia level rules out a disturbance of the ornithine cycle. Treatment — uridine (a source of UMP and, through UTP, a feedback inhibitor of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II).

topics.title: The interrelationship of carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism

goals.text: To give the student an integrated understanding of the general scheme of the catabolism of proteins, fats and carbohydrates, of the metabolism of the nitrogen-free residue of amino acids, of glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids, of the synthesis of glucose from amino acids and glycerol, of the formation of amino acids from carbohydrates and fats, of the role of insulin and cortisol in the regulation of metabolism, of the changes in metabolism in starvation and diabetes mellitus, and of the biochemical basis of the metabolic syndrome.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the common intermediate products of the catabolism of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins (pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, metabolites of the Krebs cycle);
glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids;
which substances can be converted into one another and which cannot (that glucose is not formed from fatty acids);
the metabolic cooperation between organs in the fed and the fasting state;
the main metabolic effects of insulin, glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol;
the changes in metabolism in diabetes mellitus and the metabolic syndrome.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: depict the connections between metabolites in the form of a scheme;
evaluate several blood indices at once (glucose, ketone bodies, urea, lipids) and determine the metabolic state (fed, fasting, diabetes);
analyze the results of a glucose tolerance test.

blocks.text: The catabolism of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins proceeds in three stages (topic 5): 1) breakdown of polymers into monomers; 2) conversion of the monomers into a few common intermediate products — **pyruvate, acetyl-CoA**, metabolites of the Krebs cycle; 3) the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. **Acetyl-CoA** and the **Krebs cycle** are the “crossroads” of all metabolic pathways.

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: The main points of convergence of carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: The main points of convergence:

items: **glucose-6-phosphate** — glycolysis, synthesis and breakdown of glycogen, the pentose phosphate pathway;
**dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP)** — the link between glycolysis and the synthesis of triacylglycerols (glycerol-3-phosphate);
**pyruvate** — glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, alanine metabolism (ALT), formation of acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate;
**acetyl-CoA** — synthesis of fatty acids, ketone bodies and cholesterol, and the Krebs cycle;

**oxaloacetate, α-ketoglutarate** — transamination with aspartate and glutamate, gluconeogenesis. **An important rule: the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible**, and therefore **glucose is not synthesized** from acetyl-CoA (and hence from even-chain **fatty acids**): the 2 carbons of acetyl-CoA leave the Krebs cycle as 2 CO~2~, and the net amount of oxaloacetate does not increase. The propionyl-CoA part of odd-chain fatty acids (through succinyl-CoA) and the **glycerol** part of triacylglycerols are converted into glucose.

sections.title: 2. Metabolism of the nitrogen-free residue of amino acids

blocks.text: After deamination the carbon skeleton of amino acids (α-keto acids) is converted into one of seven products: pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate.

blocks.title: Table 15.1. Classification of amino acids by their carbon skeleton
head: Group
Amino acids
Product formed
rows: Ala, Gly, Ser, Cys, Thr, Asp, Asn, Glu, Gln, Arg, His, Pro, Met, Val
Pyruvate or metabolites of the Krebs cycle → glucose
Acetyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA → ketone bodies, fatty acids

blocks.text: **Glucogenic amino acids** serve as substrates of gluconeogenesis in starvation; **ketogenic amino acids** are used for the synthesis of ketone bodies and lipids.

sections.title: 3. Synthesis of glucose from amino acids and glycerol

blocks.text: In starvation and physical exertion **gluconeogenesis** (topic 7) maintains glucose in the blood. The main substrates:

items: **amino acids** — muscle proteins break down and reach the liver and the kidney in the form of **alanine** (the glucose-alanine cycle) and **glutamine**; alanine → pyruvate → glucose;
**glycerol** — from lipolysis in adipose tissue; in the liver glycerol kinase → glycerol-3-phosphate → DHAP → glucose;
**lactate** — from muscle and erythrocytes (the Cori cycle). Thus, although fatty acids are not converted into glucose, their oxidation supplies the liver with **ATP and NADH** for gluconeogenesis.

sections.title: 4. Biosynthesis of amino acids from carbohydrates and fats

blocks.text: The body can synthesize **nonessential amino acids** from the intermediate products of carbohydrates:

items: pyruvate + transamination → **alanine**;
oxaloacetate → **aspartate** → asparagine;
α-ketoglutarate → **glutamate** → glutamine, proline, arginine;

3-phosphoglycerate → **serine** → glycine, cysteine (with the sulfur of methionine). The nitrogen is taken from other amino acids or from NH~3~ (glutamate dehydrogenase). **Essential amino acids** (valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine; in children also arginine and histidine) are not formed from carbohydrates and fats — they come only from food.

blocks.text: **Synthesis of fats from carbohydrates:** excess glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (mitochondria) → into the cytosol in the form of citrate → synthesis of fatty acids; NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway and from malic enzyme; glycerol-3-phosphate from DHAP. For this reason food rich in carbohydrates leads to obesity.

blocks.title: Table 15.2. The main metabolic effects of hormones
head: Process
Insulin
Glucagon
Adrenaline
Cortisol

blocks.text: **Insulin** is the only hypoglycemic, **anabolic** hormone: through GLUT4 it increases the entry of glucose into muscle and adipose tissue; through phosphoprotein phosphatases it activates glycogen synthase, pyruvate dehydrogenase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase; it induces the synthesis of glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase.

**Cortisol** is a **catabolic** hormone (muscle proteins are broken down) that induces the synthesis of the enzymes of gluconeogenesis (PEPCK, glucose-6-phosphatase); it is important in prolonged stress and starvation. The ratio of insulin to the contrainsular hormones (the insulin/glucagon index) determines the direction of metabolism.

sections.title: 6. Metabolism in the fed and the fasting state

blocks.text: **The absorptive period (2–4 hours after a meal):** the insulin/glucagon index is high. The liver converts glucose into glycogen and fatty acids (which it releases in VLDL); muscle stores glucose as glycogen and synthesizes protein; adipose tissue takes the triacylglycerols of chylomicrons and VLDL (lipoprotein lipase) into its stores.
**The postabsorptive period and starvation:** insulin decreases, and glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol increase.

blocks.label: Figure 15.2
blocks.caption: The change of energy sources at the different stages of starvation (drawn after Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry)

blocks.title: Table 15.3. Changes in metabolism at the stages of starvation
head: Period
Main processes
Blood indices
rows: Liver glycogen (used up in ≈ 12–24 hours), gluconeogenesis begins, lipolysis increases
Glucose at the lower limit of normal, free fatty acids ↑
Gluconeogenesis is maximal (muscle proteins → alanine, glutamine), ketone bodies ↑
The brain obtains ≈ 2/3 of its energy from ketone bodies; protein breakdown decreases (proteins are spared); renal gluconeogenesis ↑
Ketone bodies 5–7 mmol/l, urea decreases, excretion of NH~4~^+^ ↑

blocks.text: In prolonged starvation life expectancy depends mainly on the **fat store**; death occurs when ≈ 1/3–1/2 of the proteins (muscle, and then the vital organs) have been broken down.

sections.title: 7. Disturbance of metabolism in diabetes mellitus

blocks.text: **Diabetes mellitus** is chronic hyperglycemia resulting from insulin deficiency (type 1 — absolute, autoimmune damage of the β-cells) or from relative deficiency with resistance to insulin (type 2). In the absence of insulin the body works “in a state of starvation”, even though there is plenty of glucose in the blood.

blocks.title: Table 15.4. Changes in metabolism in diabetes mellitus
head: Metabolism
Change
Result
rows: Entry of glucose into tissues (GLUT4) ↓, synthesis of glycogen ↓, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis ↑
Hyperglycemia, glucosuria (when the renal threshold of ≈ 10 mmol/l is exceeded), polyuria, polydipsia
Lipolysis ↑, free fatty acids ↑, β-oxidation ↑, ketone bodies ↑; VLDL ↑ (in type 2)
Negative nitrogen balance, urea ↑, wasting, slow healing of wounds

blocks.text: **Mechanisms of the late complications:** **nonenzymatic glycosylation** of proteins (HbA~1c~, collagen, the basement membrane — microangiopathy, nephropathy, retinopathy); the **polyol pathway** — aldose reductase converts glucose into sorbitol (the lens of the eye, the nerves — cataract, neuropathy); oxidative stress.

parts.text: **HbA~1c~** (glycated hemoglobin) reflects the mean glycemia of the last 2–3 months (erythrocyte lifespan ≈ 120 days): normal < 6.0%; ≥ 6.5% — diagnostic criterion of diabetes mellitus. **Fructosamine** (glycated albumin) reflects the last 2–3 weeks.

blocks.text: **Metabolic syndrome** is a cluster of interrelated factors that develops on the basis of insulin resistance: **abdominal obesity** (waist circumference: men > 94 cm, women > 80 cm), **arterial hypertension** (≥ 130/85 mm Hg), **hyperglycemia** (fasting ≥ 5.6 mmol/l), **hypertriglyceridemia** (≥ 1.7 mmol/l), **decreased HDL cholesterol** (men < 1.0, women < 1.3 mmol/l). The diagnosis is made if three of them are present.

**Biochemical basis:** visceral adipose tissue releases many free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and adiponectin decreases → insulin signaling in muscle and liver is impaired (IRS-1 phosphorylation) → compensatory hyperinsulinemia. In the liver VLDL synthesis increases (hypertriglyceridemia, small dense LDL) and HDL decreases. Hyperinsulinemia increases renal Na^+^ reabsorption and sympathetic activity (hypertension). Complications: type 2 diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, gout, polycystic ovary syndrome.
Experiment 1: glucose tolerance test (GTT)
**Principle of the method:** glucose is measured in blood in the fasting state and after a glucose load, which allows the body's ability to utilize glucose to be assessed.

items: After the subject has fasted for 8–14 hours, determine glucose in capillary or venous blood (glucose oxidase method, topic 7).
Dissolve 75 g of anhydrous glucose in 250–300 ml of water and drink it within 5 minutes (for children 1.75 g/kg, at most 75 g).
After 2 hours (for teaching purposes — every 30 minutes) determine glucose again; plot the glycemic curve.

blocks.title: Table 15.5. Interpretation of GTT results (venous plasma, mmol/l)
head: Condition
Fasting
After 2 hours

blocks.text: **Analysis:** normally glucose peaks at 30–60 minutes (1.5–1.7 times the initial level) and returns to the initial level by 2 hours. In diabetes the peak is high and the decline is slow.
Experiment 2: determination of glucose and ketone bodies in urine (test strips)

items: Dip the test strip into fresh urine for 1–2 seconds and blot off the excess urine against the edge of the container.

After 30–60 seconds compare the color with the scale on the container. **Results and analysis:** the glucose zone — glucose oxidase–peroxidase reaction; the ketone zone — acetoacetate and acetone give a violet color with sodium nitroprusside (based on Legal’s reaction; it does not detect β-hydroxybutyrate). Simultaneous glucosuria and ketonuria is a sign of decompensated diabetes; ketonuria alone — starvation, vomiting, ketogenic diet.

skills.title: Skill: determining the metabolic state from laboratory parameters

items: Assess blood glucose, ketone bodies, free fatty acids, triacylglycerols, urea and insulin.
Fed state: glucose ↑ (≤ 7.8), insulin ↑, ketone bodies and free fatty acids ↓.
Starvation: glucose at the lower limit of normal, insulin ↓, ketone bodies ↑ (moderately), urea ↑ (days 2–5).
Decompensated type 1 diabetes: glucose ↑↑, insulin ↓↓, ketone bodies ↑↑, pH ↓.
Type 2 diabetes / metabolic syndrome: glucose ↑, insulin ↑ (resistance), triacylglycerols ↑, HDL ↓.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A healthy male volunteer, under a physician's supervision, underwent therapeutic fasting and drank only water. Blood was drawn on day 3 and in week 3. Day 3: glucose 3.9 mmol/l, ketone bodies 2.5 mmol/l, a lot of urea in the urine. Week 3: glucose 3.6 mmol/l, ketone bodies 6.5 mmol/l, urinary urea decreased, ammonium salts increased.
cases.ask: Why is there a lot of urea in the urine on day 3 and little in week 3? What are the main sources of glucose? Why did ammonium excretion increase?
cases.answer: On day 3 liver glycogen is depleted and glucose comes mainly from gluconeogenesis — muscle proteins are broken down, and alanine and glutamine go to the liver; their nitrogen is converted to urea (a lot of urea). In week 3 the brain obtains a large part of its energy from ketone bodies, the need for glucose decreases, and protein breakdown slows down (proteins are spared) — urea decreases. Sources of glucose: amino acids, glycerol (lipolysis), lactate. To compensate for ketoacidosis, glutaminase is activated in the kidney: NH~3~ excretes H^+^ as NH~4~^+^, and the carbon skeleton of glutamine is used in renal gluconeogenesis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 16-year-old girl has been drinking a lot of water and urinating a lot for a month and has lost weight; today she has abdominal pain, vomiting, deep noisy breathing (Kussmaul) and an acetone smell on the breath. Blood glucose 24 mmol/l, pH 7.15, ketone bodies 9 mmol/l; the urine contains a lot of glucose and ketone bodies.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? How are carbohydrate, lipid and protein metabolism disturbed? Why has the patient lost weight?
cases.answer: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, diabetic ketoacidosis. Without insulin, glucose does not enter muscle and adipose tissue, and glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are enhanced in the liver (hyperglycemia, glucosuria, osmotic diuresis — polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration). Lipolysis is enhanced and free fatty acids undergo β-oxidation in the liver; because oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis, acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies — ketoacidosis (Kussmaul breathing — compensation by exhaling CO~2~). Protein synthesis decreases and breakdown increases (negative nitrogen balance). The weight loss is due to the breakdown of adipose and muscle tissue and the loss of glucose in the urine (loss of energy).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 52-year-old man: height 172 cm, weight 98 kg, waist circumference 112 cm, BP 150/95 mm Hg. Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/l, triacylglycerols 3.1 mmol/l, HDL cholesterol 0.8 mmol/l, insulin elevated, uric acid 480 µmol/l.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Explain the biochemical mechanism. What complications are at risk?
cases.answer: Metabolic syndrome (abdominal obesity, hypertension, impaired fasting glycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, decreased HDL — 5 criteria). Visceral adipose tissue releases many free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines, and insulin signaling in muscle and liver is impaired — insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia. In the liver VLDL synthesis increases (triacylglycerols ↑) and HDL decreases. Hyperinsulinemia enhances renal reabsorption of Na^+^ and urate (hypertension, hyperuricemia). Complications: type 2 diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, fatty liver disease, gout. The basis of treatment is weight loss, physical activity and diet.
