topics.title: Molecular biology. DNA structure, replication, transcription

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the structure of nucleic acids (the Watson–Crick model), the role of DNA in heredity, the genetic system of mitochondria, DNA hybridization, replication and its relation to the cell cycle, post-replicative modifications (methylation, telomeres), transcription and post-transcriptional modifications of RNA, the organization of prokaryotic and eukaryotic genes, recombination, transposons and plasmids, and the use of PCR and recombinant DNA in medicine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the primary, secondary and tertiary structure of DNA and RNA and Chargaff's rules;
the structure of chromatin (nucleosome, histones);
the principles of replication (semiconservative, antiparallel, discontinuous) and its enzymes;
the importance of telomerase and DNA methylation;
the stages of transcription and the eukaryotic RNA polymerases;
the post-transcriptional modifications of mRNA, rRNA and tRNA (capping, polyadenylation, splicing);
the principle of PCR and the basics of molecular diagnostics;
the drugs that block replication and transcription.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: isolate nucleoproteins from tissue and perform qualitative reactions for their components;
write the complementary strand and the mRNA from a DNA sequence;
interpret PCR results (gel electropherogram).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Replication and transcription are “DNA → DNA” and “DNA → RNA”. Main difference: replication requires a **primer** and its substrate is **dNTP**; transcription does not need a primer and its substrate is **NTP**.

blocks.text: **Nucleic acids** are polymers formed by the joining of mononucleotides through 3’,5’-**phosphodiester bonds**. The 5’-end of the chain carries a phosphate and the 3’-end a free OH group; the sequence is written in the 5’→3’ direction.

blocks.title: Table 16.1. Differences between DNA and RNA
head: Characteristic
DNA
RNA
rows: Storage and transmission of genetic information
Implementation of information (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA), regulation (microRNA)
Hydrolyzed in alkali because of the 2’-OH

blocks.text: **Chargaff's rules:** in DNA A = T and G = C; the sum of purines equals the sum of pyrimidines (A + G = T + C); the (G + C)/(A + T) ratio is species-specific.

**Watson–Crick model (1953, B-form):** two **antiparallel** polynucleotide chains form a right-handed double helix twisted around a common axis; the bases are inside and the sugar-phosphate backbone is outside. The bases pair **complementarily**: A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds). One turn of the helix is ≈ 10 base pairs (3.4 nm), the diameter is 2 nm; the major and minor grooves are important for the binding of proteins to DNA. The helix is stabilized by hydrogen bonds and by the **stacking interactions** of the bases.

**Tertiary structure and chromatin:** DNA winds 1.7 times around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4 — 2 of each) with ≈ 146 base pairs to form a **nucleosome**; the linker histone H~1~ assembles nucleosomes into a 30 nm fibril; then come loops and metaphase chromosomes. **Euchromatin** is loosely packed and actively transcribed; **heterochromatin** is dense and inactive.

**Denaturation and hybridization:** heating (or alkali) breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the double helix — the **melting temperature (T~m~)** is higher when there are many G≡C pairs; on denaturation the absorbance at 260 nm increases (**hyperchromic effect**). On cooling, complementary strands reassociate (renaturation). The joining of complementary strands from different sources is **hybridization** (Southern blot, FISH, DNA microarrays, PCR-based methods).

**Genetic system of mitochondria:** mtDNA is circular, 16,569 base pairs, 37 genes (13 respiratory chain proteins, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs); it is inherited only **through the mother**; repair is weak and mutations are frequent — mitochondrial diseases (MELAS, Leber optic atrophy), aging.

sections.title: 2. Organization of the gene and the genome

blocks.text: A **gene** is a segment of DNA that carries information about a functional product (a polypeptide or an RNA). A eukaryotic gene consists of a **promoter** (TATA box, CAAT box), **exons** (coding regions) and **introns** (noncoding regions removed in splicing), **enhancers** and silencers.

blocks.title: Table 16.2. Differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes
head: Characteristic
Prokaryotes
Eukaryotes
rows: Transcription in the nucleus, translation in the cytoplasm

blocks.text: The human genome is ≈ 3.1 × 10^9^ base pairs (haploid), with ≈ 20,000 protein-coding genes.
Elements of genetic variability:

items: **recombination** — exchange of DNA segments (crossing-over in meiosis, V(D)J recombination of immunoglobulin genes);
**transposons** (“jumping genes”) — DNA segments that change their position within the genome; in humans, LINE and Alu elements;
**plasmids** — extrachromosomal circular DNA of bacteria; they carry **antibiotic resistance genes**; vectors in genetic engineering;
**bacteriophages** — viruses of bacteria; transduction, vectors in genetic engineering.

blocks.text: **Replication** is the copying of DNA; it takes place in the **S phase** of the cell cycle.
Principles:

items: **semiconservative** — each new molecule contains one old and one new strand (the Meselson–Stahl experiment);
**template-directed and complementary**;
**antiparallel** — the new strand is elongated only in the 5’→3’ direction;
**discontinuous (semidiscontinuous)** — the leading strand is synthesized continuously, the lagging strand as **Okazaki fragments**;
**requires a primer** — DNA polymerases cannot start synthesis; they only add nucleotides to an existing 3’-OH;
in eukaryotes there are many **origins of replication (ori)** — replicons.

blocks.label: Figure 16.1
blocks.caption: The main enzymes and processes at the replication fork (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: The substrates are **dNTPs** (dATP, dGTP, dCTP, dTTP); pyrophosphate is released and then hydrolyzed, which makes the process irreversible.

blocks.title: Table 16.3. Eukaryotic DNA polymerases
head: Polymerase
Function
rows: Primer synthesis, initiation of Okazaki fragments
Synthesis of the lagging strand; 3’→5’ exonuclease (proofreading)
Synthesis of the leading strand; 3’→5’ exonuclease (proofreading)

blocks.text: **Fidelity:** the **3’→5’ exonuclease (proofreading)** activity of DNA polymerases immediately removes a wrongly inserted nucleotide; together with mismatch repair, the error rate is ≈ 10^−9^–10^−10^.

**Relation to the cell cycle:** G~1~ → S → G~2~ → M; the transitions are controlled by **cyclins** and **cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)**; at the checkpoints the **p53** and **Rb** proteins arrest the cycle when DNA is damaged (topics 18–19). Replication licensing is granted only once per cycle.

**DNA methylation:** DNA methyltransferases (donor — S-adenosylmethionine) convert cytosine in **CpG** dinucleotides to 5-methylcytosine. Methylation of a promoter **silences** the gene — epigenetic regulation (X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting; silencing of tumor suppressor genes by methylation in tumors).

**Telomeres and telomerase:** the primer site at the 3’-end of linear DNA is not filled in, so the chromosome shortens with every division. The ends carry **telomeres** — (TTAGGG)n repeats. **Telomerase** is a **reverse transcriptase** with its own **RNA template**; it lengthens telomeres. It is active in germ cells, stem cells and **≈ 85–90% of tumor cells** (immortality), while its activity in somatic cells is low — telomere shortening is associated with **aging** (the Hayflick limit).

**Transcription** is the synthesis of RNA on a DNA template. One DNA strand (antisense, noncoding) serves as the template; the RNA is complementary to it and similar to the coding strand (with U instead of T); synthesis proceeds in the 5’→3’ direction, **no primer is required**, and the substrates are NTPs.

head: Enzyme
Location
Products
Sensitivity to α-amanitin

blocks.text: Stages:

items: **Initiation** — the general transcription factors (TFIID binds to the TATA box) and RNA polymerase II bind to the **promoter** and open the DNA over ≈ 14 base pairs; TFIIH phosphorylates the CTD domain of the polymerase.
**Elongation** — the polymerase moves along the DNA and elongates the RNA chain (≈ 40 nucleotides/s).

**Termination** — synthesis stops at termination signals (in prokaryotes, the rho factor or a GC-rich hairpin). Bacteria have a single RNA polymerase (the σ subunit recognizes the promoter) — **rifampicin** inhibits this enzyme.

blocks.label: Figure 16.2
blocks.caption: Formation and maturation of eukaryotic mRNA (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: Maturation of mRNA:

items: **5’-cap** — 7-methylguanosine attached by a 5’-5’-triphosphate bond; it protects the mRNA from exonucleases and is required for ribosome binding;
**3’-polyadenylation** — after cleavage downstream of the AAUAAA signal, poly(A) polymerase adds ≈ 200 adenylate residues; stability and export;

**splicing** — removal of introns and joining of exons; the **spliceosome** (small nuclear RNAs — snRNAs — and proteins) recognizes the GU…AG boundaries. **Alternative splicing** — several proteins are produced from one gene (for example, calcitonin and CGRP);

**RNA editing** — changes of individual nucleotides (apo B-100 in the liver, apo B-48 in the intestine — C→U editing, topic 8). **Maturation of rRNA:** the 45S precursor is cleaved in the nucleolus to form 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNAs; nucleotides are methylated.

blocks.text: **Maturation of tRNA:** the 5’- and 3’-ends are trimmed, **CCA** is added to the 3’-end (the amino acid attachment site), bases are modified (pseudouridine, dihydrouridine, inosine), and in some an intron is removed.

parts.text: Splicing defects: many forms of β-thalassemia — mutations in an intron of the β-globin gene lead to aberrant splicing. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), autoantibodies against snRNPs (anti-Sm) are produced.

sections.title: 8. Use of recombinant DNA and PCR in medicine

blocks.text: **Recombinant DNA technology: restriction enzymes** (bacterial endonucleases that cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences) are used to cut out a gene, which is joined into a **vector** (plasmid, virus) with **DNA ligase** and introduced into bacteria, yeast or animal cells. This is how the following are obtained: human **insulin**, growth hormone, erythropoietin, interferons, clotting factors (VIII), hepatitis B vaccine, monoclonal antibodies.

**Polymerase chain reaction (PCR):** in vitro amplification of a specific DNA segment. Each cycle: **denaturation** (94–95 °C) → **primer binding (annealing)** (50–65 °C) → **elongation** (72 °C, thermostable **Taq polymerase**). In 30–35 cycles the number of copies increases ≈ 2^n^ times (billions). The result is detected by agarose gel electrophoresis or in real time (fluorescent probes).

**PCR-based diagnosis:** infections (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis B and C viral load, mycobacteria of tuberculosis), hereditary diseases (mutations in cystic fibrosis and phenylketonuria), tumors (BCR-ABL), personal identification and paternity testing (forensic medicine), prenatal diagnosis. **Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR)** detects RNA viruses.

parts.text: Replication and transcription are “DNA → DNA” and “DNA → RNA”. Main difference: replication requires a **primer** and its substrate is **dNTP**; transcription does not need a primer and its substrate is **NTP**.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: isolation and hydrolysis of nucleoproteins from yeast
**Principle of the method:** nucleoproteins dissolve in weak alkali and precipitate when acid is added; on acid hydrolysis they break down into protein, purine bases, pentose and phosphoric acid.

items: Grind 5 g of yeast with 0.4% NaOH solution, stir for 20 minutes and centrifuge.
Add acetic acid to the supernatant — the nucleoproteins precipitate as white flakes.
Hydrolyze the precipitate by boiling with 10% sulfuric acid for 1 hour, cool and filter.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: qualitative reactions for the components of the hydrolysate

items: **Protein part** — the biuret reaction: a violet color when NaOH and CuSO~4~ are added to the hydrolysate.
**Purine bases** — the silver test: when ammoniacal AgNO~3~ is added, the silver salts of the purine bases form a light brown precipitate.
**Pentose** — the orcinol (Bial) reaction: a **green** color on heating with HCl and FeCl~3~ (ribose); the **diphenylamine** reaction — a **blue** color (deoxyribose, DNA).

**Phosphoric acid** — the molybdate reagent: on heating with ammonium molybdate and HNO~3~, a **yellow** crystalline precipitate (ammonium phosphomolybdate). **Results and analysis:** positive results of all the reactions confirm that nucleoproteins contain protein, nitrogenous bases, pentose and phosphate. Yeast contains mainly RNA, so the orcinol reaction is clearly positive.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: interpretation of a PCR electropherogram (case-based)

items: Identify the lanes on the gel image: marker (lengths of DNA fragments), positive control, negative control, patient samples.
Compare the band in the patient sample with the positive control (the length must be the same).

There must be no band in the negative control (if there is one — contamination, the result is invalid). **Results and analysis:** a band of the expected length in the patient lane is a positive result (pathogen DNA or a mutant allele is present).

skills.title: Skill: writing the complementary strand and the mRNA from a DNA sequence

items: Mark the direction of the given strand (5’→3’).
Write the complementary strand antiparallel: A↔T, G↔C (3’→5’).
Write the mRNA from the template strand: U instead of T; the mRNA is identical to the coding strand (with U).
Example: coding 5’-ATG GCT TAA-3’ → template 3’-TAC CGA ATT-5’ → mRNA 5’-AUG GCU UAA-3’.

skills.title: Skill: clinical interpretation of a PCR result

items: Determine the purpose of the test (infection, mutation, viral load).
Check that the controls worked correctly.
Assess a qualitative (present/absent) or quantitative result (real-time PCR: the Ct value — the smaller it is, the more starting DNA there is).
Consider the causes of false positives (contamination) and false negatives (inhibitors, sample quality).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A family ate mushrooms gathered in the forest. After 10–12 hours vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain began; on day 3 jaundice appeared, blood ALT was 3500 U/l and the prothrombin index fell sharply.
cases.ask: Which toxin is responsible? What is its molecular mechanism of action? Why is the liver specifically affected?
cases.answer: The toxin of the death cap (Amanita phalloides) — α-amanitin. It inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II: mRNA synthesis stops, proteins (including clotting factors) are not synthesized, and the cell dies. The toxin is absorbed from the intestine and reaches the liver first via the portal blood, actively enters hepatocytes through OATP transporters and acts again and again through the enterohepatic circulation — liver necrosis. The fall in the prothrombin index shows that protein synthesis in the liver is impaired.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient was diagnosed with tuberculosis and treatment with rifampicin was started. After a few weeks his urine and tears turned orange-red. The patient asked whether the drug also stops RNA synthesis in human cells.
cases.ask: What is the mechanism of action of rifampicin? Why does it have almost no effect on human cells?
cases.answer: Rifampicin binds to the β subunit of the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and blocks the initiation of transcription (the start of chain elongation). Eukaryotic RNA polymerases differ in structure and are not sensitive to rifampicin — hence its selective action. The orange color is the drug's own color (harmless). In addition, rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 in the liver — interactions with other drugs must be taken into account.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A nasopharyngeal swab was taken from a patient and tested for a viral infection by real-time RT-PCR. Result: Ct = 18 (positive control Ct = 25, no signal in the negative control).
cases.ask: How do you interpret the result? Why is the “RT” step needed to detect an RNA virus? What does the Ct value mean?
cases.answer: The result is positive: the sample contains viral RNA and the controls worked correctly. Taq polymerase cannot amplify the genome of RNA viruses — first, complementary DNA (cDNA) is synthesized from the RNA by reverse transcriptase and then amplified by PCR. Ct is the number of the cycle at which the fluorescent signal crosses the threshold; the smaller the Ct, the more starting copies there are (Ct 18 — a high viral load, the patient is likely to be infectious).

topics.title: Translation. Regulation of gene expression

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the genetic code and its properties, the components of the protein-synthesizing system, the stages of polypeptide chain synthesis on ribosomes, post-translational modification, protein folding and targeting, inhibitors of protein synthesis (antibiotics, toxins), the regulation of gene expression in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and cell differentiation.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the properties of the genetic code;
the structure of tRNA and the role of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases;
the structure of ribosomes (prokaryotic and eukaryotic);
the initiation, elongation and termination stages of translation;
the main post-translational modifications;
the antibiotics and toxins that block protein synthesis;
the operon model (the lactose operon) and the levels of regulation of gene expression in eukaryotes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine a peptide sequence from an mRNA sequence using the genetic code table;
predict the effect of a mutation on a protein;
explain the basis of the selective action of antibiotics.

sections.title: 1. The genetic code and its properties

blocks.text: The **genetic code** is the system that matches the sequence of mRNA nucleotides to the sequence of amino acids in a protein. The 4 kinds of nucleotides form 64 **codons** (triplets): 61 of them code for amino acids and 3 are **stop codons** (UAA, UAG, UGA). **AUG** is the start codon (methionine).

blocks.title: Table 17.1. Properties of the genetic code
head: Property
Meaning
rows: Each amino acid is coded by three nucleotides
One amino acid is coded by several codons (leucine, serine, arginine — 6 each); only Met and Trp — one each
Each codon codes for only one amino acid
Each nucleotide belongs to only one codon
There are no separators between codons — the reading frame is set from the start codon
The sequences in the gene and in the protein are in the same order
Almost the same in all organisms (small differences in mitochondria: UGA — tryptophan)

blocks.text: **Wobble hypothesis:** pairing between the 3rd nucleotide of the codon and the 1st nucleotide of the anticodon is less strict (for example, inosine pairs with U, C and A) — therefore the 61 codons can be read by ≈ 40 different tRNAs.

items: **Amino acids** (20 standard ones; selenocysteine — the UGA codon in a special context).
**mRNA** — the template.

**tRNA** — the “adapter”: a “cloverleaf” secondary structure and an L-shaped tertiary structure; the **anticodon loop** (recognizes the codon) and the **CCA at the 3’-end** (the amino acid is attached).

**Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases** — a separate enzyme for each amino acid; they activate the amino acid and attach it to the corresponding tRNA (2 high-energy bonds are consumed). They are the **main guarantee of the fidelity** of translation — they hydrolyze a wrongly attached amino acid (proofreading).
**Ribosomes.**
**Protein factors:** initiation (eIF), elongation (eEF), termination (eRF).
**Energy sources:** ATP (activation), GTP (initiation, elongation, termination).
Mg^2+^ and K^+^ ions.

blocks.title: Table 17.2. Structure of ribosomes
head: Characteristic
Prokaryotes
Eukaryotes

blocks.label: Figure 17.1
blocks.caption: Stages of translation (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Activation of amino acids:** amino acid + ATP → aminoacyl-AMP + PP~i~; aminoacyl-AMP + tRNA → aminoacyl-tRNA + AMP.

**Initiation (in eukaryotes):** the 40S subunit, the initiator **Met-tRNA~i~^Met^**, eIF2-GTP and other factors bind together to the **5’-cap of the mRNA** (eIF4E recognizes the cap) and move along the mRNA to the first **AUG** codon (**scanning**, the Kozak sequence). GTP is hydrolyzed and the 60S subunit joins — the **80S** initiation complex is formed, with Met-tRNAi in the **P site**. In prokaryotes the initiator is **formylmethionine-tRNA**, and 16S rRNA recognizes the **Shine–Dalgarno** sequence in the mRNA.
**Elongation** — three steps repeated for each codon:

items: The next aminoacyl-tRNA arrives at the **A site** with eEF1α-GTP (if the anticodon matches the codon, GTP is hydrolyzed).

**Peptidyl transferase** transfers the peptide in the P site to the amino group of the amino acid in the A site — a peptide bond is formed. This activity belongs to the **28S rRNA** of the 60S subunit (a **ribozyme**; in prokaryotes, 23S rRNA).

**Translocation** — under the action of eEF2-GTP the ribosome moves one codon along the mRNA; the peptidyl-tRNA moves to the P site, and the empty tRNA moves to the E site and is released. **4 high-energy bonds** are consumed for each peptide bond (2 in activation, 2 GTP in elongation). Many ribosomes read one mRNA at the same time — a **polysome**.

blocks.text: **Termination:** when a stop codon enters the A site, **release factors** (eRF1, eRF3-GTP) bind instead of a tRNA; peptidyl transferase transfers the peptide to water (hydrolysis), the polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates into subunits.

**Folding:** a polypeptide often reaches its correct conformation spontaneously; **chaperones** (heat shock proteins — Hsp70, Hsp60/chaperonins) prevent misfolding and aggregation. Misfolded proteins are degraded by the **ubiquitin–proteasome** system. Folding disorders — **prion diseases**, Alzheimer disease (β-amyloid), Parkinson disease (α-synuclein), cystic fibrosis (CFTR ΔF508).

**Targeting:** secretory and membrane proteins are directed to the **rough endoplasmic reticulum** by an N-terminal **signal peptide** (SRP — signal recognition particle) and are then sorted in the Golgi apparatus. Lysosomal enzymes are directed to lysosomes by the **mannose-6-phosphate** tag (I-cell disease — absence of this tag). Mitochondrial and nuclear proteins have special signal sequences.

Aminoacyl-tRNA analog — causes premature chain termination
Inactivates it by ADP-ribosylation — translocation stops
Removes an adenine (N-glycosidase) — the ribosome is inactive

blocks.text: The **selective action** of antibiotics is based on the difference in structure between prokaryotic (70S) and eukaryotic (80S) ribosomes. Because mitochondria contain 70S-type ribosomes, chloramphenicol can damage the bone marrow (aplastic anemia; in newborns, the “gray baby syndrome” — due to insufficient glucuronidation).

sections.title: 6. Regulation of gene expression in prokaryotes

blocks.text: An **operon** (Jacob and Monod, 1961) is a group of structural genes under the control of one promoter and operator that is transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA.

blocks.label: Figure 17.2
blocks.caption: Regulation of the lactose operon — induction (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Lactose operon (inducible):** structural genes — lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase). In the absence of lactose the **repressor** binds to the operator and blocks transcription. Lactose (more precisely, allolactose — the **inducer**) binds to the repressor and releases it from the operator — the genes are expressed. **Positive control:** when glucose is low, cAMP increases, and the **cAMP–CAP** complex binds to the promoter and enhances transcription (catabolite repression — when glucose is present, the lactose operon works weakly).

**Tryptophan operon (repressible):** when tryptophan is abundant it acts as a **corepressor**, activating the repressor, and the genes for the synthetic enzymes are switched off; an additional mechanism is **attenuation**.

sections.title: 7. Regulation of gene expression in eukaryotes

blocks.text: In eukaryotes, regulation operates at many levels:

items: **Chromatin level** — histone **acetylation** (histone acetyltransferases) loosens chromatin and activates transcription, while deacetylation silences it; **DNA methylation** (CpG) silences the gene — **epigenetic** regulation; genomic imprinting (Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes).

**Transcription level** — the main level: **transcription factors** bind to the promoter, **enhancers** (which work even thousands of base pairs away) and silencers. Examples: **steroid hormone receptors** — bind the hormone and then bind to hormone response elements in DNA (GRE); cAMP → PKA → **CREB**; metals → the metallothionein gene; hypoxia → HIF-1 → the erythropoietin gene.
**Gene amplification** — an increase in the number of gene copies (HER2, MYC in tumors; the dihydrofolate reductase gene in methotrexate resistance).
**Gene rearrangement** — V(D)J recombination of immunoglobulin genes.

**Post-transcriptional level** — alternative splicing, RNA editing, mRNA stability (the transferrin receptor mRNA is regulated by iron, topic 21), **microRNAs** and siRNAs (RNA interference) degrade mRNA or stop translation.
**Translation level** — phosphorylation of eIF2 (under stress, and in heme deficiency globin synthesis stops in reticulocytes); iron-dependent translation of ferritin mRNA (IRE/IRP).

**Post-translational level** — phosphorylation, proteolysis, degradation by ubiquitination. **Cell differentiation:** the genome is the same in all somatic cells, but in each cell type only a certain set of genes is expressed (globin in erythrocyte precursors, insulin in β-cells). This **selective expression** is provided by tissue-specific transcription factors and epigenetic marks; in ontogenesis the **homeotic (HOX) genes** determine the body plan. For example, the switch from fetal hemoglobin (HbF) to adult hemoglobin (HbA) is the silencing of the γ-globin gene and the activation of the β-globin gene.

parts.text: **Hydroxycarbamide** (hydroxyurea) in sickle cell anemia reactivates expression of the γ-globin gene and increases the amount of HbF — HbF reduces the polymerization of HbS.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: solving translation problems using the genetic code table

items: Find the first AUG codon in the given mRNA sequence — the reading frame starts there.
Divide the sequence into codons of three and determine the amino acids from the table.
Continue up to the stop codon. **Example:** 5’-GCC **AUG** UUU GGC UGG AAA UAG CC-3’ → Met–Phe–Gly–Trp–Lys (UAG — stop).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining the effect of a mutation on a protein

items: Compare the normal and mutant sequences.
Determine the type of mutation: substitution (missense, nonsense, synonymous), insertion or deletion (frameshift).

Predict its effect on the protein structure. **Example:** codon 6 of the β-globin gene GAG → GUG: glutamate → valine (missense) — HbS (sickle cell anemia). Deletion of a single nucleotide shifts the reading frame — all subsequent amino acids change, and a premature stop codon often appears.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: comparing the effects of protein synthesis inhibitors (working with a table)

items: Write the target of each antibiotic (30S, 50S, 80S, eEF2) in the table.

Mark its toxicity to humans and the reason (effect on mitochondrial ribosomes, on eukaryotic ribosomes). **Results and analysis:** substances that act selectively on prokaryotic ribosomes are used as antibiotics; those that block eukaryotic ribosomes (cycloheximide, ricin, diphtheria toxin) are toxic to humans.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An unvaccinated 6-year-old child has fever, sore throat, a gray, hard-to-remove membrane on the tonsils and swelling of the neck. A week later a heart rhythm disturbance developed (myocarditis).
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is the molecular mechanism of action of the toxin? Why is the heart affected?
cases.answer: Diphtheria. The toxin of Corynebacterium diphtheriae enters the cell by endocytosis, and its A fragment transfers an ADP-ribose residue from NAD^+^ to the elongation factor eEF2 (to the diphthamide residue) — eEF2 is inactivated, translocation and protein synthesis stop, and the cell dies. A single toxin molecule is enough to kill a cell. The toxin spreads through the blood and damages especially the myocardium and nerve tissue, where protein synthesis is active. Treatment — antitoxic serum (neutralizes the toxin before it enters the cells) and antibiotics; prevention — vaccine (toxoid).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient has pneumonia; the physician wants to choose one of the antibiotics that act on the 70S ribosome. The patient is a pregnant woman (second trimester).
cases.ask: Which antibiotics that block protein synthesis are not used in pregnancy, and why? Which group is relatively safe?
cases.answer: Tetracyclines (30S — block the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA) form chelates with calcium and accumulate in fetal bones and teeth (tooth discoloration, slowed bone growth). Aminoglycosides (30S — misreading of the code) are ototoxic to the fetus (deafness). Chloramphenicol (50S) — the “gray baby syndrome” in newborns (insufficient glucuronidation in the liver) and bone marrow suppression through mitochondrial ribosomes. Macrolides (azithromycin — 50S, blocks translocation) are considered relatively safe. The selective action is based on the structural difference between 70S and 80S ribosomes.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient has been diagnosed with sickle cell anemia. In the coding strand of the β-globin gene, codon 6 is GTG instead of GAG.
cases.ask: What kind of mutation is this? What change occurs in the protein and how does it lead to the disease? What is the basis of treatment with hydroxycarbamide?
cases.answer: A point missense mutation: GAG → GUG in the mRNA; in the protein, glutamate at position 6 (negatively charged, hydrophilic) is replaced by valine (hydrophobic) — HbS. Deoxygenated HbS molecules form long polymers through hydrophobic interactions; the erythrocytes become sickle-shaped, occlude small vessels (painful crises) and are rapidly destroyed (hemolytic anemia). Hydroxycarbamide reactivates expression of the γ-globin gene and increases the proportion of fetal hemoglobin (HbF); HbF blocks the polymerization of HbS.

topics.title: DNA damage and repair. Apoptosis. Basics of gene therapy

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the causes and types of DNA damage, molecular mutations (substitution, deletion, insertion), repair systems and their defects, genetic variability and protein polymorphism, the molecular basis of hereditary diseases, the use of DNA technologies in medicine, the differences between apoptosis and necrosis, the regulation of apoptosis, and the basics of cloning and gene therapy.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the physical, chemical and biological factors that damage DNA;
the classification of mutations and their effect on proteins;
the main repair systems (BER, NER, MMR, repair of double-strand breaks);
the diseases associated with repair defects;
protein polymorphism and its clinical importance;
the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways of apoptosis and the proteins that regulate it;
the principles and vectors of gene therapy.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the type of mutation from a sequence;
distinguish apoptosis from necrosis by biochemical features;
choose a method of molecular diagnosis for a hereditary disease.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Diseases associated with repair defects: **xeroderma pigmentosum** (NER), **Lynch syndrome** (MMR), **BRCA1/2** (homologous recombination), **ataxia-telangiectasia** (ATM), **Fanconi anemia** (cross-link repair), **Bloom syndrome** (helicase). The common feature is a predisposition to tumors.

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of DNA lesions occur in each cell per day; most of them are corrected by the repair systems.

blocks.title: Table 18.1. Factors that damage DNA
head: Factors
Examples
Type of damage
rows: Water, reactive oxygen species, replication errors
Depurination, deamination of cytosine to uracil, 8-oxoguanine, mispairing
Single- and double-strand breaks, free radicals

blocks.text: A **mutation** is a heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA. Mutations in germ cells are passed on to offspring (hereditary diseases), while somatic mutations lead to tumors and aging.
**By level:** gene (point), chromosomal (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation — the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)), genomic (aneuploidy — Down syndrome, trisomy 21).

blocks.title: Table 18.2. Molecular (gene) mutations and their effect on proteins
head: Mutation
Meaning
Effect on the protein
Example
rows: The codon changes, the amino acid does not
Because of the degeneracy of the code
A different amino acid is coded
The codon becomes a stop codon
Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of 3
Tay–Sachs disease, many forms of Duchenne muscular dystrophy

blocks.text: **Transition** — a purine is replaced by a purine or a pyrimidine by a pyrimidine; **transversion** — a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine.

blocks.label: Figure 18.1
blocks.caption: Types of DNA damage, repair systems and their defects (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Direct repair:** O^6^-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase transfers the methyl group to itself (a “suicide” enzyme); in bacteria **photolyase** splits thymine dimers under the action of light (absent in humans).

**Base excision repair (BER):** a damaged base (uracil, 8-oxoguanine, an alkylated base) is recognized by a specific **DNA glycosylase**, which cleaves the N-glycosidic bond; the resulting apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site is cut by **AP endonuclease**; DNA polymerase β fills the gap and DNA ligase seals it. This is also why DNA contains thymine instead of uracil: uracil formed by deamination of cytosine is recognized as “foreign”.

**Nucleotide excision repair (NER):** bulky lesions (thymine dimers, benzo(a)pyrene adducts) — a complex of XP proteins cuts the damaged strand on both sides and removes a fragment of ≈ 24–32 nucleotides; DNA polymerase δ/ε and ligase fill it in.

parts.text: **Xeroderma pigmentosum** is a hereditary defect of the NER enzymes (XP-A … XP-G) (autosomal recessive). Thymine dimers formed under sunlight are not repaired: the skin is very sensitive, there are freckles, and multiple **skin cancers** (basal cell carcinoma, melanoma) appear at an early age (before 10 years). Prevention — complete protection from the sun.

blocks.text: **Mismatch repair (MMR):** after replication, mispaired bases and small loops are recognized by **MSH2/MSH6**, and **MLH1/PMS2** nick the new strand; the new strand is removed by an exonuclease and resynthesized. Its defect causes **microsatellite instability** and **Lynch syndrome** (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer).
Repair of double-strand breaks:

items: **homologous recombination** — uses the sister chromatid as a template (in the S and G~2~ phases) and is accurate; the **BRCA1 and BRCA2** proteins take part — their defect sharply increases the risk of breast and ovarian cancer; the ATM kinase senses the break (ataxia-telangiectasia);

**nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ)** — Ku proteins and DNA-PK; fast, but nucleotides are sometimes lost (error-prone). **SOS repair (translesion synthesis):** special low-fidelity DNA polymerases “bypass” the damaged site — the probability of mutations is high.

parts.text: Diseases associated with repair defects: **xeroderma pigmentosum** (NER), **Lynch syndrome** (MMR), **BRCA1/2** (homologous recombination), **ataxia-telangiectasia** (ATM), **Fanconi anemia** (cross-link repair), **Bloom syndrome** (helicase). The common feature is a predisposition to tumors.

sections.title: 4. Genetic variability. The human genome. Protein polymorphism

blocks.text: **Mechanisms of genetic variability:** mutations, recombination in meiosis (crossing-over), independent assortment of chromosomes, transposons.

**The human genome:** ≈ 3.1 × 10^9^ base pairs; the protein-coding part is ≈ 1.5%; the rest consists of introns, regulatory elements, repetitive sequences (Alu, LINE, microsatellites) and pseudogenes. The genomes of two people are ≈ 99.9% identical; the differences consist mainly of **single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)** and copy number variations.
**Polymorphism** means gene variants that occur in a population with a frequency of ≥ 1%. **Protein polymorphism** means several variants (allelic forms) of one protein:

items: **AB0 blood groups** — glycosyltransferase variants;
the **HLA system** — very high polymorphism (transplantation, susceptibility to autoimmune diseases);
**hemoglobin variants** — HbS, HbC, HbE (more than 300);
**glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase** variants (topic 7);
**cytochrome P450** polymorphism (CYP2D6, CYP2C19) — “fast” or “slow” drug metabolizers (**pharmacogenetics**);
**N-acetyltransferase** — slow and fast acetylators of isoniazid;
**pseudocholinesterase** — with the atypical variant suxamethonium acts for a long time (apnea);
**α~1~-antitrypsin** variants (PiZZ — emphysema, liver cirrhosis).

blocks.text: **Monogenic diseases:** autosomal dominant (familial hypercholesterolemia, Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease), autosomal recessive (phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anemia, glycogenoses), X-linked (hemophilia A and B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency, Lesch–Nyhan syndrome). **Mitochondrial** — through the mother. **Multifactorial** — type 2 diabetes, atherosclerosis, hypertension.
DNA technologies in medicine:

items: **PCR** and real-time PCR — detection of mutations and infections (topic 16);
**restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP)** — if a mutation changes a restriction enzyme cutting site, the fragment lengths differ (diagnosis of sickle cell anemia);
**Southern blot** (DNA), **Northern blot** (RNA), **Western blot** (protein);
**sequencing** — the Sanger method, next-generation sequencing (whole exome/genome);
**FISH** — detection of chromosomal changes with fluorescent probes;
**DNA microarrays** — expression of thousands of genes or SNPs;
**genetic fingerprinting** (microsatellites) — forensic medicine, paternity testing;
**prenatal diagnosis** — chorionic villi, amniocytes, cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood.

blocks.text: **Apoptosis** is an energy-requiring, genetically programmed cell death. Its importance: embryogenesis (tissue between the fingers), the immune system (elimination of autoreactive lymphocytes), elimination of damaged and tumor cells, tissue homeostasis.

blocks.title: Table 18.3. Differences between apoptosis and necrosis
head: Characteristic
Apoptosis
Necrosis
rows: Physiological and pathological signals, DNA damage
Remains intact; phosphatidylserine moves to the outer leaflet
Condenses; DNA is cut into fragments of ≈ 180–200 base pairs (a “ladder”)
Phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies, no inflammation

blocks.label: Figure 18.2
blocks.caption: The extrinsic and intrinsic pathways of apoptosis (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Caspases** are proteases with cysteine in the active site that cleave after aspartate; they are synthesized as procaspases. **Initiator** (8, 9) and **effector** (3, 6, 7) caspases are distinguished. Effector caspases cleave cytoskeletal proteins, nuclear lamins and DNA repair enzymes (PARP) and activate **caspase-activated DNase**.
Regulation:

items: The **Bcl-2 family** — antiapoptotic (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) and proapoptotic (Bax, Bak, Bid, Bad) proteins regulate the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane;

**p53** (“guardian of the genome”) accumulates when DNA is damaged, arrests the cell cycle in G~1~ (p21) and activates repair; if the damage cannot be repaired, it triggers apoptosis through Bax, PUMA and NOXA;
**IAP** proteins (inhibitors of apoptosis) block caspases;

growth factors and the PI3K/Akt pathway — survival signals. **Disorders of apoptosis:** decreased apoptosis — tumors (overexpression of Bcl-2 in follicular lymphoma, t(14;18); p53 mutations) and autoimmune diseases; increased apoptosis — neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer, Parkinson), the penumbra zone in myocardial infarction and stroke, death of CD4 lymphocytes in AIDS.

sections.title: 7. Basics of cloning and gene therapy

blocks.text: **Cloning: gene (molecular) cloning** — inserting a gene into a vector and propagating it in bacteria or cell culture (production of recombinant proteins); **cell clones** — genetically identical cells derived from a single cell (monoclonal antibodies — hybridomas); **reproductive cloning** — somatic cell nuclear transfer (“Dolly” the sheep); **therapeutic cloning** — obtaining stem cells matched to the patient. The clinical importance of clones: monoclonal gammopathies (myeloma) and the **clonal** origin of tumors.
**Gene therapy** is the introduction of genetic material into cells in order to treat a disease.

blocks.title: Table 18.4. Strategies and vectors of gene therapy
head: Approach
Meaning
rows: Introduction of a normal copy in place of the defective gene (adenosine deaminase deficiency — the first gene therapy, 1990; spinal muscular atrophy; hemophilia B)
CRISPR-Cas9 — cutting DNA at a precise site and correcting it (increasing HbF via BCL11A in sickle cell anemia and β-thalassemia)
CAR-T cells — a gene for a receptor against a tumor antigen is introduced into the patient's T lymphocytes (B-cell leukemias)
Retroviruses and lentiviruses (integration into the genome — for stem cells; risk of insertional mutagenesis), adenoviruses, adeno-associated viruses (AAV — no integration, safer)
Ex vivo (cells are taken from the body, the gene is introduced and the cells are returned) and in vivo (the vector is delivered directly into the body)

blocks.text: Problems: immune response, insertional mutagenesis (leukemia), short duration of expression, high cost, ethical issues (modification of germ cells is prohibited).
Experiment 1: identifying the type of mutation from a sequence

items: Compare the coding strand sequences of normal and patient DNA.
Identify the differing nucleotide and its position.
Convert the codon to mRNA and find the amino acid in the genetic code table.
Name the type of mutation (synonymous, missense, nonsense, frameshift). **Example:** normal …TGG… (Trp) → mutant …TGA… (stop) — a nonsense mutation: the protein is shortened.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: diagnosis of sickle cell anemia by the RFLP method (case-based)
**Principle of the method:** the A→T mutation in the β-globin gene (GAG→GTG) destroys the cutting site of the restriction enzyme MstII.

items: Amplify the relevant part of the β-globin gene by PCR.
Treat with MstII and perform electrophoresis.

Compare the fragments. **Results and analysis:** the normal allele gives two short fragments (1.15 and 0.2 kb), and the mutant allele gives one long fragment (1.35 kb); in a heterozygote (HbAS) all three fragments are seen.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: introduction to methods for detecting signs of apoptosis (demonstration)

items: **DNA electrophoresis** — a “ladder” in apoptosis (fragments that are multiples of ≈ 180–200 base pairs) and a “smear” in necrosis.
Staining with **annexin V** — detects phosphatidylserine in the outer leaflet of the membrane (flow cytometry).
The **TUNEL method** — labels the ends of DNA breaks.
**Caspase-3 activity** — with a fluorogenic substrate. **Results and analysis:** using the methods together reliably distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis.

skills.title: Skill: choosing a method of molecular diagnosis for a hereditary disease

items: Determine the mode of inheritance of the disease and the known mutations.
If there is a single known mutation — PCR, RFLP or allele-specific PCR.
If there are many different mutations — gene sequencing.
Chromosomal changes — karyotype, FISH.
Trinucleotide expansion — special PCR or Southern blot.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing apoptosis from necrosis

items: Assess the cell volume and membrane integrity.
Determine whether there is an inflammatory reaction.
Assess the pattern of DNA fragmentation (ladder or smear).
Take caspase activity and the annexin V result into account.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An 8-year-old child has many freckles, dryness and ulcers on sun-exposed areas of the skin; a basal cell carcinoma was found on the face. The parents are related and healthy.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is its molecular basis? What is the mode of inheritance?
cases.answer: Xeroderma pigmentosum. Ultraviolet rays form covalent bonds between adjacent pyrimidines in DNA — thymine dimers. They are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) system; in this disease the XP proteins (enzymes that recognize and excise the damage) are defective — the dimers accumulate and lead to mutations during replication, including in p53 and other genes, so skin cancer develops at an early age. The inheritance is autosomal recessive (consanguineous marriage increases the risk). Treatment and prevention — complete protection from sunlight and early removal of tumors.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman's mother and maternal aunt died of breast cancer before the age of 45. Genetic testing of the woman found a frameshift mutation in the BRCA1 gene (heterozygous).
cases.ask: What is the function of the BRCA1 protein? Why does even a single mutant allele increase the risk of cancer? Which group of drugs is used in treatment?
cases.answer: BRCA1 takes part in the accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination (a tumor suppressor). In an inherited mutation one allele is inactive in all cells; if the second allele is lost by a somatic mutation during life (Knudson's “two-hit” hypothesis), homologous recombination does not work, the genome becomes unstable and a tumor develops. Therefore the inheritance appears dominant (risk ≈ 60–70%). PARP inhibitors (olaparib) are used in treatment: by blocking the repair of single-strand breaks, PARP inhibition selectively kills tumor cells with defective homologous recombination (synthetic lethality).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, an excess of the Bcl-2 protein was found in the tumor cells. The effect of chemotherapy is poor. The drug venetoclax was recommended.
cases.ask: How does Bcl-2 excess contribute to tumor growth? Why is chemotherapy ineffective? What is the mechanism of action of venetoclax?
cases.answer: Bcl-2 is an antiapoptotic protein: it blocks Bax and Bak and prevents the increase in mitochondrial membrane permeability and the release of cytochrome c. As a result, damaged tumor cells do not undergo apoptosis and accumulate. Many chemotherapy drugs damage DNA and trigger the intrinsic apoptotic pathway through p53 — when Bcl-2 is in excess, this pathway is blocked. Venetoclax is a Bcl-2 inhibitor (a BH3 mimetic): it releases the proapoptotic proteins and restores apoptosis in tumor cells.

topics.title: Biochemistry of oncogenesis

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of chemical, physical and viral carcinogenesis, the biochemical features of tumor cells, proto-oncogenes, oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, the mechanisms of neoplastic transformation and the multistage theory of carcinogenesis, invasion and metastasis, tumor markers, and the biochemical principles of tumor diagnosis and treatment.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the types of carcinogenic factors and the metabolic activation of procarcinogens;
the stages of carcinogenesis (initiation, promotion, progression);
the mechanisms by which proto-oncogenes are converted into oncogenes;
the main tumor suppressor genes (TP53, RB1, APC, BRCA);
the metabolic features of tumor cells (the Warburg effect);
the biochemical basis of invasion and metastasis;
tumor markers and their clinical importance;
the mechanism of multidrug resistance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: interpret tumor marker results;
show the activation pathway of a carcinogen in a scheme;
explain the mechanism of targeted therapy.

blocks.title: Table 19.1. Classification of carcinogenic factors
head: Group
Examples
Tumor
rows: Nitrosamines (formed from nitrites in the stomach)
Asbestos, arsenic, chromium, nickel, cadmium, benzene
Liver cancer; Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal cancer

blocks.text: Most chemical carcinogens are **procarcinogens**: they are not active themselves but are converted in the body by the **cytochrome P450** system (topic 26) into electrophilic **ultimate carcinogens**, which form covalent **adducts** with nucleophilic centers of DNA (most often the N7 or N2 atom of guanine). Direct-acting carcinogens (alkylating agents) do not require activation.

blocks.label: Figure 19.1
blocks.caption: Conversion of benzo(a)pyrene into an ultimate carcinogen and its detoxification (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Cytochrome P450 polymorphism and carcinogenesis:** smokers with highly inducible variants of CYP1A1 have a higher risk of lung cancer; gene variants of detoxifying enzymes (glutathione S-transferase GSTM1, N-acetyltransferase NAT2) affect the risk: for example, the risk is higher in smokers who lack the GSTM1 gene (null genotype); in slow acetylators, bladder cancer caused by aromatic amines is more common.

parts.text: Tobacco smoke contains more than 60 carcinogens. Benzo(a)pyrene diol epoxide causes G→T transversions at certain “hot spots” of the TP53 gene (codons 157, 248, 273) — the very same mutations are found in lung cancer in smokers. This is evidence of a direct molecular link between smoking and cancer.

sections.title: 3. Proto-oncogenes, oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes

blocks.text: **Proto-oncogenes** are normal genes that stimulate cell growth, division and differentiation. As a result of an activating mutation they become **oncogenes** (a **dominant** effect — one allele is enough; “a stuck gas pedal”).
Mechanisms of proto-oncogene activation:

items: **Point mutation** — the RAS protein loses its GTPase activity and remains permanently active (codons 12, 13, 61; in ≈ 30% of tumors);
**Gene amplification** — MYC (N-MYC in neuroblastoma), HER2/neu (≈ 20% of breast cancers);

**Chromosomal translocation** — the gene comes under a strong promoter (Burkitt lymphoma: t(8;14) — MYC next to an immunoglobulin gene) or a hybrid protein is formed (chronic myeloid leukemia: t(9;22) — **BCR-ABL**, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase);
**Integration next to a viral promoter** (insertional mutagenesis).

blocks.title: Table 19.2. Functions of proto-oncogene products
head: Group
Examples

blocks.text: **Tumor suppressor genes** are genes that stop cell division and ensure DNA repair and apoptosis (the “brakes”). For a tumor to develop, **both alleles** must be inactive (a **recessive** effect) — **Knudson's “two-hit” hypothesis**: in the hereditary form the first mutation is inborn and the second is somatic.

rows: “Guardian of the genome”: cell cycle arrest when DNA is damaged, repair, apoptosis

blocks.text: A tumor develops not as a result of a single mutation but as a result of successive changes in several (usually 4–7) genes over years (in the colon: APC → KRAS → SMAD4 → TP53 — the **Vogelstein model**: normal epithelium → adenoma → carcinoma).

blocks.label: Figure 19.2
blocks.caption: The multistage model of carcinogenesis (drawn after Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry)

blocks.text: As a result of **neoplastic transformation**, the cell acquires tumor features (the “hallmarks of cancer” according to Hanahan and Weinberg): self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals, evasion of apoptosis, unlimited division (**telomerase** activity), **angiogenesis** (VEGF), invasion and metastasis, reprogramming of energy metabolism, evasion of immune surveillance (PD-L1), genome instability, tumor-promoting inflammation.

items: **The Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis):** tumor cells break down glucose mainly to lactate even when oxygen is sufficient; they take up a lot of glucose (GLUT1, hexokinase II ↑) — this is the basis of diagnosis by **PET-CT**, which relies on the accumulation of ^18^F-fluorodeoxyglucose. Glycolytic intermediates are used for the synthesis of nucleotides, lipids and amino acids; the M2 isoform of pyruvate kinase is expressed.
**Glutamine “addiction”** — glutamine is a source of nitrogen and carbon (glutaminolysis).
**Anabolic processes are intense:** synthesis of nucleotides, DNA, protein and fatty acids (fatty acid synthase ↑); the pentose phosphate pathway is active (NADPH, ribose-5-phosphate).
**Shift of the isoenzyme spectrum to the embryonic type** (“dedifferentiation”): LDH-5 ↑, synthesis of embryonic proteins (α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen).
**Membrane changes:** loss of contact inhibition, adhesion molecules (E-cadherin) ↓, changes in the composition of glycoproteins and gangliosides.
**Mutant IDH1/2** (gliomas, leukemias) produces the “oncometabolite” 2-hydroxyglutarate, which disrupts the demethylation of DNA and histones.

**Cachexia:** the tumor “draws in” glucose and amino acids; cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) enhance lipolysis and muscle proteolysis; lactate is used for gluconeogenesis in the liver (the Cori cycle — a waste of energy).
**Detachment** — decrease in E-cadherin, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).
**Degradation of the basement membrane and the extracellular matrix** — **matrix metalloproteinases** (MMP-2, MMP-9 — type IV collagenases), plasminogen activator (uPA), cathepsins.
**Migration** — integrins, cytoskeletal rearrangement.
**Entry into blood and lymphatic vessels (intravasation)**, survival in the blood (a “coat” of platelets).
**Extravasation** and settling in a new site, **angiogenesis** (VEGF) — a metastatic focus.

blocks.text: Tumor markers are used mainly for **monitoring the effect of treatment and early detection of recurrence**; most of them are not specific enough for screening.

items: **Cytotoxic chemotherapy:** antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, 6-mercaptopurine — topic 14), alkylating agents and platinum drugs (DNA cross-links), topoisomerase inhibitors (doxorubicin, etoposide), mitotic poisons (vincristine, paclitaxel — microtubules).

**Targeted therapy: imatinib** — an inhibitor of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase (chronic myeloid leukemia); **trastuzumab** — a monoclonal antibody against HER2; gefitinib, osimertinib — EGFR inhibitors; vemurafenib — a BRAF V600E inhibitor; PARP inhibitors (in BRCA mutation); bevacizumab — against VEGF (an angiogenesis inhibitor).
**Hormonal therapy:** tamoxifen (an estrogen receptor modulator), aromatase inhibitors, androgen blockade.
**Immunotherapy:** immune checkpoint inhibitors (antibodies against PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4), CAR-T cells (topic 18).

**Enzymes:** L-asparaginase — leukemia cells cannot synthesize asparagine (asparagine synthetase is low), and asparagine in the blood is broken down. **Multidrug resistance:** in the membrane of tumor cells **P-glycoprotein** (the product of the MDR1 gene, an ABC transporter) increases and, using the energy of ATP, pumps drugs of various structures (doxorubicin, vincristine, paclitaxel) out of the cell. Other mechanisms: amplification of the target enzyme (dihydrofolate reductase with methotrexate), mutation of the target (imatinib-resistant BCR-ABL), increased glutathione S-transferase activity, enhanced repair, disruption of apoptotic pathways.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of α-fetoprotein in blood serum by enzyme immunoassay (demonstration)

**Principle of the method:** “sandwich” ELISA: the wells of the plate are coated with antibodies against AFP; AFP in the sample binds to them, and then a second, peroxidase-labeled antibody is added; when the substrate (TMB) is added, the color intensity is proportional to the amount of AFP (450 nm).

items: Pipette 50 µl of the standards and serum samples into the wells.
Add the conjugate, incubate at 37 °C for 60 minutes and wash 5 times.
Add the substrate, after 15 minutes add the stop solution and measure at 450 nm.

Find the concentration from the calibration curve. **Interpretation:** in adults the normal value is < 10 IU/ml; > 400 is highly characteristic of hepatocellular carcinoma (moderate increases are possible in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: assessment of lactate dehydrogenase isoenzymes in tumor tissue and blood serum (case-based)

items: Compare the results for total LDH activity and the isoenzyme spectrum (electrophoresis) with the normal values.

Pay attention to an increase in the proportion of LDH-4 and LDH-5. **Results and analysis:** in tumor cells the M-type isoenzymes adapted to anaerobic glycolysis (LDH-4, LDH-5) increase; in lymphomas and leukemias total serum LDH activity is an indicator of tumor mass and prognosis.

skills.title: Skill: clinical interpretation of tumor marker results

items: Determine which tumor the marker is characteristic of.
Compare the result with the normal value and assess the degree of increase.
Exclude causes of false positives (pregnancy — AFP, hCG; smoking — CEA; inflammation — CA-125).
Assess the dynamics: a decrease after treatment — effect; a renewed increase — recurrence or metastasis.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the target of a targeted therapy drug

items: Identify the molecular abnormality in the tumor (oncogene, amplification, translocation).
Choose a drug against the product of this abnormality (a kinase inhibitor or a monoclonal antibody).
Explain why a molecular test (HER2, EGFR, BCR-ABL, BRAF) is needed before the drug is used.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 35 years. Prolonged cough, hemoptysis, weight loss. Bronchoscopy shows a tumor, biopsy — squamous cell carcinoma; a G→T transversion at codon 248 of the TP53 gene was found in the tumor DNA.
cases.ask: What is the molecular mechanism of action of the carcinogen? Why is the TP53 mutation in particular important? Which stages of carcinogenesis can be identified?
cases.answer: Benzo(a)pyrene from tobacco smoke is converted in lung cells by CYP1A1 and epoxide hydrolase into the ultimate carcinogen — a diol epoxide — which forms an adduct with DNA guanine; during replication a G→T transversion occurs. TP53 is a tumor suppressor: it arrests cells with damaged DNA or sends them into apoptosis; its inactivation allows damaged cells to proliferate and new mutations to accumulate (genome instability). Initiation — DNA adducts and mutation; promotion — the chronic irritant and inflammatory effect of smoke; progression — additional mutations (KRAS and others), invasion. The long duration (decades) is consistent with the multistage theory.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old patient has a leukocyte count of 120 × 10^9^/l and an enlarged spleen. Cytogenetic testing revealed the Philadelphia chromosome. Treatment with imatinib was started; after 3 years the effect decreased.
cases.ask: What is the molecular basis of the disease? How does imatinib act? What could be the cause of resistance?
cases.answer: Chronic myeloid leukemia. As a result of the t(9;22) translocation, the BCR and ABL genes fuse to form the constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase; it activates signaling pathways (RAS-MAPK, PI3K/Akt, STAT), leading to uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells and evasion of apoptosis. Imatinib occupies the ATP-binding site of the ABL kinase and selectively inhibits it (targeted therapy). Resistance is most often due to point mutations in the kinase domain (for example, T315I), so the drug cannot bind; also BCR-ABL amplification or an increase in P-glycoprotein. In such cases next-generation inhibitors (dasatinib, nilotinib, ponatinib) are used.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 62-year-old patient was operated on for colorectal cancer. Before surgery CEA was 42 ng/ml, 1 month after surgery 3 ng/ml (normal < 5). After 8 months CEA rose to 28 ng/ml.
cases.ask: How do you interpret the CEA dynamics? Why is CEA unsuitable for screening? Which genes are involved in the multistage development of this tumor?
cases.answer: The fall of CEA to normal after surgery indicates that the tumor was completely removed; the renewed rise after 8 months is a sign of recurrence or metastasis (most often to the liver) — investigation (CT, PET-CT) is needed. CEA is not specific: it is also raised in smokers and in liver cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease and pancreatitis, and it is often normal at an early stage — so it is unsuitable for screening and is used mainly for monitoring treatment. Colorectal cancer develops according to the Vogelstein model: inactivation of APC (start of the adenoma) → activation of KRAS → loss of SMAD4 → inactivation of TP53 (carcinoma).

topics.title: Blood composition, plasma proteins. Biochemistry of the lymphoreticular system

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the functions of blood and the chemical composition of plasma, plasma proteins and enzymes, “acute phase” proteins, the role of albumin in water distribution and the mechanisms of edema, hematopoiesis and erythrocyte maturation, heme synthesis and its disorders (porphyrias), erythrocyte metabolism, hemoglobin and its derivatives, the buffer systems of blood, gas transport, the lymphoreticular and immune systems, and the metabolism of phagocytes.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the chemical composition and reference values of blood plasma and serum;
the fractions of plasma proteins and their functions;
acute phase proteins and their diagnostic importance;
oncotic pressure and the mechanisms of edema;
the stages and regulation of heme synthesis, and the porphyrias;
the features of erythrocyte metabolism;
hemoglobin derivatives (oxy-, carboxy-, methemoglobin) and Hb variants;
the buffer systems of blood and the transport of oxygen and CO~2~;
the mechanism of the “respiratory burst” in phagocytes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine total protein and albumin in blood serum;
interpret proteinogram (electrophoregram) results;
identify the types of dysproteinemia.

sections.title: 1. Functions and chemical composition of blood

blocks.text: **Functions of blood:** transport (gases, nutrients, metabolites, hormones), homeostatic (pH, osmotic pressure, temperature), protective (immunity, hemostasis), regulatory (transport of hormones and cytokines), excretory.
The blood volume is ≈ 6–8% of body weight (≈ 5 l); the **hematocrit** is 40–48% in men and 36–42% in women. **Plasma** contains fibrinogen; **serum** is the fluid after clotting, without fibrinogen.

blocks.title: Table 20.1. Main biochemical parameters of blood plasma (serum)
head: Index
Normal value

blocks.text: Most plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, most of the globulins) are synthesized in the **liver**, and γ-globulins (immunoglobulins) in **plasma cells**.
**Functions:** maintenance of oncotic pressure, transport, buffering, protection (immunoglobulins, complement), hemostasis (clotting factors), enzymatic, protein reserve.

blocks.label: Figure 20.1
blocks.caption: Electrophoregram of serum proteins (normal)

head: Fraction

blocks.text: **Albumin** is a small (66 kDa), very abundant protein of 585 amino acids; ≈ 12 g is synthesized per day, and its half-life is ≈ 20 days. **Transthyretin** (half-life ≈ 2 days) is a sensitive indicator of nutritional status; it transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein.
Plasma enzymes:

items: **secretory** (act in plasma) — clotting factors, plasmin, lipoprotein lipase (on the endothelium), lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase, pseudocholinesterase;
**excretory** — amylase, lipase (pancreas), alkaline phosphatase (liver, bone);
**intracellular (indicator)** — ALT, AST, LDH, CK; their increase in serum indicates cell damage (topics 2, 12, 23, 25).

blocks.text: In inflammation, trauma, infection and tumors, **IL-6**, IL-1 and TNF-α released from macrophages change the synthesis of acute phase proteins in the liver.

blocks.title: Table 20.3. Acute phase proteins
head: Group
Proteins
Degree of increase

blocks.text: **C-reactive protein (CRP)** reacts with the C-polysaccharide of pneumococci; it activates complement and is an opsonin. Normal < 5 mg/l; in bacterial infection > 100 mg/l; **high-sensitivity CRP** (1–3 mg/l) is used to assess cardiovascular risk. **Procalcitonin** is a specific marker of bacterial sepsis. **Ferritin** is also an acute phase protein (it can mask iron deficiency, topic 21). An increase in acute phase proteins (especially fibrinogen) causes an increase in the **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)**.

sections.title: 4. The role of albumin in the distribution of body water. Edema

blocks.text: Water exchange in capillaries is determined by **Starling forces**: at the arterial end the hydrostatic pressure (≈ 30–35 mm Hg) is greater than the oncotic pressure (≈ 25 mm Hg) — fluid moves out into the tissue; at the venous end the hydrostatic pressure (≈ 15) is lower than the oncotic pressure — fluid returns. **Albumin** provides ≈ 80% of the oncotic pressure.
Mechanisms of edema:

items: **decreased oncotic pressure** (hypoalbuminemia < 25–30 g/l): nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria), liver cirrhosis (synthesis ↓), starvation and kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), protein-losing enteropathy, burns;
increased hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction);
increased capillary permeability (inflammation, allergy);
impaired lymph flow (lymphedema).
**Hypoproteinemia** (< 60 g/l): malnutrition, liver diseases, nephrotic syndrome, blood loss, burns.
**Hyperproteinemia** (> 85 g/l): relative — dehydration; absolute — paraproteinemia (multiple myeloma), chronic infections (γ-globulins ↑).
**Dysproteinemia** is a change in the ratio of the fractions.

parts.text: **Multiple myeloma** is a tumor of a single clone of plasma cells: a **paraprotein** in serum (M spike), free light chains in urine — **Bence Jones protein** (precipitates at 60 °C and dissolves on boiling), osteolysis in bones (hypercalcemia), renal failure, anemia (the “CRAB” features).

sections.title: 6. Hematopoiesis and erythrocyte maturation. Heme synthesis

blocks.text: **Hematopoiesis** begins in the bone marrow from a pluripotent stem cell and is controlled by growth factors: **erythropoietin** (produced in the kidney in hypoxia via HIF-1), thrombopoietin (liver), G-CSF, GM-CSF and interleukins. Erythropoiesis requires iron, **B~12~ and folate** (DNA synthesis), B~6~ (heme synthesis), copper and protein.

Erythroid precursors → reticulocyte (anucleate, remnants of ribosomes and mitochondria, 1–2 days) → erythrocyte (lives ≈ 120 days). In erythroid cells the synthesis of heme and globin is coordinated: heme activates globin synthesis (it blocks the eIF2 kinase).

blocks.label: Figure 20.2
blocks.caption: Stages and regulation of heme synthesis (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: Heme is synthesized mainly in the **bone marrow** (≈ 85%) and the **liver** (for cytochromes). The first and the last three reactions take place in the mitochondria, and the intermediate reactions in the cytosol. **The key enzyme is δ-ALA synthase** (coenzyme — pyridoxal phosphate); heme inhibits it by feedback (it decreases its synthesis and its entry into the mitochondria). Hepatic ALA synthase-1 is induced by barbiturates, alcohol and some drugs (heme is needed for P450 synthesis).
**Porphyrias** are hereditary or acquired defects of the enzymes of heme synthesis; intermediate products accumulate.

items: **Acute intermittent porphyria** — PBG deaminase deficiency (autosomal dominant); severe abdominal pain, neurological and psychiatric disturbances; a lot of **δ-ALA and porphobilinogen** in the urine (the urine darkens in light); attacks are provoked by barbiturates, sulfonamides, alcohol and fasting. Treatment — hemin (inhibits ALA synthase), glucose.
**Porphyria cutanea tarda** — uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (the most common): skin photosensitivity, blisters; provoked by alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload.
**Erythropoietic protoporphyria**, congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Günther disease) — photosensitivity.

**Lead poisoning** — δ-ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase are inhibited: δ-ALA increases in the urine and protoporphyrin (zinc protoporphyrin) in erythrocytes; microcytic anemia, basophilic stippling of erythrocytes.

blocks.text: The mature erythrocyte has no nucleus, mitochondria or ribosomes — protein synthesis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation do not take place.

items: **Glucose** (GLUT1, insulin-independent) is the only energy source; ≈ 90% goes through **anaerobic glycolysis** → lactate (ATP for Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase and the membrane).

**The 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) shunt** (Rapoport–Luebering) decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen (facilitates the delivery of oxygen to tissues); it increases at high altitude and in anemia.

**Pentose phosphate pathway** (≈ 10%) — **NADPH** → glutathione reductase → reduced **glutathione** → detoxification of H~2~O~2~ and lipid peroxides (glutathione peroxidase, Se). **In G6PD deficiency**, oxidizing drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides) and legumes (favism) cause a hemolytic crisis (topic 7).
**Methemoglobin reductase** (NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase) reduces methemoglobin (Fe^3+^) back to hemoglobin (Fe^2+^).
Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase.
**Pyruvate kinase deficiency** — ATP decreases and erythrocytes undergo hemolysis (2,3-BPG increases).

blocks.text: **Hemoglobin** is a hemoprotein of 4 subunits (HbA: α~2~β~2~), each of which contains one heme (Fe^2+^ + protoporphyrin IX); it binds 4 molecules of O~2~. **Cooperativity** — the dissociation curve is S-shaped (hyperbolic for myoglobin). **Bohr effect** — an increase in H^+^ and CO~2~ decreases the affinity for O~2~ (facilitating O~2~ delivery in tissues); 2,3-BPG has the same effect.

blocks.text: **Hemoglobinopathies:** qualitative — changes in the structure of Hb (HbS, HbC, HbM); quantitative — **thalassemias** (reduced synthesis of α or β chains, microcytic anemia).

sections.title: 9. Buffer systems of blood. Gas transport

blocks.title: Table 20.6. Buffer systems of blood
head: System
Composition
Contribution
rows: ≈ 53%; an open system (the lungs regulate CO~2~, the kidneys regulate HCO~3~^-^)
≈ 5%; important inside cells and in urine

blocks.text: **System Composition Contribution**
**Henderson–Hasselbalch equation:** pH = 6.1 + lg ([HCO~3~^−^] / 0.03 × pCO~2~). Normally HCO~3~^−^ ≈ 24 mmol/l, pCO~2~ ≈ 40 mm Hg → pH ≈ 7.4.

**Disorders of acid–base balance: metabolic acidosis** (HCO~3~^−^ ↓: ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhea), **metabolic alkalosis** (HCO~3~^−^ ↑: vomiting, diuretics), **respiratory acidosis** (pCO~2~ ↑: hypoventilation), **respiratory alkalosis** (pCO~2~ ↓: hyperventilation). **Anion gap** = Na^+^ − (Cl^-^ + HCO~3~^−^), normal 8–16 mmol/l; it increases in ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis and methanol poisoning.
**Oxygen transport:** 1 g of Hb binds 1.34 ml of O~2~; 100 ml of arterial blood carries ≈ 20 ml of O~2~; very little is dissolved (0.3 ml).

**CO~2~ transport:** ≈ 70% as **bicarbonate** (in the erythrocyte, **carbonic anhydrase**: CO~2~ + H~2~O → H~2~CO~3~ → H^+^ + HCO~3~^−^; HCO~3~^−^ moves out into the plasma and Cl^-^ enters the erythrocyte — the **chloride shift**, Hamburger); ≈ 20–23% as **carbaminohemoglobin**; ≈ 7–10% dissolved. Deoxyhemoglobin binds H^+^ and CO~2~ better (the **Haldane effect**).

sections.title: 10. The lymphoreticular system. Metabolism of phagocytes

blocks.text: **The lymphoreticular (immune) system:** central organs — bone marrow and thymus; peripheral — lymph nodes, spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Functions: recognition and elimination of foreign antigens, immune memory, surveillance of tumor cells. **Lymph** is formed from tissue fluid; its composition is close to that of plasma but it contains little protein (20–40 g/l; intestinal lymph contains many chylomicrons — it is “milky”) and many lymphocytes. Age-related features: in children the thymus and lymphoid tissue are active; in old age the thymus involutes and the immune response weakens.

**Biochemical tools of the immune system:** immunoglobulins (IgG — the most abundant, crosses the placenta; IgM — primary response, a pentamer; IgA — mucous membranes, milk; IgE — allergy), the complement system, cytokines, interferons.

**Metabolism of phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages):** they obtain energy mainly from **glycolysis** (there is little oxygen at the site of inflammation); the pentose phosphate pathway is active. During phagocytosis there is a **“respiratory (oxidative) burst”**: O~2~ consumption rises sharply —

items: **NADPH oxidase** (in the membrane): 2O~2~ + NADPH → 2O~2~ •- (superoxide) + NADP^+^ + H^+^;
**superoxide dismutase**: 2O~2~ •- + 2H^+^ → H~2~O~2~ + O~2~;
**myeloperoxidase** (neutrophil granules): H~2~O~2~ + Cl^-^ → HOCl (hypochlorite) — a powerful bactericide;
NO synthase (in macrophages) — NO and peroxynitrite.

parts.text: **Chronic granulomatous disease** is a hereditary defect of NADPH oxidase (most often X-linked): phagocytes can engulf bacteria but cannot kill them — severe recurrent infections with catalase-positive microorganisms (staphylococci, Aspergillus) and granulomas. Diagnosis — the nitroblue tetrazolium test (negative) or the dihydrorhodamine test.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of total protein in blood serum by the biuret method
**Principle of the method:** in an alkaline medium peptide bonds form a violet complex with Cu^2+^ ions; the color intensity is proportional to the amount of protein (540 nm).

items: Add 1 ml of biuret reagent and 20 µl of serum to a test tube, 20 µl of standard (70 g/l) to a second tube and 20 µl of water to a third.
Keep for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Measure at 540 nm against the blank. **Calculation:** C (g/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × 70. **Normal:** 65–85 g/l.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of albumin in blood plasma on a biochemical analyzer (with bromocresol green)
**Principle of the method:** at pH 4.2 albumin binds the dye bromocresol green (BCG) and changes its color from yellow to green-blue (628 nm).

items: Select the “Albumin (BCG)” test on the analyzer; measure the calibrator and the control serum (the control values must be within the permitted range).
Place the tube with the patient's serum in the rack and enter its identifier.

The analyzer automatically mixes 5 µl of sample with 1 ml of reagent, measures after 1 minute and reports the result. **Interpretation:** normal 35–50 g/l. **Albumin/globulin ratio** = albumin / (total protein − albumin), normal 1.2–2.0; it decreases in inflammation, cirrhosis and myeloma.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: fractionation of serum proteins by electrophoresis (demonstration)

items: Apply serum to a cellulose acetate strip and run electrophoresis in veronal buffer (pH 8.6) at 200 V for 20 minutes.

Stain (amido black or Ponceau S) and read on a densitometer. **Results and analysis:** at pH 8.6 the proteins are negatively charged and move toward the anode; albumin is the fastest. Compare the proportions of the fractions with the normal values and determine the type of dysproteinemia.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting a proteinogram

items: Assess the amounts of total protein and albumin.
Compare the proportion of each fraction with the normal values.
Look for characteristic features: α~2~ ↑ (acute inflammation, nephrotic syndrome), β–γ bridge (cirrhosis), narrow M spike (myeloma), γ ↓ (immunodeficiency), α~1~ ↓ (α~1~-antitrypsin deficiency).
Draw a conclusion by comparing with the clinical picture.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing hemoglobin derivatives

items: Assess the color of the blood: cherry-red (HbCO), chocolate-brown (MetHb), dark red (deoxy-Hb).
Compare the pulse oximetry reading with arterial blood gases (with HbCO and MetHb the pulse oximeter may read falsely high).
Assess the CO-oximetry result and choose the principle of treatment (O~2~ or hyperbaric oxygenation; methylene blue).
