cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 6-year-old child has swelling of the face, legs and abdomen. Urine protein is 8 g/day. Blood total protein 42 g/l, albumin 15 g/l, cholesterol 11 mmol/l. The proteinogram shows α~2~-globulins 28%.
cases.ask: What syndrome is this? What is the mechanism of the edema? Why are α~2~-globulins and cholesterol increased?
cases.answer: Nephrotic syndrome. The glomerular filter is damaged, and albumin (a small protein) is lost in large amounts in the urine — hypoalbuminemia; the oncotic pressure falls and fluid leaves the vessels for the tissues (edema); the decrease in blood volume activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and enhances retention of Na^+^ and water. α~2~-Macroglobulin (a large molecule, 720 kDa) is not filtered, while the liver increases the synthesis of all proteins in response to the fall in oncotic pressure — a relative and absolute increase. For the same reason the synthesis of lipoproteins (LDL) in the liver increases and LPL activity decreases — hypercholesterolemia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In winter a coal stove was burning in a closed room. In the morning the family members woke up with headache, nausea and weakness; one was unconscious. The skin was pinkish red. The pulse oximeter showed SpO~2~ 98%; CO-oximetry showed HbCO 35%.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Why did the pulse oximeter show a normal value? What are the mechanism of poisoning and the principles of treatment?
cases.answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO binds to the iron of hemoglobin ≈ 200–250 times more strongly than O~2~, forming carboxyhemoglobin; the remaining hemes release O~2~ less readily (the dissociation curve shifts to the left) — tissue hypoxia. CO also inhibits cytochrome oxidase. An ordinary pulse oximeter cannot distinguish HbCO from HbO~2~ (both are red) — a falsely normal value; CO-oximetry is needed. Treatment: removal from the source of poisoning, 100% oxygen (the half-life of HbCO shortens from 4–5 hours to ≈ 1 hour), hyperbaric oxygenation in severe cases.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old woman has severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia and weakness in the legs. The attack began after she took a barbiturate for insomnia. Her urine turned red-brown on standing in the light. Urinary porphobilinogen is sharply increased.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is its biochemical basis? Why did the barbiturate provoke the attack? What is the principle of treatment?
cases.answer: Acute intermittent porphyria — PBG deaminase deficiency (autosomal dominant). Barbiturates induce the synthesis of cytochrome P450 in the liver; heme consumption increases and its amount decreases — the feedback is lost and the synthesis of δ-ALA synthase rises sharply; because of the PBG deaminase deficiency, δ-ALA and porphobilinogen accumulate. They are neurotoxic (autonomic and peripheral nervous system) — abdominal pain, polyneuropathy. In light, porphobilinogen is converted into porphyrins and porphobilin, which turn the urine red. Treatment: stopping the provoking drugs, intravenous hemin (inhibits ALA synthase by feedback) and glucose (reduces the induction of ALA synthase).

topics.title: Iron metabolism. Biochemistry of hemostasis

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the distribution, absorption, transport, storage and regulation of iron in the body, states of iron deficiency and iron overload, the vascular–platelet and coagulation components of hemostasis, the modern cell-based theory of hemostasis, the anticoagulant and fibrinolytic systems, disorders of hemostasis and the mechanisms of action of antithrombotic drugs.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the amount and distribution of iron in the body;
the absorption, transport (transferrin) and storage of iron (ferritin, hemosiderin);
the regulation of iron metabolism through hepcidin and the IRE/IRP system;
the biochemical features of iron deficiency anemia, anemia of chronic disease and hemochromatosis;
the mechanisms of platelet adhesion and aggregation;
the clotting factors and the role of vitamin K;
the stages of coagulation according to the cell-based model;
the anticoagulant and fibrinolytic systems.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine iron in blood serum and assess the parameters of iron metabolism;
interpret coagulogram results (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer).

sections.title: 1. Distribution and functions of iron in the body

blocks.text: The adult body contains ≈ 3–5 g of iron (≈ 50 mg/kg in men, ≈ 35–40 mg/kg in women).

blocks.title: Table 21.1. Distribution of iron in the body
head: Pool
Amount
Form
rows: Stores (macrophages of the liver, spleen and bone marrow)
Heme (cytochromes, catalase, peroxidase), Fe-S proteins, ribonucleotide reductase

blocks.text: **Functions:** transport and storage of oxygen (Hb, myoglobin), electron transport (cytochromes, Fe-S centers), redox reactions (P450, catalase), DNA synthesis (ribonucleotide reductase). Free iron is toxic — it forms hydroxyl radicals through the **Fenton reaction** (Fe^2+^ + H~2~O~2~ → Fe^3+^ + OH^-^ + OH^•^); therefore iron in the body is always bound to proteins.

sections.title: 2. Absorption, transport and storage of iron

blocks.label: Figure 21.1
blocks.caption: Iron metabolism and its regulation by hepcidin (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Absorption:** the daily diet supplies 10–20 mg of iron, of which only **1–2 mg** (10%) is absorbed (3–5 times more in deficiency) — mainly in the **duodenum and the initial part of the jejunum**.

items: **Heme iron** (meat, liver, fish) is well absorbed (20–30%);

**nonheme iron** (plants) — Fe^3+^ is reduced to Fe^2+^ by **duodenal cytochrome b** (a ferrireductase) on the surface of the intestinal cell and by **ascorbic acid**, and enters through **DMT1**. Gastric HCl, ascorbate, fructose and amino acids improve absorption; phytates (grain), polyphenols (tea, coffee), phosphates, calcium and antacids reduce it. In the enterocyte iron is stored as **ferritin** (the intestinal cell is shed in 2–3 days — the iron is lost) or released into the blood through **ferroportin** in the basolateral membrane; **hephaestin** (a Cu-containing protein) oxidizes it to Fe^3+^.

blocks.text: **Transport: transferrin** (a β-globulin synthesized in the liver) binds 2 Fe^3+^ ions. Normally ≈ 1/3 of transferrin is saturated (**saturation coefficient** 20–45%). Cells take up iron by endocytosis through the **transferrin receptor (TfR1)**; in the acidic medium of the endosome the iron is released, and apotransferrin and the receptor return to the membrane.

**Storage: ferritin** — up to 4500 Fe^3+^ atoms (as hydroxyphosphate) inside a shell of 24 subunits; it is water-soluble and rapidly mobilized. Serum ferritin reflects storage iron (1 µg/l ≈ 8–10 mg of storage iron). **Hemosiderin** is an insoluble aggregate formed by the breakdown of ferritin in lysosomes; it accumulates in iron overload (stains with Prussian blue).

**Recycling:** erythropoiesis requires ≈ 20–25 mg of iron per day — almost all of it is obtained from the heme of senescent erythrocytes in the macrophages of the spleen and liver (**heme oxygenase**). The body has **no** mechanism for active iron excretion: the daily loss is ≈ 1 mg (intestinal and skin epithelium), in women an additional ≈ 0.5–1 mg with menstruation, and in pregnancy ≈ 3–4 mg/day.

**Systemic regulation — hepcidin:** a peptide hormone of 25 amino acids synthesized in the liver. It binds to ferroportin and causes its endocytosis and degradation — iron absorption from the intestine and iron release from macrophages decrease.

items: Hepcidin **increases** in iron overload and **in inflammation (IL-6)** — the cause of anemia of chronic disease;

hepcidin **decreases** in iron deficiency, hypoxia, enhanced erythropoiesis (erythroferrone) and hemochromatosis (HFE, hemojuvelin defect). **Intracellular regulation — the IRE/IRP system:** when iron is low, **iron regulatory proteins (IRP)** bind to the **iron-responsive elements (IRE)** in mRNA:
binding to the IRE at the 5’-end of **ferritin** mRNA, they **stop translation** (stores decrease);
binding to the IRE at the 3’-end of **transferrin receptor** mRNA, they **stabilize** the mRNA (iron uptake increases). When iron is abundant, IRP dissociates — the opposite result.

blocks.title: Table 21.2. Parameters of iron metabolism in various conditions
head: Parameter (normal)
Iron deficiency anemia
Anemia of chronic disease
Hemochromatosis

blocks.text: **Iron deficiency anemia** is the most common anemia: chronic blood loss (menstruation, gastrointestinal bleeding — in adults a tumor must be excluded), pregnancy, periods of growth, malabsorption (celiac disease, gastric resection), diet. A **microcytic, hypochromic** anemia (MCV, MCH ↓); sideropenic signs — dry skin, hair loss, brittle nails (koilonychia), altered taste (eating chalk or ice — pica). Stages: prelatent (stores ↓ — ferritin ↓), latent (transport iron ↓), overt anemia. Treatment — oral Fe^2+^ preparations (with ascorbic acid), intravenous if necessary.
**Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)** — IL-6 → hepcidin ↑ → iron is “trapped” in macrophages (ferritin N or ↑) and does not reach erythropoiesis.

**Hemochromatosis: hereditary** — mutation of the HFE gene (C282Y, autosomal recessive): low hepcidin → persistently high iron absorption → liver (cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma), pancreas (“bronze diabetes”), heart (cardiomyopathy), skin pigmentation, joints, hypogonadism. **Secondary** — multiple blood transfusions (thalassemia), ineffective erythropoiesis. Treatment — phlebotomy (bloodletting), deferoxamine, deferasirox (chelators).
**Acute iron poisoning** (iron tablets in children): gastrointestinal injury, metabolic acidosis, liver necrosis; antidote — deferoxamine.

**Hemostasis** is the system that stops bleeding when a vessel is damaged and keeps the blood in a fluid state. Its components: the vessel wall, platelets, coagulation factors, anticoagulants, fibrinolysis.
Vascular–platelet (primary) hemostasis:

items: **Vasoconstriction** (thromboxane A~2~, serotonin, endothelin).
**Adhesion** — platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen through **von Willebrand factor** (vWF) and the GPIb-IX-V receptor, and directly to collagen through GPVI and integrin α~2~β~1~.

**Activation and secretion** — platelets change shape and release ADP, serotonin, Ca^2+^, vWF, fibrinogen and factor V from their granules; **thromboxane A~2~** is synthesized (from arachidonic acid by **cyclooxygenase-1**); phosphatidylserine of the inner leaflet of the membrane moves to the outer leaflet — a surface for the coagulation complexes.

**Aggregation** — the **GPIIb/IIIa** receptor (integrin αIIbβ~3~) is activated and links platelets to one another through **fibrinogen** bridges — the **platelet plug**. Normally the **endothelium** is antithrombotic: **prostacyclin (PGI~2~)** and **nitric oxide (NO)** stop aggregation and vasoconstriction (through cAMP and cGMP), ecto-ADPase breaks down ADP, and thrombomodulin, heparan sulfate, t-PA and tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) are produced.

blocks.title: Table 21.3. Clotting factors
head: Factor
Name
Feature
rows: Vitamin K-dependent; the shortest half-life (≈ 6 hours)
Cofactor of tenase; carried by vWF; deficiency — hemophilia A
Vitamin K-dependent; the center of prothrombinase

blocks.text: **The role of vitamin K:** in factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S, glutamate residues are converted to **γ-carboxyglutamate** in the liver by **γ-glutamyl carboxylase** (cofactor — reduced vitamin K, the hydroquinone form). γ-Carboxyglutamate binds the factors to the phospholipid membrane via Ca^2+^. The vitamin K epoxide formed is regenerated by **vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)** — **warfarin** inhibits this enzyme.
**The cell-based model (modern theory)** — clotting takes place on phospholipid surfaces (cells bearing tissue factor and activated platelets) in three stages:

blocks.label: Figure 21.2
blocks.caption: The cell-based model of hemostasis: initiation, amplification, propagation (drawn after Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry)

items: **Initiation** — when a vessel is damaged, **tissue factor** on fibroblasts and subendothelial cells forms a complex with VIIa and activates X and IX; Xa + Va generate a small amount of thrombin.
**Amplification** — this small amount of thrombin activates platelets and activates factors V, VIII (releasing it from vWF) and XI.

**Propagation** — on the surface of activated platelets **tenase** (IXa + VIIIa) generates a lot of Xa, and **prothrombinase** (Xa + Va + Ca^2+^ + phospholipid) provides the thrombin “burst”. **Fibrin formation:** thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides A and B from fibrinogen → fibrin monomers polymerize spontaneously (soluble fibrin) → **XIIIa** (activated by thrombin) forms isopeptide bonds between glutamine and lysine residues, creating a stable, insoluble fibrin mesh. Actomyosin inside the platelets (thrombosthenin) contracts the clot (**retraction**).

blocks.text: The classical “extrinsic” (TF, VII) and “intrinsic” (XII, XI, IX, VIII) pathways have been retained to explain laboratory tests: **prothrombin time (PT/INR)** — the extrinsic and common pathways (VII, X, V, II, I); **activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)** — the intrinsic and common pathways.
Physiological anticoagulants:

items: **antithrombin III** — a serpin; it inhibits thrombin, Xa, IXa and XIa; **heparin** (and heparan sulfate on the endothelium) increases its activity ≈ 1000 times;

**the protein C – protein S system** — thrombin binds to **thrombomodulin** on the endothelium and activates protein C; activated protein C (cofactor — protein S) proteolyzes Va and VIIIa. **Factor V Leiden** (Arg506Gln) is a factor V resistant to activated protein C, the most common hereditary thrombophilia;
**tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI)** — blocks the TF–VIIa–Xa complex;
α~2~-macroglobulin, heparin cofactor II.

blocks.text: **Fibrinolysis: plasminogen** (synthesized in the liver) binds to fibrin and is converted into **plasmin** by **tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA)** (endothelium) or **urokinase**; plasmin breaks down fibrin into **fibrin degradation products**, including **D-dimer**. **D-dimer** is a marker of the breakdown of stabilized (cross-linked by XIIIa) fibrin; it increases in deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and DIC.

**Antifibrinolytic system: α~2~-antiplasmin** (inhibits plasmin), **plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1)**, thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor. Drug — **tranexamic acid** (a lysine analog that blocks the binding of plasminogen to fibrin).

sections.title: 8. Disorders of hemostasis and antithrombotic drugs

items: **Hemophilia A** (factor VIII) and **B** (factor IX) — X-linked recessive; bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) and muscles; aPTT prolonged, PT normal.
**Von Willebrand disease** is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder (autosomal dominant): mucosal bleeding; bleeding time and aPTT prolonged.

**Vitamin K deficiency** — hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (no intestinal microflora, little vitamin K in breast milk — vitamin K is given in the maternity ward), obstructive jaundice (impaired fat absorption), prolonged antibiotic use, warfarin overdose; PT prolonged.
**Thrombocytopenias and thrombocytopathies** — hereditary (Glanzmann thrombasthenia — GPIIb/IIIa; Bernard–Soulier syndrome — GPIb) and acquired (aspirin, uremia, immune thrombocytopenia).

**DIC** (disseminated intravascular coagulation) — sepsis, obstetric complications, tumors: first hypercoagulation, then consumption of factors and platelets and bleeding; fibrinogen ↓, platelets ↓, PT and aPTT prolonged, D-dimer ↑↑.
**Thrombophilias** — factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, deficiency of antithrombin III, protein C and S, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperhomocysteinemia.

blocks.title: Table 21.4. Mechanisms of action of antithrombotic drugs

Target

Blockers of the ADP receptor P2Y~12~
Activates antithrombin III (thrombin and Xa); monitoring — aPTT; antidote — protamine sulfate
VKORC1 inhibitor — vitamin K-dependent factors are not carboxylated; monitoring — INR (2.0–3.0); antidote — vitamin K

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of iron in blood serum by the ferrozine method

**Principle of the method:** in an acidic medium iron is released from transferrin, and a reducing agent (ascorbic acid) converts Fe^3+^ to Fe^2+^; Fe^2+^ forms a violet complex with ferrozine (562 nm).

items: Add 1 ml of working reagent to the tubes, then 200 µl of serum, standard (17.9 µmol/l) or water.
Keep for 10 minutes at room temperature and measure at 562 nm. **Calculation:** C (µmol/l) = (Esample / Estandard) × 17.9.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** 11–30 µmol/l in men, 9–27 µmol/l in women. A hemolyzed sample is unsuitable (iron is released from erythrocytes). The diurnal variation of iron is large (higher in the morning) — therefore ferritin and transferrin saturation are also determined for diagnosis.
Experiment 2: determination of coagulogram parameters (prothrombin time and aPTT, demonstration)

**Principle of the method:** the time to clot formation after adding thromboplastin (tissue factor + phospholipid) and CaCl~2~ to citrated plasma (PT); with a kaolin–phospholipid activator and CaCl~2~ — aPTT.

items: Collect blood with 3.2% sodium citrate (9:1) and separate the plasma by centrifugation.
At 37 °C add 100 µl of thromboplastin–calcium reagent to 50 µl of plasma and record the clotting time on a coagulometer.
For aPTT add 50 µl of activator to 50 µl of plasma, incubate for 3 minutes, then add 50 µl of CaCl~2~ and record the time.

head: Index
Normal value
Prolongation
rows: Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver diseases, factor VII
Heparin, hemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, lupus anticoagulant

skills.title: Skill: determining the cause of bleeding from the coagulogram

items: Assess the platelet count and bleeding time (primary hemostasis).
PT prolonged, aPTT normal — factor VII, warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency.
aPTT prolonged, PT normal — factors VIII, IX, XI (hemophilia), heparin, von Willebrand disease.
Both prolonged, fibrinogen and platelets low, D-dimer high — DIC.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman complains of weakness, fatigue, hair loss and brittle nails; she craves chalk. Her menstrual periods are heavy and prolonged. Hb 92 g/l, MCV 68 fl, serum iron 5 µmol/l, TIBC 88 µmol/l, transferrin saturation 6%, ferritin 6 µg/l.
cases.ask: What kind of anemia is this? Explain the parameters biochemically. What are the principles of treatment?
cases.answer: Iron deficiency anemia (chronic blood loss — menorrhagia). Storage iron is exhausted (ferritin very low), transport iron is low (serum iron and transferrin saturation low); in iron deficiency the liver increases transferrin synthesis — TIBC is high. There is not enough iron for heme synthesis — the erythrocytes are small and contain little hemoglobin (microcytosis, hypochromia). Deficiency of iron-containing enzymes (in the epithelium) causes changes in the skin, hair and nails and pica. Treatment: identify and eliminate the cause of the menorrhagia; Fe^2+^ preparations with ascorbic acid, taken separately from tea and dairy products; continue for 2–3 months after Hb normalizes to replenish the stores (under ferritin control).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 68-year-old man takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. A week after he started taking an antibiotic for pneumonia, his gums began to bleed and his urine turned red. INR 7.5 (target 2–3).
cases.ask: What is the mechanism of action of warfarin? Why did the INR rise? How should help be provided?
cases.answer: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and decreases the reduced form of vitamin K; factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S are not carboxylated in the liver — they cannot bind Ca^2+^ and phospholipids, and clotting slows down. Antibiotics eliminate the intestinal microflora and reduce the source of vitamin K~2~; some of them (metronidazole, fluoroquinolones, macrolides) inhibit CYP2C9 in the liver and slow the breakdown of warfarin — its effect increases. Help: stop warfarin and give vitamin K (phytomenadione); in serious bleeding, prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma (ready-made factors).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 5-year-old boy has prolonged bleeding after minor injuries and bleeding into the knee joint. His mother's brother has the same disease. Platelets 280 × 10^9^/l, PT 13 s, aPTT 78 s, factor VIII activity 2%.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the laboratory results on the basis of the hemostasis model. What is the mode of inheritance?
cases.answer: Hemophilia A (severe form). Factor VIII is the cofactor of the tenase complex (IXa + VIIIa); without it, the “burst” of Xa and thrombin on the platelet surface does not occur in the propagation stage — a stable fibrin clot is not formed; primary (platelet) hemostasis is preserved, so what is characteristic is not bleeding from minor wounds but deep bleeding into joints and muscles. aPTT (intrinsic pathway: XII, XI, IX, VIII) is prolonged, PT (VII, X, V, II) is normal. The inheritance is X-linked recessive: the mother is a carrier, her brother is affected. Treatment — recombinant factor VIII or emicizumab (a bispecific antibody that binds IXa and X).

topics.title: Biochemistry of connective tissue

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the composition and functions of the extracellular matrix, the amino acid composition, structure, types, synthesis and breakdown of collagen, the importance of ascorbic acid, diseases associated with disorders of collagen synthesis, the structure and metabolism of elastin, the structure, functions, synthesis and breakdown of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans (mucopolysaccharidoses), and adhesive proteins.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main components of the extracellular matrix;
the specific features of the amino acid composition and structure of collagen;
the types of collagen and their location;
the intracellular and extracellular stages of collagen synthesis and the role of vitamin C and copper;
the breakdown of collagen and the diagnostic importance of hydroxyproline determination;
the properties of elastin and the role of desmosine;
the structure and functions of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans;
mucopolysaccharidoses and collagenopathies.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine hydroxyproline in urine and interpret the result;
determine glycosaminoglycans (sialic acids) in blood serum;
explain the biochemical features of connective tissue diseases.

blocks.text: **Connective tissue** consists of cells (fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteoblasts, macrophages, mast cells) and a large amount of **extracellular matrix**. Composition of the matrix:

items: **fibers** — collagen, elastin, reticulin;
**ground (amorphous) substance** — proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, water;

**adhesive glycoproteins** — fibronectin, laminin, nidogen, tenascin. **Functions:** supportive-mechanical (tendon, bone, cartilage), protective (barrier, phagocytosis), trophic (exchange of substances), water–salt balance, reparative (wound healing), signaling (storage of growth factors, cell migration and differentiation).

blocks.text: **Collagen** is the most abundant protein in the body (≈ 25–33% of total protein).
Specific features of the amino acid composition:

items: every third amino acid is **glycine** (≈ 33%): the (Gly–X–Y)n repeat; because glycine is the smallest, the three chains pack tightly along the axis of the helix;
there is a lot of **proline** and **hydroxyproline** (≈ 21%; proline is most often in position X and hydroxyproline in position Y);
**hydroxylysine** — for glycosylation and cross-links;
**no tryptophan**, little cysteine and tyrosine — collagen is not a nutritionally complete protein.

blocks.text: Structure:

items: **primary** — (Gly–X–Y)n;
**secondary** — each α-chain is a left-handed **polyproline helix** (not an α-helix; the proline ring does not allow an α-helix);

**tertiary** — three α-chains wind around one another to form a right-handed **triple helix** (superhelix) — **tropocollagen** (length 300 nm, diameter 1.5 nm); hydrogen bonds (with the participation of the OH groups of hydroxyproline) stabilize it;

**quaternary** — tropocollagen molecules are arranged in a staggered manner (shifted by 1/4 of their length) to form **fibrils** (periodic cross-striations of 67 nm in the electron microscope); fibrils combine into fibers.

blocks.title: Table 22.1. Main types of collagen
head: Type
Location
Feature
rows: Blood vessels, skin (embryonic), internal organs, reticular fibers
Fibril-forming; early stage of wound healing
Fibrils anchoring the epithelium to the basement membrane

blocks.label: Figure 22.1
blocks.caption: Stages of collagen biosynthesis (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: Intracellular stages (fibroblast):

items: Synthesis of the **preprocollagen** α-chains in the rough endoplasmic reticulum; the signal peptide is cleaved off.

**Hydroxylation** — **prolyl 4-hydroxylase**, prolyl 3-hydroxylase and **lysyl hydroxylase**; cofactors: **Fe^2+^, O~2~, α-ketoglutarate and ascorbic acid** (keeps the iron in the reduced state). Hydroxylation is possible only until the helix is formed.
**Glycosylation** of hydroxylysine residues (galactose, glucosyl-galactose).
The C-propeptides join the three chains by disulfide bonds — the **triple helix** forms like a “zipper” (from the C-end to the N-end) — **procollagen**.
**Secretion** via the Golgi apparatus. **Extracellular stages:**
**Procollagen N- and C-peptidases** cleave off the propeptides → **tropocollagen** (the propeptides enter the blood — **markers of collagen synthesis**: PINP, PICP).
The molecules assemble spontaneously into fibrils.

**Lysyl oxidase** (a copper-containing enzyme; cofactor — Cu^2+^) oxidizes the ε-amino groups of lysine and hydroxylysine to aldehydes (allysine); the aldehydes form **cross-links** with amino groups on neighboring molecules — the fibers are strengthened. With age the number of cross-links increases (skin elasticity decreases).

parts.text: **Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency)** — prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases do not work; unhydroxylated chains do not form a stable triple helix and are degraded in the cell. Collagen is scarce and fragile: swollen and bleeding gums, loosening and loss of teeth, perifollicular hemorrhages, slow wound healing, reopening of old scars, bone fragility (Möller–Barlow disease in children). Treatment — ascorbic acid.

blocks.text: **Regulation:** collagen synthesis is enhanced by **TGF-β**, insulin, somatotropin (IGF-1) and ascorbate; **glucocorticoids** reduce it (with long-term use the skin thins, wounds heal slowly, osteoporosis develops). Factors that chronically activate fibroblasts cause **fibrosis** (liver cirrhosis, pulmonary fibrosis, keloid).

Collagen turns over slowly (half-life from weeks to years), faster in bone and during growth. **Collagenases** (matrix metalloproteinases — MMP-1, MMP-8, MMP-13; Zn^2+^-containing) cut the triple helix at a specific site (into 3/4 and 1/4 fragments); then gelatinases (MMP-2, MMP-9) and lysosomal cathepsins break it down. MMPs are regulated by tissue inhibitors (TIMPs).

Because **hydroxyproline** is found almost only in collagen and is not reused, its **amount in the urine** is an indicator of collagen breakdown: normal in adults 15–50 mg/day (more in children because of growth). **It increases** with enhanced bone resorption (hyperparathyroidism, Paget disease, bone metastases, osteoporosis), collagenoses (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma), burns, thyrotoxicosis. **It decreases** in hypothyroidism, scurvy and hypopituitarism. Modern markers of bone resorption — **C-telopeptide (CTX)**, deoxypyridinoline.

sections.title: 5. Disorders of collagen synthesis and maturation

blocks.title: Table 22.2. Diseases associated with collagen
head: Disease
Defect
Main features
rows: Type I collagen genes (COL1A1, COL1A2) — most often substitution of glycine
Multiple fractures, blue sclerae, deafness, dental defects
Various types: genes of type III or V collagen, lysyl hydroxylase, procollagen peptidase
Excessive skin extensibility, joint hypermobility, fragile vessels (type III — arterial rupture)

blocks.text: **Biochemical diagnosis of collagenoses:** acute phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, seromucoid, sialic acids), proteinogram (α~2~ and γ ↑), urinary hydroxyproline ↑, autoantibodies (antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies — SLE, rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies — rheumatoid arthritis, Scl-70 — scleroderma), complement ↓.
**Elastin** is the protein that gives elasticity to the large vessels (aorta), lungs, skin and ligaments (ligamentum flavum); it stretches and then returns to its original state.

items: It contains a lot of glycine, alanine, valine and proline (hydrophobic); little hydroxyproline, no hydroxylysine and no carbohydrates.
The monomer is **tropoelastin**; outside the cell it assembles on **fibrillin** microfibrils.

**Lysyl oxidase** forms from lysine residues the characteristic cross-links that join four lysine residues — **desmosine and isodesmosine** — a three-dimensional network of randomly coiled chains (“rubber”).
It turns over very slowly (over a lifetime); it is broken down by **neutrophil elastase**; α~1~-antitrypsin inhibits elastase.

parts.text: **α~1~-Antitrypsin deficiency** — in the lungs neutrophil elastase acts uncontrolled and breaks down the elastin in the alveolar walls — early **panacinar emphysema** (smoking oxidizes and inactivates α~1~-antitrypsin and sharply increases the risk); in the PiZZ variant the misfolded protein accumulates in hepatocytes and leads to liver cirrhosis. **Marfan syndrome** — mutation of the **fibrillin-1** gene: tall stature, long fingers (arachnodactyly), dislocation of the lens, aortic aneurysm and dissection.

blocks.text: **Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)** are long unbranched polysaccharides made of repeating disaccharide units: a **uronic acid** (glucuronic or iduronic) + an **amino sugar** (N-acetylglucosamine or N-acetylgalactosamine); most of them are sulfated. They carry many negative charges (–COO^-^, –SO~3~^−^) — they strongly bind Na^+^ and **water** and form a gel.

blocks.title: Table 22.3. Main glycosaminoglycans
head: GAG
Disaccharide unit
Location and function
rows: Glucuronic acid + N-acetylglucosamine; unsulfated, not covalently bound to protein
Synovial fluid (lubrication), vitreous body, cartilage, umbilical cord; cell migration
Cartilage, bone, vessels — the most abundant GAG
Basement membranes, cell surface (syndecan) — growth factor receptor, antithrombin
Iduronic acid + glucosamine (the most highly sulfated)

blocks.text: **Proteoglycans** are GAG chains covalently bound to a core protein (protein ≈ 5%, carbohydrate ≈ 95%). In cartilage, **aggrecan** molecules attach to a hyaluronic acid chain through a link protein and form huge aggregates.

blocks.label: Figure 22.2
blocks.caption: Structure of the cartilage proteoglycan aggregate (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Biological functions:** supportive (resistance of cartilage to compression), protective (a barrier to the spread of bacteria — hyaluronic acid; bacterial **hyaluronidase** is a “spreading factor”), mechanical (lubrication of joints), binding (ordering of collagen fibrils — decorin), ion exchange (binding of Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^ — bone mineralization), filtration (heparan sulfate in the glomerular basement membrane repels albumin by its negative charge), signaling (binding of growth factors).

**Synthesis:** the core protein is synthesized in the RER; in the Golgi apparatus the chains are elongated from UDP-sugars (UDP-glucuronic acid, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine) by **glycosyltransferases**; the sulfate donor is **PAPS** (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate). Hyaluronic acid is synthesized at the plasma membrane.
**Breakdown:** in lysosomes, exoglycosidases and sulfatases degrade them step by step.

parts.text: **Mucopolysaccharidoses** are hereditary defects of lysosomal enzymes: incompletely degraded GAGs accumulate in tissues and are excreted in the urine. **Hurler syndrome** (α-L-iduronidase; autosomal recessive) — coarse facial features (“gargoylism”), corneal clouding, intellectual disability, enlarged liver and spleen, skeletal deformities. **Hunter syndrome** (iduronate-2-sulfatase; X-linked) — the cornea is clear. **Sanfilippo syndrome** — mainly severe neurological disorders. Diagnosis — increased dermatan and heparan sulfate in the urine, determination of the enzyme in leukocytes; treatment — enzyme replacement therapy, stem cell transplantation.

blocks.text: **Use of GAGs in medicine:** heparin (anticoagulant), chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine (chondroprotectors in osteoarthritis), hyaluronic acid (intra-articular — “liquid prosthesis”, ophthalmic surgery, cosmetology), hyaluronidase (softening of scars, enhancing the spread of drugs).

items: **Fibronectin** is a dimeric glycoprotein; it binds collagen, heparin, fibrin and cell **integrins** (through the RGD — Arg-Gly-Asp sequence); cell migration (embryogenesis, wound healing), opsonin.
**Laminin** is the main glycoprotein of the basement membrane (cross-shaped); it binds type IV collagen, nidogen and cells.
**Integrins** are receptors for matrix proteins (α and β subunits); they link the matrix to the cytoskeleton and transmit signals.
**Cadherins** (Ca^2+^-dependent), selectins and adhesion molecules of the immunoglobulin family (ICAM, VCAM) — cell–cell adhesion; attachment of leukocytes to the endothelium.
**Antiadhesive proteins** — **tenascin**, **thrombospondin**, **SPARC (osteonectin)** — enable cells to detach from the matrix and migrate (embryogenesis, wound healing, tumor invasion).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of hydroxyproline in urine

**Principle of the method:** urine is subjected to acid hydrolysis to convert bound hydroxyproline into the free form; it is oxidized by chloramine T to form a pyrrole, which gives a pink-red color with **Ehrlich's reagent** (p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde) (558 nm).

items: Add 1 ml of concentrated HCl to 1 ml of daily urine, hydrolyze at 110 °C for 3 hours and neutralize.
Add chloramine T solution to the hydrolysate and keep for 20 minutes at room temperature.
Add Ehrlich's reagent, heat at 60 °C for 15 minutes, cool and measure at 558 nm.
Calculate by comparison with a standard hydroxyproline solution.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** 15–50 mg/day in adults. An increase indicates enhanced bone resorption and collagen breakdown (hyperparathyroidism, metastases, collagenoses, burns). Collagen-rich foods (jelly, aspic) should not be eaten for 2 days before the test.
Experiment 2: determination of sialic acids in blood serum (Hess method)

**Principle of the method:** sialic (N-acetylneuraminic) acids are the terminal residues of the oligosaccharide chains of glycoproteins and GAGs; after the serum proteins are precipitated, the sialic acids in the hydrolysate give a colored compound when heated with a mixture of acetic and sulfuric acids.

items: Add 1 ml of 5% trichloroacetic acid to 0.1 ml of serum, boil for 5 minutes and centrifuge.
Add 5 ml of Hess reagent to 0.4 ml of supernatant and keep in a boiling water bath for 30 minutes.

Cool and measure at 540 nm against the blank; find the amount from the calibration graph. **Interpretation:** normal 2.0–2.33 mmol/l (≈ 180–200 conventional units). An increase is seen in rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis, collagenoses, acute inflammation and tumors (a nonspecific indicator of inflammatory activity).

skills.title: Skill: assessing the biochemical features of a connective tissue disease

items: Inflammatory activity: CRP, ESR, fibrinogen, sialic acids, seromucoid, proteinogram (α~2~, γ).
Collagen turnover: urinary hydroxyproline, serum PINP (synthesis), CTX (resorption).
Immunological markers: rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, complement.
Compare with the clinical diagnosis.

skills.title: Skill: identifying a hereditary connective tissue disease by its molecular defect

items: Clinical features: bone fractures and blue sclerae (type I collagen), skin extensibility and hypermobility (Ehlers–Danlos), arachnodactyly and aortic aneurysm (fibrillin-1), corneal clouding and gargoylism (Hurler).
Biochemical confirmation: urinary GAGs, enzyme activity, gene analysis.
Determine at which stage the defect lies: synthesis, hydroxylation, propeptide cleavage, cross-linking, breakdown.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old sailor returning from a long sea voyage (for several months he ate mainly dried bread and canned food) complains of swollen, bleeding gums, loose teeth and small hemorrhages on his legs. An old wound scar has reopened.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the biochemical mechanism of the symptoms.
cases.answer: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency). Ascorbic acid is the cofactor of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases: it keeps the iron in the enzyme in the Fe^2+^ state. When it is deficient, proline and lysine are not hydroxylated; without hydroxyproline the triple helix is not stabilized by hydrogen bonds and is degraded in the cell, and without hydroxylysine cross-links are not formed. Collagen is scarce and fragile: capillary walls weaken (hemorrhages, bleeding gums), the periodontal ligaments break down (loose teeth), and because scar collagen is constantly renewed, old scars reopen. Treatment — ascorbic acid, fresh fruit and vegetables.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 3-year-old child breaks bones after minor falls (6 times in two years). The sclerae are blue, and the teeth are translucent and yellowish. One of the parents also has blue sclerae and reduced hearing.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is its molecular basis? Why does a single mutant allele cause the disease?
cases.answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta (autosomal dominant). A mutation in one of the type I collagen genes (COL1A1 or COL1A2) — most often substitution of glycine in the triple helix by a larger amino acid: such a chain cannot pack tightly into the triple helix. Because the triple helix consists of three chains, the mutant chain combines with normal chains and makes the whole molecule defective (a dominant-negative effect) — most of the molecules are abnormal and are degraded. As a result, bone, the sclera (it thins and the vascular layer shows through — blue color), dentin and the auditory ossicles are weakened.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 2-year-old child has coarse facial features, corneal clouding, an enlarged liver and spleen, delayed mental development and spinal deformity. The urine contains a lot of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is its biochemical basis? What treatment is possible?
cases.answer: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I — Hurler syndrome. The lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase is deficient: iduronic acid residues at the ends of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate chains are not removed, the GAGs accumulate in lysosomes (cells enlarge, organ function is impaired), and the excess is excreted in the urine. Accumulation in cartilage, bone (skeletal deformities), the cornea (clouding), liver, spleen and brain (intellectual disability) produces the symptoms. Treatment: enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant α-L-iduronidase (it does not reach the brain), hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at an early age; prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling (autosomal recessive).

topics.title: Biochemistry of muscle and the cardiovascular system

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic proteins of muscle, the biochemical mechanisms of muscle contraction and relaxation, the extractive substances of muscle, the specific features of energy metabolism in muscle and the role of creatine phosphate, changes in muscular dystrophy and denervation, the metabolism and secretory function of the heart muscle, the diagnostic importance of cardiospecific proteins and enzymes, and endothelial factors.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure and functions of muscle proteins (myosin, actin, tropomyosin, troponin, titin, dystrophin);
the role of Ca^2+^ and ATP in muscle contraction and relaxation;
the pathways of ATP regeneration in muscle (creatine phosphate, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation);
creatine synthesis and creatinine formation;
the differences in the metabolism of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle;
the biochemical markers of myocardial infarction and their dynamics;
the importance of natriuretic peptides;
the role of endothelial factors in cardiovascular pathology.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine creatine kinase activity in blood serum;
interpret the results of myocardial infarction markers;
assess the biochemical features of myopathies.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Nitroglycerin** and other nitrates release NO in the body → cGMP → vasodilation (in angina). **Sildenafil** is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that slows the breakdown of cGMP. Using them together leads to a dangerous fall in blood pressure.

blocks.text: Muscle mass is ≈ 40% of body weight; ≈ 80% of its dry residue is protein.

Lies in the groove of actin and covers the myosin-binding sites at rest
TnC (binds Ca^2+^), TnI (inhibits actomyosin ATPase), TnT (binds to tropomyosin)

blocks.text: The I and T isoforms of cardiac and skeletal muscle troponins differ in amino acid composition — this is the basis of the high diagnostic specificity of **cardiac troponins**.

sections.title: 2. Mechanism of muscle contraction and relaxation

blocks.text: **Sliding filament theory** (Huxley): during contraction the length of the filaments does not change — the thin (actin) filaments slide between the thick (myosin) filaments, and the sarcomere shortens.

blocks.label: Figure 23.1
blocks.caption: Biochemical cycle of skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: **Excitation–contraction coupling:** the action potential spreads through the T tubules → the **dihydropyridine receptor** (voltage-sensitive) opens the **ryanodine receptor** → **Ca^2+^** is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (10^−7^ → 10^−5^ M) → Ca^2+^ binds to **troponin C** → tropomyosin shifts → the myosin heads bind to actin.

**Cross-bridge cycle:** myosin–ADP–P~i~ binds to actin → P~i~ is released and the “power stroke” occurs (the filament moves ≈ 10 nm) → ADP is released → a new **ATP** binds and detaches myosin from actin → ATP hydrolysis returns the myosin head to its initial position. Without ATP, myosin remains bound to actin — **rigor mortis**.

**Relaxation: Ca^2+^-ATPase (SERCA)** returns Ca^2+^ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (ATP is consumed); Ca^2+^ dissociates from troponin C, and tropomyosin covers the binding sites. Thus, ATP is required for both contraction and relaxation.

**Smooth muscle:** there is no troponin; Ca^2+^ combines with **calmodulin** and activates **myosin light chain kinase** — myosin is phosphorylated and interacts with actin. Relaxation — myosin phosphatase; **NO** → cGMP → PKG causes relaxation (vasodilation).
Nonprotein substances extracted from muscle with water (they give meat broth its taste and appetite-stimulating effect):

items: **nitrogenous:** ATP, ADP, AMP, **creatine phosphate and creatine**, **carnosine and anserine** (histidine dipeptides — buffer, antioxidant, activate the Ca^2+^ pump), carnitine, glutamine, free amino acids, urea, purine bases;
**non-nitrogenous:** glycogen, glucose, lactate, pyruvate, Krebs cycle acids, inositol;
**minerals:** K^+^, Mg^2+^, phosphates (abundant inside cells), Na^+^, Cl^-^ (little).

sections.title: 4. Energy metabolism in muscle. Creatine phosphate

blocks.text: The ATP reserve in muscle (≈ 5 mmol/kg) is enough for only 1–2 seconds of contraction. Pathways of ATP regeneration:

blocks.title: Table 23.2. Pathways of ATP resynthesis in muscle
head: Pathway
Rate
Duration
Feature
rows: Creatine phosphate + ADP → creatine + ATP (creatine kinase)
AMP activates PFK-1 and glycogen phosphorylase
Aerobic oxidation (glucose, fatty acids, ketone bodies)
The most efficient; requires O~2~ and mitochondria

blocks.text: **Creatine phosphate shuttle:** mitochondrial creatine kinase forms creatine phosphate using ATP from oxidative phosphorylation; it diffuses through the cytosol to the myofibrils, where creatine kinase regenerates ATP — an energy carrier.

**Creatine synthesis:** 1) in the kidney: arginine + glycine → guanidinoacetate (amidinotransferase); 2) in the liver: guanidinoacetate + S-adenosylmethionine → **creatine** (methyltransferase). Creatine is carried by the blood to muscle and brain. Creatine and creatine phosphate are converted nonenzymatically at a rate of ≈ 2% per day into **creatinine**, which is excreted by the kidneys; the daily amount of creatinine is proportional to **muscle mass** and constant (8.8–17.7 mmol/day in men, 7.1–15.9 mmol/day in women). Therefore blood creatinine is an indicator of **glomerular filtration** (topic 29).

**Types of muscle fibers: type I (red, slow)** — rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, aerobic, fatigue-resistant (postural muscles, marathon runners); **type II (white, fast)** — rich in glycogen and glycolytic enzymes, anaerobic, fatigue quickly (sprinters).
Causes of **fatigue**: depletion of creatine phosphate and glycogen, accumulation of lactate and H^+^ (acidosis weakens the binding of Ca^2+^ to troponin and PFK-1), accumulation of P~i~.

sections.title: 5. Biochemical changes in muscular dystrophy and denervation

blocks.text: **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** — X-linked recessive; a deletion or frameshift in the **dystrophin** gene (the largest gene, ≈ 2.4 million base pairs) — dystrophin is absent. The sarcolemma tears during contraction, Ca^2+^ enters and activates proteases, and the muscle fibers undergo necrosis and are replaced by fat and connective tissue. Signs at 3–5 years: weakness of proximal muscles, the **Gowers sign**, pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles; respiratory and heart failure at about 20 years. **Becker dystrophy** — in-frame mutations, partially functional dystrophin, a milder course.

**Biochemical signs of dystrophies:** serum **CK (MM) is sharply increased** (10–100 times, even before clinical signs), ALT, AST, LDH, aldolase and myoglobin are increased; muscle does not retain creatine — urinary **creatinuria** increases and **creatinine** excretion decreases (muscle mass is reduced); in muscle, myofibrillar proteins decrease and stromal (collagen) proteins increase; ATP and creatine phosphate decrease.

**Denervation** (nerve injury, poliomyelitis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis): muscle atrophy, decreased protein synthesis, enhanced proteolysis; CK is usually slightly increased; creatinuria; acetylcholine receptors spread over the entire sarcolemma.

**Other myopathies: McArdle disease** (glycogenosis type V — muscle glycogen phosphorylase is absent; pain and cramps on exertion, lactate does not rise), **carnitine and carnitine palmitoyltransferase** deficiency (myoglobinuria on prolonged exertion or fasting), mitochondrial myopathies (lactic acidosis), **statin myopathy**, **rhabdomyolysis** (trauma — “crush syndrome”, heavy exertion, alcohol, drugs): CK > 10,000 U/l, myoglobinuria (brown urine), hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury. **Myasthenia gravis** — autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors.

sections.title: 6. Metabolism and secretory function of the heart muscle

blocks.text: **Myocardial metabolism:** the heart works continuously and consumes ≈ 6 kg of ATP per day (the ATP reserve lasts a few seconds). Mitochondria occupy ≈ 35% of the cell volume; > 95% of ATP comes from **oxidative phosphorylation**. Energy sources: **fatty acids** (60–80% at rest), glucose, **lactate** (during exercise — to pyruvate via LDH-1), ketone bodies (in fasting and diabetes). In oxygen deficiency (ischemia), β-oxidation stops and anaerobic glycolysis cannot meet the ATP demand — lactate and H^+^ accumulate (anginal pain), ATP is depleted and the membrane pumps fail, and Ca^2+^ overload and free radicals (on reperfusion) lead to cardiomyocyte necrosis.

**Regulation of myocardial contraction:** β~1~-adrenoceptors → cAMP → PKA: L-type Ca^2+^ channels and **phospholamban** are phosphorylated (inhibition of SERCA is removed — rapid relaxation), and troponin I is phosphorylated. **Cardiac glycosides** (digoxin) inhibit Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase → Na^+^ ↑ in the cell → Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchange decreases → Ca^2+^ ↑ → contraction is enhanced.

**Endocrine function — natriuretic peptides: atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)** is released when the atria are stretched, and **brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)** mainly when the ventricular walls are stretched. Action: guanylate cyclase receptor → cGMP; natriuresis and diuresis, vasodilation, decreased secretion of renin, aldosterone and vasopressin — lowering blood volume and pressure. **BNP and NT-proBNP** are the main laboratory markers of **heart failure** (diagnosis, severity and prognosis): NT-proBNP < 125 pg/ml practically excludes (chronic) heart failure.

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic importance of cardiospecific proteins and enzymes

blocks.text: In myocardial necrosis the contents of cardiomyocytes are released into the blood.

blocks.label: Figure 23.2
blocks.caption: Dynamics of biochemical markers in myocardial infarction (drawn after Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry)

blocks.title: Table 23.3. Markers of myocardial injury
head: Marker
Onset of rise
Peak
Return to normal
Comment
rows: The “gold standard” — the most sensitive and specific; 0/1- or 0/2-hour algorithm
Early but nonspecific (also in skeletal muscle)

blocks.text: **Creatine kinase isoenzymes** (dimers of M and B subunits): **CK-MM** — skeletal muscle (≈ 95% of total activity), **CK-MB** — myocardium (15–40% of myocardial CK), **CK-BB** — brain, smooth muscle; there is also a mitochondrial CK. Normal total CK is < 190 U/l in men and < 170 U/l in women; CK-MB < 25 U/l or < 6% of the total.

**Modern diagnosis of myocardial infarction** (universal definition): troponin above the 99th percentile of normal with a **rise-and-fall pattern** + clinical signs of ischemia or ECG changes. Troponin can also rise in myocarditis, PE, sepsis, renal failure and heart failure (myocardial injury without infarction).
The endothelium (≈ 1.5 kg, ≈ 1000 m^2^) is an active endocrine organ; it regulates vascular tone, hemostasis, inflammation and permeability.

blocks.title: Table 23.4. Endothelial factors
head: Action
Factors
rows: Nitric oxide (NO) — synthesized by eNOS from arginine (BH~4~, NADPH) → guanylate cyclase in smooth muscle → cGMP; prostacyclin (PGI~2~); endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor; bradykinin
Endothelin-1 (the most potent), angiotensin II (ACE on the endothelium), thromboxane A~2~
NO, PGI~2~, thrombomodulin, heparan sulfate, t-PA, TFPI
von Willebrand factor, tissue factor, PAI-1
Selectins (E, P), ICAM-1, VCAM-1, IL-6, MCP-1

blocks.text: **Endothelial dysfunction** is a decrease in the formation and biological activity of NO (oxidative stress converts NO to peroxynitrite, asymmetric dimethylarginine inhibits eNOS) with a predominance of vasoconstrictor, prothrombotic and inflammatory factors. Risk factors: hypercholesterolemia (oxidized LDL), arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus (glycation products), smoking, **hyperhomocysteinemia** (deficiency of B~6~, B~12~, folate), obesity. Endothelial dysfunction is the first stage of **atherosclerosis** (topic 10) and the basis for the development of hypertension, thrombosis and coronary heart disease.

parts.text: **Nitroglycerin** and other nitrates release NO in the body → cGMP → vasodilation (in angina). **Sildenafil** is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that slows the breakdown of cGMP. Using them together leads to a dangerous fall in blood pressure.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of creatine kinase activity in blood serum (“Biotest” kit, kinetic method)

**Principle of the method (coupled reactions):** creatine phosphate + ADP → (CK) → creatine + ATP; ATP + glucose → (hexokinase) → ADP + glucose-6-phosphate; glucose-6-phosphate + NADP^+^ → (G6PD) → 6-phosphogluconate + NADPH. The rate of NADPH formation at 340 nm is proportional to CK activity. N-acetylcysteine activates CK, while AMP and diadenosine pentaphosphate inhibit erythrocyte myokinase.

items: Warm the working reagent to 37 °C; add 1 ml of reagent and 20 µl of serum to the cuvette and mix.
After 2 minutes of incubation record the absorbance at 340 nm, then measure every minute for 3 minutes.
Calculate the mean ΔE/min. **Calculation:** activity (U/l) = ΔE/min × 8095 (based on the millimolar extinction coefficient of NADPH, 6.22, and the sample dilution).

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** < 190 U/l in men, < 170 U/l in women. Hemolysis falsely increases the result (adenylate kinase and ATP from erythrocytes). Physiological increases occur after intramuscular injections and heavy physical exertion.
Experiment 2: determination of CK-MB by the immunoinhibition method (demonstration)
**Principle of the method:** antibodies against the M subunit completely inhibit CK-MM and half of CK-MB (its M part); the remaining activity (B subunit) is multiplied by 2.

items: Incubate the serum with the antibody-containing reagent.

Measure the residual activity as in Experiment 1; × 2. **Results and analysis:** CK-MB > 25 U/l and > 6% of total CK are characteristic of myocardial injury; today this method has been replaced by troponin determination.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting markers in chest pain

items: Determine the time elapsed since the onset of pain.
Determine high-sensitivity troponin on arrival and after 1–3 hours; assess the dynamics.
With early presentation (< 3 hours), a first negative result does not exclude infarction.
With late presentation (> 3–4 days), troponin is still high, while CK-MB may have returned to normal.
Detect reinfarction by a renewed rise in CK-MB.
Exclude causes of troponin elevation without infarction.

skills.title: Skill: assessing the biochemical features of a myopathy

items: Determine serum CK (MM), AST, ALT, LDH, aldolase and myoglobin.
Assess creatine and creatinine in the urine.
Very high CK (> 10,000 U/l) and brown urine — rhabdomyolysis (monitor potassium and creatinine).
Very high CK and proximal weakness in a young boy — dystrophin gene analysis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man presented with severe crushing chest pain lasting for 2 hours. On arrival high-sensitivity troponin T was 18 ng/l (normal < 14), and 74 ng/l 1 hour later; myoglobin was increased; CK-MB 28 U/l.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the dynamics of the markers. Why do myocardial cells die?
cases.answer: Acute myocardial infarction: troponin above the 99th percentile with a sharp rise within 1 hour (dynamics) together with clinical signs of ischemia. Myoglobin is a small molecule and is released the earliest, but it is also present in skeletal muscle; CK-MB rises at 3–6 hours; troponin becomes detectable at 1–3 hours and persists for 7–14 days (the sarcomere-bound fraction is released slowly). Coronary thrombosis cuts off oxygen: β-oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation stop, and anaerobic glycolysis cannot meet the ATP demand; lactate and H^+^ accumulate; Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase and Ca^2+^-ATPases fail, Na^+^ and Ca^2+^ increase inside the cell, phospholipases and proteases are activated, and the membranes are destroyed — necrosis, and the enzymes are released into the blood.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 5-year-old boy tires quickly, has difficulty climbing stairs and pushes on his legs with his hands when getting up from the floor; his calf muscles are enlarged. Serum CK 15,000 U/l, ALT and AST increased.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain the biochemical changes. How can the diagnosis be confirmed?
cases.answer: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked recessive). Because dystrophin is absent, the cytoskeleton is not linked to the sarcolemma and the extracellular matrix; the membrane tears during contraction, Ca^2+^ enters and activates calpains, and the fibers undergo necrosis — CK (MM), aminotransferases, LDH and aldolase are released into the blood (the increase in ALT/AST must not be mistaken for liver disease). The enlarged calves are a pseudohypertrophy due to fat and connective tissue; the way of getting up from the floor is the Gowers sign. Confirmation: molecular analysis of the DMD gene (deletions — MLPA, sequencing), immunohistochemical demonstration of the absence of dystrophin in a muscle biopsy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 25-year-old man presented after a marathon with severe muscle pain and weakness; his urine is dark brown. CK 85,000 U/l, potassium 6.2 mmol/l, creatinine 280 µmol/l. The urine test strip is positive for “blood”, but there are no erythrocytes on microscopy.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Explain the laboratory results. Why are the kidneys damaged?
cases.answer: Rhabdomyolysis after heavy physical exertion. As a result of ATP depletion and Ca^2+^ accumulation in muscle cells, the fibers break down and CK, myoglobin and K^+^ are released into the blood (hyperkalemia — dangerous for the heart). The test strip detects the peroxidase activity of heme — myoglobin also gives a positive result, while erythrocytes are absent (myoglobinuria). Myoglobin is filtered in the glomeruli, precipitates in the tubules in acidic urine and causes oxidative injury through heme iron; together with dehydration and vasoconstriction this leads to acute kidney injury (creatinine increased). Treatment: abundant intravenous fluids, correction of hyperkalemia, alkalinization of the urine, dialysis if necessary.

topics.title: Biochemistry of the gastrointestinal system

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the composition and functions of saliva, gastric juice, pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal juice, the biochemical regulation of taste and appetite, the regulation of digestive juice secretion, the breakdown products of organic substances in the intestine, the absorption of water and salts and its disorders, and the biochemical basis of pancreatitis, celiac disease and inflammatory bowel diseases.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the composition and functions of saliva;
taste receptors and the hormones that regulate appetite (ghrelin, leptin);
the mechanism of HCl secretion and its regulation;
the enzymes of pancreatic juice and their activation;
the composition of bile and the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids;
intestinal juice and membrane digestion;
the mechanisms of absorption of monosaccharides, amino acids, lipids, water and electrolytes;
the biochemical basis of pancreatitis, celiac disease, lactose intolerance, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform qualitative reactions for the components of saliva and bile;
interpret the results of amylase in blood and urine and of serum lipase;
identify the biochemical features of the malabsorption syndrome.

blocks.text: Saliva consists of the secretions of three pairs of major glands (parotid — serous; submandibular and sublingual — mixed) and many minor glands; 1–1.5 l is secreted per day; pH 6.4–7.4.

**Composition:** water (≈ 99.4%); organic substances — **mucin** (a glycoprotein that makes the food bolus slippery), **α-amylase** (ptyalin — breaks down starch into dextrins; activated by Cl^-^), lingual lipase (important in infants), **lysozyme** (breaks down the bacterial wall), lactoferrin, **secretory IgA**, histatins, kallikrein, growth factors (epidermal growth factor); inorganic — Na^+^, K^+^ (more than in plasma), Ca^2+^, phosphates, HCO~3~^−^, Cl^-^, **thiocyanates** (rhodanides; abundant in smokers), F-.

**Functions:** digestive (the start of carbohydrate digestion), protective (antibacterial, buffering, remineralization of enamel — saturated with Ca^2+^ and phosphate), moistening and swallowing of food, taste perception (dissolves taste substances), excretory (urea, drugs, heavy metals).

parts.text: Reduced salivary secretion (xerostomia — Sjögren syndrome, radiation, anticholinergic drugs) increases dental caries and oral infections. Caries — **lactic acid**, formed when bacteria (Streptococcus mutans) ferment sucrose, dissolves the hydroxyapatite of enamel; fluoride forms the more resistant **fluorapatite** in enamel.

sections.title: 2. Taste perception. Regulation of appetite and hunger

blocks.text: **Biochemical basis of taste perception:** there are five basic tastes. **Sweet** (T1R2/T1R3), **umami** (T1R1/T1R3 — L-glutamate) and **bitter** (the T2R family, ≈ 25 types) are G protein-coupled receptors; the G protein **gustducin** → phospholipase Cβ2 → IP~3~ → Ca^2+^ → TRPM5 channel → depolarization. **Salty** — direct entry of Na^+^ through ENaC sodium channels; **sour** — H^+^ ions (the OTOP1 proton channel). Zinc (gustin) is required for taste perception — in Zn deficiency taste is impaired (hypogeusia).
**Regulation of appetite and hunger** — two groups of neurons in the **arcuate nucleus** of the hypothalamus:

items: **orexigenic** (increase appetite): **neuropeptide Y** and AgRP;
**anorexigenic** (satiety): **POMC → α-MSH** (melanocortin-4 receptor) and CART.

blocks.text: Mechanism of HCl secretion:

blocks.label: Figure 24.1
blocks.caption: HCl secretion in the gastric parietal cell and its regulation (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: In the parietal cell, **carbonic anhydrase** forms H~2~CO~3~ from CO~2~ and H~2~O; H^+^ is pumped into the lumen by the **H^+^,K^+^-ATPase** (proton pump) in the apical membrane (against a ≈ 106-fold concentration gradient), and HCO~3~^−^ passes into the blood across the basolateral membrane in exchange for Cl^-^ (the postprandial **“alkaline tide”** — the urine becomes alkaline). Cl^-^ and K^+^ leave into the lumen through apical channels. **Stimulators:** acetylcholine (vagus nerve, M~3~), gastrin, **histamine** (from ECL cells, H~2~ receptor — cAMP); **inhibitors:** somatostatin, prostaglandin E~2~, secretin, GIP, pH < 2 (feedback).

parts.text: **Gastric and duodenal ulcer** — disturbance of the balance between aggression (HCl, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs) and protection (mucus, HCO~3~^−^, prostaglandins, blood flow). The H. pylori enzyme **urease** breaks down urea into NH~3~ and CO~2~, creating an alkaline “cloud” around the bacterium; NH~3~ damages the epithelium. Diagnosis — the ^13^C-urea breath test; treatment — proton pump inhibitors + antibiotics. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce protective prostaglandins. **Zollinger–Ellison syndrome** — a gastrin-producing tumor (gastrinoma): multiple recurrent ulcers.

blocks.text: 1.5–2 l per day; pH 7.8–8.4 (HCO~3~^−^ ≈ 120–140 mmol/l — neutralizes the acidic chyme).

blocks.text: **Protective mechanisms:** proteases are synthesized as inactive **zymogens** and stored in membrane-bound granules; the granules and the juice contain a **trypsin inhibitor** (SPINK1); activation occurs only in the intestine (enteropeptidase).
Regulation of secretion:

blocks.label: Figure 24.2
blocks.caption: Hormonal regulation of digestive juice secretion (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: 0.6–1 l is formed in the liver per day; in the gallbladder water is reabsorbed and bile is concentrated 5–10 times.

**Composition: bile acids** (bile salts — ≈ 67% of the dry residue), **phospholipids** (lecithin), **cholesterol**, **bilirubin diglucuronide** (conjugated bilirubin — the color of bile), proteins, electrolytes (HCO~3~^−^), metabolites of drugs and toxins.

**Bile acids** are synthesized in the liver **from cholesterol** (key enzyme — **7α-hydroxylase**, a cytochrome P450; topic 10): **primary** — cholic and chenodeoxycholic acids; with glycine or taurine they **are conjugated** (glycocholic and taurocholic acids — highly soluble, amphipathic). In the intestine, bacteria deconjugate them and 7-dehydroxylate them into **secondary** bile acids (deoxycholic, lithocholic).

**Functions:** **emulsification** of fats, enhancement of lipase activity, formation of **micelles** for the absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), keeping cholesterol in solution, stimulation of intestinal peristalsis, bacteriostatic action, excretion of cholesterol and bilirubin.

**Enterohepatic circulation:** ≈ 95% of bile acids are reabsorbed in the **ileum** (active transport together with Na^+^) and return to the liver via the portal vein; they circulate 6–10 times a day; only ≈ 0.5 g/day is lost with the feces — this is the main route of cholesterol elimination from the body. Sequestrants (colestyramine) bind bile acids and lower blood cholesterol.

parts.text: **Cholesterol gallstones** — an excess of cholesterol in bile relative to bile acids and phospholipids (lithogenic bile): obesity, estrogens, pregnancy, rapid weight loss, ileal resection (bile acids are lost). **Ursodeoxycholic acid** is used to dissolve small stones. **Pigment stones** — calcium bilirubinate (hemolysis, infection).

blocks.text: Intestinal juice (2–3 l/day, pH 7.5–8.0) consists of the secretion of the Brunner and Lieberkühn glands and shed epithelial cells. Digestion takes place mainly as **membrane (parietal) digestion** — by enzymes located in the brush border of the enterocyte microvilli:

items: **disaccharidases:** sucrase-isomaltase, **lactase** (β-galactosidase), maltase-glucoamylase, trehalase;
**peptidases:** aminopeptidases, dipeptidases, tripeptidases;
**enteropeptidase (enterokinase)** — activates trypsinogen;
alkaline phosphatase, nucleotidases.

Many Na^+^-dependent and Na^+^-independent transporters (for neutral, basic and acidic amino acids and imino acids); di- and tripeptides — PEPT1 (symport with H^+^)
Delivered within micelles; in the enterocyte TAG is resynthesized and released into the lymph as chylomicrons; short- and medium-chain fatty acids go directly into the portal vein
Osmotic (aquaporins) — mainly in the jejunum and ileum; the colon absorbs the rest

blocks.text: **Malabsorption syndrome** — weight loss, diarrhea, steatorrhea, anemia, osteoporosis, hypoproteinemic edema, vitamin deficiencies.

items: **Lactose intolerance** — lactase deficiency (in adults a genetically programmed decline — widespread in many populations; secondary — in intestinal diseases): after drinking milk, lactose passes into the colon, where bacteria ferment it to gases (H~2~, CO~2~) and short-chain acids — **osmotic diarrhea**, bloating. Diagnosis — the hydrogen breath test, the lactose tolerance test (blood glucose does not rise).

**Celiac disease (gluten enteropathy)** — an autoimmune response to **gliadin** peptides of wheat, barley and rye (rich in proline and glutamine, resistant to pepsin and trypsin): **tissue transglutaminase** deamidates gliadin, and T cells are activated through HLA-DQ2/DQ8; atrophy of the intestinal villi — the absorption of all substances is impaired (iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis). Diagnosis — IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase, biopsy; treatment — a **lifelong gluten-free diet**.

**Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency** (chronic pancreatitis, **cystic fibrosis** — a CFTR defect, thick secretions block the ducts): steatorrhea, decreased fecal **elastase-1**; treatment — enzyme preparations (pancreatin).
**Bile acid deficiency** (obstructive jaundice, ileal resection) — the absorption of fats and vitamins A, D, E, K is impaired (vitamin K deficiency — bleeding).

**Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis** are chronic inflammatory bowel diseases: genetic predisposition (NOD2 — a receptor that recognizes bacterial muramyl dipeptide), disturbed microbiota (dysbiosis), disturbed epithelial barrier and immune response (excess TNF-α, IL-12/23); protein loss, anemia, malabsorption (in Crohn disease, the ileum — B~12~, bile acids). Activity marker — fecal **calprotectin**. Treatment includes monoclonal antibodies against TNF-α (infliximab) and 5-aminosalicylates.

**Familial adenomatous polyposis** — mutation of the APC gene: hundreds of polyps in the colon, with a ≈ 100% chance of malignant transformation (topic 19). **Functions of the colon:** absorption of water and electrolytes; the **microbiota** (10^14^ cells) — fermentation of undigested polysaccharides (fiber) to form **short-chain fatty acids** (acetate, propionate, **butyrate** — the main energy source of colonocytes, anti-inflammatory), synthesis of vitamin K~2~ and B vitamins, transformation of bile acids and bilirubin (urobilinogen, stercobilin), **putrefaction** of amino acids (indole, skatole, phenol, cresol, putrescine, cadaverine — topic 26), a competitive barrier to pathogens.

sections.title: 8. Mechanisms of action of drugs in diarrhea and constipation

items: **Secretory diarrhea** — cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the G~s~ protein and permanently activates adenylate cyclase → cAMP ↑ → a lot of Cl^-^ and water is secreted through CFTR (up to 10–20 l per day).

blocks.text: **Oral rehydration solution** (glucose + NaCl) — based on the fact that the absorption of Na^+^ and water together with glucose through SGLT1 is preserved.

items: **Osmotic diarrhea** — unabsorbed substances (lactose, sorbitol, magnesium salts).

**Antidiarrheal drugs:** loperamide (a μ-opioid receptor agonist — peristalsis ↓, secretion ↓), adsorbents (diosmectite, activated charcoal), racecadotril (an enkephalinase inhibitor — secretion ↓), probiotics.

**Laxatives:** osmotic (lactulose — bacteria ferment it to form acids; macrogol; magnesium sulfate), bulk-forming (fiber, psyllium), stimulant (bisacodyl, sennosides — enhance epithelial secretion and peristalsis), softeners (liquid paraffin).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of the components of saliva

items: **Mucin:** add 3–4 drops of acetic acid to 2 ml of saliva — a white stringy precipitate (mucin); filter the precipitate and perform the biuret reaction (the protein part).

**Amylase:** add 1 ml of diluted (1:10) saliva to 1 ml of 1% starch solution and keep at 37 °C for 10 minutes; reaction with iodine — no color or reddish (starch has been broken down); the Trommer reaction is positive (maltose).

**Thiocyanates (rhodanides):** add 2–3 drops of HCl and 2 drops of 5% FeCl~3~ to 1 ml of saliva — a red color (Fe(SCN)3). **Results and analysis:** the saliva of smokers contains a lot of thiocyanates (a product of the detoxification of cyanides in tobacco smoke). Preserved amylase activity indicates the digestive function of saliva.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: qualitative reactions for the components of bile

items: **Bile acids — the Pettenkofer reaction:** place 2 drops of bile and 1 drop of 20% sucrose solution in a dry test tube and carefully add 1 ml of concentrated sulfuric acid down the wall — a red-violet ring at the interface (condensation of the hydroxymethylfurfural formed from sucrose with bile acids).

**Bile pigments — the Gmelin reaction:** pour 1 ml of concentrated nitric acid into a test tube and layer 1 ml of bile over it down the wall — colored rings at the interface (green, blue, violet, red, yellow) — products of successive oxidation of bilirubin (biliverdin and others).

**Reduction of surface tension by bile (Hay's test):** sprinkle sulfur powder on the surface of two test tubes containing water and diluted bile — in the bile the powder sinks (the surface tension is reduced). **Results and analysis:** the reactions confirm the presence of bile acids and pigments in bile; a positive Gmelin reaction in urine indicates conjugated bilirubinuria (obstructive and hepatocellular jaundice).

blocks.text: Experiment 3: interpretation of serum amylase and lipase results (case-based)

items: Compare the results of serum α-amylase (normal < 100 U/l; pancreatic isoenzyme < 53 U/l) and lipase (< 60 U/l) with the normal values.

Take into account the result of urinary diastase (amylase). **Results and analysis:** in acute pancreatitis amylase rises within 2–12 hours and returns to normal in 3–5 days; urinary amylase persists longer; **lipase** is more specific and stays high longer (7–14 days) — an increase of **3 times** the upper limit of normal is the diagnostic criterion. Amylase also rises in mumps, intestinal obstruction and macroamylasemia.

skills.title: Skill: biochemical diagnosis of acute pancreatitis

items: Determine lipase and amylase activity (≥ 3-fold increase).
Assess severity: glucose ↑, calcium ↓ (calcium soaps in fat necrosis), LDH ↑, leukocytosis, CRP > 150 mg/l (at 48 hours), urea ↑.
Determine the cause: gallstones (bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, ALT ↑), alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia (> 11 mmol/l), hypercalcemia.

Explain the mechanism: premature activation of trypsinogen inside the gland → activation of the other proenzymes → self-digestion of the gland (autolysis), elastase — vascular damage, phospholipase A~2~ — destruction of membranes.

skills.title: Skill: determining the cause of malabsorption

items: Confirm steatorrhea (fat in the feces — coprogram).
Determine fecal elastase-1: low — pancreatic insufficiency.
Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase — celiac disease.
Lactose tolerance or hydrogen breath test — lactase deficiency.
Assess blood albumin, iron, ferritin, B~12~, folate, calcium, vitamin D and PT.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old man presented after eating a large fatty meal and drinking alcohol with severe girdle-like pain in the upper abdomen and repeated vomiting. Serum lipase 1250 U/l (normal < 60), amylase 820 U/l, glucose 9.8 mmol/l, calcium 1.9 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the biochemical mechanism of the disease. Why is calcium decreased and glucose increased?
cases.answer: Acute pancreatitis. Alcohol and fatty food enhance secretion, raise the pressure in the ducts and damage the acinar cells; trypsinogen is converted to trypsin prematurely inside the gland and activates the other proenzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, prophospholipase A~2~) — the gland digests itself (autolysis): elastase destroys the vessels (hemorrhage), phospholipase A~2~ destroys membranes, and lipase breaks down adipose tissue. The enzymes are released into the blood (increased lipase and amylase). In foci of fat necrosis, free fatty acids form soaps with calcium, leading to hypocalcemia (a sign of a severe course). Damage to the islets of Langerhans and stress hormones cause hyperglycemia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 25-year-old woman complains of bloating, rumbling and loose stools 1–2 hours after drinking milk or eating dairy products. After 50 g of lactose, blood glucose did not rise (+ 0.6 mmol/l), and breath hydrogen rose sharply.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the biochemical mechanism of the symptoms. What recommendations would you give?
cases.answer: Lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance). Without lactase, lactose is not broken down into glucose and galactose in the small intestine — blood glucose does not rise. Lactose passes into the colon, raises the osmotic pressure and retains water (osmotic diarrhea); bacteria ferment it to H~2~, CO~2~, methane and short-chain acids (bloating, rumbling; H~2~ is absorbed into the blood and exhaled). Recommendations: limit fresh milk; fermented dairy products (yogurt, cheese — little lactose, contain bacterial β-galactosidase), lactose-free milk or lactase preparations; prevention of calcium deficiency.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 7-year-old child is growth-retarded and thin, with a large abdomen and frequent, large, fatty, foul-smelling stools. Blood Hb 88 g/l, ferritin 5 µg/l, albumin 30 g/l. IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase are sharply increased. Intestinal biopsy shows villous atrophy.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the mechanism of the disease. Why did iron deficiency and hypoalbuminemia develop? What is the treatment?
cases.answer: Celiac disease (gluten enteropathy). The gliadin peptides of wheat, barley and rye are resistant to proteases; tissue transglutaminase deamidates them, and the deamidated peptides are presented to T lymphocytes with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 — inflammation; cytotoxic lymphocytes destroy the enterocytes, and the villi become atrophic. The absorptive surface and membrane enzymes decrease: the absorption of fats (steatorrhea), iron (in the duodenum — iron deficiency anemia), amino acids (hypoalbuminemia), calcium and vitamin D is impaired — growth retardation. Treatment — a lifelong strict gluten-free diet (rice, corn and buckwheat are allowed); iron and vitamin supplementation; a decrease in antibodies shows that the diet is being followed.
