topics.title: Biochemistry of the liver. Bilirubin metabolism and jaundice

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the role of the liver in the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and amino acids and its age-related features, heme catabolism and bilirubin metabolism, the types of jaundice and their differential diagnosis, physiological and pathological jaundice in newborns, the syndromes of liver damage (cytolysis, cholestasis, mesenchymal-inflammatory, hepatocellular insufficiency), and the biochemical mechanisms of the development of hepatic coma.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main functions of the liver in metabolism;
the breakdown of heme and the formation, transport, conjugation and excretion of bilirubin;
the properties of conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin;
the biochemical differences between hemolytic, hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice;
the causes of neonatal jaundice and the hereditary hyperbilirubinemias;
the laboratory parameters of the syndromes of liver damage;
the biochemical mechanisms of hepatic coma.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine bilirubin and its fractions in blood on a biochemical analyzer;
determine bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine;
distinguish the type of jaundice by laboratory parameters.

sections.title: 1. The role of the liver in metabolism

blocks.text: The liver (≈ 1.5 kg) is the body's main “biochemical laboratory”; blood arrives through the portal vein (≈ 75%) and the hepatic artery; hepatocytes make up ≈ 80% of the cells.

blocks.title: Table 25.1. Metabolic functions of the liver
head: Metabolism
Functions
rows: Maintaining the blood glucose level (the “glucostat”): glycogen synthesis and breakdown (glucose-6-phosphatase only in the liver and kidney), gluconeogenesis; conversion of fructose and galactose to glucose; pentose phosphate pathway

Synthesis of fatty acids and TAG, formation of VLDL and HDL, synthesis of cholesterol and its conversion to bile acids, synthesis of ketone bodies (the liver does not use them itself), phospholipid synthesis
Synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin and other clotting factors, transferrin, ceruloplasmin, acute phase proteins, apolipoproteins); almost all of them except γ-globulins
Transamination, deamination, urea synthesis (the only site), creatine synthesis (the last stage), synthesis of nonessential amino acids
Conjugation of bilirubin and its excretion with bile
A, D (25-hydroxylation), B~12~ store, synthesis of K-dependent factors; store of iron and copper

blocks.text: **Age-related features:** in newborns the activity of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, some P450 isoforms and gluconeogenic enzymes is low (physiological jaundice, sensitivity to drugs, tendency to hypoglycemia); the synthesis of albumin and clotting factors is lower. In old age liver mass and blood flow decrease, and drug metabolism slows down.
≈ 250–300 mg of bilirubin is formed per day: ≈ 80% from the hemoglobin of senescent erythrocytes, the rest from myoglobin, cytochromes and ineffective erythropoiesis.

blocks.label: Figure 25.1
blocks.caption: Bilirubin metabolism (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **In macrophages** (spleen, Kupffer cells of the liver, bone marrow): **heme oxygenase** (microsomal, requires O~2~ and NADPH) cleaves the α-methene bridge of heme to form **biliverdin**, **CO** and Fe^2+^; **biliverdin reductase** (NADPH) reduces biliverdin to **bilirubin** (from green to yellow — the color change of a bruise).

**Transport in the blood:** bilirubin is insoluble in water (lipophilic) and is carried to the liver bound to **albumin** — **unconjugated (indirect, free)** bilirubin. It does not pass the renal filter — it is not found in urine. Its free (non-albumin-bound) fraction crosses the blood–brain barrier and is **neurotoxic**. Sulfonamides, salicylates and free fatty acids displace it from albumin.

**In the liver:** hepatocytes take up bilirubin with membrane transporters (OATP) and bind it inside the cell to ligandin (glutathione S-transferase); in the endoplasmic reticulum, **UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1)** attaches two glucuronic acid residues from UDP-glucuronic acid — **bilirubin diglucuronide** (**conjugated, direct** bilirubin) — which is water-soluble.
**Secretion into bile** — active transport (ATP) through the **MRP2** transporter; this is the **slowest (rate-limiting) step** of the process.

**In the intestine:** bacterial β-glucuronidase removes the glucuronic acid; bacteria reduce bilirubin to **urobilinogens** (mesobilinogen, stercobilinogen). Most of it is oxidized to **stercobilin**, which colors the feces (200–300 mg per day). Part of the urobilinogen is reabsorbed and returns to the liver (enterohepatic circulation), and a small part is excreted in the urine and oxidized to **urobilin** (the color of urine).

blocks.text: **Normal:** total bilirubin 3.4–20.5 µmol/l. **Jaundice** is yellowing of the skin, mucous membranes and sclerae; it becomes visible when bilirubin is > 34 µmol/l (earliest in the sclerae).

sections.title: 3. Types of jaundice and their differential diagnosis

blocks.text: **Physiological jaundice** is observed in ≈ 60% of full-term and ≈ 80% of preterm newborns. Causes: the large number and short lifespan (≈ 80 days) of fetal erythrocytes (HbF) — bilirubin production is 2–3 times higher than in adults; the low activity of **UDP-glucuronosyltransferase** (≈ 1% of the adult level, matures by 1–3 months); little ligandin; the intestine is sterile — urobilinogen is not formed, and bilirubin is reabsorbed under the action of β-glucuronidase. Features: it begins on **days 2–3**, peaks on days 3–5 (< 205–220 µmol/l) and resolves by days 10–14; only unconjugated bilirubin increases; the general condition is good.

blocks.label: Figure 25.2
blocks.caption: Dynamics of bilirubin in newborns (drawn after Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Signs of pathological jaundice:** appearance on the first day, a rapid rise in bilirubin (> 85 µmol/l/day), duration of more than 2 weeks in full-term and more than 3 weeks in preterm infants, an increase in conjugated bilirubin (> 25–34 µmol/l), an undulating course. Causes: **hemolytic disease** (Rh or AB0 incompatibility), G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis, infections, hypothyroidism, biliary atresia, hereditary hyperbilirubinemias.

parts.text: **Bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus)** — unconjugated bilirubin (> 340 µmol/l in full-term infants, lower in preterm infants) crosses the blood–brain barrier and accumulates in the basal ganglia: it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria — neurons die (deafness, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability). **Phototherapy** (blue light, 460–490 nm) converts bilirubin into water-soluble photoisomers (lumirubin), which are excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. In severe cases — exchange transfusion. Phenobarbital induces UGT1A1.

blocks.text: **Liver fibrosis and cirrhosis** — in chronic damage (hepatitis B, C, alcohol, fatty liver disease) **stellate (Ito) cells** are activated, transform into myofibroblasts and synthesize a lot of collagen (types I, III); nodules form. Fibrosis markers — hyaluronic acid, type III procollagen peptide, elastography.
**Hepatic encephalopathy and coma** is a disturbance of central nervous system function in acute or chronic liver failure.

items: **The ammonia hypothesis (the main one):** urea synthesis in the liver decreases, and ammonia from the intestine reaches the brain directly through portocaval shunts. In the brain, astrocytes convert NH~3~ into **glutamine** (glutamine synthetase) — glutamine accumulates and the astrocytes swell (osmotically), brain edema; **α-ketoglutarate** is consumed for glutamate — the Krebs cycle and ATP formation decrease; inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmission are disturbed (topic 13).

**False neurotransmitters:** aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan) increase in the blood (the liver does not break them down), while branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine — used in muscle) decrease — the **Fischer ratio** (BCAA/AAA) falls from 3–3.5 to < 1. Many aromatic amino acids enter the brain and form octopamine, phenylethanolamine (false transmitters) and serotonin; dopamine and norepinephrine decrease.
**Enhanced GABAergic inhibition** (endogenous benzodiazepines).
**Intestinal toxins:** mercaptans (the liver odor — “foetor hepaticus”), phenols, short-chain fatty acids, indole, skatole — the liver does not detoxify them.

Hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, alkalosis — enhances the passage of NH~3~ into the brain), acidosis, renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome). **Principles of treatment:** temporary restriction of protein (but not complete), **lactulose** (in the colon bacteria ferment it and acidify the medium: NH~3~ → NH~4~^+^ — not absorbed, excreted from the intestine; laxative effect), bowel cleansing, nonabsorbable antibiotics (rifaximin — reduces the ammonia-producing bacteria), L-ornithine L-aspartate (enhances the synthesis of urea and glutamine), branched-chain amino acids, correction of hypokalemia; in severe cases liver transplantation.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of total and direct bilirubin in blood on a biochemical analyzer (Jendrassik–Grof method)

**Principle of the method:** bilirubin forms red-violet azobilirubin with diazotized sulfanilic acid (the diazo reagent). Conjugated bilirubin reacts directly (**direct bilirubin**); unconjugated bilirubin requires an **accelerator** (caffeine benzoate) to be released from albumin — with it **total bilirubin** is determined. Indirect bilirubin = total − direct. Measurement — 546 nm (in an alkaline medium — 578 nm, blue color).

items: Select the “Total bilirubin” and “Direct bilirubin” tests on the analyzer; perform quality control with calibrators and control sera.
Place the serum sample in the rack (the sample must be protected from light — bilirubin breaks down in light).

The analyzer mixes 10–20 µl of sample with the appropriate reagents, measures after the set time and reports the result. **Interpretation:** total bilirubin 3.4–20.5 µmol/l; direct ≤ 3.4–5 µmol/l (≤ 25% of the total). Hemolysis and lipemia alter the result.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determination of bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine

items: **Bilirubin — the Rosin test:** carefully layer a 1% alcoholic iodine solution over 3 ml of urine — a **green ring** at the interface (bilirubin is oxidized to biliverdin). Test strips (diazo reaction) are also used.

**Urobilinogen — the Ehrlich reaction:** add 0.5 ml of Ehrlich's reagent (p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde + HCl) to 2 ml of urine — a red color at room temperature (a lot of urobilinogen); normally the color is faint and appears only on heating. **Results and analysis:** bilirubin in urine — conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (hepatocellular or obstructive jaundice); a lot of urobilinogen — hemolytic or hepatocellular jaundice; no urobilinogen and a lot of bilirubin — complete obstruction of the bile ducts.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of jaundice by laboratory parameters

items: Assess total bilirubin and its fractions: which fraction predominates?
Assess urinary bilirubin and urobilinogen and the stool color.
Assess the enzymes: ALT/AST (cytolysis) or alkaline phosphatase/GGT (cholestasis).
Check for signs of hemolysis: reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin.
Conclusion: hemolytic, hepatocellular or obstructive jaundice; recommend a confirmatory investigation (ultrasound, markers).

skills.title: Skill: grouping liver function tests by syndrome

items: Identify the parameters of cytolysis (ALT, AST, GLDH).
Identify the parameters of cholestasis (ALP, GGT, direct bilirubin, bile acids).
Assess the synthetic function (albumin, PT/INR, cholinesterase).
Assess the inflammatory and immune parameters (γ-globulins).
Assess the severity (Child–Pugh: bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 62-year-old patient complains of gradually increasing yellowing of the skin and sclerae, severe itching and weight loss; there is no pain. The urine is dark and the stools are colorless. Total bilirubin 285 µmol/l (direct 230), alkaline phosphatase 980 U/l, GGT 650 U/l, ALT 95 U/l, no urobilinogen in the urine. PT is prolonged and normalized after vitamin K was given. CA 19-9 is sharply increased.
cases.ask: Determine the type of jaundice. Explain the laboratory results. Why was the PT corrected by vitamin K?
cases.answer: Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice; the painless progression, weight loss and CA 19-9 point to a tumor of the head of the pancreas. Because bile flow is blocked, conjugated bilirubin returns to the blood (the direct fraction predominates), is filtered by the kidneys and darkens the urine; no bile reaches the intestine — urobilinogen and stercobilin are not formed (acholic stools, no urobilinogen in the urine). In cholestasis the synthesis of alkaline phosphatase and GGT and their release into the blood increase sharply; bile acids accumulate and cause itching. Because there are no bile acids in the intestine, fat-soluble vitamin K is not absorbed — prothrombin and other factors are not carboxylated; since the synthetic function of the liver is preserved, parenteral vitamin K corrected the PT (this does not happen with hepatocellular damage).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 3-day-old newborn (from the second pregnancy of an Rh-negative mother) developed jaundice 10 hours after birth. Total bilirubin was 150 µmol/l on day 1 and 310 µmol/l on day 2 (almost all unconjugated), Hb 105 g/l, many reticulocytes, direct Coombs test positive.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Why is the jaundice not physiological? What is the danger and how should help be provided?
cases.answer: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh incompatibility): the mother's IgG antibodies against the Rh antigen cross the placenta and destroy the fetal erythrocytes (Coombs positive). The jaundice began on the first day, bilirubin is rising by > 85 µmol/l per day, and there is anemia — it is pathological. A lot of heme is broken down and unconjugated bilirubin is formed; the newborn's low UGT1A1 activity cannot conjugate it in time. The danger is bilirubin encephalopathy (> 340 µmol/l; free bilirubin exceeding the albumin capacity enters the brain). Help: intensive phototherapy, intravenous immunoglobulin, exchange transfusion (removal of antibodies and bilirubin, replacement of erythrocytes); avoidance of drugs that occupy albumin binding sites (sulfonamides, ceftriaxone). Prevention — anti-D immunoglobulin for the Rh-negative mother.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis developed drowsiness, confusion, hand tremor (“flapping”) and a peculiar sweetish-musty breath odor after bleeding from esophageal varices. Blood ammonia 145 µmol/l (normal < 50), albumin 26 g/l, PT prolonged.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Why did the condition worsen after the bleeding? What are the biochemical mechanism and the principles of treatment?
cases.answer: Hepatic encephalopathy (precoma). Blood in the intestine is a large protein load: bacteria break it down and form a lot of ammonia; in cirrhosis urea synthesis in the liver is reduced, and NH~3~ reaches the brain through portocaval shunts. In the brain, astrocytes convert NH~3~ into glutamine and swell; α-ketoglutarate is consumed and ATP formation decreases; aromatic amino acids increase and false neurotransmitters are formed; GABAergic inhibition is enhanced. Mercaptans — the liver odor. Albumin and PT show the decline in the synthetic function of the liver. Treatment: stopping the bleeding, bowel cleansing, lactulose (elimination as NH~4~^+^), rifaximin, L-ornithine L-aspartate, correction of electrolytes and glucose, temporary protein restriction.

topics.title: Detoxification of toxic substances in the liver

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the mechanisms of detoxification (biotransformation) of xenobiotics — microsomal oxidation and conjugation reactions, the detoxification of toxic products formed by the putrefaction of amino acids in the colon, the inactivation of normal metabolites and hormones, the biotransformation of drugs and the factors that affect it, inducers and inhibitors of cytochrome P450, P450 polymorphism and personalized treatment, and ethanol metabolism.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: phases I and II of biotransformation;
the composition and mechanism of the microsomal oxidation system;
the main conjugation reactions and their donors;
the detoxification of putrefaction products such as indole, skatole, phenol and cresol;
the inactivation of hormones and bilirubin in the liver;
the clinical importance of P450 inducers and inhibitors;
pharmacogenetic polymorphisms (CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, NAT2, TPMT);
ethanol metabolism and the metabolic effects of alcohol.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine hippuric acid in urine (based on the Quick test);
predict drug–drug interactions on the basis of P450;
explain the biochemical mechanism of paracetamol poisoning.

blocks.text: **Xenobiotics** are substances foreign to the body: drugs, industrial poisons, pesticides, food additives, carcinogens. Most of them are **lipophilic** — even when filtered in the kidneys they are reabsorbed in the tubules, and they accumulate in membranes and adipose tissue. The aim of biotransformation is to convert them into **hydrophilic** (water-soluble) compounds and excrete them in the urine or bile.

blocks.label: Figure 26.1
blocks.caption: The two phases of xenobiotic detoxification (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **Phase I (functionalization)** — polar groups (–OH, –NH~2~, –COOH, –SH) are introduced into the molecule or unmasked: **oxidation** (mainly cytochrome P450), reduction (nitro and azo compounds), **hydrolysis** (esterases, amidases, epoxide hydrolase).
**Phase II (conjugation)** — a small endogenous molecule is attached to the polar group; the product is highly water-soluble and usually inactive.
**Phase III** — export of the conjugates from the cell by membrane transporters (P-glycoprotein, MRP). Besides the liver, detoxification also takes place in the intestine, kidneys, lungs and skin.

blocks.text: **Microsomes** are fragments of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum isolated from a cell homogenate. The **monooxygenase** (mixed-function oxidase) reaction:
RH + O~2~ + NADPH + H^+^ → ROH + H~2~O + NADP^+^
One oxygen atom goes to the substrate and the other to water.

**Electron transport chain:** NADPH → **NADPH–cytochrome P450 reductase** (a flavoprotein: FAD, FMN) → **cytochrome P450** (a hemoprotein). The second electron can also be donated by cytochrome b5 (via NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase).

**The cytochrome P450 cycle:** the substrate binds to Fe^3+^-P450 → first electron (Fe^2+^) → O~2~ binds → second electron → the O–O bond is broken, one O atom forms water → the active iron–oxo complex hydroxylates the substrate → the product is released. The name “P450”: its reduced form bound to CO gives an absorption peak at 450 nm.

**The P450 family:** 57 genes in humans; mainly the **CYP1, 2, 3** families take part in xenobiotic metabolism: **CYP3A4** (≈ 50% of drugs), CYP2D6 (≈ 25%), CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP1A2, CYP2E1 (ethanol, paracetamol, organic solvents). Other P450s take part in the synthesis of endogenous substances: steroid hormones (adrenal glands, gonads), bile acids (7α-hydroxylase), hydroxylation of vitamin D, eicosanoids.
**Types of reactions:** aliphatic and aromatic hydroxylation, epoxidation, N-, O- and S-dealkylation, deamination, N- and S-oxidation, dehalogenation.

**Toxic activation (lethal synthesis):** some substances become more toxic under the action of P450: benzo(a)pyrene → diol epoxide (a carcinogen, topic 19), paracetamol → NAPQI, CCl~4~ → trichloromethyl radical (lipid peroxidation, liver necrosis), methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid (blindness, acidosis), ethylene glycol → oxalate (kidney).
**Difference from mitochondrial oxidation:** microsomal oxidation does not produce ATP (energy is consumed — NADPH), has low substrate specificity and is inducible.

blocks.text: **Urinary indican** (the Obermayer reaction, topic 11) reflects the intensity of putrefaction in the intestine and the detoxifying activity of the liver: it increases in constipation, intestinal obstruction, achylia and dysbiosis.

sections.title: 5. Detoxification of normal metabolites and hormones

items: **Bilirubin** — glucuronidation (topic 25).

**Steroid hormones:** the cortisol ring is reduced and conjugated with glucuronic acid (17-hydroxycorticosteroids in the urine); androgens — 17-ketosteroids (sulfate and glucuronide conjugates); estrogens — hydroxylation, methylation, glucuronidation (enterohepatic circulation).
**Catecholamines** — catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) and monoamine oxidase (MAO) → vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
**Peptide hormones** (insulin, glucagon, somatotropin) — proteolysis (insulinase); ≈ 50% of insulin is degraded in the liver on first pass.

**Thyroid hormones** — deiodination, glucuronidation, sulfation. **Clinical importance:** in liver cirrhosis the inactivation of estrogens decreases — gynecomastia in men, “spider angiomas”, palmar erythema; the inactivation of aldosterone decreases — retention of Na^+^ and water (ascites); the breakdown of insulin decreases.

blocks.text: **Age-related features:** in newborns P450 and UGT activity is low (chloramphenicol — the “gray baby syndrome”, physiological jaundice); in children some P450s are more active; in the elderly liver mass, blood flow and phase I reactions decrease — drug doses must be reduced.

sections.title: 6. Biotransformation of drugs and the factors that affect it

blocks.text: **Influencing factors:** age, sex (pregnancy), genetic polymorphism, liver and kidney diseases, nutrition (protein deficiency decreases P450; aromatic hydrocarbons in grilled meat induce CYP1A2), smoking (CYP1A2 induction), alcohol (CYP2E1 induction), other drugs (induction and inhibition), circadian rhythm.

**The “first-pass” effect:** when an orally administered drug passes through the intestinal wall and the liver, a large part of it is broken down (nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine) — therefore it is given sublingually or parenterally.

**Prodrugs** are inactive drugs that are activated in the body: codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), clopidogrel → active thiol metabolite (CYP2C19), enalapril → enalaprilat (esterases), cyclophosphamide (CYP2B6).

The effect of other drugs decreases: oral contraceptives fail, the warfarin dose must be increased; the activity of prodrugs increases; paracetamol toxicity increases

blocks.text: Phenobarbital is used as an inducer in neonatal jaundice and Crigler–Najjar type II (induction of UGT1A1).
Because of pharmacogenetic polymorphism, people are divided into **poor**, **intermediate**, **normal** and **ultrarapid** metabolizers of drugs.

items: **CYP2D6** — poor metabolizers (≈ 7% in Europe): toxicity of β-blockers and antidepressants, codeine is ineffective (not converted to morphine); in **ultrarapid** metabolizers (many gene copies), codeine is converted to large amounts of morphine and depresses the respiratory center (deaths in children).
**CYP2C19** — in poor metabolizers **clopidogrel** is not activated (risk of thrombosis); proton pump inhibitors act more strongly.
**CYP2C9** and **VKORC1** — the dose of **warfarin** is chosen according to the genotype.
**NAT2** — in slow acetylators, isoniazid polyneuropathy (protection with B~6~), and lupus-like syndrome with hydralazine and procainamide.
**TPMT** — in its deficiency 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine cause severe bone marrow suppression — genotyping before treatment is recommended.
**UGT1A1*28** (Gilbert) — irinotecan toxicity.
**Pseudocholinesterase** — in the atypical variant suxamethonium causes prolonged apnea.
**G6PD** — hemolysis with oxidizing drugs (topic 7). **Personalized medicine** — choosing the drug and the dose on the basis of pharmacogenetic tests and preventing adverse effects.

sections.title: 8. Detoxification of ethanol in the liver

blocks.label: Figure 26.2
blocks.caption: Pathways of ethanol metabolism and its metabolic consequences (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: ≈ 90% of ethanol is oxidized in the liver (2–10% is excreted unchanged by the lungs and in the urine); the rate is ≈ 7–10 g/hour (0.1–0.15‰ per hour).

items: **Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** — cytosol, NAD^+^; the main pathway (also a small amount in the stomach; women have less gastric ADH).

**The microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) — CYP2E1** — NADPH, O~2~; it is induced 5–10 times by chronic drinking (“tolerance”); it generates free radicals and alters the metabolism of paracetamol and other drugs.

**Catalase** — in peroxisomes, with H~2~O~2~ (of little importance). **Acetaldehyde** is the most toxic intermediate: adducts with proteins, DNA and phospholipids, damage to microtubules, depletion of glutathione. **Aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)** oxidizes it to acetate: **ALDH2** — mitochondrial, low K~m~, the main one; ALDH1 — cytosolic.

parts.text: The **ALDH2*2** (Glu487Lys) variant occurs in ≈ 40% of the East Asian population: the enzyme is almost inactive, and after alcohol acetaldehyde accumulates and causes facial flushing, tachycardia and nausea (a protective factor, but the risk of esophageal cancer increases). **Disulfiram**, by inhibiting ALDH, causes the same reaction — it is used in the treatment of alcoholism; metronidazole and some cephalosporins also have a disulfiram-like effect.

blocks.text: **Acetate** is converted to acetyl-CoA in various tissues.
**The metabolic consequences of alcohol** are mainly due to an **increase in the NADH/NAD^+^ ratio** in the cytosol and mitochondria:

items: pyruvate is converted to lactate — **lactic acidosis**; lactate competes with urate secretion in the kidney — **hyperuricemia** (gout attack);
gluconeogenesis stops (pyruvate and oxaloacetate are reduced) — **hypoglycemia** when drinking on an empty stomach (dangerous, especially in children and diabetic patients);
β-oxidation and the Krebs cycle slow down, and the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate and fatty acids increases — triacylglycerols accumulate: **fatty liver**, hyperlipidemia;
a lot of acetyl-CoA and little oxaloacetate — **alcoholic ketoacidosis**;

in chronic drinking: CYP2E1 induction, oxidative stress, activation of stellate cells — **alcoholic hepatitis** and **cirrhosis**; deficiency of thiamine (Wernicke–Korsakoff), folate and B~6~; pancreatitis; in methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning ethanol acts as an **antidote** as a competitive substrate for ADH (fomepizole — an ADH inhibitor). **Markers of chronic alcoholism:** GGT ↑, AST/ALT > 2, MCV ↑ (macrocytosis), **carbohydrate-deficient transferrin** (CDT) ↑, triacylglycerols and uric acid ↑.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determination of hippuric acid in urine (assessment of the detoxifying function of the liver — based on the Quick–Pytel test)

**Principle of the method:** the liver conjugates benzoic acid with glycine and converts it into **hippuric acid**. The amount of hippuric acid excreted in the urine after a sodium benzoate load reflects the conjugating activity of the liver. Hippuric acid crystallizes in an acidic medium.

items: The subject drinks 4 g of sodium benzoate dissolved in 30 ml of water on an empty stomach (for teaching purposes a prepared urine sample is used).
Urine is collected for 4 hours and its volume is measured.
Add 1 g of NaCl and acetic acid (or HCl) to 20 ml of urine and keep in an ice bath for 30 minutes — hippuric acid precipitates as needle-shaped crystals.

Filter the crystals, wash with a small amount of cold water, dry and weigh (or titrate with 0.1 M NaOH in the presence of phenolphthalein: 1 ml of 0.1 M NaOH = 17.9 mg of hippuric acid). **Interpretation:** in a healthy person ≈ 65–85% of the administered sodium benzoate (≈ 3–3.5 g calculated as benzoic acid) is excreted as hippuric acid within 4 hours. A decrease is seen with damage to the liver parenchyma (hepatitis, cirrhosis) or with glycine deficiency; kidney function must be preserved.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: analysis of paracetamol metabolism (case-based)

items: Write the metabolic pathways of paracetamol at a therapeutic dose: glucuronidation (≈ 55%), sulfation (≈ 30%), NAPQI via CYP2E1 (≈ 5–10%) → conjugation with glutathione → mercapturic acid.
Show which pathways become saturated at a toxic dose (> 150 mg/kg) and the fate of NAPQI.
State the mechanism of action of N-acetylcysteine.

blocks.text: **Results and analysis:** the conjugation pathways become saturated, a lot of NAPQI is formed and the glutathione store is exhausted (< 30%) — NAPQI binds covalently to the cysteine residues of hepatocyte proteins — centrilobular liver necrosis. N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis and binds NAPQI directly; it is very effective if given within 8–10 hours. Chronic alcoholism (CYP2E1 induction, decreased glutathione) and fasting increase the risk.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old girl in a depressed state took 20 tablets of paracetamol (10 g). On the first day she had no complaints other than nausea. On day 3 jaundice and pain under the right costal margin appeared: ALT 6800 U/l, AST 5200 U/l, bilirubin 85 µmol/l, INR 3.8.
cases.ask: What is the biochemical mechanism of the liver damage? Why did the symptoms appear late? How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: At a therapeutic dose paracetamol is detoxified mainly by glucuronidation and sulfation; a small part is converted by CYP2E1 into reactive NAPQI, which is immediately bound by glutathione. At a high dose the conjugation pathways become saturated, a lot of NAPQI is formed and the glutathione in hepatocytes is exhausted; NAPQI binds covalently to the cysteine residues of proteins, damages the mitochondria and causes oxidative stress — necrosis of the cells in the center of the liver lobules (where CYP2E1 is abundant). The necrosis and its signs (a sharp rise in ALT, impaired synthesis — INR) develop within 24–72 hours; the early period is almost asymptomatic, which makes it dangerous. The antidote is N-acetylcysteine: a source of cysteine for glutathione synthesis, and it binds NAPQI directly; it is most effective when given early (within 8–10 hours). The patient also needs psychiatric care.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman with tuberculosis who is taking rifampicin became pregnant even though she was taking an oral contraceptive. In addition, she takes warfarin, and her INR has fallen to 1.3 (target 2–3).
cases.ask: How do you explain these situations? What is the mechanism? What measures should be taken?
cases.answer: Rifampicin is a potent P450 inducer: through the nuclear receptor PXR it enhances the synthesis of CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and other enzymes, as well as UGT and P-glycoprotein. As a result, the estrogens and progestins of the contraceptive (CYP3A4) are broken down rapidly and their blood concentration falls below the effective level — contraception fails. Warfarin (its S-enantiomer via CYP2C9) is metabolized rapidly — the anticoagulant effect decreases (INR fell, risk of thrombosis). Measures: barrier methods of contraception during treatment and for 4 weeks after it ends; increasing the warfarin dose under INR control (and reducing the dose again after rifampicin is stopped, as the induction wears off over 2 weeks — otherwise there is a risk of bleeding).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 50-year-old man has been drinking large amounts of alcohol for 20 years. He was brought in confused after heavy drinking on an empty stomach in the morning. Blood glucose 2.1 mmol/l, lactate 5.8 mmol/l, β-hydroxybutyrate 4.5 mmol/l, uric acid 560 µmol/l, triacylglycerols 4.8 mmol/l, GGT 420 U/l, MCV 104 fl.
cases.ask: Explain all the biochemical changes in relation to alcohol metabolism.
cases.answer: When ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase, a lot of NADH is formed and the NADH/NAD^+^ ratio rises. As a result, pyruvate is reduced to lactate (lactic acidosis) and oxaloacetate to malate — substrates for gluconeogenesis are lacking; when the glycogen store is exhausted on an empty stomach, hypoglycemia develops (confusion). Lactate competes with urate secretion in the kidney — hyperuricemia. β-Oxidation slows because of the excess NADH, glycerol-3-phosphate increases and TAG synthesis is enhanced — hypertriglyceridemia and fatty liver. Acetyl-CoA formed from acetate is converted to ketone bodies when oxaloacetate is lacking, and NADH reduces acetoacetate to β-hydroxybutyrate — alcoholic ketoacidosis. The increase in GGT is due to the induction of CYP2E1 and microsomal enzymes and to liver damage; macrocytosis is due to the direct effect of alcohol on the bone marrow and folate deficiency. Treatment: thiamine before giving glucose (to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy).

topics.title: Physiologically active substances and biochemistry of the endocrine system

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the classification of physiologically active substances, substances of peptide nature (cytokines, growth factors), amino acid derivatives, the hierarchy of regulatory systems and the hypothalamic–pituitary system, the classification of hormones by chemical nature, function and mechanism of action, the interrelation of the endocrine and nervous systems, the synthesis and catabolism of steroid hormones, the mechanism of action of sex hormones, the detoxification of hormones in the liver, and the determination of chorionic gonadotropin in urine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of physiologically active substances (hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines, growth factors, eicosanoids);
the classification of hormones by chemical nature;
the mechanisms of action through membrane and intracellular receptors;
the hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary and the feedback principle;
the stages and enzymes of steroid hormone synthesis;
the synthesis, transport and mechanism of action of sex hormones;
the structure, function and diagnostic importance of β-hCG.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine chorionic gonadotropin in urine with an immunochromatographic test and interpret the result;
explain the mechanism of hormone action through second messengers;
determine the type of hormonal disorder (primary, secondary) on the basis of feedback.

blocks.text: **Physiologically active substances** are signaling molecules that regulate cell activity at very low concentrations (10^−6^–10^−12^ M).

blocks.title: Table 27.1. Classification of signaling molecules by range of action
head: Type
Definition
Examples
rows: Through the blood to distant target cells
Somatostatin (in the islets), histamine, NO, growth factors
To the cell that produced it
A ligand on the cell surface with a receptor on a neighboring cell

blocks.text: Locally acting substances (tissue hormones):

items: **eicosanoids** (from arachidonic acid): prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes (cyclooxygenase pathway), leukotrienes (lipoxygenase pathway) — inflammation, pain, fever, hemostasis, bronchial tone (topic 9);
**biogenic amines:** histamine, serotonin;
**kinins:** bradykinin, kallidin — vasodilation, permeability, pain;
**nitric oxide (NO)**. **Substances of peptide nature:**

**cytokines** — interleukins (IL-1, IL-6 — acute phase, fever), interferons (antiviral), tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α), chemokines, colony-stimulating factors; they act mainly through the JAK-STAT pathway;

**growth factors** — epidermal growth factor (EGF), platelet-derived (PDGF), insulin-like (IGF-1), fibroblast (FGF), vascular endothelial (VEGF), transforming (TGF-β), nerve growth factor (NGF), erythropoietin; mainly through tyrosine kinase receptors;

**neuropeptides** — endorphins, enkephalins (opioid peptides), substance P, neuropeptide Y. **Amino acid derivatives:** from tyrosine — catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and **thyroid hormones**; from tryptophan — **serotonin** and **melatonin**; from histidine — **histamine**; from glutamate — **GABA**; from arginine — NO.

blocks.title: Table 27.2. Classification of hormones by chemical nature
head: Group
Examples
Features
rows: Insulin, glucagon, somatotropin, prolactin, PTH, calcitonin, hypothalamic hormones, vasopressin, oxytocin
Synthesized as prohormones, stored in granules, water-soluble, membrane receptors
Common α subunit, specific β subunit
Catecholamines — membrane receptors; thyroid hormones — nuclear receptors
Cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone, calcitriol
From cholesterol, not stored, transported by carrier proteins, nuclear receptors

blocks.text: **By biological function:** regulators of carbohydrate, lipid and protein metabolism (insulin, glucagon, cortisol, somatotropin), of water–salt metabolism (aldosterone, vasopressin, natriuretic peptides), of calcium–phosphate metabolism (PTH, calcitonin, calcitriol), of reproductive function (sex hormones, gonadotropins), and of other endocrine glands (tropic hormones).

blocks.label: Figure 27.1
blocks.caption: Mechanisms of hormone action through receptors (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: Through membrane receptors (hydrophilic hormones):

items: **G protein-coupled receptors** (7 transmembrane domains):
**G~s~ → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A** — glucagon, epinephrine (β), ACTH, TSH, PTH, vasopressin (V~2~), LH, FSH;
**G~i~** — inhibits adenylate cyclase (epinephrine α~2~, somatostatin);

**G~q~ → phospholipase Cβ** → phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate → **IP~3~** (releases Ca^2+^ from the endoplasmic reticulum; Ca^2+^–calmodulin) + **DAG** (protein kinase C) — epinephrine (α~1~), vasopressin (V~1~), angiotensin II, oxytocin, releasing hormones. cAMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase (inhibited by caffeine and theophylline).
**Tyrosine kinase receptors** — insulin, IGF-1, EGF, PDGF: autophosphorylation → IRS, PI3K/Akt, Ras-MAPK pathways.
**Tyrosine kinase-associated receptors (JAK-STAT)** — somatotropin, prolactin, erythropoietin, leptin, cytokines.

**Guanylate cyclase receptors** — natriuretic peptides (membrane), NO (soluble guanylate cyclase) → cGMP → PKG. **Through intracellular (nuclear) receptors (lipophilic hormones):** steroids, T~3~, calcitriol and retinoids cross the membrane by diffusion and bind to cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors; the hormone–receptor complex (released from Hsp90) forms a dimer, binds to **hormone response elements (HRE)** in DNA and changes the transcription of target genes. The action is slow (hours) and long-lasting.

sections.title: 4. Hierarchy of regulatory systems. The hypothalamic–pituitary system

blocks.text: **Hierarchy:** cerebral cortex → **hypothalamus** (releasing and inhibiting hormones) → **pituitary** (tropic hormones) → **peripheral endocrine glands** → target tissues. Regulation is based on the principle of **negative feedback**: the peripheral hormone inhibits the secretion of the hypothalamus and pituitary.

blocks.title: Table 27.3. Hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary
head: Hypothalamus
Pituitary (anterior lobe, adenohypophysis)
Target and action
rows: ACTH (from POMC; together with β-lipotropin, β-endorphin, α-MSH)
Liver — IGF-1; growth, anabolism, lipolysis, contrainsular effect
Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) — synthesized in the hypothalamus and transported along axons: vasopressin (ADH), oxytocin
Kidney (water reabsorption), vessels; uterine contraction, milk ejection

blocks.text: **Level of disorders: primary** (peripheral gland) — the peripheral hormone is low and the tropic hormone is **high** (feedback); **secondary** (pituitary) or **tertiary** (hypothalamus) — both are low. For example, in primary hypothyroidism TSH ↑, T~4~ ↓; in secondary TSH ↓, T~4~ ↓.

sections.title: 5. Interrelation of the endocrine and nervous systems. Ontogenesis

blocks.text: The hypothalamus is the center that links the nervous and endocrine systems: its neurons produce neurohormones (**neurosecretion**). The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion (acetylcholine from preganglionic fibers triggers epinephrine secretion). Hormones affect brain function (thyroid hormones — brain development, cortisol — mood and memory, sex hormones — behavior); in stress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal system and the sympathoadrenal system are activated together. Circadian rhythms (cortisol high in the morning, melatonin at night) are controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

**Changes in ontogenesis:** in the fetal period thyroid hormones are crucial for brain and skeletal development (congenital hypothyroidism — cretinism; newborn screening — TSH); in childhood somatotropin and IGF-1 ensure growth; at puberty gonadoliberin pulsatility begins and sex hormones increase; in old age somatotropin (somatopause), sex hormones (menopause, andropause) and DHEA decrease, and insulin sensitivity declines.

sections.title: 6. Synthesis and catabolism of steroid hormones

blocks.text: All steroid hormones are synthesized **from cholesterol** (obtained mainly through LDL). The key (rate-limiting) step is the transport of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane by the **StAR protein** and its conversion to **pregnenolone** by **CYP11A1** (the side-chain cleavage enzyme); this step is stimulated through cAMP by ACTH (adrenal gland) and LH (gonads). The enzymes of synthesis belong mainly to the cytochrome P450 family.

blocks.label: Figure 27.2
blocks.caption: Main pathways of steroid hormone synthesis (drawn after Severin E.S.)

items: **Zona glomerulosa: aldosterone** (aldosterone synthase — CYP11B2; stimulated by angiotensin II and K^+^);
**zona fasciculata: cortisol** (17α-, 21- and 11β-hydroxylases; ACTH);
**zona reticularis:** androgens (DHEA, androstenedione);
**testes (Leydig cells): testosterone** (LH); in target tissues **5α-reductase** converts it into the more active **dihydrotestosterone** (prostate, external genitalia, hair follicles);

**ovaries:** theca cells synthesize androgens (LH), and granulosa cells convert them into **estradiol** with **aromatase** (CYP19) (FSH); the corpus luteum — **progesterone**; adipose tissue also contains aromatase (the source of estrogens after menopause).

parts.text: **Congenital adrenal hyperplasia** — most often **21-hydroxylase** deficiency (autosomal recessive): cortisol and aldosterone are not synthesized; by feedback ACTH increases, the gland becomes hyperplastic and the accumulated 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is converted into androgens — virilization of the external genitalia in girls, salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia). Newborn screening — blood 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Treatment — replacement with glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.

blocks.text: **Transport:** in the blood most steroids are bound to proteins: cortisol — to **transcortin** (≈ 90%) and albumin; testosterone and estradiol — to **sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)** and albumin; only the free fraction (1–3%) is active.

**Catabolism (in the liver):** reduction of ring A, hydroxylation, then conjugation with **glucuronic acid** or **sulfate** — water-soluble metabolites are excreted in the urine: **17-hydroxycorticosteroids** from cortisol, **17-ketosteroids** from androgens and part of cortisol, **pregnanediol** from progesterone, and estriol glucuronides from estrogens. The daily urinary free cortisol is a screening test for Cushing syndrome. In liver cirrhosis the inactivation of estrogens decreases (topic 26).

sections.title: 7. Mechanism of action of sex hormones

blocks.text: **Androgens** (testosterone, dihydrotestosterone) bind to the androgen receptor (nuclear): formation of the male genitalia in the fetal period, secondary sexual characteristics at puberty, spermatogenesis (together with FSH), **anabolic effect** (muscle protein synthesis, erythropoiesis, bone mass), libido. **Androgen receptor defect** — complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (genotype XY, female phenotype).

**Estrogens** (estradiol, estrone, estriol) — estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ): development of the female genitalia and mammary glands, endometrial proliferation (the 1st phase of the menstrual cycle), reduction of bone resorption (osteoporosis after menopause), raising HDL and lowering LDL (atheroprotective), increasing the hepatic synthesis of transport proteins (SHBG, transcortin, thyroxine-binding globulin) and clotting factors (risk of thrombosis with oral contraceptives).

**Progesterone** — progesterone receptor: secretory phase of the endometrium, maintenance of pregnancy (reduces myometrial excitability), development of the alveoli of the mammary glands, thermogenic effect (rise in basal temperature).

**Pharmacological use:** oral contraceptives (estrogen + progestin — suppress gonadotropin secretion by feedback), tamoxifen (an estrogen antagonist in the breast), aromatase inhibitors (letrozole), 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride — in prostatic adenoma), antiandrogens, anabolic steroids (abuse — liver, heart, infertility).

**Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)** is a glycoprotein produced by the **syncytiotrophoblast**; its α subunit is identical to that of LH, FSH and TSH, while the **β subunit** is specific (that is why tests detect β-hCG). Its function is to act like LH and maintain the **corpus luteum** and progesterone secretion during the first 8–10 weeks of pregnancy (after that the placenta produces progesterone itself). It is detectable in the blood 8–10 days after fertilization, doubles every 48–72 hours and peaks at 8–10 weeks. At high concentrations it stimulates TSH receptors (signs of hyperthyroidism in hyperemesis of pregnancy).

**Diagnostic importance:** early detection of pregnancy; ectopic (extrauterine) pregnancy — hCG rises slowly; threatened miscarriage; trophoblastic diseases (**hydatidiform mole**, **choriocarcinoma** — very high hCG; a tumor marker); embryonal tumors of the testis; prenatal screening (elevated in Down syndrome in the 2nd trimester).
Experiment 1: determination of chorionic gonadotropin in urine with an immunochromatographic test

**Principle of the method:** the test strip contains monoclonal antibodies against β-hCG labeled with gold particles. Urine moves along the membrane by capillary action: if hCG is present, it forms a complex with the labeled antibodies and is captured by the immobilized second antibodies in the “test” zone — a colored line appears (a “sandwich”). Antiglobulins in the “control” zone capture the excess conjugate — this shows that the test has worked correctly.

items: Collect morning urine (the highest concentration) in a clean container.
Dip the test strip into the urine up to the indicated mark for 10–15 seconds (do not go beyond the mark).

Place it on a flat horizontal surface and read the result after 3–5 minutes (a result read after 10 minutes is unreliable). **Interpretation:** two lines — positive (hCG ≥ 10–25 IU/l); only the control line — negative; no control line — the test is invalid. The test is reliable from the first day of a missed period. False negative — too early, dilute urine; false positive — treatment with hCG preparations, trophoblastic tumors, a recent abortion.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: analysis of hormone mechanisms of action using a scheme (case-based)

items: For the given hormone (glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, insulin, vasopressin), determine its chemical nature and receptor type.
Write down the second messenger and the final effector protein.

Show the speed of the response (fast or slow) and the metabolic result. **Results and analysis:** hydrophilic hormones act quickly through membrane receptors and second messengers, and lipophilic hormones act slowly through nuclear receptors by changing gene expression.

skills.title: Skill: determining the level of an endocrine disorder

items: Assess the peripheral hormone (T~4~, cortisol, testosterone) and the corresponding tropic hormone (TSH, ACTH, LH).
Peripheral hormone ↓ + tropic hormone ↑ — primary (glandular) insufficiency.
Peripheral hormone ↓ + tropic hormone ↓ — secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic).
Peripheral hormone ↑ + tropic hormone ↓ — primary hyperfunction (tumor, autoimmune stimulation).

Assess the dynamics: an increase of ≈ 2 times in 48 hours — normal pregnancy; a slow increase — ectopic or nonviable pregnancy.
Very high for the gestational age — multiple pregnancy or hydatidiform mole.
hCG outside pregnancy — tumor (choriocarcinoma, testicular tumor).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In the maternity ward a newborn (XX karyotype) has ambiguous external genitalia. In the 2nd week vomiting and dehydration began: Na^+^ 124, K^+^ 6.8 mmol/l, glucose 2.8 mmol/l. Blood 17-hydroxyprogesterone is sharply increased, and ACTH is high.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain all the signs on the basis of the steroid synthesis scheme. What is the principle of treatment?
cases.answer: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia — 21-hydroxylase deficiency, salt-wasting form. Progesterone and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone are not 21-hydroxylated: cortisol (hypoglycemia) and aldosterone (Na^+^ loss, K^+^ retention, dehydration) are not synthesized. Because of the low cortisol, ACTH increases by feedback and the gland becomes hyperplastic; the accumulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone is diverted to the androgen synthesis pathway — the excess androgens virilize the external genitalia of the girl in the fetal period. Treatment: glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone — replaces cortisol and, by lowering ACTH, stops the overproduction of androgens), a mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone), table salt; in a crisis — intravenous fluids, glucose, hydrocortisone.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 27-year-old woman's period is 2 weeks late; she has one-sided lower abdominal pain and bloody discharge. Blood β-hCG 1200 IU/l, and 1350 IU/l 48 hours later. Ultrasound did not detect a gestational sac in the uterine cavity.
cases.ask: What condition is suspected? Explain the hCG dynamics. What is the physiological role of hCG in pregnancy?
cases.answer: Extrauterine (ectopic, probably tubal) pregnancy. In a normal intrauterine pregnancy β-hCG roughly doubles every 48–72 hours in the early weeks; here it hardly rose (≈ 12%) — the trophoblast is not developing adequately; the absence of a gestational sac in the uterus at this hCG level indicates an ectopic location. hCG secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum through LH receptors and ensures progesterone secretion; progesterone maintains the endometrium and stops menstruation. An ectopic pregnancy requires urgent treatment because of the risk of tubal rupture and internal bleeding.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 40-year-old patient has extreme fatigue, weight loss, nausea, arterial hypotension and dark pigmentation of the skin and gums. Blood Na^+^ 128, K^+^ 5.9 mmol/l, morning cortisol 60 nmol/l (normal 140–690), ACTH sharply increased.
cases.ask: At what level is the disorder? What is the biochemical cause of the pigmentation? Explain the electrolyte changes.
cases.answer: Primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease, most often autoimmune). Low cortisol and high ACTH — the disorder is in the peripheral gland (feedback is preserved, and the pituitary produces a lot of ACTH). ACTH is formed from proopiomelanocortin (POMC); when POMC is cleaved, α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone also increases, and ACTH itself stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors — melanin synthesis is enhanced (pigmentation; absent in secondary insufficiency). Aldosterone is also deficient: renal Na^+^ reabsorption and K^+^ secretion decrease — hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia and hypotension. Treatment — lifelong replacement therapy with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.

topics.title: Hormonal regulation of metabolism. Functions of the peripheral glands and their disorders

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the hormonal regulation of carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism and its age-related features, thyroid hormones and the effect of their deficiency on growth and development, the regulation of calcium–phosphate metabolism and rickets, the regulation of water–salt metabolism, locally acting hormones, the pathogenesis of endemic goiter and hypothyroidism, and the determination of insulin by enzyme immunoassay.
By the end of the class the student should know:

the role of PTH, calcitonin and calcitriol in calcium–phosphate metabolism;

goals.text: The student should be able to:

sections.title: 1. Hormonal regulation of carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism

blocks.text: **Insulin** — in the **β-cells** of the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas: preproinsulin → proinsulin (A and B chains + C-peptide) → insulin + **C-peptide** (released in equal amounts; C-peptide is an indicator of endogenous insulin secretion). **Mechanism of secretion:** glucose enters through GLUT2 → glucokinase → glycolysis and oxidation → ATP/ADP ↑ → ATP-sensitive K^+^ channels close (sulfonylurea drugs act in the same way) → depolarization → Ca^2+^ channels open → exocytosis of granules. Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) enhance secretion; epinephrine (α~2~) and somatostatin inhibit it.

**Mechanism of insulin action:** tyrosine kinase receptor → autophosphorylation → **IRS-1/2** → **PI3K → Akt (PKB)**: translocation of GLUT4 to the membrane (muscle, adipose tissue), inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (glycogen synthesis ↑), activation of phosphodiesterase 3B (cAMP ↓ — lipolysis ↓), mTOR (protein synthesis ↑), inactivation of FOXO1 (gluconeogenesis genes ↓); **Ras-MAPK** — growth and division.

blocks.title: Table 28.1. Metabolic effects of the contrainsular hormones
head: Hormone
Mechanism
Main metabolic effects
rows: Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver ↑, glycolysis and lipogenesis ↓, ketogenesis ↑
Glycogenolysis (liver and muscle), lipolysis, gluconeogenesis ↑; insulin secretion ↓ (α~2~); “fight or flight”

Gluconeogenic enzymes (PEPCK, G-6-phosphatase) ↑, muscle proteolysis ↑, peripheral glucose uptake ↓; central lipogenesis, peripheral lipolysis (“permissive” effect); suppresses inflammation and immunity
Protein synthesis ↑ (via IGF-1), lipolysis ↑, glucose uptake ↓ (diabetogenic), growth
Basal metabolism ↑, all processes are accelerated

blocks.text: **Diabetes mellitus** (topic 15): **type 1** — autoimmune destruction of β-cells (antibodies to GAD, insulin, IA-2), absolute insulin deficiency, tendency to ketoacidosis, low C-peptide; **type 2** — insulin resistance + relative deficiency, often with obesity, C-peptide normal or high; **gestational**, MODY (mutations in glucokinase and other genes) and other types. **Diagnostic criteria:** fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/l, ≥ 11.1 at 2 hours in the GTT, random ≥ 11.1 (with symptoms), HbA~1c~ ≥ 6.5%.

**Acute complications:** diabetic ketoacidosis (type 1), hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (type 2; glucose > 33 mmol/l, osmolality > 320, no ketosis — the small amount of insulin stops lipolysis), lactic acidosis (metformin, hypoxia), **hypoglycemia** (overdose of insulin or a sulfonylurea; < 3.9 mmol/l — the most dangerous for the brain).

**Age-related features:** in newborns the glycogen store is small and the gluconeogenic enzymes are immature — a tendency to hypoglycemia (especially in preterm infants and infants of diabetic mothers — fetal hyperinsulinism); type 1 diabetes is more common in children; in the elderly insulin sensitivity declines and muscle mass decreases — type 2 diabetes becomes more common.

blocks.label: Figure 28.1
blocks.caption: Biosynthesis of thyroid hormones (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **Synthesis:** follicular cells concentrate iodide from the blood 20–40 times through the **Na^+^/I^-^ symporter (NIS)**; **thyroperoxidase** (heme-containing, requires H~2~O~2~) oxidizes iodide and iodinates the tyrosine residues within **thyroglobulin** (mono- and diiodotyrosine), then condenses them — T~4~ and T~3~ are stored in the colloid as part of thyroglobulin. Under the action of TSH the hormones are released into the blood by endocytosis of colloid and lysosomal proteolysis (mainly T~4~, ≈ 80–90%). The daily iodine requirement is **150 µg** (250 µg in pregnancy and lactation).

**Transport:** > 99% is bound to proteins (thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, albumin); the active forms are **free T~4~** and **free T~3~**. In the periphery **deiodinases** (selenoproteins) convert T~4~ into the more active **T~3~** (10 times higher affinity for the receptor) or into inactive reverse T~3~.
**Mechanism of action and effects:** T~3~ binds to nuclear receptors (TR, a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor) and changes gene transcription:

items: **basal metabolism and thermogenesis ↑** — synthesis of Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase, mitochondrial biogenesis, uncoupling proteins;
carbohydrates — absorption, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis ↑;
lipids — lipolysis ↑, hepatic LDL receptors ↑ (cholesterol ↓);
proteins — at physiological doses synthesis ↑ (growth), in excess catabolism ↑;
**growth and development** — expression of the somatotropin gene, ossification, **brain development** (myelination, synaptogenesis — in the fetus and the first 2–3 years of life);
heart — β-adrenoceptors and myosin heavy chain α ↑ (tachycardia).

blocks.text: **Endemic goiter** is enlargement of the thyroid gland in iodine-deficient regions (mountainous areas, including some regions of Central Asia). **Pathogenesis:** when iodine is lacking, T~4~ synthesis decreases → TSH increases by feedback → the follicular cells undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia (the gland enlarges); the gland adapts by producing more T~3~ (which requires less iodine); if this continues for a long time, hypothyroidism develops. Iodine deficiency in pregnant women leads to impaired brain development in the fetus. Goitrogenic substances (thiocyanates and goitrin in cabbage and radish family plants) reduce iodine uptake. **Prevention** — **iodized table salt** (universal salt iodization), potassium iodide for risk groups. **Treatment** — potassium iodide, levothyroxine; surgery for nodules.

The body contains ≈ 1 kg of calcium (99% in bones as hydroxyapatite) and ≈ 0.6 kg of phosphorus (85% in bones). Total blood calcium is 2.15–2.55 mmol/l: ≈ 45% is **ionized** (active, 1.1–1.3 mmol/l), ≈ 40% is bound to albumin, and ≈ 15% forms complexes with anions. Alkalosis reduces ionized calcium (tetany).

blocks.text: **Disorders: primary hyperparathyroidism** (adenoma) — hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, kidney stones, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer (“bones, stones, abdominal groans, psychic moans”); **hypoparathyroidism** (after surgery) — hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, tetany (Chvostek and Trousseau signs); **chronic kidney disease** — low calcitriol, phosphate retention — secondary hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy.

**Rickets in children** is impaired mineralization of growing bone. **Causes:** vitamin D deficiency (little exposure to the sun, especially in those born in winter, dark skin, prolonged exclusive breastfeeding without prophylaxis, malnutrition, prematurity), malabsorption, liver and kidney diseases (impaired hydroxylation), hereditary forms (defects of 1α-hydroxylase or the vitamin D receptor — **vitamin D-dependent rickets**; **X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets** — FGF-23 excess, vitamin D-resistant). **Pathogenesis:** absorption of Ca^2+^ and phosphate decreases → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → phosphaturia and hypophosphatemia, bone resorption; the osteoid is not mineralized. **Biochemical signs:** blood phosphate ↓, calcium N or ↓, **alkaline phosphatase ↑↑** (osteoblast activity), PTH ↑, 25(OH)D ↓ (< 30 nmol/l). **Clinical signs:** sweating, restlessness, softening of the skull (craniotabes), the “rachitic rosary”, bowing of the legs, delayed tooth eruption, muscle hypotonia. **Prevention and treatment** — vitamin D (prophylactic dose 400–500 IU/day), sunlight, calcium-rich food. The same condition in adults is **osteomalacia**.

Water makes up ≈ 60% of body weight in adults (≈ 75–80% in newborns); intracellular (≈ 2/3) and extracellular (interstitial and plasma) fluids. The main cation outside the cells is Na^+^, and inside — K^+^.

items: **Vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone)** is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma **osmolality rises** (osmoreceptors; even 1–2% is enough) and when blood volume falls sharply. In the renal collecting ducts: V~2~ receptor → cAMP → **aquaporin-2** moves to the apical membrane → water is reabsorbed (concentrated urine). V~1~ — vasoconstriction. **Diabetes insipidus** — vasopressin deficiency (central) or renal insensitivity to it (nephrogenic — V~2~ or AQP2 mutations, lithium): 5–20 l of dilute urine per day (specific gravity < 1.005), thirst, hypernatremia. The syndrome of inappropriate vasopressin secretion — hyponatremia.

**The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system:** when blood pressure and Na^+^ fall (and via sympathetic β~1~), the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney release **renin** → angiotensinogen (liver) → **angiotensin I** → (**angiotensin-converting enzyme**, mainly in the pulmonary endothelium) → **angiotensin II**: powerful vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, thirst and vasopressin, proximal Na^+^ reabsorption. **Aldosterone** (a nuclear receptor) — synthesis of ENaC and Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase in the distal tubules and collecting ducts: Na^+^ and water are retained, K^+^ and H^+^ are excreted. ACE inhibitors (enalapril), angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan), aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) — in hypertension and heart failure.

**Natriuretic peptides** (ANP, BNP) oppose the RAAS: natriuresis, vasodilation (topic 23). **Age-related features:** in newborns the concentrating ability of the kidney is low and the relative water content and turnover are high — very prone to dehydration (with diarrhea, vomiting); in the elderly thirst and concentrating ability decline.

blocks.text: **Eicosanoids** (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes), histamine, serotonin, kinins, NO and gastrointestinal hormones (gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin, GIP, GLP-1, somatostatin — topic 24) act at the site of formation or at a short distance and are rapidly inactivated. **Prostaglandin E~2~** — fever (hypothalamus), pain, gastric protection, maintenance of renal blood flow; NSAIDs reduce it and can cause gastric ulcer and kidney damage.
Experiment 1: determination of serum insulin by enzyme immunoassay (based on a video)

**Principle of the method (“sandwich” ELISA):** the wells of the plate are coated with monoclonal antibodies against one epitope of insulin. Insulin in the sample binds to them; a second, **peroxidase-labeled** antibody against another epitope is added. After washing, the substrate (tetramethylbenzidine + H~2~O~2~) gives a blue color, which turns yellow when the stop acid is added (450 nm). The color intensity is **directly proportional** to the amount of insulin.

items: Pipette 25 µl of the calibrators (0–300 µIU/ml), the control and the patient's serum (taken fasting) into the wells.
Add 100 µl of conjugate (peroxidase–anti-insulin) and incubate with shaking for 60 minutes at room temperature.
Wash the wells 5 times with wash buffer.
Add 100 µl of substrate and keep in the dark for 15 minutes; add 50 µl of stop solution.

Measure the absorbance at 450 nm; find the concentration from the calibration curve. **Interpretation:** fasting insulin 2–25 µIU/ml (≈ 14–174 pmol/l). **HOMA-IR** = [glucose (mmol/l) × insulin (µIU/ml)] / 22.5; > 2.5–2.7 — insulin resistance. Insulin ↓ (C-peptide ↓) — type 1 diabetes; ↑ — insulin resistance (type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, polycystic ovary syndrome), insulinoma (together with hypoglycemia). In patients treated with insulin preparations, endogenous secretion must be assessed by **C-peptide**.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: interpretation of thyroid hormone and TSH results (case-based)

items: Assess TSH first (the most sensitive screening test; normal 0.4–4.0 mIU/l).
Assess free T~4~ (≈ 10–22 pmol/l) and, if necessary, free T~3~.

Take antibodies (to TPO, to the TSH receptor) into account. **Results and analysis:** TSH ↑ + free T~4~ ↓ — primary hypothyroidism; TSH ↑ + free T~4~ N — subclinical hypothyroidism; TSH ↓ + free T~4~ ↑ — thyrotoxicosis; TSH ↓ + free T~4~ ↓ — secondary hypothyroidism (pituitary).

skills.title: Skill: assessing the type of diabetes and insulin secretion

items: Confirm the diagnosis of diabetes by glucose and HbA~1c~.
Assess C-peptide and insulin: low — type 1 (insulin deficiency), high or normal — type 2.
Check for antibodies against β-cells (GAD).
Calculate HOMA-IR.
Assess ketosis and acid–base status (risk of decompensation).

skills.title: Skill: identifying a disorder of calcium–phosphate metabolism

items: Assess total and ionized calcium, phosphate and albumin (albumin-corrected calcium).
Determine PTH, 25(OH)D, alkaline phosphatase and creatinine.

Ca ↑ + PTH ↑ — primary hyperparathyroidism; Ca ↓ + PTH ↓ — hypoparathyroidism; Ca ↓/N + phosphate ↓ + PTH ↑ + 25(OH)D ↓ + ALP ↑ — vitamin D deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia); phosphate ↑ + creatinine ↑ + PTH ↑ — kidney failure.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman living in a mountainous region was found to have an enlarged thyroid gland in the neck; weakness, cold intolerance and dry skin. TSH 9.8 mIU/l, free T~4~ 9 pmol/l, antibodies to TPO negative, urinary iodine 35 µg/l (normal > 100). She does not use iodized salt.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the mechanism of development of goiter and hypothyroidism. What are the measures for prevention and treatment?
cases.answer: Endemic (iodine deficiency) goiter with hypothyroidism. When iodine is lacking, thyroperoxidase cannot iodinate thyroglobulin sufficiently — T~4~ synthesis decreases; by negative feedback the pituitary secretes a lot of TSH; TSH stimulates the growth and division of the follicular cells — the gland enlarges (goiter). As an adaptation the gland synthesizes more T~3~, but if the iodine deficiency persists, hypothyroidism develops: basal metabolism and thermogenesis decrease (cold intolerance, weakness), and GAGs accumulate in the skin. The negative antibodies exclude autoimmune thyroiditis. Prevention — iodized table salt; treatment — potassium iodide, levothyroxine if necessary; iodine intake is especially important when planning a pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 10-month-old child (born in winter, exclusively breastfed, no vitamin D prophylaxis) sweats, is restless, has a bald patch on the back of the head, a “rosary” on the ribs and bowed legs, and has no teeth yet. Blood calcium 2.0 mmol/l, phosphate 0.8 mmol/l (normal 1.3–2.1), alkaline phosphatase 1100 U/l, PTH increased, 25(OH)D 15 nmol/l.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain the mechanism of the biochemical changes. What are the treatment and prevention?
cases.answer: Vitamin D-deficiency rickets. Because of little sunlight (winter) and insufficient vitamin D in the diet (it is low in breast milk), not enough D~3~ was obtained from the skin and food — 25(OH)D and calcitriol are low. Intestinal absorption of Ca^2+^ and phosphate decreases — hypocalcemia stimulates the parathyroid glands (secondary hyperparathyroidism): PTH mobilizes calcium from bone (calcium is kept close to normal) and enhances renal phosphate excretion — hypophosphatemia. Because the calcium × phosphate product is low, the osteoid is not mineralized; the osteoblasts are activated compensatorily and release a lot of alkaline phosphatase; the bones soften and become deformed. Treatment — therapeutic doses of vitamin D, calcium, sunbathing; prevention — vitamin D for all infants in the first year of life (400–500 IU/day).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a head injury a patient is passing 9 l of colorless urine per day and has intense thirst. Urine specific gravity 1.002, osmolality 90 mOsm/kg; blood Na^+^ 152 mmol/l, osmolality 305 mOsm/kg, glucose 5.1 mmol/l. After desmopressin was given, the urine volume fell sharply and the specific gravity rose to 1.018.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Why is the urine dilute? What does the desmopressin test show?
cases.answer: Central (hypothalamic–pituitary) diabetes insipidus — the synthesis or secretion of vasopressin is impaired because of the injury. Without vasopressin the V~2~ receptor → cAMP → aquaporin-2 pathway in the collecting ducts does not work and water is not reabsorbed — a large amount of low-osmolality urine is excreted; the water loss raises plasma osmolality and Na^+^ and stimulates the thirst center. Glucose is normal (not diabetes mellitus). The response to the synthetic vasopressin analog desmopressin (concentration of the urine) shows that the renal receptors are preserved and the defect is central; in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus there is no response. Treatment — desmopressin.
