topics.title: Biochemistry of the kidney. Normal and pathological components of urine

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the mechanism of urine formation (filtration, reabsorption, secretion), the role of the kidneys in maintaining acid–base balance, the specific features of metabolism and energy supply in the kidney, the endocrine functions of the kidney, the general properties of urine and their age-related features, the normal and pathological chemical composition of urine, and the formation and prevention of kidney stones.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the mechanisms of glomerular filtration and tubular reabsorption and secretion;
the pathways by which the kidney excretes H^+^ and regenerates bicarbonate (ammoniagenesis);
the features of metabolism and energy supply in renal tissue;
the endocrine functions of the kidney (renin, erythropoietin, calcitriol);
the physical properties and normal chemical composition of urine;
pathological components (protein, glucose, ketone bodies, bilirubin, blood) and their diagnostic importance;
the types of kidney stones and the biochemical basis of their prevention.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: detect normal and pathological components of urine with test strips;
calculate the GFR from creatinine;
interpret the results of urinalysis.

blocks.text: ≈ 1.2 l of blood passes through the kidneys per minute (≈ 20–25% of the cardiac output). Each kidney has ≈ 1 million **nephrons**.

blocks.label: Figure 29.1
blocks.caption: The main functions of the parts of the nephron (drawn after Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry)

blocks.text: **1. Glomerular filtration** — under hydrostatic pressure, plasma passes through the glomerular filter (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane — type IV collagen, negatively charged heparan sulfate, podocytes). Substances with a molecular mass < 60–70 kDa that are not negatively charged pass through the filter; albumin (66 kDa, negative charge) hardly passes. **Primary urine** is ≈ 180 l per day — its composition is close to that of protein-free plasma. The **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is 90–120 ml/min/1.73 m^2^; it is the main indicator of kidney function.
**2. Tubular reabsorption** — ≈ 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed:

items: **proximal tubule** — glucose (**SGLT2**, SGLT1; completely), amino acids, ≈ 65% of Na^+^ and water, HCO~3~^−^ (≈ 80%), K^+^, phosphate, urate, small proteins (endocytosis — megalin, cubilin), vitamins; the energy comes from Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase;

**loop of Henle** — in the descending limb water, in the ascending limb Na^+^, K^+^ and 2Cl^-^ via **NKCC2** (the target of furosemide); the countercurrent mechanism creates an osmotic gradient in the renal medulla (urea also contributes);
**distal tubule** — NaCl (**NCC**, the target of thiazides), Ca^2+^ (PTH);

**collecting ducts** — Na^+^ (ENaC, aldosterone), water (**aquaporin-2**, vasopressin). **Renal threshold:** when the maximum capacity of the transporters is exceeded, the substance passes into the urine — for glucose ≈ 8.9–10 mmol/l in the blood. **SGLT2 inhibitors** (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) deliberately increase glucosuria, treating type 2 diabetes and protecting the heart and kidneys.

blocks.text: **3. Secretion** — active transport from the blood into the tubular lumen: H^+^, K^+^, NH~3~, organic anions (urate, para-aminohippurate, penicillin, diuretics — OAT transporters) and cations (creatinine partly, metformin — OCT2).

**Clearance** is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance in 1 minute: C = (U × V) / P (U — concentration in urine, P — concentration in plasma, V — urine flow per minute). Inulin clearance = GFR; para-aminohippurate clearance — renal plasma flow. In practice GFR is estimated from **creatinine** (the CKD-EPI formula; age and sex are taken into account) or from **cystatin C**.

sections.title: 2. The role of the kidneys in acid–base balance

blocks.text: ≈ 50–100 mmol of nonvolatile acids (sulfuric acid from sulfur-containing amino acids, phosphoric acid, organic acids) are formed in the body per day; only the kidneys can excrete them (the lungs excrete only CO~2~).

blocks.label: Figure 29.2
blocks.caption: H^+^ excretion and bicarbonate regeneration in the kidney (drawn after Severin E.S.)

blocks.text: In the tubular cells **carbonic anhydrase** forms H~2~CO~3~; H^+^ is secreted into the urine (Na^+^/H^+^ exchanger NHE3 — proximal; H^+^-ATPase and H^+^,K^+^-ATPase — intercalated cells of the collecting ducts), and HCO~3~^−^ passes into the blood. In the urine H^+^ is bound in three ways:

items: **Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate** — H^+^ + HCO~3~^-^ → H~2~CO~3~ → CO~2~ + H~2~O (brush-border carbonic anhydrase); CO~2~ enters the cell.
**Titratable acids** — H^+^ is bound mainly by the phosphate buffer: HPO~4~^2-^ + H^+^ → H~2~PO~4~^-^ (≈ 10–30 mmol per day).

**Ammoniagenesis** (the main adaptive mechanism) — in the proximal tubules **glutamine** → **glutaminase** → glutamate + NH~3~ → (glutamate dehydrogenase) α-ketoglutarate + NH~3~; NH~3~ binds H^+^ and is excreted as **NH~4~^+^** (≈ 30–50 mmol per day, up to 300 mmol in acidosis). α-Ketoglutarate is used in gluconeogenesis, and **new HCO~3~^-^** is formed. Urine pH is normally 5.0–7.0 (on average ≈ 6.0); acidic with a meat diet, alkaline with a plant and dairy diet.

blocks.text: **Renal tubular acidosis:** type I (distal) — H^+^ secretion is impaired, urine pH > 5.5, nephrocalcinosis and stones; type II (proximal) — HCO~3~^−^ reabsorption is impaired (together with Fanconi syndrome: glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia); type IV — aldosterone deficiency or resistance, hyperkalemia.

sections.title: 3. Specific features of metabolism and energy supply in the kidney

items: The kidneys make up ≈ 0.5% of body weight but consume ≈ 10% of the body's oxygen; ≈ 70–80% of the energy is spent on the work of **Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase** (which drives secondary active transport).
**Cortex** (proximal tubules) — aerobic; energy sources: **fatty acids**, ketone bodies, lactate, glutamine, citrate; many mitochondria; little glycolysis.
**Medulla** — little oxygen, **anaerobic glycolysis** predominates (glucose is the main source) — very sensitive to ischemia (papillary necrosis).
The kidney is an organ of **gluconeogenesis** (second after the liver; in prolonged fasting and acidosis up to 40% of blood glucose); substrates — glutamine, lactate, glycerol.
Amino acid metabolism: **the first step of creatine synthesis** (guanidinoacetate), synthesis of **arginine** from citrulline, metabolism of glycine and serine.

Small proteins and peptide hormones (insulin, PTH, β~2~-microglobulin) are reabsorbed in the tubules and degraded in lysosomes — in kidney failure the insulin requirement decreases. **Endocrine functions of the kidney: renin** (RAAS, topic 28), **erythropoietin** (in hypoxia — HIF; anemia in kidney failure), **calcitriol** (1α-hydroxylase), prostaglandins (vasodilation), kinins (kallikrein), urodilatin.

blocks.text: **The role of the kidneys in calcium, phosphorus and bicarbonate metabolism:** ≈ 98% of Ca^2+^ is reabsorbed (in the distal part it is regulated by PTH and calcitriol); phosphate — in the proximal tubule via NaPi-IIa (PTH and FGF-23 reduce it); bicarbonate — reabsorption and formation of new bicarbonate. **In chronic kidney disease:** phosphate is retained and calcitriol decreases → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy; metabolic acidosis (excretion of NH~4~^+^ decreases); anemia (low erythropoietin); hyperkalemia; uremia — urea, creatinine and “uremic toxins” (indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate, guanidines) accumulate.

sections.title: 4. General properties of urine and their age-related features

blocks.title: Table 29.1. Physical properties of urine (in adults)
head: Index
Normal value
Changes
rows: Polyuria > 2 l (diabetes mellitus and insipidus); oliguria < 0.5 l; anuria < 0.1 l
Dark brown — bilirubin; red — blood, hemoglobin, myoglobin, beetroot; colorless — polyuria
High — glucosuria, proteinuria, dehydration; low (< 1.005) — diabetes insipidus; fixed at 1.010 (isosthenuria) — kidney failure
Alkaline — plant diet, urinary tract infection (urease), type I tubular acidosis

blocks.text: **Age-related features:** in newborns there is oliguria in the first days, a low specific gravity (1.002–1.006 — the concentrating ability is immature), physiological proteinuria and the “uric acid infarct” (topic 14); the daily diuresis is approximately: up to 1 year 300–600 ml, ≈ 900 ml at 5 years, ≈ 1200 ml at 10 years; creatinine excretion increases with muscle mass. In the elderly GFR decreases by ≈ 1 ml/min per year, the concentrating ability declines, and nocturia appears.
≈ 50–70 g of dry matter is excreted in the urine per day.

blocks.title: Table 29.2. The main organic and inorganic components of urine (daily)
head: Component
Amount
Comment
rows: ≈ 85–90% of nitrogen; depends on protein intake and catabolism

blocks.text: **Proteinuria** — urine protein > 150 mg/day (in a healthy person albumin < 30 mg/day).

items: **Glomerular** — damage to the filter (glomerulonephritis, **diabetic nephropathy**, amyloidosis): selective (albumin) or nonselective (large proteins as well); **nephrotic syndrome** — > 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia (topic 20).
**Tubular** — small proteins (β~2~-microglobulin, α~1~-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein) are not reabsorbed: pyelonephritis, heavy metals, nephrotoxic drugs.
**Overflow (prerenal)** — many small proteins in the blood: **Bence Jones protein** (myeloma), myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), hemoglobin (intravascular hemolysis).
**Postrenal** — inflammation of the urinary tract, blood.
**Functional** — physical exertion, fever, orthostatic (in adolescents).

parts.text: **Microalbuminuria** (albumin 30–300 mg/day or an albumin/creatinine ratio of 3–30 mg/mmol) is the earliest sign of **diabetic nephropathy** and an indicator of cardiovascular risk; it is checked every year in diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Ordinary test strips do not detect it.

blocks.text: **Glucosuria** — when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (diabetes mellitus, steroids, stress) or when the threshold is lowered (**renal glucosuria** — SGLT2 gene mutation, pregnancy, Fanconi syndrome, SGLT2 inhibitors).

**Ketonuria** — acetoacetate and acetone: decompensated diabetes mellitus, starvation, repeated vomiting (hyperemesis of pregnancy), ketogenic diet, acetonemic vomiting in children, alcoholic ketoacidosis.
**Bilirubinuria** (conjugated only) — hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice; **urobilinogenuria** — hemolytic and hepatocellular jaundice (topic 25).

**Hematuria** (erythrocytes — glomerulonephritis, stones, tumors, infection), **hemoglobinuria** (intravascular hemolysis: G6PD deficiency, incompatible blood transfusion, burns), **myoglobinuria** (rhabdomyolysis) — the “blood” zone of the test strip is positive in all three (peroxidase activity of heme); microscopy is needed to distinguish them.
**Leukocyturia and nitrites** — urinary tract infection: gram-negative bacteria (E. coli) reduce nitrates to nitrites.

**Other pathological components:** phenylpyruvate (phenylketonuria — green color with FeCl~3~), homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria — the urine darkens in air), porphyrins and porphobilinogen (porphyrias), cystine, aminoaciduria (Fanconi, Hartnup disease), oxalates, orotic acid (topic 14), GAGs (mucopolysaccharidoses), 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (carcinoid tumor), vanillylmandelic acid (pheochromocytoma), hCG (pregnancy).

sections.title: 7. Kidney stones and the biochemical basis of their prevention

blocks.text: Stone formation results from **supersaturation** of the urine with salts, a lack of crystallization inhibitors (citrate, Mg^2+^, Tamm–Horsfall protein, nephrocalcin, GAGs) and impaired urine flow.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: detection of the normal and pathological components of urine with test strips
**Principle of the method:** on multiparameter test strips each zone works through its own specific chemical reaction.

blocks.title: Table 29.4. Reactions of the test strip zones
head: Zone
Basis of the reaction
Comment
rows: Specific; ascorbate gives a false negative result

items: Take fresh, well-mixed morning urine (test it within 2 hours).
Dip the test strip into the urine for 1–2 seconds until all the zones are immersed, and remove the excess by touching the edge of the container.
Holding the strip horizontally, compare each zone with the color scale on the container at the indicated time (30–120 seconds) (or read it on a urine analyzer).

Record the results in a table and compare them with the normal values. **Results and analysis:** normally glucose, protein (traces possible), ketone bodies, bilirubin, blood, nitrites and leukocytes are negative; urobilinogen — traces; pH 5–7; specific gravity 1.010–1.025. The causes of positive results are given in section 6; pathological results are confirmed by laboratory methods and microscopy.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: estimation of GFR from creatinine (calculation)

items: Determine creatinine in blood (the Jaffe reaction — an orange color with picric acid in an alkaline medium, or an enzymatic method) and creatinine and diuresis in daily urine.
Calculate the clearance: C = (U × V) / P, V — ml/min.

The Cockcroft–Gault formula: CrCl (ml/min) = [(140 − age) × weight (kg)] / [72 × creatinine (mg/dl)]; × 0.85 for women. (If creatinine is in µmol/l: mg/dl = µmol/l / 88.4.) **Results and analysis:** GFR ≥ 90 — normal; 60–89 — mildly decreased; < 60 ml/min/1.73 m^2^ for more than 3 months — chronic kidney disease; < 15 — kidney failure (dialysis). Drug doses must be adjusted to the GFR.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting a urinalysis

items: Assess the physical properties: volume, color, clarity, specific gravity, pH.
Assess the chemical components: protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen, blood, nitrites, leukocytes.

Group the results into syndromes: diabetes (glucose + ketones + high specific gravity), nephrotic (a lot of protein), nephritic (protein + blood), infection (leukocytes + nitrites + alkaline pH), jaundice (bilirubin, urobilinogen).
Compare with the blood tests (glucose, creatinine, bilirubin).

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of kidney stone and its prevention

items: Assess the urine pH and the crystals in the sediment.
Determine calcium, oxalate, urate, citrate and cystine in daily urine.
Assess blood calcium, PTH and uric acid.
Recommend a diet and drug prophylaxis appropriate to the type of stone.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old patient has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 15 years. Edema of the face and legs. Blood glucose 11.2 mmol/l, HbA~1c~ 9.1%, creatinine 210 µmol/l, albumin 28 g/l, potassium 5.6 mmol/l, Hb 98 g/l. Urine protein 4.2 g/day, glucose positive.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? What is the biochemical mechanism of the kidney damage? Explain the cause of the anemia and hyperkalemia.
cases.answer: Diabetic nephropathy with nephrotic-range proteinuria and chronic kidney disease. Prolonged hyperglycemia nonenzymatically glycates the proteins of the glomerular basement membrane (advanced glycation end products), the mesangial matrix increases via TGF-β, and negatively charged heparan sulfate decreases; hyperfiltration and hypertension damage the glomeruli — first microalbuminuria, then heavy proteinuria (hypoalbuminemia, edema), then GFR decreases (creatinine increased). Anemia is due to decreased renal production of erythropoietin; K^+^ secretion is impaired because of the decreased GFR and the hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism that is common in diabetes — hyperkalemia. Treatment: control of glycemia and BP, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, SGLT2 inhibitors (depending on GFR).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 40-year-old man presented with sudden severe colicky pain radiating from the loin to the groin. The urine contains many erythrocytes, pH 5.0, uric acid crystals. Blood uric acid 520 µmol/l. No stone was visible on X-ray; CT showed an 8 mm stone in the renal pelvis.
cases.ask: What type of stone is this? Why is it not visible on X-ray? What are the mechanism of stone formation and its treatment?
cases.answer: A urate (uric acid) stone. Urate stones absorb little X-ray radiation (radiolucent) and are visible on CT. Hyperuricemia and high urate excretion together with persistently acidic urine (at pH < 5.5 the solubility of uric acid is low, as it is un-ionized) lead to crystallization; in the metabolic syndrome ammoniagenesis is reduced and the urine is more acidic. Treatment: plenty of fluids, alkalinization of the urine with potassium citrate to pH 6.5–7 (urate stones dissolve — unlike other stones), allopurinol, restriction of purines and alcohol; pain relief.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 6-year-old child has fever, vomiting and abdominal pain. The urine smells of acetone. On the test strip ketone bodies are +++, glucose negative. Blood glucose 3.8 mmol/l. The child has eaten almost nothing for 2 days.
cases.ask: What is the cause of the ketonuria? Why is there no glucosuria? How is it distinguished from diabetes mellitus?
cases.answer: An acetonemic state (ketosis) against the background of fasting and vomiting. Children have a small glycogen store that is quickly exhausted; insulin decreases and glucagon and cortisol increase — lipolysis is enhanced, and β-oxidation of fatty acids in the liver forms a lot of acetyl-CoA, which, because oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis, is converted into ketone bodies; acetoacetate and acetone are detected in the urine. Blood glucose is normal or low — because it does not exceed the renal threshold, there is no glucosuria. In diabetes mellitus, by contrast, ketonuria is accompanied by hyperglycemia (> 11 mmol/l) and glucosuria. Treatment: drinking and glucose-containing fluids (also intravenously), antiemetic measures — glucose restores insulin secretion and stops ketogenesis.

topics.title: Biochemistry of the central and peripheral nervous system

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the specific features of nervous system function, the structural components of the central and peripheral nervous system, the protein and lipid composition of nervous tissue, the features of metabolism and energy exchange in nerve cells, the biochemical differences between neurons and neuroglia, signal transmission across synapses and neurotransmitters, the biochemistry of sensory systems, and the biochemical basis of mental and neurological diseases.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the chemical composition of nervous tissue and the properties of myelin;
the specific features of energy metabolism in the brain (dependence on glucose, ketone bodies);
the structure and function of the blood–brain barrier;
the metabolic cooperation between neurons and glial cells;
the synthesis, inactivation and receptors of the main neurotransmitters;
the biochemical basis of vision, hearing, smell and taste;
the biochemical basis of Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, depression, schizophrenia and epilepsy and the mechanism of action of drugs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: isolate lipids from brain tissue and perform qualitative reactions for them;
interpret the biochemical analysis of cerebrospinal fluid;
explain the mechanism of drugs that act on neurotransmitters.

sections.title: 1. Specific features and structural components of the nervous system

blocks.text: The **central nervous system** is the brain and spinal cord; the **peripheral** one consists of nerves, ganglia and nerve endings. Cellular composition: **neurons** (≈ 86 billion) and **neuroglia** — astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (myelin in the CNS), Schwann cells (myelin in the periphery), microglia (immune defense), ependyma.

**The blood–brain barrier (BBB)** — **tight junctions** between capillary endothelial cells (claudin, occludin), basement membrane, pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Glucose (GLUT1), amino acids and ketone bodies (MCT1) cross via specific transporters; small lipophilic substances by diffusion (ethanol, anesthetics, nicotine); proteins, most drugs and conjugated bilirubin do not cross. **P-glycoprotein** pumps many drugs back out. In newborns the BBB is immature (risk of kernicterus). Dopamine does not cross the BBB — in Parkinson disease its precursor **L-DOPA** is given.

**Cerebrospinal fluid** — ≈ 500 ml is formed per day in the choroid plexuses; protein 0.15–0.45 g/l (≈ 200 times less than in plasma), glucose 2.2–3.9 mmol/l (≈ 60% of blood glucose), chlorides 120–130 mmol/l.
The brain contains ≈ 78% water (≈ 84% in gray matter, ≈ 70% in white matter); half of the dry residue is **lipids** (≈ 55% in white matter), and the rest is proteins.

**Lipids:** phospholipids (phosphatidylethanolamine, plasmalogens, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylcholine), **sphingolipids** — sphingomyelin, **cerebrosides** (galactosylceramide — specific to myelin), sulfatides, **gangliosides** (contain sialic acid; in gray matter, in neuronal membranes), **cholesterol** (in free form; the brain contains ≈ 25% of the body's cholesterol, synthesized locally). The brain contains **almost no triacylglycerols** — fatty acids are not an energy source. Membranes are rich in ω-3 **docosahexaenoic acid** (retina, synapses).

**Myelin** is the multilayered wrapping of the membrane of an oligodendrocyte or Schwann cell around an axon; ≈ 70–80% lipid (cholesterol, cerebrosides, plasmalogens), ≈ 20–30% protein (**myelin basic protein**, proteolipid protein); electrical insulation — saltatory conduction (speeds up to 100 m/s). **Demyelination:** multiple sclerosis (autoimmune response to myelin proteins), Guillain–Barré syndrome, B~12~ deficiency (spinal cord), leukodystrophies; **sphingolipidoses** (defects of lysosomal enzymes): Tay–Sachs (hexosaminidase A — GM2 ganglioside), Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase), Niemann–Pick (sphingomyelinase), Krabbe (galactocerebrosidase).

**Proteins:** neurospecific proteins — **S100** (astrocytes; a marker of brain injury), neuron-specific enolase, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), tubulin and **tau protein** (microtubules), neurofilaments, synaptic proteins (synapsins, SNARE), ion channels and pumps, receptors, neuropeptides. Axonal transport (kinesin — anterograde, dynein — retrograde) requires ATP.

sections.title: 3. Specific features of energy metabolism in nervous tissue

items: The brain makes up ≈ 2% of body weight but at rest consumes **≈ 20% of the oxygen** and ≈ 25% of the glucose (≈ 120 g per day).
≈ 50–60% of the energy is spent on the work of **Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase** — to restore the membrane potential; the rest goes to the synthesis and reuptake of transmitters and to axonal transport.

The main substrate is **glucose** (GLUT1 — BBB, GLUT3 — neurons; insulin-independent), which is completely oxidized aerobically. **The glycogen store is very small** (in astrocytes), and there is no oxygen store: if the circulation stops, consciousness is lost in 10 seconds and irreversible damage occurs in 4–5 minutes.
**In prolonged starvation** the brain obtains ≈ 2/3 of its energy from **ketone bodies** (topic 15); in newborns (breast milk fats) ketone bodies are also an important source.
Fatty acids cross the BBB poorly and are hardly used for energy.

**Hypoglycemia** (< 2.8–3.0 mmol/l) — headache, confusion, seizures, coma; if prolonged, neurons die. **Hypoxia and ischemia** (stroke) — ATP is depleted, depolarization, a lot of glutamate is released — **excitotoxicity** (Ca^2+^ influx through NMDA receptors, proteases, free radicals) — necrosis and apoptosis of neurons.
Thiamine (B~1~) deficiency (the coenzyme of pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) — **Wernicke–Korsakoff encephalopathy** (in alcoholism).

sections.title: 4. Biochemical cooperation between neurons and neuroglia

items: **Astrocytes:** take up K^+^ from the synaptic cleft; take up glutamate and GABA and convert them into glutamine (the **glutamate–glutamine cycle**); **detoxify ammonia** (glutamine synthetase — topics 13 and 25); store glycogen and produce **lactate** by glycolysis, which they give to neurons (the “astrocyte–neuron lactate shuttle”); produce the antioxidant glutathione; form the BBB.
**Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells** — myelin synthesis, nourishment of axons.
**Microglia** — phagocytosis, cytokines, synaptic “pruning”.

blocks.text: **The nerve impulse:** resting potential (≈ −70 mV; K^+^ permeability and Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase) → depolarization (voltage-gated Na^+^ channels) → repolarization (K^+^ channels). Local anesthetics (lidocaine) block Na^+^ channels, and tetrodotoxin blocks them from the outside.

parts.text: **Organophosphorus compounds** (pesticides, sarin) irreversibly phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase: acetylcholine accumulates, causing muscarinic (miosis, salivary and bronchial secretion, bradycardia, diarrhea) and nicotinic (muscle twitching, paralysis) signs and CNS disturbance; death — respiratory failure. Antidotes: **atropine** (an M-cholinergic blocker) and **reactivators** (pralidoxime — restores the enzyme before “aging”). Reversible inhibitors (neostigmine) — in myasthenia, donepezil — in Alzheimer disease.

blocks.text: **Vision:** in the rods **rhodopsin** = opsin + **11-cis-retinal** (vitamin A). A quantum of light isomerizes 11-cis-retinal into **all-trans-retinal** → metarhodopsin II → the G protein **transducin** → **cGMP phosphodiesterase** is activated → cGMP decreases → cGMP-gated Na^+^/Ca^2+^ channels close → **hyperpolarization** → glutamate release decreases → signal. One photon activates hundreds of transducin molecules (amplification). The visual cycle: all-trans-retinal → retinol → converted back to 11-cis-retinal in the pigment epithelium. **Vitamin A deficiency** — night blindness (hemeralopia), xerophthalmia. Cones contain three kinds of iodopsin (color vision); the genes are on the X chromosome — color blindness.

**Hearing:** sound waves bend the stereocilia of the hair cells → mechanosensitive channels open and K^+^ enters (the endolymph is rich in K^+^ — 150 mmol/l, produced by the stria vascularis) → depolarization → glutamate is released. Aminoglycosides and furosemide are ototoxic.
**Smell:** ≈ 400 kinds of odorant receptors (G protein-coupled; the largest gene family) → G~olf~ → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → cation channels open.
**Taste** — topic 24: sweet, umami, bitter (G protein — gustducin), salty and sour (ion channels).

**Pain (nociception):** TRPV1 (capsaicin, heat), TRPA1, acid-sensing channels; mediators — prostaglandin E~2~ (increases sensitivity — the basis of NSAID action), bradykinin, substance P, glutamate; endogenous analgesia — enkephalins, endorphins.

blocks.text: **Routes of biochemical diagnosis:** cerebrospinal fluid analysis (protein, glucose, lactate, cells; Aβ~42~, tau — Alzheimer disease; oligoclonal IgG — multiple sclerosis), neurospecific proteins in the blood (S100, NSE, neurofilament light chain — brain injury), transmitter metabolites in the urine (VMA, homovanillic acid — neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma; 5-HIAA — carcinoid), therapeutic drug monitoring (lithium, antiepileptics), genetic tests, PET (glucose metabolism, amyloid).
Experiment 1: isolation of lipids from brain tissue and qualitative reactions for them
**Principle of the method:** lipids dissolve in organic solvents; cholesterol and phospholipids give characteristic reactions.

items: Grind 1 g of brain tissue with 10 ml of chloroform–methanol mixture (2:1) and filter (extract).

**Cholesterol — the Salkowski reaction:** carefully add 1 ml of concentrated H~2~SO~4~ to 1 ml of the (chloroform) extract — the chloroform layer turns red and the acid layer gives a yellow-green fluorescence. **The Liebermann–Burchard reaction:** with acetic anhydride and H~2~SO~4~ — a blue-green color (the basis of cholesterol determination in serum).
**Phosphate (phospholipids):** evaporate the extract, heat the residue with HNO~3~ and add ammonium molybdate — a yellow precipitate (phosphomolybdate).

**The acrolein test** (glycerol): heat the residue with KHSO~4~ — a pungent odor (glycerol of the glycerophospholipids). **Results and analysis:** the brain extract contains a lot of cholesterol and phospholipids (the Salkowski and molybdate reactions are clearly positive); this confirms the high lipid content of the brain and the composition of its membranes (myelin).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus went to training after injecting insulin without eating. 1 hour later he developed sweating, tremor and confusion, then seizures and loss of consciousness. Blood glucose 1.9 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Why is the brain especially sensitive to hypoglycemia? How should help be provided?
cases.answer: Hypoglycemic coma. The brain obtains its energy almost exclusively from the aerobic oxidation of glucose; its glycogen store is very small, it cannot use fatty acids, and the use of ketone bodies develops only as an adaptation to prolonged starvation (here insulin has also stopped ketogenesis). When glucose falls, ATP formation decreases, Na^+^,K^+^-ATPase stops working and the neurons depolarize — confusion, seizures (a lot of glutamate is released), coma; if prolonged, irreversible damage. Sweating and tremor are a contrainsular adrenergic reaction. Help: if conscious, a sweet drink; if unconscious, 40% glucose intravenously or glucagon intramuscularly (hepatic glycogenolysis); then a carbohydrate meal and analysis of the cause.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 65-year-old man has a resting hand tremor, slowness of movement, muscle rigidity and short steps when walking. Parkinson disease was diagnosed and levodopa + carbidopa was prescribed.
cases.ask: What is the biochemical basis of the disease? Why is levodopa given rather than dopamine itself? Why is carbidopa added?
cases.answer: The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra die (because of α-synuclein aggregates, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress), and dopamine decreases in the striatum; the balance with acetylcholine is disturbed, and movement disorders appear. Dopamine does not cross the blood–brain barrier, whereas its precursor L-DOPA crosses through an amino acid transporter and is converted to dopamine in the brain by DOPA decarboxylase (B~6~). Carbidopa is a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor (it does not cross the BBB): it stops the conversion of L-DOPA into dopamine in the blood, ensuring that more of it reaches the brain, and reduces the peripheral adverse effects (nausea, arrhythmia). Protein-rich food competes with L-DOPA for absorption and for crossing the BBB.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A farmer working in the field was brought in after spraying pesticide with blurred vision, sharply constricted pupils, profuse salivation, shortness of breath, diarrhea and muscle twitching. Blood cholinesterase activity is sharply decreased.
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? What is the biochemical mechanism of the symptoms? What are the principles of treatment?
cases.answer: Acute poisoning with an organophosphorus compound. The poison phosphorylates the serine in the active site of acetylcholinesterase and inhibits it irreversibly; acetylcholine accumulates in the synapses. Through M-cholinergic receptors — miosis, blurred vision, increased salivary and bronchial secretion, bronchospasm, bradycardia, diarrhea; through N-receptors — muscle fibrillation, then paralysis (respiratory muscles); in the CNS — agitation, seizures, coma. A decrease in blood cholinesterase activity confirms the diagnosis. Treatment: washing the poison off the skin, high-dose atropine (stops the muscarinic signs), oxime reactivators (pralidoxime — detaches the phosphate group from the enzyme, effective if given early), benzodiazepines (seizures), artificial ventilation.
